en: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.1 1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga Anubuddhasutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who has awakened after another; the one who has awakened by himself; the one who has fallen away from what was awakened to; and the one who has never awakened. And how, monks, is one a person who has awakened after another? Here, monks, a certain person has heard thus: ‘The Dhamma and Discipline taught by the Blessed One is well-expounded, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves. Having heard this, he goes to the Blessed One and, having approached him, pays homage to him and sits down at one side. As he is sitting there, the Blessed One teaches him the Dhamma, inspires him, rouses him, gladdens him, and clarifies it for him.

Then, having been taught, inspired, roused, gladdened, and clarified by the Blessed One, he attains a measure of confidence in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Having attained a measure of confidence in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, he reflects thus: ‘It would be good if I were to go forth in the presence of the Blessed One. He then approaches the Blessed One and, having approached him, says: ‘Venerable sir, I wish to go forth under the Blessed One; I wish to receive the full admission. Then the Blessed One gives him the going-forth and the full admission. Once he has received the full admission, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults. He trains himself by undertaking and following the training rules of the bhikkhus. He is content with robes for the body, almsfood for the belly, and dwelling in seclusion. He applies energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the cultivation of wholesome states, steadfast, firm in effort, not shirking the burden of wholesome states. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. By realizing for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless through the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who has awakened after another. And how, monks, is one a person who has awakened by himself? Here, monks, a certain person does not hear thus: ‘The Dhamma and Discipline taught by the Blessed One is well-expounded…’ Rather, he himself seeks out the Dhamma, examines it, and investigates it with his mind. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’… ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. By realizing for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless through the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who has awakened by himself. And how, monks, is one a person who has fallen away from what was awakened to? Here, monks, a certain person has heard thus: ‘The Dhamma and Discipline taught by the Blessed One is well-expounded…’ Having heard this, he goes to the Blessed One and, having approached him, pays homage to him and sits down at one side. As he is sitting there, the Blessed One teaches him the Dhamma, inspires him, rouses him, gladdens him, and clarifies it for him. Then, having been taught, inspired, roused, gladdened, and clarified by the Blessed One, he attains a measure of confidence in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Having attained a measure of confidence in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, he reflects thus: ‘It would be good if I were to go forth in the presence of the Blessed One. He then approaches the Blessed One and, having approached him, says: ‘Venerable sir, I wish to go forth under the Blessed One; I wish to receive the full admission. Then the Blessed One gives him the going-forth and the full admission. Once he has received the full admission, he dwells unrestrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, lacking proper conduct and resort, seeing no danger in unwholesome states. He does not train himself by undertaking and following the training rules of the bhikkhus. He is discontented with robes for the body, almsfood for the belly, and dwelling in seclusion. He does not apply energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the cultivation of wholesome states, but is lax, weak in effort, shirking the burden of wholesome states. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’… ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Not understanding as it really is, he falls away from those wholesome qualities that he had previously attained. This, monks, is called a person who has fallen away from what was awakened to. And how, monks, is one a person who has never awakened? Here, monks, a certain person does not hear thus: ‘The Dhamma and Discipline taught by the Blessed One is well-expounded…’ Nor does he seek out the Dhamma, examine it, or investigate it with his mind. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’… ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Not understanding as it really is, he does not realize for himself with direct knowledge, here and now, the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless through the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who has never awakened. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjis at Bhaṇḍagāma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus.
"Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating four things that we and you have thus wandered and transmigrated for such a long time.
What are these four?
“Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating noble virtue that we and you have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time.
Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating noble concentration that we and you have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time.
Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating noble wisdom that we and you have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time.”
“Bhikkhus, it was through not awakening to and not penetrating the noble liberation that we and you have wandered and transmigrated for such a long time.
But now, bhikkhus, the noble virtue has been awakened to and penetrated; the noble concentration has been awakened to and penetrated;
the noble wisdom has been awakened to and penetrated; the noble liberation has been awakened to and penetrated.”
“Craving for existence has been severed; the conduit to existence is exhausted; now there is no further becoming.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
“Virtue, concentration, and wisdom,
and unsurpassed liberation—
these states have been fully awakened to.”
By the renowned Gotama.
Thus the Buddha, having directly known through higher knowledge,
proclaimed the Dhamma to the bhikkhus.
“The Teacher, the Eyeful One, who brought an end to suffering, has attained final Nibbāna.
Thus ends the first [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.2 1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga Papatitasutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who has fallen away from both ends; the person who has fallen away from one end but not from the other;

the person who has not fallen away from either end; and the person who has fallen away from neither end. And how, monks, is a person one who has fallen away from both ends? Here, monks, a certain person does not enjoy himself in the present life nor does he experience the fruit of recluseship. This, monks, is called a person who has fallen away from both ends. And how, monks, is a person one who has fallen away from one end but not from the other? Here, monks, a certain person enjoys himself in the present life but does not experience the fruit of recluseship. This, monks, is called a person who has fallen away from one end but not from the other. And how, monks, is a person one who has not fallen away from either end? Here, monks, a certain person enjoys himself in the present life and also experiences the fruit of recluseship. This, monks, is called a person who has not fallen away from either end. And how, monks, is a person one who has fallen away from neither end? Here, monks, a certain person does not enjoy himself in the present life, yet he experiences the fruit of recluseship. This, monks, is called a person who has fallen away from neither end. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, one who does not possess four qualities is said to have fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya. Which four? [The Buddha continued:]”
“Monks, one who is not endowed with noble virtue is said to have fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Monks, one who is not endowed with noble concentration is said to have fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Monks, one who is not endowed with noble wisdom is said to have fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
“Monks, one who does not possess noble liberation is said to have ‘fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Monks, one who does not possess these four qualities is said to have ‘fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Monks, one who possesses four qualities is said to have ‘not fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.’”
Which four?
One endowed with noble virtue, monks, is said to be "not fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
One endowed with noble concentration, monks, is said to be "not fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya."
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses noble wisdom is said to be ‘not fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Bhikkhus, one who possesses noble liberation is said to be ‘not fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.
It is by possessing these four qualities, bhikkhus, that one is said to be ‘not fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya.’”
The leaves fall and those that have fallen fall again,
while the greedy ones return;
what was to be done has been done, and it is delightful and beautiful.
“Accompanied by happiness, it is happiness.
The second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.3
1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga: The First Discourse on the Wound (Paṭhamakhatasutta) (AN 4.3, PTS AN ii 2)

“Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man, maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.
What are the four?
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, he speaks praise of one who deserves dispraise.”
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks dispraise of one who deserves praise;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one conceives confidence in a matter that inspires lack of confidence;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one conceives lack of confidence in a matter that inspires confidence.

“Monks, possessed of these four qualities, a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man, maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.

Monks, possessed of four qualities, a wise person, a competent person, a true man, maintains himself unwounded and uninjured; he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit.
What are the four?”
Having investigated and scrutinized, one speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise;
having investigated and scrutinized, one speaks praise of one who deserves praise;
and having investigated and scrutinized, one expresses lack of confidence regarding a matter that merits lack of confidence.
Having investigated and scrutinized, he manifests confidence in a matter that inspires confidence.
It is by possessing these four qualities, monks, that a wise, competent, and true person preserves himself unscarred and uninjured;
he is blameless and beyond reproach to the wise, and he generates much merit.
He who praises one who deserves blame,
or blames one who deserves praise,
gathers misfortune with his own mouth.

Even if one were to lose everything, including one's very self,
this alone is the greatest misfortune:
to harbor a mind of malice toward those who have attained the Good State.
For one hundred thousand nirabbudas,
and thirty-six plus five abbudas,
does he who reviles the noble ones go to hell.
“Having directed one’s speech and mind toward what is evil.
The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.4.
1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga The Second Discourse on the Pit (Dutiyakhatasutta) (AN 4.4, PTS AN ii 4)

“Bhikkhus, when a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man, practices wrongly in four respects, he maintains himself in a state of injury and ruin; he becomes blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.
What are the four?

Bhikkhus, when a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man, practices wrongly toward his mother, he maintains himself in a state of injury and ruin; he becomes blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.”
Bhikkhus, one who behaves wrongly toward his father... [and so on] ...one who behaves wrongly toward a Tathāgata...
[and so on] ...one who behaves wrongly toward a disciple of the Tathāgata is a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man;
he maintains himself in a state of injury and ruin, he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.

“Bhikkhus, when a foolish, incompetent, unvirtuous person practices wrongly regarding these four things, he maintains himself in a state of injury and ruin; he becomes blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.

When a wise, competent, virtuous person practices rightly regarding these four things, he maintains himself in a state free from injury and ruin; he becomes blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit.
What are the four?”

“Bhikkhus, when a wise, competent, true person practices rightly toward his mother, he preserves himself unscarred and uninjured; he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit.

Bhikkhus, when one practices rightly toward his father… Bhikkhus, when one practices rightly toward the Tathāgata… Bhikkhus, when a wise, competent, true person practices rightly toward a disciple of the Tathāgata, he preserves himself unscarred…”
He preserves himself unharmed; he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit.
Monks, when a wise, competent, and true person practices rightly in these four ways, he preserves himself unscarred and unharmed;
he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit.
He who behaves wrongly toward his mother or father, or toward the Tathāgata,
the perfectly enlightened one—
Or else, toward his disciples;
such a man produces much demerit.
On account of that unrighteous conduct toward his mother and father,
the wise censure him even here in this world.
He goes to a state of woe after death—
he who behaves rightly toward both mother and father.
Whether toward a Tathāgata, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, or his disciple,
he generates much merit.
Such a person is meritorious.
Through that practice of the Dharma toward their mother and father, the wise—
“Right here they praise him,
and after passing away, he rejoices in heaven.
Thus ends the fourth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.5 1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga Anusotasutta “Monks, there are these four floods. What four? The flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. These, monks, are the four floods. “Monks, there are these four yokes. What four?

The yoke of sensuality, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance. These, monks, are the four yokes. “Monks, there are these four bonds. What four? The bond of sensuality, the bond of existence, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance. These, monks, are the four bonds. “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? One who goes with the stream, one who goes against the stream, one who stands firm, and one who has crossed over and gone beyond. “And how, monks, is one a person who goes with the stream? Here, monks, a certain person pursues what is unwholesome, does not pursue what is wholesome; pursues what is blameworthy, does not pursue what is blameless; pursues what is agreeable to the foolish, does not pursue what is agreeable to the wise. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who goes with the stream. “And how, monks, is one a person who goes against the stream? Here, monks, a certain person does not pursue what is unwholesome, but pursues what is wholesome; does not pursue what is blameworthy, but pursues what is blameless; does not pursue what is agreeable to the foolish, but pursues what is agreeable to the wise. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who goes against the stream. “And how, monks, is one a person who stands firm? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind well-restrained regarding the six bases of contact. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who stands firm. “And how, monks, is one a person who has crossed over and gone beyond? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters and become a non-returner, one who will attain final nibbāna there without returning from that world. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who has crossed over and gone beyond.”
“Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world. Which four? [The text continues with the description of each.]”

The person who goes with the stream, the person who goes against the stream, the person established in themselves, and the brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land.
And what, bhikkhus, is the person who goes with the stream?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and performs evil deeds.
This, monks, is called the person who goes with the stream.
And what, monks, is the person who goes against the stream?
Here, monks, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not perform evil deeds.
Even with suffering and even with mental distress, even weeping with a tearful face, he leads the full and pure holy life.
This, monks, is called the person who goes against the stream.
And what, monks, is the person who is established in himself?
"Here, monks, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
This, monks, is called the person who is established in himself.
And what, monks, is the person who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land—the brahmin?"

In this case, monks, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
This, monks, is called a person who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land—a brahmin.
These, monks, are the four persons found existing in the world.
Those people who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures,
who have not yet transcended passion here while indulging in sense-desires,
go again and again to birth and old age.
Overcome by craving, they go with the stream.
Therefore, the wise person, established in mindfulness here,
should not indulge in sensual pleasures or evil deeds.
Even with difficulty one should abandon sensual desires;
such a person they call "one who goes against the stream.
Indeed, he who has abandoned the five defilements...
One who has fulfilled the training, whose nature is not subject to decline,
who has attained mastery over the mind and whose faculties are concentrated—
he indeed is called a man of steadfastness.
He for whom high and low phenomena have been fully understood,
extinguished, and have passed away so that they no longer exist—
he is indeed a sage who has lived the holy life.
“He is called one who has gone to the end of the world, one who has reached the further shore.
The fifth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.6
1. Bhaṇḍagāma Chapter: Appassuta Sutta (The Discourse on the One of Little Learning) (AN 4.6, PTS AN ii 6)
“Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Which four?
One who has heard little and is not perfected in what he has heard;”
One who has heard little but is endowed with what he has heard;
one who has heard much but is not endowed with what he has heard;
and one who has heard much and is endowed with what he has heard.
And how, monks, is a person one who has heard little and is not proficient in what he has heard?
Here, monks, a certain person has heard little—
that is, the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical expositions.
Thus, having understood neither the meaning nor the Dhamma of that little he has heard, he does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
In this way, monks, a person is one who has heard little and has not mastered what he has heard.
And how, monks, is a person one who has heard little but has mastered what he has heard?
In this case, monks, a certain person has heard little—
that is, the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical expositions.
Having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma of that little he has heard, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
"In this way, monks, a person has heard little but is established in what he has heard.
And how, monks, is a person learned but not established in what he has heard?
Here, monks, a certain person has heard much—"

The discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical teachings (vedalla).
One who has heard much of this, yet without having understood its meaning or its Dhamma, does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is one who has heard much but is not established in what he has heard.
And how, monks, is a person one who has heard much and is endowed with what he has heard?
Here, monks, a certain person has heard much—

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" passages (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical treatises (vedalla).
Thus, having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma of that great learning, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is one of great learning who has become perfected through learning.
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.
If one is both of little learning and unconcentrated in moral conduct,
people censure him for both reasons.
In virtue and in learning.
Even if one has heard little,
if one is well-composed in the precepts;
They praise him for his virtue,
and his learning bears fruit; even if he is very learned, [he must still be virtuous].
One who is not established in the virtues is censured for his lack of virtue,
and his learning does not bear fruit.
If one is both learned and well-composed in moral virtues,
people praise them for both qualities.
In virtue and in learning.
One who is well-versed in the scriptures, a bearer of the Dhamma,
possessed of wisdom— such a one is a disciple of the Buddha.
Like a gem from the Jambu River,
who would be worthy to criticize you?
Even the gods praise him.
“Even by Brahmā has he been praised.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.7
1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga: The Discourse on the Beautiful (Sobhanasutta) (AN 4.7, PTS AN ii 8)
“Bhikkhus, these four who are competent, disciplined, confident, learned, bearers of the Dhamma, and practitioners of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, beautify the Saṅgha.
Which four?
A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who is competent, disciplined, confident, learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and a practitioner of the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, beautifies the Saṅgha.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhunī who is competent, disciplined, confident, learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, beautifies the Saṅgha.
A lay follower who is competent, disciplined, confident, learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, beautifies the Saṅgha.
A female lay follower who is competent, disciplined, confident, learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma, beautifies the Saṅgha.”
“Monks, these four—being competent, disciplined, confident, and learned; being bearers of the Dhamma and practicing in accordance with the Dhamma—beautify the Saṅgha.
He who is both competent and confident, and who is also learned and a bearer of the Dhamma...”
One who practices in accordance with the Dhamma is called one who beautifies the Saṅgha;
such a bhikkhu is endowed with virtue.
A bhikkhunī who is learned,
a faithful layman,
and a faithful laywoman;
"These indeed adorn the Saṅgha; for these are the adornments of the Saṅgha.
The seventh.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.8 1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga Vesārajjasutta (The Discourse on Confidences) “Monks, there are these four confidences of a Tathāgata. What four? ‘I am a Tathāgata; for me there is no ground for others to legitimately accuse me thus: “While you claim to be a Tathāgata, you have not fully awakened to all things. This is the first confidence of a Tathāgata. ‘I have destroyed the taints; for me there is no ground for others to legitimately accuse me thus: “While you claim to have destroyed the taints, these taints have not been destroyed by you. This is the second confidence of a Tathāgata. ‘These are the obstructive phenomena that I have declared to be obstructive; for me there is no ground for others to legitimately accuse me thus: “While these phenomena have been declared by you to be obstructive, they do not actually become obstacles when one engages with them. This is the third confidence of a Tathāgata. ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering; for me there is no ground for others to legitimately accuse me thus: “This is not the path leading to the cessation of suffering as declared by you”; or, “By following this path, one does not fully realize the cessation of suffering as it truly is. This is the fourth confidence of a Tathāgata. These, monks, are the four confidences of a Tathāgata.”

“Bhikkhus, there are these four grounds of self-confidence possessed by a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel. What are the four? [The text continues with the four specific grounds.]”
“‘If anyone— whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world— should rightfully challenge me, who claims to be a perfectly awakened Buddha, saying:
“These things have not been fully realized by you,”’ monks, I do not perceive any ground for such a sign.”
Not perceiving any such ground for this, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence:

"If anyone— a monk, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world— should rightfully challenge me regarding my claim that 'the taints are exhausted,' saying, 'These taints are not yet exhausted in you,' this would be the ground [for such a challenge]."
"Monks, I do not see any such ground.
Not seeing any such ground, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-confidence.
As for those things called 'obstructive states,' which were said by me to be obstructive for one who indulges in them—I do not see any ground for that either."
“Monks, I do not see any ground on which anyone in the world—whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else at all—could rightfully challenge me, saying:
‘You have not attained this. Monks, seeing no such ground, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence.”

"Monks, I do not see any ground on which a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could rightfully challenge me, saying: 'But for what purpose was the Dhamma taught by you? It does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.'"
Not perceiving any such ground for this, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence.

These, monks, are the four grounds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata, possessed of which the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Whatever paths of dispute there may be, variously established...
Those ascetics and brahmins who rely on [such views] no longer exist once they have reached the Tathāgata—
the one who is confident and has transcended the path of discourse.
To him who, being all-encompassing and compassionate toward all beings, set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma having overcome [all obstacles]—
to such a one, the best among gods and humans, [I pay homage].
“Beings pay homage to those who have gone beyond existence.
(The Eighth) Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.9

1. Bhaṇḍagāmavagga Taṇhuppādasutta (AN 4.9, PTS AN ii 10) At Bhaṇḍagāma, the Blessed One said this: “Monks, when craving arises, it arises in dependence upon these six bases. When craving ceases, it ceases in dependence upon these same six bases. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, does craving arise in dependence upon these six bases? And how does craving cease in dependence upon these same six bases? “Here, monk, the eye is the basis for the arising of craving; it is in dependence upon the eye that craving arises. The ear is the basis... the nose is the basis... the tongue is the basis... the body is the basis... the mind is the basis for the arising of craving; it is in dependence upon the mind that craving arises. Thus, monk, craving arises in dependence upon these six bases. Furthermore, monk, the eye is the basis for the cessation of craving; it is in dependence upon the eye that craving ceases. The ear is the basis... the nose is the basis... the tongue is the basis... the body is the basis... the mind is the basis for the cessation of craving; it is in dependence upon the mind that craving ceases. “Bhikkhus, there are these four origins of craving where craving arises in a bhikkhu as it arises.
What are the four?
Craving arises in a bhikkhu on account of robes;”
“Monks, craving arises in a monk because of almsfood; craving arises in a monk because of lodgings;
or craving arises in a monk because of the pursuit of this or that state of existence.”
These, monks, are the four origins of craving where craving arises in a monk as it arises.
Craving is the companion of man as he wanders through the long course of saṃsāra.
From this state to another state,
one does not transcend saṃsāra.
Having understood such dangers as these, [one should practice].
Craving is the origin of suffering;
free from craving and without grasping,
let the mindful bhikkhu wander forth.
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.10 1.
Bhaṇḍagāmavagga (The Chapter on Bhaṇḍagāma)
The Discourse on the Fetter (Yogavagga Sutta), AN 4.10 (PTS AN ii 10):
“Bhikkhus, there are these four fetters.”
Which four?
The bond of sensual desire, the bond of existence, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance.
And what, monks, is the bond of sensual desire?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures.
For one who does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding sensual pleasures,
whatever sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, sensual craving, and sensual fever there is toward sensual pleasures—
The clinging to sensual pleasures, namely sensual craving, lies latent within one.
This, monks, is called the yoke of sensual pleasure.
Such is the yoke of sensual pleasure.
And how does the bond of existence come about?
Here, monks, a certain person does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the various forms of existence.
For one who does not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the various forms of existence...

In one who does not understand, whatever lust for existence, delight in existence, affection for existence, infatuation with existence, thirst for existence, fever for existence, clinging to existence,
and craving for existence persists among states of being—
this, monks, is called the yoke of existence.
Thus there is the bond of sensual desire and the bond of existence.
And how does the bond of views come to be?
Here, monks, a certain person does not understand, as it really is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding views.
For one who does not understand, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these views,
that lust for views, delight in views, affection for views, infatuation with views, thirst for views, fever for views, clinging to views,
and craving for views remain latent within them.
This, monks, is called the yoke of views.
Thus there is the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, and the yoke of views.
And how does the yoke of ignorance come to be?
"Here, monks, a certain person does not understand, as they really are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact.

Because he does not understand, as they really are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, the ignorance and lack of knowledge concerning those six bases of contact underlie his mind.
This, monks, is called the bond of ignorance."

Thus there is the bond of sensual desire, the bond of existence, the bond of views, and the bond of ignorance—one who is fettered by these evil, unwholesome states which are defiling, conducive to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death. Therefore, one is called "one who has not attained security from bondage.
These, monks, are the four bonds.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four dissociations. What four?
Dissociation from the bond of sensual desire, dissociation from the bond of existence, dissociation from the bond of views, and dissociation from the bond of ignorance.”
And what, bhikkhus, is the dissociation from the bond of sensual pleasures?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person understands, as it really is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures.
For him, having understood the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures as they really are...
For one who understands, whatever sensual lust, sensual delight, sensual affection, sensual infatuation, sensual thirst, sensual fever, sensual clinging,
and sensual craving there is regarding sense pleasures does not underlie them.
This, monks, is called the dissociation from the bond of sensuality.
Thus is the dissociation from the bond of sensual desire.
And how does the dissociation from the bond of existence come about?
Here, monks, a certain person understands, as it truly is, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding states of existence.
For one who understands, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger,

and the escape regarding these states of existence, that lust for existence, delight in existence, affection for existence, infatuation with existence, thirst for existence, fever for existence, clinging to existence,
and craving for existence do not underlie their mind.
This, monks, is called the dissociation from the bond of existence.
Thus there is dissociation from the bond of sensual desire and dissociation from the bond of existence.
And how does dissociation from the bond of views come about?

In this case, monks, a certain person understands, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding views. For one who thus understands the origin,
the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding views as they truly are,
whatever lust for views, delight in views, affection for views, infatuation with views, and thirst for views there may be—
The fever of views, the clinging to views, and craving for views—these do not underlie it.
This, monks, is called the dissociation from the bond of views.
Thus there is dissociation from the bond of sensual desire, dissociation from the bond of existence, and dissociation from the bond of views.
And how does there come to be the dissociation from the bond of ignorance?
Here, monks, a certain person understands, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact.

For one who understands, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, that ignorance and lack of knowledge which exists regarding the six bases of contact does not underlie them.
This, monks, is called the dissociation from the bond of ignorance.

Thus, through dissociation from the bond of sensual desire, dissociation from the bond of existence, dissociation from the bond of views, and dissociation from the bond of ignorance, one is dissociated from evil, unwholesome states—those which are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death. Therefore, one is called "one who has attained security from bonds."
"These, monks, are the four dissociations.
Bound by the yoke of sensual desire,
and by both the yokes of existence,"
Bound by the yoke of views and preceded by ignorance,
beings wander through saṃsāra.
Those who go to birth and death,
and those who, having fully understood sensual pleasures,
have completely abandoned the fetter of existence.
Having utterly uprooted the yoke of views and having dispelled ignorance,
those who are disjoined from all bonds—
“Those indeed are the sages who have transcended all bonds. Tenth.
The First Chapter on the Village of Bhaṇḍa.
Its summary verse:
Anubuddha, Papatita—two;
Khatā, with Anusota as the fifth.
And for one of little learning, confidence;
and through the bond of craving, those ten.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.11

2. The Chapter on Conduct: Discourse on Conduct (Carasutta) “Monks, there are these two kinds of conduct. What two? Mundane conduct and supramundane conduct. And what, monks, is mundane conduct? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This, monks, is called mundane conduct. And what, monks, is supramundane conduct? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind not obsessed by sensual lust, without burning with sensual lust; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This, monks, is called supramundane conduct. These, monks, are the two kinds of conduct.”
“Monks, even while walking, if sensual thought, ill will, or harmful thought arises in a bhikkhu, and if he tolerates it,
does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to vanish,
then that bhikkhu, while walking, is said to be one who is without ardor, without self-reproach, constantly and continuously lazy, and lacking in energy.
“Monks, even if a sensual thought, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty should arise in a monk who is established [in concentration],
if he tolerates it, does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end,
and does not cause it to vanish, then such a monk, though established, is called ‘one who is without ardor, without self-reproach, constantly and continuously lazy, and lacking in energy.’”
“Monks, if a thought of sensual desire, or a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty arises in a monk while he is sitting,
and if that monk tolerates it, does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to vanish,
then such a monk, monks, even while sitting, is called one who is without ardor, without self-reproach, constantly and continuously lazy, and of inferior energy.”
“Bhikkhus, if a sleeping but wakeful bhikkhu gives rise to a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty,
and if he tolerates it, does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not eliminate it,
then that sleeping but wakeful bhikkhu, being thus, is said to be ‘without ardor, without self-respect, constantly and continuously lazy, and of inferior energy.’”
"Monks, even if a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty should arise in a monk while he is walking,
if that monk does not tolerate it, but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease to exist,
then such a monk, monks, even while walking, is called 'ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute. "
“Monks, even if a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty should arise in a monk who is established [in mindfulness],
if he does not tolerate it, but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease,
then such a monk, though established, is called ‘ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.’”
“Monks, if a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty arises in a monk while he is sitting,
and if that monk does not tolerate it, but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end,
and makes it non-existent— then, monks, such a monk while sitting is called ‘ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.’”
“Monks, even if a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty should arise in a monk who is lying down but awake,
if he does not tolerate it, but abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and causes it to cease to exist,
then that monk, monks, while lying down but awake, is called ‘ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.’”
Whether walking or standing,
sitting or lying down,
whoever thinks a thought—
Evil and based on the household life,
he has entered upon a wrong path,
infatuated with things that lead to delusion.
Such a bhikkhu is incapable of touching the supreme enlightenment,
whether walking or standing.
Whether sitting or lying down,
having stilled discursive thoughts,
he delights in the subsiding of thought.
Such a bhikkhu as that is capable of touching the supreme enlightenment.
Thus is the first [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.12 2.

Caravagga Sīlasutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is virtuous but not learned; the person who is learned but not virtuous; the person who is neither virtuous nor learned; and the person who is both virtuous and learned. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Monks, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha;
dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfected in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and train yourselves by undertaking the rules of training.
Monks, as you dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha, and restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha...”
For those who dwell perfected in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and training by undertaking the rules of training—what further task remains for them to do?

Monks, even if a bhikkhu, while walking, is free from covetousness and ill will, free from sloth and torpor... free from restlessness and remorse... [the same applies to standing, sitting, and lying down].
… doubt has been abandoned, energy is aroused and unflagging, mindfulness is established and unconfused,
the body is tranquil and unagitated, and the mind is concentrated and one-pointed. Even while walking, monks,
a bhikkhu who is thus becomes called "ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute."
“Bhikkhus, even if a bhikkhu is standing, if his covetousness and ill will have vanished, if his sloth and torpor… restlessness and remorse… and doubt have been abandoned;

if his energy is aroused and unflagging, his mindfulness established and unmuddled, his body tranquil and unaroused, and his mind concentrated and one-pointed— then a bhikkhu who is standing and has become thus, bhikkhus, [is said to be well-established].”
“He is called one who is ardent, possessed of shame, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute. Monks, even if a bhikkhu is seated, if his covetousness and ill will have vanished,

if his sloth and torpor… his restlessness and remorse… and his doubt have been abandoned, and if his energy is aroused and unflagging, and mindfulness is established… [he is called one who is ardent, possessed of shame, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute].”
Being mindful and clearly comprehending, with a body tranquil and unagitated, and with a mind concentrated and one-pointed— even when sitting, monks,
a bhikkhu who is thus becomes called "ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.
And even for a bhikkhu who is lying down and awake, if covetousness and ill will have vanished, and sloth and torpor...
… restlessness and remorse … doubt have been abandoned; energy has been aroused, unflagging;
mindfulness is established, unconfused; the body is tranquil and unaroused; the mind is concentrated and one-pointed.
Even when lying down, monks, a bhikkhu who is thus awake is called “ardent, ashamed, constantly and continuously energetic, and resolute.”
Let the bhikkhu move with restraint, stand with restraint,
sit with restraint, lie down with restraint,
and bend his limbs with restraint.
One should stretch out this [body]—
upward, across, and toward the west—
as far as the range of the world extends.
And having contemplated the arising and passing away of phenomena and the aggregates,
[he attains] the mastery of mental tranquility.
Always mindful in training—
such a person they call a bhikkhu who is constantly resolute.
The Second [Discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.13 2.
Caravagga (The Chapter on Wanderers)
The Discourse on Exertion (Padhānasutta).
“Monks, there are these four right exertions.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
he generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states.
One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states;
one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, applies the mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states.
These, monks, are the four right strivings.
Those who have conquered Mara’s realm through right exertion,
they are unattached and have gone beyond the fear of birth and death;
having defeated Mara along with his host, they are joyful and imperturbable.
“Having completely transcended all the power of Namuci, they are happy.
The third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.14

2. Caravagga Saṃvarasutta (AN 4.14, PTS AN ii 16) “Monks, there are these five kinds of restraint. What five? Restraint by the eye, restraint by the ear, restraint by the nose, restraint by the tongue, and restraint by the body. These, monks, are the five kinds of restraint.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four efforts.
What are the four?
The effort of restraint, the effort of abandoning, the effort of development, and the effort of protection.”
And what, monks, is the striving for restraint?
Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For, if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when he has heard a sound with the ear... smelled an odor with the nose... [corresponding unwholesome] states were to flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye faculty, he attains restraint over the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... [he practices for its restraint; he guards the nose faculty, he attains restraint over the nose faculty].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If, when one dwells with this faculty of mind unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states were to flow in,
one practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of mind, and achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
This, monks, is called the striving of restraint.
And what, bhikkhus, is the striving for abandonment?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent.
[He does not tolerate] an arisen thought of ill will... [and so forth].
He does not tolerate a thought of cruelty that has arisen...
[and so on] ...he does not tolerate whatever evil, unwholesome states that have arisen; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, and makes them non-existent.
This, monks, is called the effort for abandoning.
And what, monks, is the effort for development?
Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in relinquishment;
he develops the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor...
He develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture … he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility …

He develops the concentration factor of enlightenment … he develops the equanimity factor of enlightenment, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment.
This, monks, is called the exertion of development.
And what, monks, is the effort of preservation?

Here, monks, a monk preserves a favorable sign of concentration that has arisen: the perception of a skeleton, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, and the perception of a bloated corpse.
This, monks, is called the effort of preservation.
"These, monks, are the four efforts:
restraint, abandoning,
development, and protection."
These are the four exertions taught by the Kinsman of the Sun;
by means of which a bhikkhu here, being ardent, [attains his goal].
“May one reach the destruction of suffering.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.15

2. Caravagga: Paññattisutta (AN 4.15, PTS AN ii 17) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these four modes of designation. What four? Designation by way of name, designation by way of clan, designation by way of occupation, and designation by way of craft. These, monks, are the four modes of designation.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four designations of the foremost. What four?
Bhikkhus, this is the foremost among personal existences, namely—”
Rāhu, the lord of the asuras.
And this, monks, is the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures:
namely, King Mandhātā.
“Bhikkhus, this is the foremost of those who exercise sovereignty,
namely, Māra the Evil One.

In the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among the generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost.”
These, monks, are the four foremost designations:
Rāhu among those with physical forms,
and Mandhātā among those who enjoy sensual pleasures.
Māra blazed with sovereignty,
with psychic power, and with glory—
above, across, and behind.
To whatever extent there is a destination for the world,
including the world of the devas,
the Buddha is declared the foremost.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.16 2.
Caravagga (The Chapter on Wandering)
The Discourse on Refinement (Sokhummasutta):
“Monks, there are these four refinements.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a monk possesses the supreme subtlety of form;
and by means of that subtlety of form, he does not perceive any other subtlety of form as superior or more refined.
And by means of that subtlety of form, he does not long for another subtlety of form that is more excellent or more sublime.
He is endowed with a supreme subtlety of feeling;
and by means of that subtlety of feeling, he does not perceive another subtlety of feeling that is more excellent or more sublime.
And by means of that subtlety of feeling, he does not long for another subtlety of feeling that is more excellent or more sublime.
He possesses the supreme subtlety of perception;
and by means of that subtlety of perception, he does not regard any other subtlety of perception as more excellent or more sublime.
And by means of that subtlety of perception, he does not aspire to any other subtlety of perception as being higher or more sublime.
He possesses the supreme subtlety of volitional formations;
and by means of that subtlety of volitional formations, he does not regard any other subtlety of volitional formations as being higher or more sublime.
And by means of that subtlety of formations, one does not long for another subtlety of formations that is more excellent or more sublime.
"These, monks, are the four kinds of subtlety.
Having known the subtlety of form...
The origin of feelings,
and that from which perception arises,
and where it goes to its end.
Having understood formations as external,
as suffering, and not as self—
he is indeed a bhikkhu who sees rightly.
The virtuous ones, delighting in the state of peace,
bear their final body,
having conquered Māra and his host.
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.17 2.
Caravagga (The Chapter on Wanderers)
Paṭhamagatisutta (AN 4.17,
PTS AN ii 18): “Bhikkhus,
there are these four ways of going to ruin.
Which four?
One goes to a wrong course through desire, one goes to a wrong course through hatred, one goes to a wrong course through delusion, and one goes to a wrong course through fear.
These, monks, are the four ways of going to a wrong course.
Whoever transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
his fame diminishes.
“Like the moon in the dark fortnight.
The seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.18

2. Chapter on Caravans: The Second Discourse on Destinations (AN 4.18, PTS AN ii 18) “Monks, there are these four destinations for a person who has passed away. What four? One who is a killer of living beings, one who takes what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, one who speaks falsely—such a person, monks, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in a place of suffering, even in hell. This, monks, is the first destination for a person who has passed away. Furthermore, monks, one who is a killer of living beings, one who takes what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, and one who speaks truthfully—such a person, monks, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This, monks, is the second destination for a person who has passed away. Furthermore, monks, one who abstains from killing living beings, one who abstains from taking what is not given, one who abstains from sexual misconduct, and one who abstains from false speech—such a person, monks, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This, monks, is the third destination for a person who has passed away. Furthermore, monks, one who abstains from killing living beings, one who abstains from taking what is not given, one who abstains from sexual misconduct, and one who abstains from false speech—such a person, monks, by the destruction of the taints, in this very life enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for oneself with direct knowledge. This, monks, is the fourth destination for a person who has passed away. These, monks, are the four destinations for a person who has passed away.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of not going astray.
What are the four?
One does not go astray through desire, one does not go astray through hatred, one does not go astray through delusion, and one does not go astray through fear.”
"These, monks, are the four ways of not going to a bad destination.
He who does not transgress the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion."
His fame increases,
like the moon during the waxing fortnight.
Thus ends the eighth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.19 2. Caravagga Tatiya-agatisutta (The Third Discourse on Non-Going) “Monks, there are these four kinds of non-going. What four? One who does not go to hell; one who does not go to the animal realm; one who does not go to the sphere of afflicted spirits; and one who does not go to the plane of misery, the evil destination, the lower world, or perdition. These, monks, are the four kinds of non-going. And what, monks, is the person who does not go to hell? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. This, monks, is the person who does not go to hell. And what, monks, is the person who does not go to the animal realm? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. This, monks, is the person who does not go to the animal realm. And what, monks, is the person who does not go to the sphere of afflicted spirits? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. This, monks, is the person who does not go to the sphere of afflicted spirits. And what, monks, is the person who does not go to the plane of misery, the evil destination, the lower world, or perdition? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. This, monks, is the person who does not go to the plane of misery, the evil destination, the lower world, or perdition. These, monks, are the four kinds of non-going.”
“Monks, there are these four ways of going to ruin.
What are the four?
One goes to a wrong course through lust, one goes to a wrong course through hatred, one goes to a wrong course through delusion, and one goes to a wrong course through fear.
These, monks, are the four ways of going to a wrong course.
There are, monks, these four ways of not going to a wrong course.
Which four?
One does not go by way of bias through desire, one does not go by way of bias through hatred, one does not go by way of bias through delusion, and one does not go by way of bias through fear.
These, monks, are the four ways of not going astray.
Whoever transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
his fame diminishes.
Like the moon in the dark fortnight,
he who does not overstep the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
“His fame increases,
like the moon in the bright fortnight.
Thus ends the ninth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.20 2. Caravagga Bhattuddesakasutta: The Discourse on the Designator of Almsfood At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these four kinds of designators of almsfood. What four? The one who designates out of favoritism, the one who designates out of ill will, the one who designates out of delusion, and the one who designates out of fear. These, monks, are the four kinds of designators of almsfood. “Monks, there are these four kinds of designators of almsfood. What four? The one who designates out of favoritism, the one who designates out of ill will, the one who designates out of delusion, and the one who designates out of fear. And how, monks, is one a designator of almsfood out of favoritism? Here, monks, a certain person, out of favoritism, designates almsfood for a specific monk, saying: ‘This almsfood is for such-and-such a monk. Thus, monks, one is a designator of almsfood out of favoritism. “And how, monks, is one a designator of almsfood out of ill will?

Here, monks, a certain person, out of ill will toward a specific monk, designates almsfood for another monk, saying: ‘This almsfood is for such-and-such a monk. Thus, monks, one is a designator of almsfood out of ill will. “And how, monks, is one a designator of almsfood out of delusion? Here, monks, a certain person, out of delusion, designates almsfood, thinking: ‘By this gift, may I be reborn in heaven! Thus, monks, one is a designator of almsfood out of delusion. “And how, monks, is one a designator of almsfood out of fear? Here, monks, a certain person, out of fear, designates almsfood, thinking: ‘If I do not designate almsfood, they will harm me or take my life.
