“Bhikkhus, one who is possessed of four qualities, as an assigner of meals, is deposited in hell just as if he were placed there. Which four? [The text continues with the list of qualities.]”
"He goes astray through desire, he goes astray through hatred, he goes astray through delusion, and he goes astray through fear.
Possessing these four qualities, monks, the distributor of meals is deposited in hell as if carried there by his own burden.
Possessing four qualities, monks, the distributor of meals is deposited in heaven as if carried there by his own burden."
Which four?

He does not follow a wrong course through desire, he does not follow a wrong course through hatred, he does not follow a wrong course through delusion, and he does not follow a wrong course through fear.
It is by possessing these four qualities, monks, that a distributor of meals causes [the donor] to go to heaven, just as if they had been placed there according to their deserts.
Those people who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures,
who are unrighteous and hold the unrighteous in high esteem,
follow the path of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.
And he is called "one with a face like a mask.
For thus it was said by the knowing ascetic:
"Therefore, those true men are indeed to be praised."
Those who, established in the Dhamma,
do no evil— neither out of desire, nor hatred, nor delusion, nor fear—
they are called the cream of the assembly.
"Thus indeed has it been said by the knowing ascetic.
Tenth. The Second Chapter on Wandering.
Its summary verse:
Walking, virtue, the exertions,
restraint, and the fifth is the formal designation.
Three kinds of delicacies,
ten ways of assigning meals—
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.21.

3. Uruvelavagga Paṭhama-uruvelasutta (AN 4.21, PTS AN ii 20) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, before his enlightenment. At that time, many people were bathing in the river Nerañjarā. Having bathed, some were ascending the bank, some were descending, and some were splashing about in the water. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in his mind: “It is wonderful, it is marvelous! This river Nerañjarā is so full of people; yet here, no one is crying out, making a noise, or uttering a sound. Then, having risen from seclusion in the evening, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, did you hear many people bathing in the river Nerañjarā? Having bathed, some were ascending the bank, some were descending, and some were splashing about in the water? “Yes, venerable sir,” they replied. “Bhikkhus, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind: ‘It is wonderful, it is marvelous! This river Nerañjarā is so full of people; yet here, no one is crying out, making a noise, or uttering a sound. “Venerable sir, this is indeed wonderful and marvelous! How could such a thing be? “Bhikkhus, those who have not seen the Tathāgata or one who has seen the Tathāgata, and who have not heard the Dhamma or one who has heard the Dhamma, do not know the Tathāgata as he really is, nor do they understand the Dhamma as it really is. But those who have seen the Tathāgata or one who has seen the Tathāgata, and who have heard the Dhamma or one who has heard the Dhamma, know the Tathāgata as he really is, and they understand the Dhamma as it really is. “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of sensual pleasures. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; sounds cognizable by the ear... odors cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of sensual pleasures. “Now, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple understands these five kinds of sensual pleasures as they really are, and understands the origin of these five kinds of sensual pleasures as it really is, the cessation of these five kinds of sensual pleasures as it really is, and the way leading to the cessation of these five kinds of sensual pleasures as it really is—he is called a noble disciple who has understood the Dhamma, who sees the Dhamma, who has reached this Dhamma, who dwells in this Dhamma, who has transcended doubt, who has put away uncertainty, who has gained intrepidity, and who has become independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation. “Just as, bhikkhus, a river flowing down from a mountain slope, carrying along much gravel and pebbles, would empty into the great ocean; even so, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple understands these five kinds of sensual pleasures as they really are, and understands their origin, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation as they really are—he is called a noble disciple who has understood the Dhamma... and who has become independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had gone, a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda and said: “Friend Ānanda, just now, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in his mind: ‘It is wonderful, it is marvelous! This river Nerañjarā is so full of people; yet here, no one is crying out, making a noise, or uttering a sound. “Friend, this is indeed wonderful and marvelous! How could such a thing be? For the Blessed One, friend, is one who has abandoned the five lower fetters, one who has cut off craving, severed the bonds, and by completely breaking through conceit, has made an end of suffering in this very life. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported what had occurred. “Ānanda, it is just as you say. It is wonderful and marvelous that the bhikkhu has spoken thus. For the Tathāgata, Ānanda, is one who has abandoned the five lower fetters, one who has cut off craving, severed the bonds, and by completely breaking through conceit, has made an end of suffering in this very life. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, the bhikkhus delighted in the words of the Blessed One. The First Discourse at Uruvelā is concluded.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Bhikkhus, on one occasion I was dwelling at Uruvelā, by the bank of the Nerañjarā River, at the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree, having just attained full enlightenment.
Then, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘It is indeed suffering to dwell without respect and without deference.’”
‘What ascetic or brahmin might I honor, revere, and live in dependence upon?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Since my aggregate of virtue is not yet fulfilled, for the sake of fulfilling it, I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon another ascetic or brahmin.’”
Yet, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans, I do not see another ascetic or brahmin more perfect in virtue than myself,
whom I might honor, revere, and dwell in dependence upon.
If the aggregate of concentration were not yet fulfilled, I would honor, revere, and rely upon another ascetic or brahmin for its fulfillment. However,
I do not see any other ascetic or brahmin in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans— anyone more perfected in concentration than myself.
Having honored, revered, and relied upon him, I would dwell [under his guidance].
For the sake of fulfilling the aggregate of wisdom that is as yet unfulfilled, I would honor, revere, and rely upon another ascetic or brahmin.
Yet, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, who—
In this world with its devas and humans, there is no other ascetic or brahmin more perfected in wisdom than myself,
whom I might honor, revere, and live in dependence upon. Indeed,
for the sake of fulfilling the aggregate of liberation that is as yet unfulfilled, I would honor, revere, and live in dependence upon another ascetic or brahmin.
‘Yet, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans, I do not see any other ascetic or brahmin more accomplished in liberation than myself,
whom I might honor, revere, and dwell in dependence upon.’”
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
"What if I were to dwell honoring, respecting, and relying upon that very Dhamma which has been fully awakened to by me?
Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, knowing with his own mind the reflection in my mind—just as...
“Just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm,
even so, having vanished from the Brahma-world, he appeared before me. Then, monks,
Brahmā Sahampati arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and extending his joined palms toward me, said this to me:”
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
Those who were the Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past, Blessed Ones, they too dwelt having honored, revered, and relied upon the Dhamma alone.
Those who will be the Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future, Blessed Ones, they too will dwell having honored, revered, and relied upon the Dhamma alone.”
“May the Blessed One too, Bhante, who is now an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell honoring, respecting, and relying upon the Dhamma alone.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said.
Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“Those who were the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past,
those Buddhas who are yet to come,
and he who is the Perfectly Enlightened One now— ”
The destroyer of the sorrow of many.
All those who revere the true Dhamma have lived and still live [in this way].
And they will continue to dwell thus;
this is the nature of the Buddhas.
Therefore, by one who desires their own welfare,
By one desiring the highest greatness,
the true Dhamma should be held in reverence,
remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.
"This, monks, is what Brahmā Sahampati said.
Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished right there.

Then, monks, having understood Brahmā’s exhortation and knowing what was appropriate for myself, I honored, revered, and relied upon that very Dhamma which had been fully awakened to by me, and I dwelt [therein]."
"But when, monks, the Saṅgha too has attained greatness, then I have reverence for the Saṅgha as well.
The first.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.22
3. Uruvelavagga The Second Discourse at Uruvelā (AN 4.22, PTS AN ii 22)
“Bhikkhus, on one occasion I was dwelling at Uruvelā, by the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the Goatherd’s Banyan tree, having just attained full enlightenment.

Then, bhikkhus, a number of brahmins—old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the end of their lifespan and come to the final stage of life—approached me; having approached, they exchanged greetings with me.
When they had concluded their polite and amiable conversation, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, bhikkhus, those brahmins said this to me:”
“Master Gotama, we have heard this:
‘The ascetic Gotama does not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, nor does he rise for them or invite them to a seat.
And so it is, Master Gotama.”
“Master Gotama does not pay homage to brahmins who are aged, elderly, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life, nor does he rise up for them or invite them to a seat.
This, Master Gotama, is indeed not proper.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘These venerable ones do not know an elder, nor the qualities that make one an elder.
Even if, monks, one is old— eighty, ninety, or a hundred years by birth— if he speaks at the wrong time,

speaks what is untrue, speaks what is useless, speaks what is contrary to the Dhamma, speaks what is contrary to the Vinaya, and utters speech that is ungrounded, untimely, indefinite, and unbeneficial;
Yet he is reckoned as merely a "foolish elder.
But even if, monks, one is young, a youth with black hair, endowed with the bloom of early manhood and in the prime of life;

and if he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya; if he utters speech that is well-founded, timely, reasoned, limited, and connected with the goal—[he is to be honored].
Then he indeed comes to be reckoned as "the wise elder.
Monks, there are these four qualities that constitute an elder.
What are the four?

In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

He is learned, one who has retained what he has heard, one who has accumulated what he has heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings as these he [masters].
They have become very learned in the teachings; they retain them in memory, master them through speech, examine them with the mind, and penetrate them thoroughly through right view.
They are able to attain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

Through the destruction of the taints, they realize for themselves through direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, they dwell therein.
“Monks, these are the four qualities that make one an elder.
Whoever, with an agitated mind,
speaks much frivolous chatter;”
One whose intention is unconcentrated,
who delights in what is not the true Dhamma,
and who is deluded— that person is far from steadfastness.
One with evil views is disrespectful;
but one who is endowed with virtue,
learned, and eloquent—
The wise one, restrained in all phenomena,
clearly perceives the meaning through wisdom;
he has gone beyond all things.
He is entirely wise and possessed of ready eloquence;
having abandoned birth and death,
he is perfected in the holy life.
I call him an elder who has no taints;
through the destruction of the taints, he is a bhikkhu.
Thus he is called an elder.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.23

3. Uruvelavagga Lokasutta (AN 4.23, PTS AN ii 23) “Monks, this world is led by mind, drawn along by mind, and has mind as its master. If one speaks or acts with a defiled mind, suffering follows one even as the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the cart. Monks, this world is led by mind, drawn along by mind, and has mind as its master. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind, happiness follows one even as one’s shadow that never departs.”
“Monks, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is detached from the world.
The origin of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.”
The origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata.
The cessation of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
The cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata.
“Monks, the path leading to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
The path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata.
That which, monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins...”
Whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by mind among the generation consisting of devas and humans—
all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.”

Monks, whatever the Tathāgata speaks, utters, or explains during the interval between the night he awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night he attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue—
all that is exactly so and not otherwise.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.
Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so does he act; as he acts, so does he speak.
Thus, as he speaks, so does he act; as he acts, so does he speak.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.

In this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, and the wielder of power.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.”
Having directly known the entire world,
and the entire world as it truly is,
he is completely detached from the entire world.
Unattached to the entire world,
he is indeed the wise one who has overcome all and is liberated from all bonds.
For one who has touched it, there is supreme peace,
Nibbāna, free from fear from any quarter.
He is the Buddha whose taints are destroyed.
Free from affliction, with doubts severed,
he has attained the destruction of all karma and is liberated through the exhaustion of the substrata of existence.
He is that Blessed One, the Buddha;
he is the unsurpassed lion for the world including its devas.
He set in motion the Wheel of Brahma.
Thus, both gods and humans who have gone for refuge to the Buddha—
Gathering together, they pay homage to him—
the great one who is free from timidity;
the tamed one, the best among those who tame.
The Sage is the best among those who have attained peace;
the Liberated One is the foremost among those who liberate;
the Crossed-Over One is the most excellent among those who help others cross over.
Thus do they pay homage to him,
the great one who is free from timidity,
in this world together with its devas.
“There is no one who is my equal.
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.24
3. The Chapter at Uruvelā:
The Discourse on the Dark Wood Monastery (Kāḷakārāmasutta) (AN 4.24, PTS AN ii 24)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāketa in the Kāḷaka Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins...”
Whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or pondered by the mind among this generation with its devas and humans—
that I know. Whatever, monks,
in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins...
Whatever has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or pondered by the mind among this generation with its devas and humans—that I have directly known.
That is understood by the Tathāgata; that does not obsess the Tathāgata.
"Bhikkhus, if I were to say, 'Whatever in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind—
that I do not know,' that would be a falsehood on my part."
“Bhikkhus, regarding that which... [as before] ...if I were to say, ‘I both know it and do not know it,’ that would be just like that. Bhikkhus, regarding that which...
[as before] ...if I were to say, ‘I neither know it nor do I not know it,’ that would be a failure for me.

Thus, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has seen what is to be seen; he does not conceive of what is seen, he does not conceive of what is not seen, he does not conceive of what is to be seen, and he does not conceive of the seer.”

Having heard what is to be heard, one does not conceive of what has been heard, one does not conceive of what has not been heard, one does not conceive of that which is to be heard, and one does not conceive of the hearer.

Having sensed what is to be sensed, one does not conceive of what has been sensed, one does not conceive of what has not been sensed, one does not conceive of that which is to be sensed, and one does not conceive of the sensor.

Having cognized what is to be cognized, one does not conceive of what has been cognized, one does not conceive of what has not been cognized, one does not conceive of that which is to be cognized, and one does not conceive of the cognizer.
"Thus, monks, the Tathāgata is indeed one who is the same (tādī) regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
And I say that there is no other one who is the same superior to or more excellent than that same one.
Whatever is seen or heard or sensed..."
Truth or falsehood spoken to others that is clung to—
such a person does not harm them, for they are themselves restrained.
Truth or even falsehood would not burn another in such a case.
Having seen this arrow and having removed it—
that to which people are attached and entangled—
I know and see it exactly as it is.
“Tathāgatas have nothing to which they are attached.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.25

3. Uruvelavagga: Brahmacariyasutta (AN 4.25, PTS AN ii 26) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these three kinds of holy life. What three? The holy life that is for the sake of the present life, the holy life that is for the sake of the next life, and the holy life that is for the sake of the ultimate goal. And what, monks, is the holy life for the sake of the present life? Here, someone is a thief, a robber, one who has gone over to the side of thieves; he is violent, bloody-handed, a destroyer of villages, a plunderer of the countryside. He thinks: ‘If I were to go forth into homelessness under the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, I would be one who lives the holy life for the sake of the present life. This, monks, is called the holy life for the sake of the present life. And what, monks, is the holy life for the sake of the next life? Here, someone is a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, given to violence toward living beings. He thinks: ‘If I were to go forth into homelessness under the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, I would be one who lives the holy life for the sake of the next life. This, monks, is called the holy life for the sake of the next life. And what, monks, is the holy life for the sake of the ultimate goal? Here, someone is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. He thinks: ‘If I were to go forth into homelessness under the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, I would be one who lives the holy life for the sake of the ultimate goal. This, monks, is called the holy life for the sake of the ultimate goal. These, monks, are the three kinds of holy life.”

“Monks, this holy life is not lived for the sake of deceiving people, nor for the sake of flattering people, nor for the sake of gain, honor, and renown, nor for the sake of the benefit of escaping from debate, nor with the thought, ‘Let people know me thus.
Rather, monks, this holy life is lived for the sake of restraint, for the sake of abandoning, for the sake of dispassion, and for the sake of cessation.
[It is] for the sake of restraint, for the sake of abandoning...”
The Blessed One taught the holy life, which is not based on mere tradition,
leading to the depths of Nibbāna.
This is the path followed by the great ones, the great seers;
and those who practice it—
Just as taught by the Buddha:
"Those who act according to the Teacher’s instruction will make an end of suffering."
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.26 3.
Uruvela Vagga (The Chapter at Uruvelā)
The Kuha Sutta (AN 4.26): “Those monks, bhikkhus, who are deceitful, stubborn, boasters, arrogant, haughty, and unconcentrated— they, bhikkhus, are not my monks.”
“Monks, those monks have departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya, and they do not attain growth, increase, or abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
But those monks, monks, who are guileless, free from chatter, steadfast, undeluded, and well-composed—they, monks, are my monks.
They have not departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya, and they do attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
Deceitful, stubborn, talkative, and sharp-tongued,
arrogant and unconcentrated—
such qualities do not grow in them.
Taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One:
free from guile, free from chatter, steadfast, without arrogance, and well-composed.
"These qualities indeed flourish in one who has been taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Thus ends the sixth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.27 3. Uruvela Vagga Santuṭṭhi Sutta: Contentment “Monks, there are these four kinds of contentment. What four? Contentment with any kind of robes; contentment with any kind of almsfood; contentment with any kind of lodging; and contentment with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick. These, monks, are the four kinds of contentment.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things that are few, easy to obtain, and blameless.
What are the four?
“Bhikkhus, among robes, the rag-robe is little and easy to obtain, and it is blameless.
Among foods, almsfood is little and easy to obtain, and it is blameless.
Among lodgings, the foot of a tree is little and easy to obtain, and it is blameless.”
"Decayed urine, monks, is a medicine that is both little and easy to obtain, and it is blameless.
These, monks, are the four things that are little, easy to obtain, and blameless.
When, monks, a monk is content with what is little and easy to obtain, I say that this is one factor of the ascetic life for him."
For one who is content with what is blameless,
meager, and easy to obtain,
there is no concern regarding lodgings.
With robes, drink, and food,
there is no obstruction to the mind,
and it is not hindered in any direction.
And those teachings which have been proclaimed,
which are conducive to the state of a recluse,
having mastered them, he is content.
“For one who trains with diligence.
The seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.28

3. Uruvelā Vagga: The Discourse on the Noble Lineages (Ariyavaṃsa Sutta) At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages. What four? (1) Here, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of robe, and he declares that noble lineage: ‘I am content with any kind of robe. This is called the first noble lineage. (2) Again, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of almsfood, and he declares that noble lineage: ‘I am content with any kind of almsfood. This is called the second noble lineage. (3) Again, a bhikkhu is content with any kind of lodging, and he declares that noble lineage: ‘I am content with any kind of lodging. This is called the third noble lineage. (4) Again, a bhikkhu delights in and takes delight in non-distraction, and he declares that noble lineage: ‘I delight in and take delight in non-distraction. This is called the fourth noble lineage. These, bhikkhus, are the four noble lineages.”

“Monks, there are these four noble lineages—ancient, long-standing, traditional, and original; unadulterated and never before adulterated; not being adulterated now, nor will they be adulterated; and they are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins. What are the four?
Here, monks, a monk is content with whatever robe he receives; through contentment with whatever robe he receives...”
He speaks in praise of robes, yet he does not engage in improper or unsuitable search for the sake of robes; not obtaining robes, he is not distressed,
and having obtained robes, he uses them without attachment, infatuation, or clinging, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
And by virtue of that contentment with whatever robe he receives, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—this, monks, is called a monk established in the ancient, primordial noble lineage.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with whatever almsfood he receives; through contentment with whatever almsfood he receives...
He speaks in praise [of such conduct], yet he does not engage in improper search for almsfood for its sake; when he does not obtain almsfood,
he is not distressed, and when he obtains almsfood, he consumes it without being attached, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
And by means of that contentment with whatever almsfood may be obtained, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, he, monks, is said to be a monk established in the ancient, primordial noble lineage.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with whatever lodging may be obtained; through contentment with whatever lodging may be obtained...
He speaks in praise of lodgings, yet he does not resort to improper means for the sake of lodgings; not obtaining a lodging, he does not become anxious,
and having obtained a lodging, he uses it without attachment, infatuation, or clinging, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
And by means of that contentment with any kind of lodging, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—he, monks, is called a monk established in the ancient, primordial lineage of the noble ones.
Furthermore, monks, a monk delights in development and rejoices in development; he delights in relinquishment and rejoices in relinquishment.
And because of that delight in meditation and delight in development, and because of that delight in abandoning and delight in relinquishment, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others.
For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—that one, monks, is said to be a monk established in the ancient, primordial noble lineage.

These, monks, are the four noble lineages—ancient, long-standing, traditional, original, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated now, and not to be adulterated; they are uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.
And furthermore, monks, a monk endowed with these four noble lineages, even if he dwells in the eastern direction, overcomes discontent and discontent does not overcome him;
even if he dwells in the western direction, he overcomes discontent and discontent does not overcome him;
even if he dwells in the northern direction, he overcomes discontent and discontent does not overcome him.
Even if he dwells in the southern direction, he overcomes discontent; discontent does not overcome him.
Why is that? Because, monks, the wise person is one who overcomes both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Discontent does not overcome the steadfast;
the steadfast overcomes discontent;
it is the steadfast alone who overcomes discontent.
For the wise man indeed endures discontent.
Who can prevent one who has abandoned all kamma from having it dispelled?
Like a necklace of pure gold from the Jambu river,
who would be fit to censure him?
Even the gods praise him.
“He was even praised by Brahmā.
The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.29
3. Uruvelavagga: Dhammapadasutta (AN 4.29, PTS AN ii 29)

“Bhikkhus, there are these four footprints of the Dhamma that are foremost, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, and will not be adulterated; they are not reviled by wise recluses and brahmins.
What are the four?

“Non-covetousness, monks, is a footprint of the Dhamma, primeval, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated; it is not being adulterated, nor will it be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins alike.

Non-ill will, monks, is a footprint of the Dhamma, primeval, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated and never before adulterated; it is not being adulterated, nor will it be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins alike.”

“Right mindfulness, bhikkhus, is a footprint of the Dhamma that is foremost, ancient, traditional, original, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, and never to be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.

Right concentration, bhikkhus, is a footprint of the Dhamma that is foremost, ancient, traditional, original, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, and never to be adulterated; it is uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.”
“Monks, these four Dhamma-footings are foremost, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated;
they are not being adulterated, nor will they be adulterated; they are uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins.”
One should dwell without covetousness,
with a mind free from ill will,
mindful and with a one-pointed mind.
“Fully concentrated within.
The ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.30
3. Uruvelavagga: The Discourse on Wanderers (Paribbājakasutta) (AN 4.30, PTS AN ii 29)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, many well-known and famous wanderers were residing in the Wanderers’ Park on the bank of the Sippinikā River, namely:
Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyin, and other well-known wanderers.
These were well-known wanderers.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the wanderers’ park on the bank of the Sappinikā River.
Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Once seated, the Blessed One said this to those wanderers:

“Monks, there are these four Dhamma-phrases that are foremost, ancient, traditional, original, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, and never to be adulterated; they are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins.
What are the four?
“Non-covetousness, wanderers, is a footprint of the Dhamma— primeval, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, not to be adulterated,
unrepudiated by wise ascetics and brahmins. Non-ill will, wanderers, is a footprint of the Dhamma … Right mindfulness, wanderers,
is a footprint of the Dhamma … Right concentration, wanderers, is a footprint of the Dhamma— primeval, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated.”
"Never before defiled, not being defiled now, nor will it be defiled in the future; it is unreviled by wise recluses and brahmins.

These, wanderers, are the four footprints of Dhamma that are foremost, long-standing, traditional, ancient, undefiled, never before defiled, not being defiled now, nor will they be defiled in the future; they are unreviled by wise recluses and brahmins."
“Monks, if anyone were to say:
‘Setting aside this verse of Dhamma regarding non-covetousness, I shall point out a recluse or brahmin who is covetous and possessed of intense lust for sensual pleasures,’ then I would say to him:
‘Let him come; let him speak; let him declare it, and we shall see his power.’”

“Indeed, wanderers, it is impossible that one could point to a recluse or a brahmin who, having rejected the Dhamma-footprint of non-covetousness, is covetous and possesses intense lust for sensual pleasures;
no such case exists. Wanderers, if anyone were to say:
‘Having rejected this Dhamma-footprint of non-ill will, I shall point to a recluse or a brahmin whose mind is full of ill will and whose intentions are corrupt,’ I would say to him regarding that:”
‘Let him come, let him speak, let him declare it; we shall see his power.
Monks, it is impossible that one who has rejected the Dhamma-footprint of non-ill will would designate a recluse or a brahmin as having a mind of ill will and a corrupt intention.
Monks, if anyone were to say this: [it is impossible].”
‘Having rejected this verse of the Dhamma on right mindfulness, I shall point out a recluse or brahmin who is muddle-minded and lacking in clear comprehension’—regarding such a person, I would say:
‘Let him come, let him speak, let him declare it; we shall see his power.

For it is impossible, O wanderers, that one who has rejected this verse of the Dhamma on right mindfulness should point out a recluse or brahmin who is muddle-minded and lacking in clear comprehension; no such case exists.
“Monks, if anyone were to say:
‘Setting aside this footstep of the Dhamma that is right concentration, I shall point out a recluse or brahmin who is unconcentrated and of wandering mind,’ then regarding him I would say:
‘Let him come, let him speak, let him declare it; we shall see his power.’”

“Indeed, wanderers, it is impossible that one would designate a recluse or a brahmin as being of undistracted mind and concentrated while rejecting this verse of the Dhamma, which is right concentration.

Wanderers, if anyone should think that these four verses of the Dhamma are to be censured or rejected, there are four legitimate grounds for censure that apply to him in this very life. What are the four?
[The four grounds follow.]”

If you revile and reject the verse of the Dhamma concerning non-covetousness, then those recluses and brahmins who are covetous and intensely lustful for sensual pleasures are to be honored by you, they are to be praised by you.

If you revile and reject the verse of the Dhamma concerning non-ill will, then those recluses and brahmins who have minds full of ill will and corrupt intentions are to be honored by you, they are to be praised by you.

If you, sir, revile and reject the verse of the Dhamma concerning right mindfulness, then those recluses and brahmins who are muddle-minded and lacking clear comprehension are the ones worthy of your honor and praise.

If you, sir, revile and reject the verse of the Dhamma concerning right concentration, then those recluses and brahmins who are unconcentrated and of wandering minds are the ones worthy of your honor and praise.
Monks, if anyone should think that these four Dhamma-footings are to be censured or rejected, then in this very life four legitimate grounds for censure will accrue to him.

Even those wanderers who were the Ukkalā Vassabhajjā—proponents of non-causality, proponents of non-action, and proponents of nihilism—even they did not think that these four Dhamma-footings were to be censured or rejected. Why is that?
From blame, reproach, censure, and fear—
being free from malice, always mindful,
and well-composed within, [one overcomes them].
One who trains in the subduing of covetousness is called "heedful.
Thus ends the tenth [sutta].
The Third Chapter: Uruvelā.
Its summary verse:
Two on Uruvelā, Loka, and Kāḷaka.
The fifth [chapter] is on the holy life (brahmacariya);
then on hypocrisy, contentment, and the lineage, and the Chapter on the Dhamma-footprint (Dhammapada), along with that on the wanderer (paribbājaka).
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.31 4.

Cakkavagga Cakkasutta (The Discourse on the Wheel) “Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels that, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of greatness, to the attainment of abundance, to the attainment of sovereignty, and to the attainment of the supreme state among human beings. What four? The wheel of noble lineage, the wheel of noble wealth, the wheel of noble virtue, and the wheel of noble wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the four wheels that, when developed and cultivated, lead to the attainment of greatness, to the attainment of abundance, to the attainment of sovereignty, and to the attainment of the supreme state among human beings.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels, possessed of which gods and humans turn the fourfold wheel; possessed of which gods and humans before long attain greatness and abundance in wealth.
What are the four? [Text follows]”
"Living in a suitable locality, relying on true persons, right resolve for oneself, and having performed merit in the past—these, monks, are the four wheels.
Possessed of these, the four wheels turn for gods and humans; possessed of these, gods and humans before long attain greatness and abundance in wealth.
One should dwell in a suitable locality.
One should cultivate noble friends;
a person endowed with right aspiration who has performed merit in the past;
“Grain, wealth, fame, and renown—
this happiness attends him. Thus ends the first [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.32 4. Cakkavagga Saṅgahasutta:

The Discourse on Gathering “Monks, there are these four ways of gathering. What four? Gathering through giving; gathering through kind speech; gathering through beneficial conduct; and gathering through consistency between words and deeds. These, monks, are the four ways of gathering.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of sympathy. Which four?
Generosity, kindly speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—
these, monks, are the four bases of sympathy.
Generosity and kindly speech...
And here, acting for the welfare of others,
and impartiality toward all things,
as is appropriate in each case.
These indeed are the means of integration in the world,
like the linchpin of a moving chariot;
were these means of integration not to exist, [the world would fall apart].
Neither a mother nor a father would receive honor or worship for the sake of their son.
And because the wise examine these means of integration,
they therefore attain greatness.
“And they become praised.
The second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.33

4. Cakkavagga Sīhasutta (AN 4.33, PTS AN ii 33) “Monks, just as the lion, the king of beasts, when lying down, sitting, or pacing back and forth, surveys the four quarters with a leonine gaze, so too, monks, a bhikkhu who is an arahant—one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, one completely liberated through final knowledge—when lying down, sitting, or pacing back and forth, surveys the four quarters with a leonine gaze. And why? Because he is free from fear and free from trembling. Monks, this is the leonine gaze of a bhikkhu who is an arahant.”
“Bhikkhus, in the evening time the lion, the king of beasts, emerges from his lair.
Having emerged from his lair, he stretches himself.
Having stretched himself, he surveys the four quarters all around.
Having surveyed the four directions all around, he roars his lion’s roar three times.
Having roared his lion’s roar three times, he sets out for his range.
And those creatures of the animal realm, bhikkhus, who hear the sound of the lion, the king of beasts, roaring, mostly fall into fear, agitation, and terror.
Those who dwell in holes enter their holes; those who dwell in water enter the water; those who dwell in the forest enter the forest; and birds resort to the sky.

Even those royal elephants, bhikkhus, who are bound by strong leather thongs in villages, market towns, and royal capitals—even they, having snapped and torn apart those bonds, being terrified, discharge urine and dung.
They flee here and there.
Thus, monks, the lion, king of beasts, is of such great psychic power among animals, of such great authority, and of such great majesty.
Even so, monks, when a Tathāgata arises in the world—an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct—
The Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, teaches the Dhamma thus:
“Such is identity, such is the origin of identity, such is the cessation of identity, such is the way leading to the cessation of identity.

And even those gods, bhikkhus, who are long-lived, beautiful, abundant in happiness, and dwell for a long time in lofty palaces—even they, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part fall into fear, a sense of urgency, and terror.
‘Alas, sirs, being impermanent, we indeed imagined ourselves to be permanent;
alas, sirs, being unstable, we indeed imagined ourselves to be stable;
alas, sirs, being non-eternal, we indeed imagined ourselves to be eternal.’
‘We, sir, are indeed impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and included within identity.
Thus, monks, the Tathāgata is of such great psychic power in the world with its devas, of such great authority, and of such great majesty.
When the Buddha, having realized through direct knowledge—
He set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
the Teacher of the world with its devas, the peerless one.
Personal existence and its cessation,
the origin of personal existence,
and the Noble Eightfold Path—
Which leads to the subsiding of suffering.
Even those gods who are long-lived,
beautiful, and glorious;
Terrified, they fell into a state of panic,
like other animals before a lion;
they had not yet transcended personal existence.
“Truly, we are impermanent, O sir!”—
having heard the words of the Arahant,
the one who is utterly liberated and steadfast.
The Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34 4.
The Chapter on the Wheel (Cakkavagga)
The Discourse on Supreme Confidence (Aggappasādasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these four supreme confidences.”
Which four?
Monks, however many beings there are—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless;
whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among them.
He is the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Monks, those who have faith in the Buddha have faith in the foremost.
And for those who have faith in the foremost, the result is foremost.
“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be the foremost among them.
Those who have confidence in the Noble Eightfold Path, bhikkhus, have confidence in the foremost.
And for those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.”
"Monks, whatever phenomena there are, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared the foremost among them;

that is to say, the crushing of intoxication, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the cycle of existence, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
Those who have confidence, monks, in these phenomena of dispassion, have confidence in the foremost."
Moreover, for those with faith in the foremost, the result is foremost.
Monks, whatever assemblies or groups there may be, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them;
that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples, worthy of offerings.
He is worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Those, monks, who have faith in the Saṅgha have faith in the foremost.
For those who have faith in the foremost, the result is foremost.
"These, monks, are the four supreme confidences.
For those who have supreme confidence and who understand the supreme Dhamma..."
For those with faith in the Supreme Buddha,
the unsurpassed one worthy of offerings;
for those with faith in the Supreme Dhamma...
In the bliss of the pacification of dispassion,
for those with faith in the supreme Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit.
For those giving the foremost gift,
the foremost merit increases;
the foremost lifespan and the foremost beauty [increase as well].
Fame, renown, happiness, and strength belong to the wise giver of the foremost [gift],
who is established in the foremost Dhamma.
Whether become a god or a human,
one who has reached the summit rejoices. Thus ends the fourth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.35 4. Cakkavagga Vassakārasutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, when they had concluded their polite and amiable conversation, sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Vassakāra said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a world of ruin, even in hell? “Brahmin, it is because of three things that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a world of ruin, even in hell. What three? Here, brahmin, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, and engages in sexual misconduct. These are the three things because of which some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a world of ruin, even in hell. “What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world? “It is because of three things, brahmin, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. What three? Here, brahmin, someone abstains from destroying life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct. These are the three things because of which some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. When this was said, the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last.”
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, we recognize a man of great wisdom, a Great Man, by four qualities.
What are these four?"
In this case, Master Gotama, one is learned;
one knows the meaning of various things heard and of various things spoken, thinking: "This is the meaning of this speech; this is the meaning of that speech.
Furthermore, one is mindful; one remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago.

Furthermore, regarding those domestic duties that must be performed, he is skillful and diligent therein, endowed with the appropriate means of investigation, capable of acting and capable of providing for them.
It is on account of these four qualities, Master Gotama, that we designate one as a man of great wisdom, a Great Man.
If it seems right to you, Master Gotama, may Master Gotama grant me his approval.
"But if, Master Gotama, it is to be rejected by me, let Master Gotama reject it.
"I neither approve of you, brahmin, nor do I reject you.
Rather, brahmin, I describe one who possesses four qualities as a man of great wisdom, a Great Man."
Which four?
Here, brahmin, one practices for the welfare of many people and for the happiness of many people;
much of the populace has been established by him in the noble way, namely, in the state of wholesome qualities and virtuous qualities.
Thus, whatever thought he wishes to think, that thought he thinks; whatever thought he does not wish to think, that thought he does not think.
Whatever intention he wishes to intend, that intention he intends; whatever intention he does not wish to intend, that intention he does not intend.
In this way, he has attained mastery over the mind regarding the pathways of thought.
He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
Regarding this, brahmin, I neither approve nor do I reject it.
“Brahmin, it is by means of these four qualities that I define one as a great man of great wisdom.
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
How well this has been spoken by Master Gotama!”
And for these four reasons, Master Gotama, we hold you, Master Gotama, to be endowed with these qualities:
for Master Gotama practices for the welfare of many people and for the happiness of many people;
and a great multitude of people have been established by him in the noble method, namely, in the state of wholesome qualities and skillful qualities.
For Master Gotama thinks whatever thought he wishes to think;
he does not think any thought that he does not wish to think. He intends whatever intention he wishes to intend;
he does not intend any intention that he does not wish to intend.
"For Master Gotama has attained mastery over the mind regarding the paths of thought.
For Master Gotama is one who gains at will, without difficulty or trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

For Master Gotama, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it."
“Certainly, brahmin, I have spoken to you with words that were offensive and provocative.
Nevertheless, I shall answer you:
‘For I, brahmin, am practicing for the welfare of many people and for the happiness of many people.’”
"A great many people have been established by me in the noble way, namely, in the state of wholesome qualities and skillful qualities.
For I, brahmin, think whatever thought I wish to think;
I do not think whatever thought I do not wish to think. I intend whatever intention I wish to intend..."
I direct that intention which I intend; I do not direct that intention which I do not wish to intend.
For I, brahmin, have attained mastery over the mind regarding the pathways of thought.
For I, brahmin, am one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas—states of higher consciousness that provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

"For I, brahmin, having realized for myself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, free from taints through the destruction of the taints,
abide therein. He who knows the release of all beings from the snare of death—
He proclaimed the Dhamma, the method, which is beneficial for gods and humans;
indeed, having seen and heard it, [one attains peace].
Many people find confidence [in him].
Skilled in what is the path and what is not the path,
he has accomplished his task and is free from taints.
“The Buddha, whose body is his last,
is called the one of great wisdom, the Great Man.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.36 4. Cakkavagga Doṇasutta “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a man who, having filled a granary with grain, would consume it all; yet another man would fill that same granary again and consume it all. In this way, bhikkhus, that man would consume the grain from that granary for a hundred years, or even more than a hundred years. Yet, bhikkhus, the amount of dust on the surface of the earth would be far more than the amount of grain consumed by that man. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a man who, having covered the entire earth as far as its ocean boundaries with a layer of grass, leaves, or wood one span high, would set fire to it. That fire, fanned by the wind, would burn for a hundred years, or even more than a hundred years. Yet, bhikkhus, the amount of dust remaining after that fire has gone out would be far more than the amount of grass, leaves, or wood consumed by that fire. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a man who, having filled the great ocean with water, would drink it all; yet another man would fill that same ocean again and drink it all. In this way, bhikkhus, that man would drink the water from that great ocean for a hundred years, or even more than a hundred years. Yet, bhikkhus, the amount of dust on the surface of the earth would be far more than the amount of water drunk by that man. “Just so, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. “When a noble disciple possesses these four things, bhikkhus, he is called a stream-enterer, no longer bound to the nether world, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the highway between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā.
And the brahmin Doṇa was also traveling along the highway between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā.
The brahmin Doṇa saw on the Blessed One’s feet wheels with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs, perfect in every detail;
having seen them, this thought occurred to him:
“It is wonderful, indeed! It is marvelous, indeed!”
"These cannot be the footprints of one who has become a human being.
Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the path, sat at the foot of a certain tree, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Then the brahmin Doṇa, following the Blessed One's footprints, saw the Blessed One at that certain spot.
Seeing him sitting at the foot of a tree— inspiring, inspiring confidence, with tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind, having attained the highest self-control and composure,
tamed, guarded, with senses restrained, a true Naga—
he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Will you, sir, become a deva?
“No, brahmin, I shall not become a deva.
“Will you, sir, become a gandhabba?”
“I shall not become a gandhabba, brahmin.
“Then will you become a yakkha, sir?
“I shall not become a yakkha, brahmin.”
“Will your lordship become a human being?
“No, brahmin, I shall not become a human being.
“Then will your lordship become a deva? Being asked thus:
“You said, brahmin, ‘I shall not become a deva.
When asked, ‘Will you then become a gandhabba?’,
you replied, ‘No, brahmin, I shall not become a gandhabba.’”
When asked, "Will you become a *yakkha*, sir?
you replied, "No, brahmin, I will not become a *yakkha*.
When asked, "Will you become a human, sir?"...
“‘I shall not be a human being, brahmin,’ you say. Then what indeed will you become?

“Brahmin, those taints (*āsava*) by the non-abandonment of which I might have become a deva—those taints have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to future non-arising.”
“Brahmin, those taints (*āsava*) through the non-abandonment of which I might have become a *gandhabba*, or a *yakkha*, or a human—
those taints of mine have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent,
and are subject to non-arising in the future.”
"Just as, brahmin, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus, born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsullied by the water—
even so, brahmin, though born in the world and grown in the world, I dwell having overcome the world,
unsullied by the world. 'Buddha,' brahmin, you should remember me."
By what means one would be reborn as a god,
or as a gandhabba, or as a bird;
by what means one might go to the state of a yakkha—
And I have attained the human state;
those taints of mine are exhausted,
shattered, and rendered baseless.
Just as a lovely white lotus is not defiled by water,
so am I not defiled by the world.
"Therefore, O brahmin, I am a Buddha.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.37

4. Cakkavagga Aparihāniyasutta (AN 4.37, PTS AN ii 39) “Monks, there are these seven factors of non-decline. What seven? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will toward one quarter; likewise toward the second, the third, and the fourth quarter; thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with compassion... with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy... with a mind imbued with equanimity, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will toward one quarter; likewise toward the second, the third, and the fourth quarter; thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells with a mind imbued with equanimity, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. These, monks, are the seven factors of non-decline.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with four qualities is incapable of decline and is close to Nibbāna itself.
With which four?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue; he guards the doors of his sense faculties; he is moderate in eating; and he is devoted to wakefulness.
And how, monks, is a monk accomplished in virtue? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous;
he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is accomplished in virtue.
And how, monks, is a monk one who guards the doors of the sense faculties?
Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its general appearance nor grasp at its secondary details.
For if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.
If states of covetousness and dejection were to flow in upon him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the eye and achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If, when the mind-faculty is left unguarded, covetousness, dejection, and other evil, unwholesome states might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the mind-faculty; he attains restraint over the mind-faculty.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one whose doors of the sense-faculties are guarded.
And how, monks, is a monk moderate in eating?
Here, monks, a monk reflects wisely before partaking of food:
"Not for sport, not for intoxication, not for smartening, not for adornment, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body."
"For the maintenance of this body, for the cessation of affliction, and for the support of the holy life:
'Thus I shall terminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and there will be for me sustenance, blamelessness, and a comfortable dwelling.
In this way, monks, a monk is moderate in eating.
And how, monks, is a monk devoted to wakefulness?
Here, monks, during the day a monk purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and sitting;
during the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and sitting.

During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising.
During the last watch of the night, having risen, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by means of walking and sitting.
In this way, monks, a monk is devoted to wakefulness.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these four qualities is incapable of decline and is in the very presence of Nibbāna.
A monk established in virtue and restrained in the sense faculties...”
Knowing moderation in food,
he devotes himself to wakefulness;
dwelling thus, ardent—
Day and night, without sloth,
cultivating wholesome states for the attainment of security from bondage.
The bhikkhu who delights in heedfulness and sees danger in negligence is incapable of decline.
“...in the very vicinity of Nibbāna.
The seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.38.

4. Cakkavagga Patilīnasutta (AN 4.38, PTS AN ii 41) “Monks, when a bhikkhu is secluded, he delights in seclusion; when he is aloof from society, he delights in aloofness; when he is content, he delights in contentment; when he has attained the path, he delights in the path; when he has attained the fruit, he delights in the fruit; when he has attained Nibbāna, he delights in Nibbāna. But when a bhikkhu is not secluded, he does not delight in seclusion; when he is not aloof from society, he does not delight in aloofness; when he is not content, he does not delight in contentment; when he has not attained the path, he does not delight in the path; when he has not attained the fruit, he does not delight in the fruit; when he has not attained Nibbāna, he does not delight in Nibbāna. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall be secluded and we shall delight in seclusion; we shall be aloof from society and we shall delight in aloofness; we shall be content and we shall delight in contentment; we shall attain the path and we shall delight in the path; we shall attain the fruit and we shall delight in the fruit; we shall attain Nibbāna and we shall delight in Nibbāna. Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.”
“Monks, a monk who has dispelled his individual truths is called one who has completely renounced seeking, whose bodily formations have been stilled, and who is withdrawn.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has dispelled his individual truths?
Here, monks, whatever various individual truths there are among the many ordinary recluses and brahmins—namely:”
"Or that the world is eternal, or that the world is non-eternal, or that the world is finite, or that the world is infinite;
or that the soul and the body are the same, or that the soul is one thing and the body another;
or that a Tathāgata exists after death, or that a Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death."
or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—
all these are shaken off, dispelled, abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and cast aside.
In this way, monks, a monk has dispelled his individual dogmatic assertions.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has completely abandoned seeking?
Here, monks, a monk’s seeking for sense-pleasures is abandoned, his seeking for existence is abandoned, and his seeking for the holy life has subsided.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has completely abandoned seeking.
And how, monks, is a monk one whose bodily formations have become tranquil? Here, monks,
with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
In this way, monks, a monk has tranquilized the bodily formations.
And how, monks, is a monk withdrawn?
Here, monks, a monk’s conceit “I am” has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
In this way, monks, a monk is withdrawn.
A monk who has dispelled his individual dogmatic views, who has utterly abandoned seeking, whose bodily formations have been stilled—he is called "withdrawn. [The three seekings are:
the seeking of sensual pleasures, the seeking of existence, and the seeking of a holy life.
The quest for the holy life,
along with the clinging to truth—
these are the standpoints of views, these lofty edifices.
For one who is detached from all lust,
liberated through the destruction of craving,
seeking has been relinquished.
The bases of views have been uprooted.
He is indeed a peaceful, mindful bhikkhu,
tranquil and unconquered.
The Buddha, through the realization of conceit,
is said to be “withdrawn.
Thus ends the eighth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.39 4. Cakkavagga Ujjayasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, bhikkhus, a person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare?

Here, bhikkhus, a person does not destroy life, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. But he encourages others to destroy life, to take what is not given, to engage in sexual misconduct, to speak falsely, and to indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, bhikkhus, a person destroys life... [as above] ...and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. And he encourages others to destroy life... [as above] ...and to indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, bhikkhus, a person does not destroy life... [as above] ...and does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. And he encourages others to abstain from destroying life... [as above] ...and to abstain from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “One who destroys life, who takes what is not given, Who engages in unchastity, who speaks falsehood, Who indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants— Such a person is intent on his own welfare, but not on that of others. One who does not destroy life, who does not take what is not given, Who is celibate, who speaks truth, Who does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants— Such a person is intent on the welfare of others, but not on his own. One who destroys life, who takes what is not given, Who engages in unchastity, who speaks falsehood, Who indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants— Such a person is intent neither on his own welfare nor on that of others. One who does not destroy life, who does not take what is not given, Who is celibate, who speaks truth, Who does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants— Such a person is intent both on his own welfare and on that of others. These are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world; Of these, the fourth is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the supreme, and the finest. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. This is the third discourse in the Chapter on the Wheel. The Chapter on the Wheel is finished. The Fourth Book is finished. Then the brahmin Ujjaya approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Ujjaya said this to the Blessed One:
“Does Master Gotama also praise sacrifice?
“I do not, brahmin, praise every kind of sacrifice;
nor, brahmin, do I fail to praise every kind of sacrifice.”
"In whatever kind of sacrifice, brahmin, cattle are slaughtered, goats and sheep are slaughtered, chickens and pigs are slaughtered, and various living beings meet their destruction—
in such a violent sacrifice, brahmin, I do not praise it. And for what reason?"
For such a violent sacrifice, brahmin, neither the Arahants nor those who have entered the path to arahantship would attend.

But as for a sacrifice, brahmin, where no cattle are slain, no goats or sheep are slain, no chickens or pigs are slain, and no various living beings are brought to slaughter—such a non-violent sacrifice, brahmin, do I praise:
namely, the perpetual gift and the family sacrifice.
For what reason?
Because, brahmin, it is to such a sacrifice free from violence that Arahants or those who have entered the path to Arahantship approach.
[Such as] the horse-sacrifice and the human-sacrifice...
The Sammāpāsa, the Vājapeyya, and the Niraggaḷa—
these great sacrifices involving great exertion do not yield great fruit.
Where goats, sheep, and cattle of various kinds are slaughtered—
that sacrifice is not one of those who have gone the right way.
The great seers approach those who perform sacrifices without violence,
sacrificing always in accordance with their lineage.
Neither goats nor cattle,
nor various other creatures, are slain therein;
that sacrifice is well-performed by those who have gone the right way.
The great seers approach.
A wise person should sacrifice this;
this sacrifice is of great fruit.
For this is better for the sacrificer, not worse:
that the sacrifice becomes vast.
"And the deities are pleased.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.40.

4. Cakkavagga Udāyīsutta (AN 4.40, PTS AN ii 43) At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Udāyī, if you would abandon three things and cultivate three things, then this would lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. What are these six? They are: sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty. If you would abandon these three things and cultivate their opposites—non-sensual desire, non-ill will, and non-cruelty—then this would lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘If you would abandon three things and cultivate three things, then this would lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. Then the Venerable Udāyī, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the Venerable Udāyī had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to say: ‘I cannot find any other single thing so blameworthy as the three unwholesome roots: greed, hatred, and delusion. That man would be speaking rightly. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, when these three unwholesome roots are present, various evil unwholesome states come to be; and when these three unwholesome roots are absent, those various evil unwholesome states do not come to be.
