Then the brahmin Udāyī approached the Blessed One; having approached, after being greeted by the Blessed One... [and] sitting to one side, the brahmin Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
"Does Master Gotama also praise sacrifice?
"I do not praise every kind of sacrifice, brahmin."
But I do not, brahmin, praise every kind of sacrifice.
For whatever sacrifice, brahmin, involves the slaughter of oxen, the slaughter of goats and sheep, the slaughter of chickens and pigs, and where various living beings meet their destruction—
such a violent sacrifice, brahmin, I do not praise.
For what reason?
Because, brahmin, Arahants or those who have entered the path to arahantship do not approach such a violent sacrifice.

But in a sacrifice of such a kind, brahmin, where neither cows are slaughtered, nor goats and sheep are slaughtered, nor chickens and pigs are slaughtered, and where various living beings do not undergo slaughter;
"O Brahmin, it is such a sacrifice free from violence that I praise—namely, constant giving and family sacrifices.
And why is that? Because, O Brahmin, it is to such a sacrifice free from violence that the Arahants or those who have entered the path to Arahantship approach."
A sacrifice that is well-prepared, free from violence,
and appropriate for the time—
such a one they attend.
Those who are self-restrained and lead the holy life,
who have uncovered the veil in this world and have transcended family and destiny—
The Buddhas, who are skilled in sacrifice, praise this sacrifice—
whether it be at a sacrificial rite or at a funeral offering.
Having prepared the sacrificial offering as is appropriate,
one with a clear mind makes the sacrifice among those who practice the holy life, which is a fertile field.
That which is well-offered, well-sacrificed,
and well-bestowed upon those worthy of offerings—
such a sacrifice becomes vast.
And the deities are pleased.
Having sacrificed thus, the wise person,
with a mind full of faith and liberated, [attains the higher realms].
The wise person is reborn in a world that is free from affliction and full of happiness.
Thus ends the tenth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.41 5. Rohitassavagga Samādhibhāvanāsutta (The Discourse on the Development of Concentration) “Monks, there are these four kinds of development of concentration. What four? There is, monks, a development of concentration that leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension. There is a development of concentration that leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision. There is a development of concentration that leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension. There is a development of concentration that leads to the destruction of the taints. And what, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life and to mindfulness and clear comprehension. And what, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision? Here, monks, a bhikkhu concentrates on the perception of light, with a mind imbued with luminosity, he develops the mind for the sake of the attainment of knowledge and vision. This, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision. And what, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension? Here, monks, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension. And what, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to the destruction of the taints? Here, monks, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and mental unification, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. This, monks, is the development of concentration that leads to the destruction of the taints.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four developments of concentration. What four? [The passage continues as follows:]”
“Monks, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
there is, monks, a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision;
there is, monks, a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension.”
“Monks, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints.
And what, monks, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life?
Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
“Monks, this development of concentration, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
And what, monks, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision?
Here, monks, a monk attends to the perception of light and fixes his mind on the perception of day.”
"As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.
Thus, with a mind that is open and unenveloped, he develops a luminous mind.
This, monks, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision.
And what, monks, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension?
Here, monks, a monk’s feelings arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known;
perceptions arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known; thoughts arise known, they persist known, and they pass away known.
“Monks, this development of concentration, when developed and cultivated, leads to mindfulness and clear comprehension.
And what, monks, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging:”
‘Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form;
such is feeling, such is the arising of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling;
such is perception, such is the arising of perception, such is the passing away of perception.’
‘Such are volitional formations, such is the origin of volitional formations, such is the passing away of volitional formations;
such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.
Monks, this development of concentration, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of the taints.
“Monks, these are the four developments of concentration.
And it was with reference to this, monks, that it was said in the *Pārāyana*, in the *Puṇṇaka* inquiry:
‘Having discerned, in this world, the high and the low...’”
“He who has no agitation anywhere in the world,
who is peaceful, smokeless, free from distress, and without longing—
he has crossed over birth and old age; thus I say.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.42 5. Rohitassavagga
Pañhabyākaraṇasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these four ways of answering questions.
Which four? There is, monks, a question that is to be answered categorically;
there is, monks, a question that is to be answered by way of analysis.
“Monks, there is a question that is to be answered by counter-questioning;
there is, monks, a question that is to be set aside.
These, monks, are the four ways of answering questions.”
One [type of] speech is categorical, another is analytical;
the third one should be answered with a counter-question.
But one should set aside the fourth.
And whoever among them knows the accordance with the Dhamma in each particular case;
One who is skilled in the four questions—
such a one they call a bhikkhu;
difficult to approach and difficult to overcome.
Profound and difficult to overcome;
moreover, he is skilled in both the meaning and the non-meaning.
The wise person avoids what is harmful and grasps what is beneficial;
through the realization of the goal, the steadfast one—
“He is called wise. The second [sutta].

5. Rohitassavagga First Discourse on Being Overcome by Anger (Paṭhamakodhagarusutta) “Monks, there are these five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. What five? Here, monks, a monk who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness dwells with anger and resentment; he dwells with contempt and insolence; he dwells with envy and avarice; he dwells with deceit and guile; and he dwells with evil desires and wrong views. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. But, monks, there are these five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. What five? Here, monks, a monk who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness does not dwell with anger and resentment; he does not dwell with contempt and insolence; he does not dwell with envy and avarice; he does not dwell with deceit and guile; and he does not dwell with evil desires and wrong views. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four?

One who values anger rather than the true Dhamma; one who values malice rather than the true Dhamma; one who values gain rather than the true Dhamma; and one who values honor rather than the true Dhamma.”
“Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Monks, there are these four persons found existing in the world.
Which four?”

One who values the true Dhamma does not value anger; one who values the true Dhamma does not value hypocrisy; one who values the true Dhamma does not value gain; one who values the true Dhamma does not value honor.
These, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.
Monks who value anger and hypocrisy...
Those who are attached to gain,
honor, and respect do not grow in the Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
And those who are devoted to the true Dhamma,
who have lived and still live [in accordance with it],
they indeed cause that Dhamma to grow.
“Taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.44.

5. Rohitassavagga The Second Discourse on Being Heavy with Anger (Dutiyakodhagarusutta) “Monks, there are these five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. What five? Here, monks, a monk is heavy with anger; he does not endure being spoken to harshly, and he does not patiently accept insults, abuse, and threats. He is heavy with resentment; he does not endure being spoken to harshly, and he does not patiently accept insults, abuse, and threats. He is heavy with malice; he does not endure being spoken to harshly, and he does not patiently accept insults, abuse, and threats. He is heavy with conceit; he does not endure being spoken to harshly, and he does not patiently accept insults, abuse, and threats. He is heavy with craving; he does not endure being spoken to harshly, and he does not patiently accept insults, abuse, and threats. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. But, monks, there are these five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness. What five? Here, monks, a monk is not heavy with anger; he endures being spoken to harshly and patiently accepts insults, abuse, and threats. He is not heavy with resentment; he endures being spoken to harshly and patiently accepts insults, abuse, and threats. He is not heavy with malice; he endures being spoken to harshly and patiently accepts insults, abuse, and threats. He is not heavy with conceit; he endures being spoken to harshly and patiently accepts insults, abuse, and threats. He is not heavy with craving; he endures being spoken to harshly and patiently accepts insults, abuse, and threats. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things contrary to the true Dhamma. Which four?

Reverence for anger, not reverence for the true Dhamma; reverence for hypocrisy, not reverence for the true Dhamma; reverence for gain, not reverence for the true Dhamma; reverence for honor, not reverence for the true Dhamma.”
These, monks, are the four things that are not the true Dhamma.
There are, monks, these four things that are the true Dhamma. Which four?

Reverence for the true Dhamma, not reverence for anger; reverence for the true Dhamma, not reverence for hypocrisy; reverence for the true Dhamma, not reverence for gain; reverence for the true Dhamma, not reverence for honor.
These, monks, are the four things that constitute the true Dhamma.
A monk who values anger and hypocrisy...
Gain, honor, and respect—
like a rotten seed in a fertile field,
these do not grow within the True Dhamma.
Those who are devoted to the true Dhamma,
who have lived and still live [in accordance with it],
they indeed cause that Dhamma to grow.
“Like medicinal herbs imbued with moisture.
The fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.45.
5. Rohitassavagga Rohitassasutta (AN 4.45, PTS AN ii 47)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, when the night had advanced, the young deva Rohitassa, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.
He stood to one side. Standing there, the young deva Rohitassa addressed the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, is it possible by traveling to know, see, or reach the end of the world—that place where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear?

“Friend, regarding that place where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear, I say that it is not possible by traveling to know, see, or reach the end of the world.”
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!
How well this has been stated by the Blessed One:
‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn—I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.’”
“Formerly, Bhante, I was a seer named Rohitassa, the son of a Bhoja, possessed of psychic power and able to travel through the air.
My speed, Bhante, was such that it was as if a skilled, well-trained archer, practiced and experienced with a light arrow, could easily shoot across the shadow of a palm tree.
My stride, Bhante, was such that it was as if from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.”
"Venerable sir, while I was endowed with such speed and such a stride, this desire arose in me:
'I shall reach the end of the world by means of traveling.
Then, venerable sir, apart from eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, and apart from the business of defecation and urination,"

Except for the removal of fatigue from sleep, though he had a lifespan of a hundred years, lived for a hundred years, and traveled for a hundred years, he passed away in the interval without having reached the end of the world.
It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
“Venerable sir, this was well-spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.
“‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.’”
"And yet, friends, I do not say that the end of suffering can be reached without reaching the end of the world.

Rather, friends, it is in this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, that I declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.
It is not to be reached by traveling."
There is no end to the world at any time;
and without reaching the end of the world,
there is no release from suffering.
Therefore, indeed, the wise one who knows the world,
having reached the end of the world and lived the holy life,
being a sage who has pacified himself, knowing the end of the world—
"One does not desire this world nor the next.
Thus [ends] the fifth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.46

5. Rohitassavagga The Second Discourse on Rohitassa (AN 4.46) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there is this path leading to the origination of the world, and there is this path leading to the cessation of the world. What, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the origination of the world? It is this: ‘I was, indeed, not, and it was not that I am not; I shall be, indeed, and it will not be that I shall not be. This, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the origination of the world. “And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the cessation of the world? It is this: ‘I was, indeed, not, and it was not that I am not; I shall be, indeed, and it will not be that I shall not be. This, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the cessation of the world. When this was said, the Venerable Rohitassa said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, as to this path leading to the origination of the world and this path leading to the cessation of the world, it is by means of this very path that I have come from the far shore to the near shore. “How is it, Rohitassa, how is it? the Blessed One asked. “Venerable sir, I was once a brahmin named Rohitassa, a master of the Three Vedas, skilled in the phonology, rituals, and etymologies, and a teacher of the hymns. I had a pupil named Rohineyya. He was diligent, energetic, and resolute. “Then, venerable sir, I said to my pupil Rohineyya: ‘Come, Rohineyya, I wish to go from the far shore to the near shore. ‘But, master, how far away is the far shore? he asked. ‘Rohineyya, the far shore is as far away as the end of the world,’ I replied. ‘Very well, master,’ he said, and he set out. “For a long time, venerable sir, Rohineyya traveled on foot, striving and making effort, until he reached a certain place. There he saw a footprint of a man. Seeing it, he thought: ‘This is surely the path by which people go from the far shore to the near shore. “He followed that path for a long time, striving and making effort, until he reached a certain place. There he saw a footprint of a cow. Seeing it, he thought: ‘This is surely the path by which people go from the far shore to the near shore. “He followed that path for a long time... until he reached a certain place. There he saw a footprint of a buffalo... a footprint of a wild ox... a footprint of a tiger... a footprint of a leopard... a footprint of a lion. Seeing it, he thought: ‘This is surely the path by which people go from the far shore to the near shore. “He followed that path for a long time, striving and making effort, until he reached a certain place. There he saw a footprint of a human being. Seeing it, he thought: ‘This is surely the path by which people go from the far shore to the near shore.

Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

"Bhikkhus, during this night, as the night was ending, the young deva Rohitassa, of surpassing beauty, having illuminated the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached me; having approached, he paid homage to me."
He stood to one side. Standing to one side, monks, the young deva Rohitassa said this to me:
“Venerable sir, where there is no birth, no aging, no death, no passing away, and no reappearing—is it possible, venerable sir, by traveling, to know, see, or reach the end of the world?
When this was said, monks, I said this to the young deva Rohitassa:

‘Where, friend, one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—to that end of the world, I say, it is not possible to go in order to know it, to see it, or to reach it.
When this was said, monks, the young deva Rohitassa said to me:
‘It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!’”
“Bhante, this was well-spoken by the Blessed One:
‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.
Bhante, in the past I was a seer named Rohitassa, the son of a Bhoja, possessed of psychic power and able to travel through the air.”
“Bhante, I possessed such speed that it was as if a skilled archer, well-trained, practiced, and experienced, with a light arrow, could effortlessly shoot across the shadow of a palm tree.
Bhante, I possessed such a stride that it was as if from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
Bhante, while I was endowed with such speed and such a stride, this kind of desire arose in me:”
‘I shall reach the end of the world by traveling.

Yet, venerable sir, having lived for a hundred years, having a lifespan of a hundred years, and having traveled for a hundred years—apart from eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; apart from the business of defecation and urination; and apart from dispelling drowsiness and fatigue—I [did not reach the end].”
"Without having reached the end of the world, he passed away along the way.
It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How well-spoken this was by the Blessed One: [that one who has abandoned the five lower fetters will not return to this world]."
“‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—there, I say, the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.
When this was said, monks, I said to the young god Rohitassa:
‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—there, I say, the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.’”
"And yet, friends, I do not say that the making an end of suffering can be achieved without reaching the end of the world.

Rather, friends, it is in this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, that I declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.
It is not to be reached by traveling."
There is no end to the world at any time;
and without reaching the end of the world,
there is no release from suffering.
Therefore, indeed, the wise one who knows the world,
having reached the end of the world and lived the holy life,
being a peaceful sage who has understood the end of the world—
“He would not desire this world nor the next.
Thus ends the sixth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.47

5. Rohitassavagga Suvidūrasutta (AN 4.47, PTS AN ii 50) “Bhikkhus, there are these four things that are very far apart. What four? The ocean is very far from the earth; the sky is very far from the earth; the world of the gods is very far from the world of humans; and Nibbāna is very far from the mind of one who is untrained. These, bhikkhus, are the four things that are very far apart.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things that are extremely remote from one another. Which four?
The sky and the earth, bhikkhus;”
This is the first instance of what is very far away.
And, monks, this near shore of the ocean and that far shore—
this is the second instance of what is very far away.
And where, monks, the sun rises and where it sets—
this is the third [pair] that is very far apart.
And the Dhamma of the virtuous, monks, and the Dhamma of the unvirtuous— [this is the fourth].
This is the fourth [thing] that is very far away.
"Monks, these indeed are the four things that are very far away:
the sky is far and the earth is far..."
They say the further shore of the ocean is far away;
yet even farther than that is where the sun rises,
the light-maker, and where he sets.
Therefore, they say that the Dhamma of the virtuous and the Dhamma of the unvirtuous are indeed far apart.
The meeting of the virtuous is never-ending.
Even if one remains [with them], it is just the same;
for the company of the wicked passes away quickly.
Therefore, the Dhamma of the virtuous is far removed from the unrighteous.
The Seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.48 5. Rohitassavagga
The Visākha Sutta (AN 4.48).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta was in the assembly hall instructing,
exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dhamma— speech that was polished, clear, flawless,
intelligible, comprehensive, and independent.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Sitting there, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, who is it that instructs and exhorts the bhikkhus in the assembly hall with a discourse on the Dhamma?"
“Does he exhort and gladden them with words that are courteous, clear, unambiguous, intelligible, comprehensive, and independent?
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta does so; he instructs the bhikkhus in the assembly hall with a discourse on the Dhamma.”
“He encourages, inspires, and gladdens [them] with speech that is polite, distinct, flawless,
intelligible, comprehensive, and independent.
Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Visākha Pañcāliputta:
“Excellent, excellent, Visākha! It is good indeed that you,
Visākha, instruct, exhort, inspire, and gladden the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk—
using speech that is polished, clear, flawless, intelligible, comprehensive, and independent.”
They do not recognize the wise man when he remains silent, mingled among fools;
yet they recognize him when he speaks.
Proclaiming the deathless state,
let him illuminate and clarify the Dhamma,
and raise high the banner of the Seers.
The sages have well-spoken words as their banner;
for the Dhamma is indeed the banner of the sages.
Thus ends the eighth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.49 5. Rohitassavagga Vipallāsasutta (The Discourse on the Perversions) “Bhikkhus, there are these four perversions of perception, perversions of mind, and perversions of view. What four? Perceiving the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view. Perceiving the suffering as happiness is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view. Perceiving the non-self as self is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view. Perceiving the unattractive as attractive is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view. These, bhikkhus, are the four perversions of perception, perversions of mind, and perversions of view.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four perversions of perception, perversions of mind, and perversions of view. What are the four? [The text continues with the specific perversions].”
Monks, to perceive the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view;
monks, to perceive suffering as happiness is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view;
monks, to perceive what is non-self as self is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
“Monks, to perceive the beautiful in the foul is a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
These, monks, are the four perversions of perception, perversions of mind, and perversions of view.
Monks, there are these four things that are not perversions of perception, not perversions of mind, and not perversions of view.”
Which four?
Monks, regarding the impermanent as impermanent: this is the non-perversion of perception, the non-perversion of mind, and the non-perversion of view.
Regarding the suffering as suffering: this is the non-perversion of perception, the non-perversion of mind, and the non-perversion of view.
“Bhikkhus, regarding what is non-self, [perceiving] ‘non-self’ is neither a perversion of perception, nor a perversion of mind, nor a perversion of view.
Regarding what is unattractive, [perceiving] ‘unattractive’ is neither a perversion of perception, nor a perversion of mind, nor a perversion of view.
These, bhikkhus, are the four that are not perversions of perception, not perversions of mind, and not perversions of view.”
Perceiving the impermanent as permanent,
perceiving suffering as happiness,
and perceiving what is non-self as self—
Perceiving the foul as beautiful,
beings are struck down by wrong view,
their minds distracted and their perceptions distorted.
Those people who are joined to Māra and have not attained security from bondage—
those beings go on in saṃsāra.
Those who go through birth and death.
But when Buddhas, the light-bringers, arise in the world;
They proclaim this Dhamma that leads to the subsiding of suffering;
having heard it from them, those possessed of wisdom—
Having regained their own minds,
they saw the impermanent as impermanent and saw suffering as suffering.
Seeing the non-self as non-self,
and the foul as foul—
by undertaking right view, [one attains peace].
"Has transcended all suffering.
Thus [ends] the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.50

5. Rohitassavagga: Upakkilesasutta (AN 4.50, PTS AN ii 53) “Bhikkhus, there are these ten imperfections of the mind. What ten? Lust is an imperfection of the mind; hatred is an imperfection of the mind; delusion is an imperfection of the mind; anger is an imperfection of the mind; hostility is an imperfection of the mind; denigration is an imperfection of the mind; insolence is an imperfection of the mind; envy is an imperfection of the mind; miserliness is an imperfection of the mind; and false view is an imperfection of the mind. These, bhikkhus, are the ten imperfections of the mind.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four defilements of the moon and the sun, by which defilements being defiled, the moon and the sun do not shine, do not glow, and do not radiate.
What are the four?
Clouds, bhikkhus, are a defilement of the moon and the sun, by which defilement being defiled, the moon and the sun do not shine, do not glow, and do not radiate.”
“Monks, mist is an obscuration of the moon and sun, by which obscuration the moon and sun are defiled and do not glow, shine, or radiate.
Smoke and dust, monks, are obscurations of the moon and sun, by which obscuration the moon and sun are defiled and do not glow, shine, or radiate.
Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, monks, is an obscuration of the moon and sun, by which obscuration the moon and sun are defiled and do not glow, shine, or radiate.”
“Monks, these are the four defilements of the moon and sun, by which defilements the moon and sun are obscured, so that they do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.

Even so, monks, there are these four defilements of some ascetics and brahmins, by which defilements some ascetics and brahmins are obscured, so that they do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.
What are the four?”
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who drink fermented liquor and spirits; they do not abstain from drinking fermented liquor and spirits.
This, bhikkhus, is the first defilement of some recluses and brahmins, by which defilement some recluses and brahmins are defiled and do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.
There are, bhikkhus, some recluses and brahmins who indulge in sexual intercourse; they do not abstain from sexual intercourse.”
This, monks, is the second defilement of some ascetics and brahmins, by which defilement some ascetics and brahmins are soiled that they do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.
There are, monks, some ascetics and brahmins who approve of gold and silver, who are not refrained from accepting gold and silver.
This, monks, is the third defilement of some ascetics and brahmins, by which defilement some ascetics and brahmins are soiled that they do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who live by wrong livelihood, not abstaining from wrong livelihood.
This, bhikkhus, is the fourth defilement of recluses and brahmins, by which some recluses and brahmins, being defiled, do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.
These, bhikkhus, are the four defilements of recluses and brahmins, by which some recluses and brahmins, being defiled, do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.”
Some recluses and brahmins, defiled by lust and hatred,
are persons shrouded in ignorance.
Delighting in pleasant forms,
they drink strong liquor and fermented spirits,
and indulge in sexual intercourse.
The ignorant accept silver and gold;
they live by wrong livelihood.
Some ascetics and brahmins [say this].
These are the defilements spoken of by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun.
Because of these defilements,
some recluses and brahmins do not glow, nor do they speak.
Impure, full of dust, like wild beasts,
shrouded in darkness,
slaves to craving, and bound by the leash.
They increase the terrible cemetery and take up further existence.
Thus ends the tenth [sutta].
The fifth chapter, the Rohitassa-vagga.
Its summary verse:
Two on the questions regarding concentration, two on anger.
Two others are Rohitassa;
with Suvidūra, Visākha, and Vipallāsa,
these ten are [reckoned] by way of the secondary defilement (upakkilesa).
The First Fifty-Section is completed.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.51.
Chapter 6: The Flood of Merit.
The First Discourse on the Overflowing of Merit (Paṭhamapuññābhisandasutta).
Setting at Sāvatthī.

“Bhikkhus, there are these four outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven, which lead to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
What are the four?
Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, while using a robe, enters upon a measureless concentration of mind...”

He dwells [thus]; for him there is an immeasurable outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness—leading to heaven, ripening as happiness, conducive to heaven—which leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
Monks, when a monk, while consuming almsfood, enters upon an immeasurable concentration of mind...

He dwells there; for him there is an immeasurable outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness—leading to heaven, having a happy result, conducive to heaven, and leading to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
Monks, when a monk, while using a lodging, enters upon an immeasurable concentration of mind...
He dwells [thus]; for him there is an immeasurable outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness, leading to heaven, having a happy result, conducive to heaven;
it leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
For that monk, monks, who is consuming medicinal requisites as support for the sick, there is an immeasurable...

He dwells having attained mental concentration; for him there is an immeasurable outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness—leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, conducive to heaven, and leading to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.

These, monks, are the four outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nourishments for happiness—leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, conducive to heaven, and leading to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
And furthermore, monks, for a noble disciple endowed with these four outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, it is not easy to grasp the measure of that merit, saying:

"So great is this outflow of merit, this outflow of the wholesome—a nourishment for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening as happiness, conducive to heaven, for what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and... [the attainment of nibbāna]."
“...it conduces to happiness. Rather, it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.
Just as, monks, it is not easy to take the measure of the water in the great ocean, saying:
“There are so many *āḷhaka* measures of water, or so many hundreds of *āḷhaka* measures of water, or so many thousands of *āḷhaka* measures of water.”
"or 'there are this many hundreds of thousands of water-measures,' but rather it is reckoned simply as an incalculable, immeasurable mass of great water;

even so, monks, for a noble disciple endowed with these four floods of merit, these four floods of the wholesome, it is not easy to grasp the measure of his merit, saying: 'This much is the flood of merit, this much is the flood of the wholesome.'"
“‘The nutriment of happiness leads to heaven, has a happy result, and conduces to heaven; it leads to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
Thus, it is reckoned as an incalculable, immeasurable, great mass of merit.
It is like the great ocean, immeasurable, a vast lake.”
Tremendously fearsome, the abode of the finest jewels;
just as many rivers frequented by throngs of people flow toward the ocean, so do they enter it.
Thus, upon the wise man who gives food,
drink, and clothing, and who is a donor of beds,
seats, and coverlets, streams of merit flow.
"Just as rivers carrying water flow into the ocean.
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.52
6. Puññābhisanda Vagga The Second Discourse on the Overflow of Merit (Dutiyapuññābhisandasutta) (AN 4.52, PTS AN ii 56)

“Monks, there are these four floods of merit, floods of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven, which lead to what is desirable, beloved, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
What are the four?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha:”

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

This, monks, is the first outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness—leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven—which leads to what is desirable, pleasing, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
Furthermore, monks, the noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma:
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves.

This, monks, is the second stream of merit, a stream of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; it leads to what is desired, beloved, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:

‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing in the right way;

the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing with propriety—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts.’
“Worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

This, monks, is the third stream of merit, a stream of the wholesome, a nutriment of happiness—leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven—that leads to what is desired, loved, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.

Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones: unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.

“Monks, this is the fourth outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a nourishment for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven; it leads to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.

Monks, these four outflows of merit, outflows of the wholesome, nourishments for happiness, leading to heaven, ripening in happiness, conducive to heaven, lead to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
For one who has faith in the Tathāgata...”
It is immovable and well-established:
the virtue of one who is noble,
beloved by the Ariyas, and praised.
He who has faith in the Saṅgha and whose vision is upright—
him they call "not poor."
His life is not in vain.
Therefore, [one should cultivate] faith and virtue,
serenity and the vision of the Dhamma.
The wise person should apply themselves,
remembering the teaching of the Buddhas. Thus ends the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.53 6.

Puññābhisanda Vagga First Discourse on Living Together “Monks, there are these four ways of living together. What four? Living together with one who is miserly, stingy, and greedy; living together with one who is immoral, of bad conduct; living together with one who is of wrong view, holding perverted views; and living together with one who is learned, of good conduct, and of right view. These, monks, are the four ways of living together.”
(AN 4.53, PTS AN ii 57) On one occasion the Blessed One was traveling along the highway between Madhurā and Verañjā.
A large number of householders and housewives were also traveling along the highway between Madhurā and Verañjā.
Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
The householders and housewives saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of that tree.

Having seen him, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One said this to those householders and housewives:
“Householders, there are these four kinds of cohabitation. Which four?
A wretch cohabits with a wretch;”
A lowly man lives with a noble woman;
a noble man lives with a lowly woman;
a noble man lives with a noble woman.
And how, householders, does a wretch live together with a wretch?

Here, householders, the husband is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence;
he is immoral, of evil character, and dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, being one who reviles and insults ascetics and brahmins.

His wife, too, is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehoods, and one who indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants that cause negligence;
she is immoral, of evil character, and dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, being abusive and insulting toward recluses and brahmins.
In this way, householders, a wretch lives together with a wretch.
And how, householders, does a wretched man live together with a celestial woman?
Here, householders, the husband is one who takes life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants that cause negligence;
he is immoral, of evil character, dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, and is one who reviles and insults ascetics and brahmins.
His wife abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence; she is virtuous, of beautiful character,
dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, and does not revile or disparage ascetics and brahmins.
In this way, householders, a wretch dwells together with a goddess.
And how, householders, does a god dwell together with a wretch?
Here, householders, the husband is one who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
He abstains from false speech, abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence;
he is virtuous, of lovely character, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, not reviling or abusing ascetics and brahmins.

Yet his wife is a killer of living beings... [and so on] ...she indulges in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence; she is immoral, of evil character, dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, and she reviles and abuses ascetics and brahmins.
In this way, householders, a deva dwells together with a female ghost.
And how, householders, does a deva dwell together with a goddess?

Here, householders, the husband abstains from taking life... [as before] ...he is virtuous, of good character, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, not reviling or disparaging ascetics and brahmins.
His wife, too, abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...abstains from fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness;
she is virtuous, of beautiful character, dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, and does not revile or abuse ascetics and brahmins.
In this way, householders, a deva dwells together with his queen.
These, householders, are the four types of co-residents:
both are immoral,
stingy, and abusive.
They become husband and wife,
wretched ones who have come together to live; the husband is of immoral conduct.
The miserly man is a reviler;
his wife, however, is virtuous,
generous, and free from stinginess.
That queen also dwells together with her husband, though he is but a corpse;
yet her husband is virtuous.
He is generous and free from stinginess,
while his wife is immoral,
miserly, and abusive.
She too dwells together with her husband, the god;
both are faithful and generous.
Self-restrained and living according to the Dhamma,
they become husband and wife who speak kindly to one another.
One's goals become abundant,
comfort arises,
and enemies become dejected.
Of those two who are equal in virtue.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
both being equal in virtue and observance;
“Nanda rejoices in the world of the gods,
delighting in whatever he desires. Thus ends the third [verse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.54 6. Puññābhisanda Vagga Second Discourse on Association “Monks, there are these four kinds of association. What four?

Association with a miserly person, monks, does not lead to one’s welfare or happiness for a long time; association with a stingy person does not lead to one’s welfare or happiness for a long time; association with a deceitful person does not lead to one’s welfare or happiness for a long time; association with a crafty person does not lead to one’s welfare or happiness for a long time. But association with a person who is generous does lead to one’s welfare and happiness for a long time; association with a person who is open-handed does lead to one’s welfare and happiness for a long time; association with a person who is honest does lead to one’s welfare and happiness for a long time; association with a person who is straightforward does lead to one’s welfare and happiness for a long time. These, monks, are the four kinds of association.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of living together. What four?
A fool dwells together with a fool;
a fool dwells together with a goddess;
a god dwells together with a fool.
A god dwells together with a goddess.
And how, monks, does a wretch dwell together with a wretch?
Here, monks, the husband is a taker of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehoods, and a speaker of divisive speech.
He is harsh in speech, a gossip, covetous, malevolent in mind, and holds wrong views.
Being immoral and of evil character, he dwells at home with a heart overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess, reviling and abusing ascetics and brahmins.
His wife, too, is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, an indulger in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehood, and one who speaks divisively.
Harsh in speech, a gossip, covetous, malevolent in heart, holding wrong views, immoral, and of evil character,
she dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, abusive and insulting toward recluses and brahmins.
In this way, monks, a wretch dwells together with a wretch.
And how, monks, does a wretch live together with his queen?

Here, monks, the husband is one who takes life... [and so on] ...is of wrong view, immoral, of evil character, dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess, and is an abuser and reviler of recluses and brahmins;
whereas his wife is one who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
They abstain from false speech, abstain from malicious speech, abstain from harsh speech, and abstain from idle chatter;

they are free from covetousness, possess a mind free from ill will, and hold right view. Being virtuous, endowed with wholesome qualities, and dwelling at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, they do not revile or disparage ascetics and brahmins.
In this way, monks, a wretch dwells together with a goddess.
And how, monks, does a god dwell together with a wretch?
Here, monks, the husband abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
He abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter;
he is free from covetousness, possesses a mind without ill will, and holds right view.
Being virtuous and of beautiful character, he dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess, not reviling or disparaging ascetics and brahmins.

His wife is a killer of living beings... [and so on] ...she holds wrong views, is immoral, of evil character, and dwells at home with a mind obsessed by the stain of stinginess; she is one who reviles and insults ascetics and brahmins.
In this way, monks, a deva dwells together with a wretched woman.
And how, monks, does a deva dwell together with a goddess?

"Here, monks, the husband abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...he has right view, is virtuous, of good character, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, not reviling or disparaging ascetics and brahmins;

his wife also abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...she has right view, is virtuous, of good character, and dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, not reviling or disparaging ascetics and brahmins.
In this way, monks, a god dwells together with a goddess."
These, monks, are the four kinds of communal living:
both are immoral,
stingy, and abusive.
They become husband and wife,
joined together in a wretched union;
the husband is one of immoral conduct.
[He is] stingy and abusive;
[but] his wife is virtuous,
generous, and free from avarice.
That queen also dwells together with her husband, though he is but a corpse;
yet her husband is virtuous.
He is generous and free from stinginess,
yet his wife is immoral,
miserly, and abusive.
She too dwells together with her husband, the god;
both are faithful and generous.
Self-restrained and living according to the Dhamma,
they become husband and wife who speak kindly to one another.
One's aims become abundant,
ease arises,
and enemies become dejected.
Of both who are equal in virtue.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
both being equal in virtue and observance;
“Nanda rejoices in the world of the gods, delighting in his desires. Thus ends the fourth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.55 6. Puññābhisanda Vagga First Discourse on the Samajīvis “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons who live the life of a *samajīvī* (one who lives according to the world). What four? Here, monks, some person who lives the life of a *samajīvī* is one who, when he sees a gift being given to others, thinks: ‘It is good that this gift is being given; it is well that this gift is being given. Having seen that gift being given, he approves of it. But when he himself is asked for something, he does not give even a little. This, monks, is the first kind of person who lives the life of a *samajīvī*. Furthermore, monks, here some person who lives the life of a *samajīvī* is one who, when he sees a gift being given to others, thinks: ‘It is good that this gift is being given; it is well that this gift is being given. Having seen that gift being given, he approves of it. And when he himself is asked for something, he gives a little. This, monks, is the second kind of person who lives the life of a *samajīvī*. Furthermore, monks, here some person who lives the life of a *samajīvī* is one who, when he sees a gift being given to others, thinks: ‘It is good that this gift is being given; it is well that this gift is being given. Having seen that gift being given, he approves of it. And when he himself is asked for something, he gives more than he receives. This, monks, is the third kind of person who lives the life of a *samajīvī*. Furthermore, monks, here some person who lives the life of a *samajīvī* is one who, when he sees a gift being given to others, thinks: ‘It is good that this gift is being given; it is well that this gift is being given. Having seen that gift being given, he approves of it. And when he himself is asked for something, he gives much more than he receives. This, monks, is the fourth kind of person who lives the life of a *samajīvī*. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons who live the life of a *samajīvī*. Of these four, monks, the latter is superior to the former.”
(AN 4.55, PTS AN ii 61) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas in the Deer Park at Bhesakalā Grove, near the village of Susumāragira.
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, went to the residence of the householder Nakulapitā. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the householder Nakulapitā and the housewife Nakulamātā approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side...
The householder Nakulapita said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, ever since Nakulamātā, the housewife, was brought to me as a young bride for a young man, I do not recall ever having transgressed against Nakulamātā, the housewife, even in thought, let alone in body.
Venerable sir, we wish to see one another in this very life, and we wish to see one another in the future life as well."
Nakulamātā, the housewife, also said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, ever since I was brought as a young girl to the young householder Nakulapitā, I do not recall ever having transgressed against the householder Nakulapitā even in thought, let alone in body.
Venerable sir, we wish to see one another in this very life, and we wish to see one another in the life to come.”
“Householders, if both husband and wife should wish to see one another in this very life and to see one another in the life to come,
and if they both possess equal faith, equal virtue, equal generosity, and equal wisdom,
then they will see one another in this very life and they will see one another in the life to come.”
Both husband and wife are endowed with faith, generous,
self-restrained, and live according to the Dhamma;
they become such a couple.
Speaking kindly to one another,
they become abundant in wealth,
and well-being arises for them.
Enemies become dejected toward those who possess equal virtue;
having practiced the Dhamma here in this world, [they attain happiness].
“Both being equal in virtue and observances,
they rejoice in the world of the gods, delighting in their desires.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.56 6.
The Chapter on the Overflow of Merit (Puññābhisanda-vagga)
The Second Discourse on Living Together (AN 4.56): “Bhikkhus,
if both husband and wife should wish to see one another in this very life, [they should live together in harmony].”
And in the future life, both may see one another, being equal in faith, equal in virtue, equal in generosity, and equal in wisdom;
they see one another both in this present life and in the future life.
Both are endowed with faith and are generous.
Self-restrained and living according to the Dhamma,
they become husband and wife who speak kindly to one another.
One's needs become abundant,
comfort arises,
and enemies become dejected.
Of those two who are equal in virtue.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
both being equal in virtue and observance;
“Nanda rejoices in the world of the gods, delighting in all that he desires.
Thus ends the sixth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.57 6. Puññābhisanda Vagga Suppavāsā Sutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, was dwelling at Icchānaṅgala, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. When he had walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his alms round, after his meal he approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, is dwelling at Icchānaṅgala, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.

It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit her out of compassion. The Blessed One consented by silence. Then the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from his alms round, after his meal he set his resting place in order, took his bowl and robe, and set out for Icchānaṅgala with a number of bhikkhus. Now at that time the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, had been lying down on a couch. Seeing the Blessed One approaching from afar, she tried to get up from her couch. The Blessed One said to her: “Enough, Suppavāsā, do not try to get up from your couch. There are seats prepared; I will sit down there. He sat down on the prepared seat. When she was seated, the Blessed One said to her: “I hope you are bearing up, Suppavāsā, I hope you are getting better. I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding, not their increase, is to be seen. “I am not bearing up, venerable sir, I am not getting better. My painful feelings are intense and increasing, not subsiding; their increase, not their subsiding, is to be seen. “Therefore, Suppavāsā, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will be intent on wholesome states, not intent on unwholesome states. It is in such a way, Suppavāsā, that you should train yourself. “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Therefore, Suppavāsā, you should train yourself thus: “I will be intent on wholesome states, not intent on unwholesome states. “Suppavāsā, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on unwholesome states, not intent on wholesome states; the person who is intent on wholesome states, not intent on unwholesome states; the person who is neither intent on wholesome states nor intent on unwholesome states; and the person who is intent on wholesome states and intent on wholesome states. These are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Blessed One then explained each of these types in detail. “Suppavāsā, when a person is intent on unwholesome states and not intent on wholesome states, what kind of result does he experience? He experiences a result that is harmful and unwholesome. When a person is intent on wholesome states and not intent on unwholesome states, what kind of result does he experience? He experiences a result that is beneficial and wholesome. When a person is neither intent on wholesome states nor intent on unwholesome states, what kind of result does he experience? He experiences a result that is indeterminate. When a person is intent on wholesome states and intent on wholesome states, what kind of result does he experience? He experiences a result that is exceedingly beneficial and wholesome. [The Blessed One then spoke further on the benefits of giving, the fruits of generosity, and the rewards of meritorious deeds. When the Blessed One had instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, with a talk on the Dhamma, he rose from his seat and departed. Then the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, followed the Blessed One from behind, crying out: “Wait, Blessed One! Wait, Fortunate One! The Blessed One stopped. The nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I give this child, my son, to the Blessed One as a novice monk. The Blessed One accepted the child. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let the child be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The Venerable Ānanda had the child given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let the child be given to the Order of bhikkhunīs. The Venerable Ānanda had the child given to the Order of bhikkhunīs. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let the child be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. The Venerable Ānanda had the child given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let the child be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, and male lay followers. The Venerable Ānanda had the child given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, and male lay followers. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let the child be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers. The Venerable Ānanda had the child given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let the child be given to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers, and let him be named ‘Saṅghadatta. The Venerable Ānanda gave the child to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers, and he was named ‘Saṅghadatta. Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with a talk on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter, has given this child, her son, to the Blessed One as a novice monk. She has given him to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, to the Order of bhikkhunīs, to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, and male lay followers, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers;

and he has been named ‘Saṅghadatta. “It is wonderful, Ānanda! It is amazing, Ānanda! How well this has been stated by the nun Suppavāsā, the Koliyan daughter: ‘I give this child, my son, to the Blessed One as a novice monk. For, Ānanda, by giving a child as a novice monk to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers, one acquires great merit, great fruit, great advantage, and great splendor. [The Blessed One then spoke further on the various merits of giving, including gifts of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, bedding, dwellings, and lamps. “Ānanda, suppose a woman or a man were to fill this Jambudīpa with the seven treasures and give it as a gift to the Tathāgata or to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus
(AN 4.57, PTS AN ii 62) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Koliyans at a town of the Koliyans named Pajjanika.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of Suppavāsā, the daughter of the Koliyans. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter, with her own hands, satisfied and served the Blessed One with excellent hard and soft foods.
When the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter sat down to one side.
As she was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter:
“Suppavāsā, when a noble female disciple gives food, she gives four things to those who receive it.
What are the four?
She gives life, she gives beauty, she gives happiness, and she gives strength.”
Moreover, by giving life, one becomes a partaker of life, whether divine or human;
by giving beauty, one becomes a partaker of beauty, whether divine or human;
by giving happiness, one becomes a partaker of happiness, whether divine or human.
By giving strength, she becomes a partaker of strength, whether divine or human.
Suppavāsā, when a noble female disciple gives food, she gives these four things to the recipients.
She who gives well-prepared food—
Pure, excellent, and endowed with the finest flavors—
such an offering, when given to those who have attained uprightness,
who are endowed with noble conduct, and who are magnanimous, [yields great fruit].
When merit flows together with merit,
it is praised by the knowers of the world as yielding great fruit.
Recalling such a sacrifice, [they attain the heavenly world].
Those born of the Vedas who wander in the world,
having eradicated the stain of stinginess along with its root,
blameless, they go to the heavenly state.
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.58.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [paid homage to] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, when a noble disciple gives food, he gives four things to those who receive it.
What are the four?”
It gives life, it gives beauty, it gives happiness, and it gives strength.
Having given life, one partakes of life, whether divine or human.
Having given beauty... having given happiness... having given strength, one partakes of strength, whether divine or human.
“Householder, when a noble disciple gives food, he gives these four things to those who receive it:
‘He who gives food at the proper time and with respect to those who are self-restrained and live on what is given by others;’”
He bestows four things:
longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength.
He is a giver of longevity, a giver of beauty.
The person who gives happiness and strength becomes long-lived and renowned wherever they are reborn.

The Discourse on Food (Bhojanasutta): “Monks,
when a donor gives food, he gives four things to the recipients.”
Which four?
He gives long life, he gives beauty, he gives happiness, and he gives strength.
And having given long life, he partakes of long life, whether divine or human.
"By giving beauty... by giving happiness... by giving strength, one becomes a partaker of strength, whether divine or human.
Monks, when a donor gives food, he gives these four things to the recipients.
To those who are self-restrained and live on what is given by others..."
One who gives food respectfully at the proper time bestows four things:
longevity, beauty, happiness, and strength.
Thus, the person who gives life, who gives beauty,
and who bestows happiness and strength,
becomes long-lived and renowned.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Householder, a noble disciple endowed with four qualities is practicing the way of a householder’s duty, which brings about the acquisition of fame and leads to heaven."
Which four?
Here, householder, a noble disciple attends upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes;
he attends upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with almsfood; he attends upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with lodgings; he attends upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus...
He is provided with medicinal requisites for use in sickness.
Householder, a noble disciple endowed with these four qualities has entered upon the way of conduct befitting a householder, which leads to the acquisition of fame and conduces to heaven.
This is the way of conduct befitting a householder.
The wise practice accordingly;
they serve with robes those who have entered the right path and possess virtue.
With alms-food, lodging, and requisites for the sick—
for them, by day and by night—
Merit always increases;
having performed auspicious kamma, one goes to the heavenly realm, the place of stability.
The tenth.

two co-residences and a shared livelihood;
Suppavāsā and Sudatta.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [approached] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, there are these four things that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
Which four?”
"May wealth accrue to me in accordance with the Dhamma"—this is the first quality that is desirable, lovely, dear, and rare in the world.
"Having obtained wealth in accordance with the Dhamma, may fame come to me along with my kinsmen and preceptors"—this is the second quality that is desirable, lovely, dear, and rare in the world.

"Having obtained wealth in accordance with the Dhamma and having obtained fame along with my kinsmen and preceptors, may I live long and enjoy a long lifespan"—this is the third quality that is desirable, lovely, dear, and rare in the world.
"Having obtained wealth through righteous means, having obtained fame together with my kinsmen and preceptors, having lived long and maintained a full lifespan,
at the breaking up of the body after death, may I be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world"—
this is the fourth quality that is desirable, lovely, dear, and rare in the world.
"These four things, householder, are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
Householder, there are four things that lead to the acquisition of these four things which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
Which four?"
Perfection of faith, perfection of virtue, perfection of generosity, and perfection of wisdom.
And what, householder, is the perfection of faith?
Here, householder, the noble disciple is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with clear vision and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
This, householder, is called accomplishment in faith.
And what, householder, is accomplishment in virtue?
"Here, householder, a noble disciple abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...he abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
This, householder, is called accomplishment in virtue.
And what, householder, is accomplishment in generosity?"
"Here, householder, a noble disciple dwells at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess, open-handed, pure in hand, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to giving, and fond of sharing.
This, householder, is called the perfection of generosity.
And what, householder, is the perfection of wisdom?"
“Householder, one who dwells with a mind overcome by covetousness and improper greed does what should not be done and neglects what should be done.
By doing what should not be done and neglecting what should be done, one falls away from fame and happiness.
One who dwells with a mind overcome by ill will, householder, does what should not be done and neglects what should be done.”
One who does what should not be done and neglects what should be done falls away from fame and happiness.
Living with a mind overcome by sloth and torpor, householder, one does what should not be done and neglects what should be done.
Doing what should not be done and neglecting what should be done, one falls away from fame and happiness.
“Householder, one who dwells with a mind overcome by restlessness and remorse does what should not be done and neglects what should be done.
By doing what should not be done and neglecting what should be done, one falls away from fame and happiness.
Householder, one who dwells with a mind overcome by doubt does what should not be done and neglects what should be done.”
By doing what should not be done and neglecting what should be done, one falls away from fame and happiness.
Householder, that noble disciple, having understood that covetousness and improper greed are an imperfection of the mind, abandons covetousness and improper greed as an imperfection of the mind.
Having understood that ill will is an imperfection of the mind, he abandons ill will as an imperfection of the mind.
"Torpor and drowsiness are a defilement of the mind"—having understood this, he abandons torpor and drowsiness as a defilement of the mind.
"Restlessness and remorse are a defilement of the mind"—having understood this, he abandons restlessness and remorse as a defilement of the mind.
"Doubt is a defilement of the mind"—having understood this, he abandons doubt as a defilement of the mind.

But when, householder, a noble disciple has understood that covetousness and improper greed are an affliction of the mind, and having understood this, covetousness and improper greed as an affliction of the mind have been abandoned.
Having understood that ill will is an affliction of the mind, and having understood this, ill will as an affliction of the mind has been abandoned.
Having understood that sloth and torpor are an affliction of the mind, and having understood this, sloth and torpor as an affliction of the mind have been abandoned.
"Restlessness and remorse are a defilement of the mind"—having understood this, restlessness and remorse as a defilement of the mind are abandoned.
"Doubt is a defilement of the mind"—having understood this, doubt as a defilement of the mind is abandoned.
This, householder, is called a noble disciple of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, one who sees at once, one endowed with wisdom.
This, householder, is called the perfection of wisdom.
Householder, these four things—which are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world—lead to the acquisition of those four things.

Furthermore, householder, that noble disciple, with wealth acquired through exertion and energy, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, and righteously obtained, performs the four appropriate deeds.
Which four?

Here, householder, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow—righteous wealth, righteously gained—the noble disciple makes himself happy and pleased, and maintains himself in comfort.
He makes his mother and father happy and pleased, and maintains them in comfort.
He comforts, satisfies, and properly provides for the well-being of his wives, children, slaves, laborers, and servants.
He comforts, satisfies, and properly provides for the well-being of his friends and colleagues.
This is the first instance of his wealth that has come into his possession and been acquired, which he enjoys according to its proper sphere.
Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired by energetic striving,
amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow— righteous wealth, lawfully obtained— the noble disciple is able to weather such calamities as those arising from fire,
water, kings, thieves, or unloved heirs. Thus he conduces to the clearing away of such misfortunes.
He makes himself secure.
This is his second instance of what has been acquired, attained, and used according to its proper application.

Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired through exertion and energy, gathered by the strength of his own arms, earned through sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained, the noble disciple performs the fivefold offering:
The offering to relatives, the offering to guests, the offering to the departed ancestors, the offering to kings, and the offering to deities.
This is his third instance of what has been acquired, obtained, and consumed from its source.
Furthermore, householder, with wealth acquired through initiative and energy, gathered by the strength of one’s own arms...

With wealth that is free from the stain of greed, righteous, and rightfully obtained, one establishes an elevated offering among those ascetics and brahmins who abstain from intoxication and negligence,
who are established in patience and gentleness, and who tame themselves alone, calm themselves alone, and bring themselves alone to final Nibbāna;
such an offering is conducive to heaven, has a pleasant result, and leads to rebirth in the celestial realms.
