This is his fourth instance where [wealth] has reached its destination, been acquired, and been utilized through a proper sphere of application.

Householder, that noble disciple, with wealth acquired through exertion and vigor, gathered by the strength of his own arms, shed with sweat, righteous, and righteously obtained, performs these four appropriate deeds.

Householder, whatever wealth of anyone else comes to exhaustion apart from these four appropriate deeds is called, householder, wealth that has not reached its destination, has not been acquired, and has not been utilized through a proper sphere of application.

“Householder, when anyone’s wealth comes to exhaustion through these four appropriate uses of wealth, it is said, householder, that those riches have reached their destination, reached their proper end, and have been enjoyed according to their scope:
‘My riches have been enjoyed, my dependents have been supported,
and I have overcome calamities.’”
Generous offerings were given with uplifted hearts,
and the five-fold bali-oblation was performed;
those possessed of virtue were attended upon.
Restrained in their practice of the holy life,
whatever purpose for wealth a wise person living at home might desire—
Thus my purpose has been attained;
what was to be done has been done without regret.
Remembering this, a mortal—
The person established in the noble Dhamma is praised even here in this world,
and after passing away, he rejoices in heaven.
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.62 7.
The Chapter on Appropriate Deeds (Pattakamma-vagga)
The Discourse on Freedom from Debt (Ānaṇyasutta).
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [paid homage to] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Householder, there are these four kinds of happiness to be attained by a layperson enjoying sensual pleasures, from time to time and according to circumstances.
What are the four?
The happiness of possession, the happiness of enjoyment, the happiness of debtlessness, and the happiness of blamelessness.
And what, householder, is the happiness of possession?
Here, householder, a clansman possesses wealth acquired by initiative and energy, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, and righteously obtained.

Thus, thinking, "I have wealth acquired through initiative and energy, amassed by the strength of my arms, born of sweat, righteous, and righteously gained," he attains happiness and attains gladness.
This, householder, is called the happiness of possession.
And what, householder, is the happiness of enjoyment?

In this case, householder, a clansman enjoys wealth acquired through initiative and energy, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, and gained in accordance with the Dhamma; he performs meritorious deeds.

Thinking, "I enjoy wealth acquired through initiative and energy, amassed by the strength of my arms, earned by the sweat of my brow, righteous, and gained in accordance with the Dhamma, and I perform meritorious deeds," he attains happiness and attains joy.
This, householder, is called the happiness of wealth.
And what, householder, is the happiness of debtlessness?
Here, householder, a clansman owes nothing to anyone, whether little or much.
Thinking, "I owe nothing to anyone, whether little or much," he attains happiness and attains joy.
This, householder, is called the happiness of debtlessness.
And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness?
Here, householder, a noble disciple is endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, and endowed with blameless mental action.
Thus, thinking, "I am endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, and endowed with blameless mental action," one attains happiness and attains gladness.
This, householder, is called the happiness of blamelessness.
These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness to be attained by a layperson enjoying sensual pleasures, from time to time and according to occasion.
Having known the happiness of debtlessness and the supreme happiness of possession,
a mortal may enjoy the happiness of wealth.
Then wisdom sees clearly.
Seeing clearly, the wise one knows both kinds of wealth.
"This does not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of blamelessness. Thus ends the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.63 7. The Chapter on Worthy Deeds The Discourse on Brahmā "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? "The person who dwells in the company of Brahmā; the person who dwells in the company of those who have reached the Brahma-faring; the person who dwells in the company of those who have entered upon the way; and the person who dwells in the company of those who have entered upon the way and attained the fruit. "And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell in the company of Brahmā? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, he places faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is worthy and rightly self-awakened, consummate in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, an expert in the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is called a person who dwells in the company of Brahmā. "And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell in the company of those who have reached the Brahma-faring? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults. Having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is called a person who dwells in the company of those who have reached the Brahma-faring. "And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell in the company of those who have entered upon the way? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has developed the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he has developed the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he has developed the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he has developed the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. This is called a person who dwells in the company of those who have entered upon the way. "And how, bhikkhus, does a person dwell in the company of those who have entered upon the way and attained the fruit? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has realized the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arahantship. This is called a person who dwells in the company of those who have entered upon the way and attained the fruit. "These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."
“Bhikkhus, those families in whose homes mother and father are honored by their children are as if they were accompanied by Brahmā. Bhikkhus,
those families in whose homes mother and father are honored by their children are as if they were accompanied by their original teachers.”
"Bhikkhus, those families have the devas as their forerunners in whose home mother and father are honored by their children.

Bhikkhus, those families are worthy of gifts from the world, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, and worthy of reverential salutation—in whose home mother and father are honored by their children.
For 'Brahmā,' bhikkhus, is a designation for mother and father."
“‘Former teachers,’ monks, is a designation for mother and father.
‘Former deities,’ monks, is a designation for mother and father.
‘Those worthy of offerings,’ monks, is a designation for mother and father.”
And why is that? Because, monks, parents are of great service to their children; they are their nurturers, their sustainers, and those who show them this world.
Parents are called "Brahmā."
They are called the ancient teachers;
they are worthy of offerings and are compassionate toward their children and offspring.
Therefore, a wise person should indeed honor and revere them with food and drink.
With clothing and with bedding;
with anointing and bathing,
and with the washing of the feet.
By such service toward their mother and father,
the wise are praised right here in this very world.
“Having passed away, one rejoices in heaven.
Thus ends the third [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.64.

7. Pattakamma-vagga Niraya-sutta (AN 4.64, PTS AN ii 71) “Monks, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who has done what leads to hell; the person who has done what leads to heaven; the person who has done what leads to Nibbāna; the person who has done both what leads to hell and what leads to heaven; and the person who has done neither what leads to hell nor what leads to heaven. And how, monks, is one a person who has done what leads to hell? Here, monks, someone is possessed of immoral conduct in body, speech, and mind. This, monks, is called a person who has done what leads to hell. And how, monks, is one a person who has done what leads to heaven? Here, monks, someone is possessed of moral conduct in body, speech, and mind. This, monks, is called a person who has done what leads to heaven. And how, monks, is one a person who has done what leads to Nibbāna? Here, monks, someone is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as their destination. This, monks, is called a person who has done what leads to Nibbāna. And how, monks, is one a person who has done both what leads to hell and what leads to heaven? Here, monks, someone is a once-returner who, having returned to this world once more, will make an end of suffering. This, monks, is called a person who has done both what leads to hell and what leads to heaven. And how, monks, is one a person who has done neither what leads to hell nor what leads to heaven? Here, monks, someone is a non-returner who, having passed away from this world, will attain final Nibbāna in the realm of the devas. This, monks, is called a person who has done neither what leads to hell nor what leads to heaven. These, monks, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.
What are the four?
One is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, and one who speaks falsehood.”
“Monks, one who is possessed of these four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.
They are: the taking of life, the taking of what is not given, and what is called false speech.”
“Going to another’s wife as well,
the wise do not praise.
The fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.65 7. The Chapter on Appropriate Action (Pattakamma-vagga) The Discourse on Form (Rūpa-sutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent upon form, devoted to form, bound by form, and infatuated with form; the person who is intent upon feeling, devoted to feeling, bound by feeling, and infatuated with feeling; the person who is intent upon perception, devoted to perception, bound by perception, and infatuated with perception; the person who is intent upon volitional formations, devoted to volitional formations, bound by volitional formations, and infatuated with volitional formations. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four? [The text continues with the description of each.]”
One who takes form as the measure and has faith in form; one who takes sound as the measure and has faith in sound; one who takes coarseness as the measure and has faith in coarseness;
and one who takes the Dhamma as the measure and has faith in the Dhamma. These, monks, are the four persons found existing in the world.
And those who have taken form as the measure...
And those people who have followed after mere sound,
possessed as they are by desire and lust, do not understand.
One who does not know within and does not see without is a fool,
obstructed on all sides.
He is indeed carried away by sound;
he does not know within,
yet he looks outward with insight.
One who sees external fruits is also carried away by sound;
yet one understands within.
And he sees outwardly;
seeing with an unobstructed vision,
he is not carried away by mere report.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.66 7.
The Chapter on Appropriate Action (Pattakamma-vagga)
Sarāgasutta: “Bhikkhus,
these four persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four? One who is lustful, one who is hateful, one who is deluded,
and one who is conceited— these, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.
Attached to things that cause passion,
delighting in forms that are dear,
beings are shrouded by delusion.
Those who are ignorant increase their bondage—
bondage born of lust, born of hatred,
and born of delusion.
Performing unwholesome karma,
which is fraught with distress and results in suffering—
people shrouded in ignorance, [act thus].
Blinded and sightless;
though things remain as they are,
they do not conceive themselves as such.
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.67 7.
The Chapter on Worthy Deeds (Pattakamma-vagga)
The Discourse to the King of Snakes (Ahirājasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain monk in Sāvatthī had been bitten by a snake and passed away.

Then a number of monks approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, here in Sāvatthī, a certain monk has been bitten by a snake and has passed away."
“Indeed, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu must not have suffused the four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness.

For if, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu had suffused the four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness, he would not have died from being bitten by a snake. Which four? [The four royal families of snakes.]”
The royal family of Virūpakkha, the royal family of Erāpatha, the royal family of Chabyāputta, and the royal family of Kaṇhāgotamaka.
Surely, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu did not pervade these four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness.
For if, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu had pervaded these four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness, he would certainly not have died from being bitten by a snake.
"I allow you, monks, to pervade these four royal families of nāgas with a mind of loving-kindness for your own protection, your own preservation, and your own safeguarding:
'May there be loving-kindness from the Virūpakkhas toward me;
may there be loving-kindness from the Erāpathas toward me.'"
I have loving-kindness for the Chabyāputtas,
and loving-kindness for the Kaṇhāgotamakas;
I have loving-kindness for those who are footless.
May there be loving-kindness toward my two-footed beings;
may there be loving-kindness toward my four-footed beings,
and loving-kindness toward my many-footed beings.
Let not the footless harm me,
let not the two-footed harm me;
let not the four-footed harm me.
May no many-footed creature harm me.
May all beings, all living things,
and all creatures whatsoever—
May all behold auspicious things;
may no evil come to anyone.
Boundless is the Buddha.
The Dharma is immeasurable;
the Saṅgha is immeasurable;
creeping reptiles are finite.
The snake, the scorpion, the centipede,
the spider, the sarabū, and the rat—
protection has been made for me, a safeguard has been made for me.
May the spirits depart!
I pay homage to the Blessed One;
homage to the seven perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
The Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.68 7.
The Chapter on Appropriate Action (Pattakamma-vagga)
The Discourse to Devadatta (Devadattasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed.
There, concerning Devadatta, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"For his own destruction, bhikkhus, did gain, honor, and fame arise for Devadatta.
For his ruin, bhikkhus, did gain, honor, and fame arise for Devadatta."
“Just as, monks, the plantain tree bears fruit for its own destruction and bears fruit for its ruin;
even so, monks, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction and arose for his ruin.
Just as, monks, the bamboo bears fruit for its own destruction and bears fruit for its ruin;”
In the same way, monks, Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his own destruction; Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his ruin.

Just as a reed gives fruit for its own destruction and gives fruit for its ruin, even so, monks, Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his own destruction; Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his ruin.
"Just as, monks, a mule conceives for her own destruction, conceives for her own ruin;
even so, monks, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own ruin.
Indeed, the fruit destroys the plantain tree."
Fruit destroys the bamboo, fruit destroys the reed;
honor kills the base man,
just as the fetus destroys the mule.
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.69 7.
The Chapter on Worthy Deeds (Pattakamma-vagga)
The Discourse on Exertion (Padhānasutta):
“Monks, there are these four exertions.”
Which four?
The effort of restraint, the effort of abandoning, the effort of development, and the effort of protection.
And what, monks, is the effort of restraint?
"Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states.
This, monks, is called the striving of restraint.
And what, monks, is the striving of abandonment?"
"Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen.
This, monks, is called the striving for abandoning.
And what, monks, is the striving for development?"
"Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen.
This, monks, is called the effort of development.
And what, monks, is the effort of preservation?"

"Here, monks, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the stability, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen.
This, monks, is called the effort of preservation."
"These, monks, are the four strivings:
restraint, abandoning,
development, and protection."
These are the four exertions taught by the Kinsman of the Sun;
for whatever bhikkhu here is ardent,
“May one reach the destruction of suffering.
Thus [ends] the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.70

7. Pattakamma-vagga: Adhammika-sutta (AN 4.70, PTS AN ii 74) “Monks, there are these five kinds of persons who are unrighteous. What five? Here, monks, some person is unrighteous in body, unrighteous in speech, and unrighteous in mind. This is the first kind of person who is unrighteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is unrighteous in body and unrighteous in speech, but righteous in mind. This is the second kind of person who is unrighteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is unrighteous in body and unrighteous in mind, but righteous in speech. This is the third kind of person who is unrighteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is unrighteous in speech and unrighteous in mind, but righteous in body. This is the fourth kind of person who is unrighteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is righteous in body, righteous in speech, and righteous in mind. Yet, he dwells with a mind that is not fully liberated from the underlying tendencies toward lust, hatred, and delusion. This is the fifth kind of person who is unrighteous. These, monks, are the five kinds of persons who are unrighteous. There are, however, monks, these five kinds of persons who are righteous. What five? Here, monks, some person is righteous in body, righteous in speech, and righteous in mind. This is the first kind of person who is righteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is righteous in body and righteous in speech, but unrighteous in mind. This is the second kind of person who is righteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is righteous in body and righteous in mind, but unrighteous in speech. This is the third kind of person who is righteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is righteous in speech and righteous in mind, but unrighteous in body. This is the fourth kind of person who is righteous. Furthermore, monks, some person is righteous in body, righteous in speech, and righteous in mind. And he dwells with a mind that is fully liberated from the underlying tendencies toward lust, hatred, and delusion. This is the fifth kind of person who is righteous. These, monks, are the five kinds of persons who are righteous.”
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion kings are unrighteous, on that occasion the king’s officials are also unrighteous.
When the king’s officials are unrighteous, on that occasion the brahmins and householders are also unrighteous.
When the brahmins and householders are unrighteous, on that occasion the people of the towns and countryside are also unrighteous.”
When the merchants and the people are unrighteous, the moon and sun move irregularly.
When the moon and sun move irregularly, the lunar mansions and the forms of the stars move irregularly.
When the lunar mansions and the forms of the stars move irregularly, night and day move irregularly.
When nights and days turn irregularly, months and fortnights turn irregularly.
When months and fortnights turn irregularly, seasons and years turn irregularly.
When seasons and years turn irregularly, winds blow irregularly and inauspiciously.
When the winds blow irregularly and the quarters are unsettled, the deities become agitated.
When the deities are agitated, the rain-god does not release his showers properly.
When the rain-god does not release his showers properly, the crops ripen unevenly.
“Monks, when people consume crops that ripen unevenly, they become short-lived, ugly, and afflicted with many ailments.
Monks, at whatever time kings are righteous, those appointed by the king are also righteous at that time.
When those appointed by the king are righteous, the brahmins and householders are also righteous at that time.”
When the brahmins and householders are righteous, at that time the people of the towns and the countryside are also righteous.
When the people of the towns and the countryside are righteous, the moon and sun move in their proper courses.
When the moon and sun move in their proper courses, the constellations and the forms of the stars move in their proper courses.
As the constellations and the forms of the stars revolve evenly, nights and days revolve evenly.
As nights and days revolve evenly, months and fortnights revolve evenly.
As months and fortnights revolve evenly, seasons and years revolve evenly.
When the seasons and the years revolve evenly, the winds blow evenly and clearly.
When the winds blow evenly and the clear-weather days are even, the deities remain unprovoked.
When the deities are unprovoked, the rain-god pours down rain properly.
"When rain falls in due measure, the crops ripen evenly.
When people consume crops that have ripened evenly, monks, they become long-lived, beautiful, strong, and free from illness.
If cattle are crossing in haste...
When the leader goes crookedly,
they all go crookedly,
since the guide has gone crookedly.
In the same way, among human beings,
if he who is considered the best practices unrighteousness,
How much more so the rest of the people;
the entire kingdom lies in suffering if the king is unrighteous.
If, among those who are hurrying along,
the leader goes straight,
they all go straight.
When one has gone straight and upright—
just so it is among human beings,
regarding him who is considered the best.
Thus, if the king practices the Dhamma,
how much more so the rest of his people;
the entire kingdom dwells in happiness.
“And if the king is righteous.
Tenth. The second chapter on “Appropriate Action” is finished.
Its summary verse:
The one who has done the deed,
the debtless one, The Brahmin, Niraya, and the fifth is Rūpa.
King Devadatta was full of lust;
he practiced striving in an unrighteous manner.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.71)

8. Apaṇṇakavagga Padhānasutta (AN 4.71, PTS AN ii 76) “Monks, there are these four right endeavors. What four? Here, monks, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. He generates desire for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states, for their non-decline, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development; he makes an effort, exerts his mind, and applies his energy. These, monks, are the four right endeavors.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a bhikkhu has entered upon the way that is unmistakable and has laid the foundation for the destruction of the taints.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he is learned; he is energetic; and he is wise.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses these four qualities has entered upon the unerring way and has laid a foundation for the destruction of the taints.
Thus was the first [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.72

8. Apaṇṇakavagga Sammādiṭṭhisutta (AN 4.72, PTS AN ii 76) “Bhikkhus, there is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. What is that one thing? Right view. This, bhikkhus, is that one thing which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a bhikkhu has entered upon the way that is unmistakable, and the basis for the destruction of the taints has been initiated in him.
What are the four? They are:
thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, thoughts of non-cruelty, and right view.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses these four qualities has entered upon the unmistakable way and has laid a foundation for the destruction of the taints.
The second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.73

8. Apaṇṇakavagga Sappurisasutta (AN 4.73, PTS AN ii 77) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a rotten seed; the person who is like a withered leaf; the person who is like a person who has been struck by lightning; and the person who is like a good person. And how, monks, is one a person like a rotten seed? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, bamboo workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or waste-removers—one that is poor, destitute, and lacking in sustenance, where food and clothing are obtained with great difficulty. And he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he is weak, sickly, and often ill; and he does not live long. This, monks, is called a person like a rotten seed. And how, monks, is one a person like a withered leaf? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family—a family of aristocrats, brahmins, or householders—one that is rich, with great wealth and many possessions, abundant in gold and silver, with vast stores of money and property, and with many fields and lands. But he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he is weak, sickly, and often ill; and he does not live long. This, monks, is called a person like a withered leaf. And how, monks, is one a person like a person who has been struck by lightning? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family—a family of aristocrats, brahmins, or householders—one that is rich, with great wealth and many possessions, abundant in gold and silver, with vast stores of money and property, and with many fields and lands. And he is handsome, attractive, and fair to look upon; he is strong, healthy, and rarely ill; and he lives long. Yet, having fallen from his own home, he goes forth into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, possessing the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life. But he does not realize, as it really is, ‘This is suffering’; he does not realize, as it really is, ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he does not realize, as it really is, ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not realize, as it really is, ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He does not realize, as it really is, ‘These are the taints’; he does not realize, as it really is, ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he does not realize, as it really is, ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he does not realize, as it really is, ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. He does not, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which is without clinging and is free from fermentation. This, monks, is called a person like a person who has been struck by lightning. And how, monks, is one a person like a good person? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family—a family of aristocrats, brahmins, or householders—one that is rich, with great wealth and many possessions, abundant in gold and silver, with vast stores of money and property, and with many fields and lands. And he is handsome, attractive, and fair to look upon; he is strong, healthy, and rarely ill; and he lives long. Having fallen from his own home, he goes forth into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells detached from sensual pleasures, detached from unwholesome states, possessing the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life. And he realizes, as it really is, ‘This is suffering’; he realizes, as it really is, ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he realizes, as it really is, ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he realizes, as it really is, ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He realizes, as it really is, ‘These are the taints’; he realizes, as it really is, ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he realizes, as it really is, ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he realizes, as it really is, ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. He, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters upon and abides in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which is without clinging and is free from fermentation. This, monks, is called a person like a good person. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses four qualities is to be known as a person of no integrity. Which four?
Here, bhikkhus, a person of no integrity reveals the dispraise of another even when unasked, let alone when asked.”
Furthermore, when questioned and pressed with a question, he speaks of another’s faults in full detail, without omission or reservation.
Monks, it should be understood that this person is an untrue man.
Moreover, monks, an untrue man does not even acknowledge another’s praise when asked about it, let alone when unasked.
Furthermore, when questioned and pressed with a question, he speaks of another’s praise in a way that is deficient, faltering, incomplete, and not detailed.
Monks, it should be understood: "This person is an untrue man.
Moreover, monks, an untrue man does not even reveal his own dispraise when asked, let alone when unasked.
Furthermore, when questioned and pressed with a question, he speaks of his own dispraise in a way that is incomplete, deficient, and lacking in detail.
Monks, it should be understood that this person is an untrue man.
Moreover, monks, an untrue man makes his own dispraise manifest even when unasked, let alone when asked.
Furthermore, when questioned and pressed with a question, he speaks of his own excellence fully and in detail, without omitting anything or holding back.
Monks, it should be understood that this person is an untrue man (*asappurisa*).
Monks, by these four qualities one should recognize an untrue man.
“Bhikkhus, a true person is to be recognized by four qualities.
By which four?
Here, bhikkhus, when a true person hears disparagement of another, he does not reveal it even when asked, let alone when unasked.”
Furthermore, when questioned and pressed with a question, he speaks of another’s dispraise in an incomplete and unelaborated manner, omitting and leaving out [details].
Monks, it should be understood: “This one is a true person.
Moreover, monks, a true person reveals the praise of another even when not asked, let alone when asked.
Furthermore, when questioned and led by a question, he speaks of another’s praise in its full extent and detail, without omitting anything or holding back.
Monks, it should be understood that this person is a true man.
Moreover, monks, a true man reveals his own dispraise even when unasked, let alone when asked.
Furthermore, when questioned and pressed with a question, he speaks of his own faults fully and in detail, without omitting or withholding anything.
Monks, it should be understood that this person is a true man.
Moreover, monks, a true man does not even reveal his own virtues when asked, let alone when unasked.
But when questioned and pressed with a question, he speaks of his own excellence in a way that is deficient, faltering, and not fully detailed.
Monks, it should be understood: "This one is a true person.
Monks, by these four qualities is a true person to be known.
“Just as, monks, when a bride is brought home, whether by night or by day,
at that very moment a keen sense of shame and dread of blame arises in her toward her mother-in-law, her father-in-law, and her husband, and even toward the slaves,
laborers, and servants; yet after some time, through living together and becoming familiar, she speaks thus to her mother-in-law, her father-in-law, and her husband:”
"Go away! What do you know?

In the same way, monks, here a certain monk, from the very moment he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness—whether by night or by day—intense shame and dread of wrongdoing are established within him toward the monks.

Toward the bhikkhunīs, the male lay followers, the female lay followers, and even toward the monastery attendants and novice monks—after some time, through living together and through intimacy—he says this even to his teacher or preceptor:
"Go away! What do you know?"
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
'We shall dwell with a mind like that of a newly arrived bride.
It is in this way, monks, that you should train yourselves."
The Third [Sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.74.
8. The Chapter on the Infallible (Apaṇṇakavagga).
Paṭhamaaggasutta (AN 4.74,
PTS AN ii 79): “Bhikkhus,
there are these four foremost things.
Which four? The summit of virtue, the summit of concentration, the summit of wisdom,
and the summit of liberation— these, monks, are the four summits.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.75 8. The Chapter on the Incontrovertible (Apaṇṇakavagga)
The Second Discourse on the Foremost (Dutiya-aggasutta). “Bhikkhus,
there are these four foremost things.
Which four? The peak of form, the peak of feeling, the peak of perception,
and the peak of existence— these, monks, are the four peaks.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.76 8.
The Chapter on the Infallible (Apaṇṇakavagga)
The Kusināra Discourse (AN 4.76).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusinārā in the Upavattana, the sal-tree grove of the Mallas, between the twin sal trees, at the time of his final nibbāna.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“It may be, monks, that even a single monk has doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice. Ask, monks; do not later feel regret, saying:
‘The Teacher was present before us, yet we were unable to question the Blessed One in his presence.’”
When this was said, those bhikkhus became silent.
A second time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“It may be, bhikkhus, that even a single bhikkhu has doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice. Ask, bhikkhus; do not later have cause for regret.”
"Our Teacher was present before us, yet we were not able to question the Blessed One in his presence.
A second time, those bhikkhus remained silent.
A third time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, it may be that even a single bhikkhu has doubt or uncertainty regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice. Ask, bhikkhus; do not later feel regret, thinking:
‘The Teacher was present before us, yet we were unable to question the Blessed One in his presence.
For a third time, those bhikkhus remained silent.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“It may be, bhikkhus, that out of respect for the Teacher you do not ask; let one friend, bhikkhus, inform another.
When this was said, those bhikkhus remained silent.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Bhante; it is marvelous, Bhante!

I am so confident, Bhante, that there is not even a single bhikkhu in this Saṅgha who has any doubt or perplexity regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, or regarding the path or the practice.”
“You speak out of faith, Ānanda. For here, Ānanda, it is the Tathāgata’s knowledge that:
‘In this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, there is not even a single bhikkhu who has any doubt or perplexity regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the path, or the practice.’”
“Ānanda, among these five hundred bhikkhus, even the most junior bhikkhu is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.77

8. Apaṇṇakavagga Acinteyyasutta (AN 4.77, PTS AN ii 80) “Monks, these four things are inconceivable and not to be reasoned about; one who reasons about them would meet with vexation and trouble. What four? The range of the Buddhas is inconceivable and not to be reasoned about; one who reasons about it would meet with vexation and trouble. The result of kamma is inconceivable and not to be reasoned about; one who reasons about it would meet with vexation and trouble. The world of sentient beings is inconceivable and not to be reasoned about; one who reasons about it would meet with vexation and trouble. The meditative absorption of a monk who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling is inconceivable and not to be reasoned about; one who reasons about it would meet with vexation and trouble. These four things, monks, are inconceivable and not to be reasoned about; one who reasons about them would meet with vexation and trouble.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four inconceivable things that should not be thought about; one who thinks about them would partake of madness and frustration.
What are the four?
The domain of the Buddhas, bhikkhus, is an inconceivable thing that should not be thought about;”
If one were to contemplate it, one would partake of madness and distress.
Monks, the domain of jhāna for one who meditates is inconceivable;
it is not to be contemplated, for if one were to contemplate it, one would partake of madness and distress.
“The ripening of kamma, bhikkhus, is inconceivable;
it should not be pondered. One who ponders it would partake of madness and vexation.
Speculation about the world, bhikkhus, is inconceivable; it should not be pondered.”
“Reflecting upon which, one would partake of madness and distress.
These, monks, are the four inconceivable things that should not be reflected upon; reflecting upon which, one would partake of madness and distress.
The seventh.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.78 8. The Chapter on the Infallible (Apaṇṇakavagga) The Discourse on the Offering (Dakkhiṇasutta) “Monks, there are these four kinds of offerings. What four? The offering that is inferior in both the present life and in the future life;

the offering that is superior in the present life but inferior in the future life; the offering that is inferior in the present life but superior in the future life; and the offering that is superior both in the present life and in the future life. And how, monks, is an offering inferior in both the present life and in the future life? Here, monks, one gives a gift with a mind of impurity, and it is given to one who is impure in virtue. This, monks, is called an offering that is inferior in both the present life and in the future life. And how, monks, is an offering superior in the present life but inferior in the future life? Here, monks, one gives a gift with a pure mind, but it is given to one who is impure in virtue. This, monks, is called an offering that is superior in the present life but inferior in the future life. And how, monks, is an offering inferior in the present life but superior in the future life? Here, monks, one gives a gift with a mind of impurity, but it is given to one who is pure in virtue. This, monks, is called an offering that is inferior in the present life but superior in the future life. And how, monks, is an offering superior both in the present life and in the future life? Here, monks, one gives a gift with a pure mind, and it is given to one who is pure in virtue. This, monks, is called an offering that is superior both in the present life and in the future life. These, monks, are the four kinds of offerings.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four purifications of offerings. What four?
“Monks, there is a gift that is purified by the giver, not by the recipient;
there is a gift, monks, that is purified by the recipient, not by the giver;
there is a gift, monks, that is purified neither by the giver nor by the recipient.”
“Monks, there is an offering that is purified both by the giver and by the recipient.
And how, monks, is an offering purified by the giver but not by the recipient?
Here, monks, the giver is virtuous and of good character, while the recipients are immoral and of evil character.”
"In this way, monks, an offering is purified by the giver, not by the recipient.
And how, monks, is an offering purified by the recipient, not by the giver?
Here, monks, the giver is immoral and of evil character, while the recipients are virtuous and of good character."
"In this way, monks, an offering is purified by the recipient, not by the donor.
And how, monks, is an offering purified neither by the donor nor by the recipient?
Here, monks, the donor is immoral and of evil character, and the recipients are also immoral and of evil character."
"In this way, monks, a gift is purified neither by the giver nor by the recipient.
And how, monks, is a gift purified both by the giver and by the recipient?
Here, monks, the giver is virtuous and of good character, and the recipients are also virtuous and of good character."
“Thus, monks, a gift is purified both by the giver and by the recipient.
These, monks, are the four purifications of a gift.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.79 8. The Chapter on the Incontrovertible (Apaṇṇakavagga) The Discourse on Trade (Vaṇijjasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of traders. What four? The trader who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the trader who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the trader who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others;

and the trader who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a trader intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, bhikkhus, a trader himself knows what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, what is base and what is noble, and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. But he does not encourage others in this way: ‘Come, friends, know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome… and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. Thus, bhikkhus, a trader is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a trader intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, bhikkhus, a trader does not himself know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome… and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. But he encourages others in this way: ‘Come, friends, know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome… and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. Thus, bhikkhus, a trader is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, bhikkhus, is a trader intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, bhikkhus, a trader does not himself know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome… and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. Nor does he encourage others in this way: ‘Come, friends, know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome… and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. Thus, bhikkhus, a trader is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a trader intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, bhikkhus, a trader himself knows what is wholesome and what is unwholesome… and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. And he encourages others in this way: ‘Come, friends, know what is wholesome and what is unwholesome… and what leads to the welfare and happiness of oneself and of others for a long time. Thus, bhikkhus, a trader is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of traders.”
(AN 4.79, PTS AN ii 81) Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why for some person here such a trade, when engaged in, results in loss?”
“But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some such trade, though engaged in, does not turn out according to one’s intention?
What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some such trade, though engaged in, turns out according to one’s intention?
And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some such trade, though engaged in, turns out contrary to one’s intention?”
“Here, Sāriputta, a certain person approaches a recluse or a brahmin and invites them, saying: ‘Venerable sir, please accept a requisite. Yet he does not give what he has invited.
If, after passing away from there, he returns to this state of existence, whatever trade he engages in will result in loss for him.

But here, Sāriputta, another person approaches a recluse or a brahmin and invites them, saying: ‘Venerable sir, please accept a requisite. Yet he does not give what he has invited according to his intention.”
If, having passed away from there, he comes back to this state of being, whatever trade he engages in, it does not turn out according to his intention.

But here, Sāriputta, someone approaches a recluse or a brahmin and invites them, saying: "Venerable sir, please speak of a requisite. Whatever he invites him to speak of, he gives that according to his intention.
If, having passed away from there, he comes back to this state of being, whatever trade he engages in, it turns out according to his intention.

“Here, Sāriputta, a certain person approaches a recluse or a brahmin and invites them, saying: ‘Venerable sir, please speak for the sake of a requisite. Whatever he invites [the other] for, he gives with ulterior motives.
If, having passed away from there, he comes back to this state of being, whatever trade he engages in, that trade of his turns out to be one with ulterior motives.
This, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the condition, why a certain person here, when engaging in such a trade, finds it to be ruinous.”
"But this, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the condition, by which for some here, such a trade as they have undertaken does not turn out according to their intention.
And this, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the condition, by which for some here, such a trade as they have undertaken turns out according to their intention.
And this, Sāriputta, is the cause, this is the condition, by which for some here, such a trade as they have undertaken turns out contrary to their intention."
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.80 8.
The Chapter on the Inevitable (Apaṇṇakavagga)
The Kambhoja Sutta (AN 4.80, PTS AN ii 82).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“What, Bhante, is the cause, what is the reason, why women do not sit in the assembly hall, do not engage in business, and do not go to Kamboja?
“Ānanda, women are prone to anger.”
Ānanda, women are envious;
Ānanda, women are stingy;
Ānanda, women are lacking in wisdom.
“This, Ānanda, is the cause, this is the reason why women do not sit in the assembly hall, do not engage in business, and do not go to Kamboja.
Tenth. The Third Chapter on the Inevitable (Apaṇṇaka-vagga).
Its summary verse:
Effort, views, the true person,
the bride, and two others— these are the foremost topics.
“Kusinārā is inconceivable,
as are alms-giving, trade, and Kamboja.
— Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.81
9. Macala Chapter:
Discourse on the Destruction of Life (AN 4.81, PTS AN ii 83)
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.
What are the four?
One is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, and one who speaks falsehood.”
“Monks, one who possesses these four qualities is placed in hell as if carried there.
Monks, one who possesses four qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there.
Which four?”
“He abstains from taking life, he abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from sexual misconduct, and he abstains from false speech.
Possessing these four qualities, monks, one is deposited in heaven as if carried there. Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.82 9.

The Chapter on the Unsteady The Discourse on False Speech “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who speaks falsely; the person who speaks divisively; the person who speaks harshly; and the person who speaks idle chatter. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. What are the four? [The Buddha said:]”
He is a speaker of falsehood, he is a speaker of malicious speech, he is a speaker of harsh speech, and he is a frivolous talker—
it is one endowed with these four qualities, monks, who is placed in hell as if carried there.
Endowed with four qualities, monks, one is placed in heaven as if carried there.
"By which four?
He abstains from false speech, he abstains from malicious speech, he abstains from harsh speech, and he abstains from idle chatter.
It is by possessing these four qualities, monks, that one is placed in heaven as if carried there."
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.83 9.
Macalavagga (The Chapter on the Unsteady)
The Discourse on One Deserving of Dispraise (Avaṇṇārahasutta):
“Monks, one endowed with four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. What four? [The text continues with the four qualities.]”
Which four?
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in praise of one who deserves blame;
without investigating and without scrutinizing, one speaks in dispraise of one who deserves praise.
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, one conceives confidence in a matter that does not inspire confidence;

without investigating and without scrutinizing, one conceives lack of confidence in a matter that inspires confidence—it is by possessing these four qualities, monks, that one is placed in hell as if carried there.
By possessing four qualities, monks, one is placed in heaven as if carried there.
Which four?
Having investigated and scrutinized, one speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise;
having investigated and scrutinized, one speaks praise of one who deserves praise.
"Having investigated and scrutinized, one shows lack of confidence in a matter that merits lack of confidence;
having investigated and scrutinized, one shows confidence in a matter that merits confidence.
Possessing these four qualities, monks, one is placed in heaven as if carried there."
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.84 9. Macalavagga (The Chapter on the Unsteady)
Kodhagarusutta (AN 4.84,
PTS AN ii 84): “Bhikkhus,
one who possesses four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.
Which four?
One values anger and not the true Dhamma; one values hypocrisy and not the true Dhamma; one values gain and not the true Dhamma; one values honor and not the true Dhamma.
Possessing these four qualities, monks, one is deposited in hell as if carried there.
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with four qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the four?
One values the true Dhamma and not anger; one values the true Dhamma and not hypocrisy; one values the true Dhamma and not gain; one values the true Dhamma and not honor.”
“Monks, one who possesses these four qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.85
9. Macala Chapter:
The Discourse on Darkness upon Darkness (AN 4.85, PTS AN ii 85)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?
One who is dark with a dark destination;”
One whose destination is darkness from light,
one whose destination is light from darkness,
and one whose destination is light from light.
And how, monks, is a person one who is dark and has a dark destination?
Here, monks, a certain person is reborn into a low family— a family of caṇḍālas, or a family of bamboo-workers,
or a family of hunters, or a family of chariot-makers, or a family of refuse-removers— one that is poor, lacking food and drink, and where livelihood is difficult.
Where food and clothing are obtained only with great difficulty;
and where he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, and afflicted by many diseases— whether one-eyed, or with a withered arm,
or lame, or paralyzed— he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps.
Thus, he engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is dark and has darkness as his destination.
And how, monks, is a person one who is in darkness but has light as their destination?
Here, monks, a certain person is reborn into a low family— a family of caṇḍālas, or a family of bamboo-workers,
or a family of hunters, or a family of chariot-makers, or a family of refuse-removers— one that is poor, lacking food and drink, and where livelihood is difficult.
Where almsfood and clothing are obtained only with great difficulty;
and where he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, afflicted by many illnesses— whether blind in one eye, or with crooked limbs, or lame, or paralyzed—
he does not obtain food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lighting.
Thus he practices good conduct by body, he practices good conduct by speech, and he practices good conduct by mind.

Having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
In this way, monks, a person is dark with a bright future destiny.
And how, monks, is a person bright but with darkness as his destination?
Here, monks, a certain person is reborn into a high family— a prominent khattiya family, or a prominent brahmin family,
or a prominent householder family— wealthy, with great riches and vast enjoyments, possessing abundant gold and silver.
He possesses abundant wealth and resources, abundant money and grain;

he is handsome, attractive, pleasing, endowed with the highest beauty of complexion; he is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lighting.
Yet he engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Thus, having practiced misconduct by way of body, having practiced misconduct by way of speech, and having practiced misconduct by way of mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even hell.
In this way, monks, a person is bright but has darkness as his destination.
And how, monks, is a person bright and has brightness as his destination?
In this case, monks, a certain person is reborn into a high family— a prominent khattiya family, a prominent brahmin family,
or a prominent householder family— one that is wealthy, of great fortune and great possessions,
with abundant gold and silver, abundant means and equipment, and abundant wealth and grain.

He is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion; he is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps.
He practices good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, and good conduct by mind.

Having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, and having practiced good conduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“Thus, monks, a person is bright and has a bright destination.
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.
The fifth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.86 9. The Chapter on the Unsteady (Macalavagga) The Discourse on the Bent and the Crooked (Oṇatoṇatasutta) "Bhikkhus, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world.

What four? "The person who is bent and crooked; the person who is crooked but not bent; the person who is bent but not crooked; and the person who is neither bent nor crooked. "And how, bhikkhus, is a person bent and crooked? Here, someone is of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. This is called a person who is bent and crooked. "And how, bhikkhus, is a person crooked but not bent? Here, someone is of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Yet he harbors thoughts of ill will, harmfulness, and sensual desire. This is called a person who is crooked but not bent. "And how, bhikkhus, is a person bent but not crooked? Here, someone is of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. Yet he harbors no thoughts of ill will, harmfulness, or sensual desire. This is called a person who is bent but not crooked. "And how, bhikkhus, is a person neither bent nor crooked? Here, someone is of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. He harbors no thoughts of ill will, harmfulness, or sensual desire. This is called a person who is neither bent nor crooked. "These, bhikkhus, are the four types of persons found existing in the world."
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What are the four? [Text continues].”
Bent down and bent down, bent down and stretched out,
stretched out and bent down.
The one who weaves out and weaves in...
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.
Thus ends the sixth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.87 9. Macalavagga Puttasutta (The Discourse on Sons) “Monks, there are these four kinds of sons found existing in the world. What four? The son who is a burden; the son who is a source of anxiety; the son who is a source of both joy and anxiety; and the son who is a source of joy. And how, monks, is a son a burden? Here, monks, a son comes from a good family, well-born on both his maternal and paternal sides, pure in descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth. But he does not possess wealth acquired by energetic striving, amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained. When his parents are deceased, he squanders whatever property they left behind. This, monks, is called a son who is a burden. And how, monks, is a son a source of anxiety? Here, monks, a son comes from a good family... [as above] ...righteous wealth righteously gained. But he is addicted to women, addicted to strong drink, addicted to gambling, and is a friend of bad companions. He squanders whatever property his parents left behind. His mother and father, hearing of him, are anxious and distressed: ‘Alas, our son is lost! Alas, our son is ruined! This, monks, is called a son who is a source of anxiety. And how, monks, is a son a source of both joy and anxiety? Here, monks, a son comes from a good family... [as above] ...righteous wealth righteously gained. He is not addicted to women, nor to strong drink, nor to gambling, and is a friend of good companions. He does not squander whatever property his parents left behind. His mother and father, hearing of him, are both joyful and anxious: ‘Oh, what will happen to our son? Will he be able to maintain the family estate? This, monks, is called a son who is a source of both joy and anxiety. And how, monks, is a son a source of joy? Here, monks, a son comes from a good family... [as above] ...righteous wealth righteously gained. He is not addicted to women, nor to strong drink, nor to gambling, and is a friend of good companions. He maintains whatever property his parents left behind. His mother and father, hearing of him, are joyful: ‘Our son has prospered! Our son has succeeded! This, monks, is called a son who is a source of joy. These, monks, are the four kinds of sons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? [Text continues].”
The ascetic Macala, the ascetic Puṇḍarīka, the ascetic Paduma, and the ascetic Sukhumāla among ascetics.
And how, bhikkhus, is a person an ascetic Macala?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a trainee (sekha) who has entered upon the path.
He dwells aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Just as, monks, the eldest son of a consecrated Khattiya king who is destined for the coronation remains unsettled until he has been consecrated,
even so, monks, a monk is a trainee practicing the way, dwelling while aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage.
In this way, monks, a person is an unshakable ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a white-lotus ascetic?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them here and now.
Having personally realized the Dhamma through direct knowledge, he enters upon and dwells in it, yet he does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with his body.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is a white-lotus ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a red-lotus ascetic?

"Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon them; and he dwells having touched the eight liberations with his body.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is a lotus-like ascetic."
And how, monks, is a person a delicate ascetic among ascetics?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu for the most part uses robes only when asked, seldom without being asked;
he for the most part consumes almsfood only when asked, seldom without being asked; he for the most part uses lodgings only when asked.
He makes use of medicinal requisites for the sick—such as medicines and provisions—mostly when asked, and only rarely without being asked.
Furthermore, with regard to those fellow celibates with whom he dwells, they mostly treat him with agreeable bodily actions and only rarely with disagreeable ones;
they mostly treat him with agreeable verbal actions and only rarely...
They treat one with agreeable mental action mostly, and with disagreeable [mental action] little;
they offer agreeable offerings mostly, and disagreeable [offerings] little.
Furthermore, as for those feelings that arise from bile, or arise from phlegm, or arise from wind...

Whether they be born of bile, phlegm, wind, or their combination; whether born of seasonal change, of irregular lifestyle, of external injury, or as the result of kamma—such ailments do not arise in him to any great extent. He is free from illness.
He is one who obtains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that are mental states belonging to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.

With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, remains therein.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is a refined ascetic among ascetics.
For if anyone, monks, speaking rightly were to say, "A refined ascetic among ascetics," it is of me alone that one should rightly say this, monks: "A refined ascetic among ascetics."
For I, monks, for the most part use robes only when they have been requested, seldom when they have not been requested;

I use almsfood for the most part only when it has been requested, seldom when it has not been requested; I use lodgings for the most part only when they have been requested, seldom when they have not been requested;
I use medicinal requisites for the sick for the most part only when they have been requested, seldom when they have not been requested.
Furthermore, those monks with whom I dwell mostly treat me with agreeable bodily action and only rarely with disagreeable;
they mostly treat me with agreeable verbal action and only rarely with disagreeable;
they mostly treat me with agreeable mental action and only rarely with disagreeable; and they mostly offer what is agreeable.
They bring about little that is unpleasant.
Furthermore, those feelings which arise from bile, or from phlegm, or from wind, or from a combination of these,
or born of changes in the weather, or born of improper conduct, or born of exertion, or born as the result of kamma— these too are unpleasant.
Or rather, those [ailments] do not arise in me very often. I am free from illness.
Furthermore, I am one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that are higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life.
And, with the destruction of the taints, I dwell having realized for myself through direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
“Monks, if one were speaking rightly, saying of anyone among ascetics, ‘He is a delicate ascetic,’ it is of me alone that one would rightly say this, monks: ‘He is a delicate ascetic among ascetics.
These, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.
The seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.88 9.

Macalavagga Saṁyojanasutta (The Fetter) “Bhikkhus, there are these four fetters. What four? The fetter of lust, the fetter of hatred, the fetter of delusion, and the fetter of conceit. These, bhikkhus, are the four fetters.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four? [Text continues].”
The ascetic Macala, the ascetic Puṇḍarīka, the ascetic Paduma, and the ascetic Sukhumāla among ascetics.
And how, bhikkhus, is a person an ascetic Macala?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, through the total destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.
"In this way, monks, a person is an unshakable ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a white-lotus ascetic?

Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, is a once-returner; having returned to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering."
In this way, monks, a person is a white-lotus ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a red-lotus ascetic?
Here, monks, a monk, through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
In this way, monks, a person is a *paduma* ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a delicate ascetic among ascetics?

Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
"Thus, monks, a person is a delicate ascetic among ascetics.
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.
This is the eighth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.89 9.
The Chapter on the Unsteady (Macalavagga) The Discourse on Right View (Sammādiṭṭhisutta)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?
The ascetic Macala, the ascetic Puṇḍarīka, the ascetic Paduma, and the ascetic Sukhumāla among ascetics.
And how, monks, is a person an ascetic Macala?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu possesses right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
"Thus, monks, is a person an unshakable ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a white-lotus ascetic?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu possesses right view, right intention, and right speech."
He possesses right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge,
and right liberation, yet he does not dwell having personally realized the eight liberations with his body.
In this way, monks, a person is a white-lotus ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a *paduma* ascetic?
Here, monks, a monk possesses right view … [as before] … and possesses right liberation; he dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with his body.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is a *paduma* ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a delicate ascetic among ascetics?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu for the most part uses a robe only when it has been requested, and seldom when it has not been requested...
[as before] ...For if anyone, monks, speaking rightly were to say of anyone: "He is a delicate ascetic among ascetics," it is of me alone that one might rightly say this.
“Monks, speaking rightly, one might say: ‘Among ascetics, he is a delicate ascetic.
These, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.
The ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.90 9.

Macalavagga Khandhasutta "Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging."
“Bhikkhus, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world. What are the four? [Text continues].”
The ascetic Macala, the ascetic Puṇḍarīka, the ascetic Paduma, and the ascetic Sukhumāla among ascetics.
And how, bhikkhus, is a person an ascetic Macala?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a trainee (sekha) who has not yet attained his heart’s goal; he dwells aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage.
"Thus, monks, a person is an ascetic who is immovable.
And how, monks, is a person an ascetic who is a white lotus?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging: "Thus, monks, a person is an ascetic who is a white lotus."
‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling … such is perception …’ and so forth.
"Such is volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away";
yet he does not dwell having personally realized the eight liberations with his body.
In this way, monks, a person is a white-lotus ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a red-lotus ascetic?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging:
‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away;
such is feeling … [and so on] … such is perception …’ … [and so on] …
“Such is volitional formations...
such is consciousness, such its origin, such its passing away”;
and he dwells having personally realized the eight liberations with his body.
In this way, monks, a person is a *paduma* ascetic.
And how, monks, is a person a delicate ascetic among ascetics?

Here, monks, a bhikkhu mostly uses robes that have been specifically requested for him, and only rarely those not so requested... [as before] ...It is of such a person, monks, that one speaking rightly would say: "A delicate ascetic among ascetics."
“Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Tenth. The Fourth Chapter on the Unsteady One.
Its summary verse:
Killing living beings, false speech,
disparagement, anger, and timidity.
The son, the fetter,
and views— these ten, according to the aggregates.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.91)
10. Asura Chapter:
The Discourse on Asuras (AN 4.91, PTS AN ii 92)
“Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Which four? One who is not an asura and has no retinue of asuras;”
An asura with a retinue of gods; a god with a retinue of asuras;
a god with a retinue of gods.
And how, monks, is a person an asura with an asura retinue?
Here, monks, a certain person is immoral and of evil character, and his assembly is also immoral and of evil character.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is an asura with an asura retinue.
And how, monks, is a person an asura with a retinue of gods?
Here, monks, a certain person is immoral and of evil character, yet his assembly is virtuous and of good character.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is an asura with a retinue of gods.
And how, monks, is a person a deva with an asura retinue?
Here, monks, a certain person is virtuous and of beautiful character, yet his assembly is immoral and of evil character.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is a deva with an asura retinue.
And how, monks, is a person a god with a retinue of gods?
Here, monks, a certain person is virtuous and of beautiful character, and his assembly is also virtuous and of beautiful character.
In this way, monks, a person is a god with a retinue of gods.
“Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Thus was the first [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.92

10. The Chapter on Asuras The First Discourse on Concentration (Paṭhamasamādhisutta) “Monks, there are these five factors that lead to the non-arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the decline of concentration that has already arisen. What five? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind overwhelmed by sensual lust; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This is the first factor that leads to the non-arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the decline of concentration that has already arisen. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind overwhelmed by ill will; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. This is the second factor... Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind overwhelmed by sloth and torpor; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor. This is the third factor... Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. This is the fourth factor... Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind overwhelmed by doubt; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This is the fifth factor that leads to the non-arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the decline of concentration that has already arisen. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the non-arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the decline of concentration that has already arisen. Monks, there are these five factors that lead to the arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the non-decline of concentration that has already arisen. What five? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind detached from sensual lust; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. This is the first factor that leads to the arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the non-decline of concentration that has already arisen. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind detached from ill will; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. This is the second factor... Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind detached from sloth and torpor; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor. This is the third factor... Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind detached from restlessness and remorse; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. This is the fourth factor... Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind detached from doubt; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This is the fifth factor that leads to the arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the non-decline of concentration that has already arisen. These, monks, are the five factors that lead to the arising of concentration that has not yet arisen, and to the non-decline of concentration that has already arisen.”
