“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person gains internal tranquility of mind but does not gain higher wisdom consisting in insight into phenomena.”

“Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*), but is not a possessor of internal tranquility of mind (*ajjhattaṃ cetosamatha*).
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is neither a possessor of internal tranquility of mind nor a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is both a possessor of internal tranquility of mind and a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom.”
“Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world.
The second [sutta].
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.93.
10. Asura Chapter:
The Second Discourse on Concentration (AN 4.93, PTS AN ii 92)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person gains internal tranquility of mind, but does not gain higher wisdom consisting in insight into phenomena.
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom, but is not a possessor of internal mental serenity.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is neither a possessor of internal mental serenity nor a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person is both a possessor of internal mental serenity and a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom."
In this regard, monks, when a person possesses internal serenity of mind but does not possess higher wisdom and insight into phenomena,
that person, having established himself in internal serenity of mind, should apply himself to higher wisdom and insight into phenomena.
After some time, he comes to possess both internal serenity of mind and higher wisdom and insight into phenomena.
In this regard, monks, for that person who has attained higher wisdom and insight into phenomena but has not attained internal serenity of mind,
that person, having established themselves in higher wisdom and insight into phenomena,
should apply themselves to internal serenity of mind.
Then, at a later time, he becomes an attainer of both higher wisdom and insight into phenomena (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) and an attainer of internal tranquility of mind (*ajjhattaṃ cetosamatha*).
In this regard, monks, as for that person who is neither an attainer of internal tranquility of mind nor an attainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena—
that person, monks, [should apply himself] to those very same wholesome states...
For the sake of attainment, there must be intense desire, effort, exertion, ardor, indefatigability, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension. Just as, monks,
one whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would act toward that very clothing or head—
One should exercise superior desire, effort, energy, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of its extinguishing;

even so, monks, that person must exercise superior desire, effort, energy, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of obtaining those very same wholesome states.
Then, at a later time, he becomes one who gains internal tranquility of mind and gains higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.
In this regard, monks, that person who has gained both internal tranquility of mind and higher wisdom through insight into phenomena— by that person, monks, regarding those very wholesome states...
"Having established himself therein, one should apply oneself further to the destruction of the taints.
These, monks, are the four persons found existing in the world. Thus was the third [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.94 10.
Asura Vagga Tatiya Samādhi Sutta (The Third Discourse on Concentration)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What are the four? [Text continues].”
“Here, monks, a certain person gains internal tranquility of mind but does not gain higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.
Here, monks, another person gains higher wisdom through insight into phenomena but does not gain internal tranquility of mind.
Here, monks, yet another person gains neither internal tranquility of mind nor higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.”
But here, monks, a certain person is one who has attained both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena.

In this regard, monks, that person who has attained internal serenity of mind but has not attained the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena should approach the person who has attained the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena and say this:
‘Friend, how indeed should volitional formations be viewed?
How should volitional formations be comprehended?
How should volitional formations be seen with insight?’”
He explains to him what has been seen and what has been understood:
“In this way, friend, formations are to be viewed; in this way, formations are to be comprehended; in this way, formations are to be insighted.
At a later time, he becomes a possessor of internal mental serenity and a possessor of higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.
In that regard, monks, when there is a person who has attained higher wisdom through insight into phenomena but has not attained internal serenity of mind,
that person should approach the one who has attained internal serenity of mind and speak to him thus:
“Friend, how indeed should the mind be steadied?
How should the mind be settled?
How should the mind be made one-pointed?”
‘How should the mind be concentrated?
He explains to him according to what he has seen and known:
‘In this way, friend, the mind should be steadied; in this way the mind should be settled; in this way the mind should be unified; in this way the mind should be concentrated.’”

Then, at a later time, he becomes both a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*) and a possessor of internal mental tranquility (*ajjhattaṃ cetosamatha*).

In this regard, monks, that person who is neither a possessor of internal mental tranquility nor a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom— compared to that person, monks, [the one] who is indeed a possessor...
To one who has attained internal mental tranquility and possesses higher wisdom and insight into phenomena, one should approach him and say this:
"Friend, how indeed should the mind be steadied?
How should the mind be settled?"
How should the mind be made one-pointed?
How should the mind be concentrated?
How should formations be viewed?
‘How should volitional formations be comprehended?
How should volitional formations be seen with insight?
He explains to him according to how he has seen and how he has known it:
‘In this way, friend, the mind should be steadied; in this way the mind should be settled; in this way the mind should be unified;
in this way the mind should be concentrated; in this way formations should be viewed;
in this way formations should be comprehended; in this way formations should be seen with insight.’”
Then, at a later time, he becomes one who gains internal tranquility of mind and gains higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.
In that regard, monks, as for that person who gains both internal tranquility of mind and higher wisdom through insight into phenomena, by that person, regarding those very wholesome states...
Having established oneself therein, one should further apply oneself to the destruction of the taints.
These, monks, are the four persons found existing in the world. Thus ends the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.95 10. Asura Vagga Chavālāta Sutta: The Branding Stick “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a branding stick; the person who is like a firebrand; the person who is like a torch; and the person who is like a meteor. And how, monks, is a person like a branding stick? Here, monks, someone is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This, monks, is called a person who is like a branding stick. And how, monks, is a person like a firebrand? Here, monks, someone is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. But he does not give gifts, nor perform meritorious deeds, nor fulfill wholesome practices. This, monks, is called a person who is like a firebrand. And how, monks, is a person like a torch? Here, monks, someone is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. However, he gives gifts, performs meritorious deeds, and fulfills wholesome practices. This, monks, is called a person who is like a torch. And how, monks, is a person like a meteor? Here, monks, someone is one who does not destroy life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, or indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. He gives gifts, performs meritorious deeds, and fulfills wholesome practices. This, monks, is called a person who is like a meteor. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four? [Text continues].”
One who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others;
one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit;
and one who practices for both his own benefit and for the benefit of others.
He practices for his own welfare and for the welfare of others.
Monks, just as a brand from a funeral pyre, burning at both ends and smeared with excrement in the middle, serves neither as firewood in the village nor as fuel in the forest;
even so, monks, I say of this person that he is one who practices neither for his own welfare nor for the welfare of others.
In this regard, monks, the person who practices for the benefit of others but not for their own benefit is more excellent and more sublime than these two persons.
In this regard, monks, the person who practices for their own benefit but not for the benefit of others is more excellent and more sublime than these three persons.

In this regard, monks, the person who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent among these four persons.

Just as, monks, from a cow comes milk, from milk curds, from curds butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee—and the cream of ghee is declared to be the preeminent among them; so it is with this person.

"In the same way, monks, this person who practices both for their own benefit and for the benefit of others is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent among these four persons.
These, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.
Thus ends the fifth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.96 10. Asura Vagga Rāgavinaya Sutta:

The Taming of Lust “Monks, there are these four taming of lusts. What four? The taming of lust for forms, the taming of lust for sounds, the taming of lust for odors, and the taming of lust for tastes. These, monks, are the four tamings of lust. When, monks, a noble disciple has abandoned lust for forms, abandoned lust for sounds, abandoned lust for odors, and abandoned lust for tastes, he is called a noble disciple who has tamed lust, who has crossed over attachment, who has gone beyond craving, and who stands having transcended the realm of Mara.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? [Text continues].”
One who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others;
one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit;
and one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others.
One who is practicing for both their own benefit and the benefit of others.
And how, monks, is a person practicing for their own benefit but not for the benefit of others?
Here, monks, a certain person practices for the removal of their own lust, but does not encourage another to remove their lust.
He practices for the sake of subduing his own hatred, but does not encourage others to subdue their hatred;
he practices for the sake of subduing his own delusion, but does not encourage others to subdue their delusion.
In this way, monks, a person practices for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.
And how, monks, is a person practicing for the benefit of others but not for their own benefit?
Here, monks, a certain person does not themselves practice for the removal of lust, yet they encourage another in the removal of lust;
they do not themselves practice for the removal of hatred, yet they encourage another in the removal of hatred.
One does not practice for the removal of one’s own delusion, yet one encourages others to remove their delusion.
In this way, monks, a person practices for the benefit of others, but not for their own benefit.
And how, monks, does a person practice neither for their own benefit nor for the benefit of others?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not practice for the removal of his own lust, nor does he encourage others to practice for the removal of lust;
he does not practice for the removal of his own hatred, nor does he encourage others to practice for the removal of hatred;
he does not practice for the removal of his own delusion, nor does he encourage others to practice for the removal of delusion.
In this way, monks, a person practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others.
And how, monks, does a person practice both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others?
Here, monks, a certain person practices himself for the removal of lust and encourages others to practice for the removal of lust.
He himself practices for the removal of hatred, and he encourages others to remove hatred;
he himself practices for the removal of delusion, and he encourages others to remove delusion.
In this way, monks, a person practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others.
“Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world.
The sixth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.97.

10. Asura Chapter: The Discourse on Quick Understanding (Khippanisanti-sutta) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these five qualities that lead to quick understanding. What five? Here, monks, a monk possesses faith; he is virtuous; he has heard much; he is one who has attained the attainments; and he is wise. These, monks, are the five qualities that lead to quick understanding.”
“Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Which four?
One who is practicing for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others;”
One who practices for the benefit of others but not for their own benefit;
one who practices neither for their own benefit nor for the benefit of others;
and one who practices both for their own benefit and for the benefit of others.
And how, monks, is a person practicing for their own benefit, but not for the benefit of others?
Here, monks, a certain person is quick to comprehend wholesome states; they are of a nature to retain the teachings they have heard;
and having retained those teachings, they examine their meaning and, having understood the meaning, [act accordingly].
Having understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma;
yet he is not one of beautiful speech, nor is he possessed of eloquence, of speech that is polished, clear, flawless, and expressive of the meaning;
nor does he instruct, encourage, inspire, and gladden his fellow celibates.
"In this way, monks, a person practices for their own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.
And how, monks, does a person practice for the benefit of others, but not for their own benefit?
Here, monks, a certain person is not one who quickly gains confidence in wholesome states."
He is not one who retains the teachings he has heard, nor does he examine the meaning of the teachings he has retained;
nor, having understood both the meaning and the teaching, does he practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

Yet he is a speaker of what is good, possessed of a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is polished, clear, articulate, and expressive of the meaning; and he is one who instructs, urges, rouses, and encourages his fellow celibates.
In this way, monks, a person practices for the benefit of others, but not for their own benefit.
And how, monks, does a person practice neither for their own benefit nor for the benefit of others?
Here, monks, a certain person is not one who quickly gains confidence in wholesome states.
He is not one who retains the teachings he has heard; nor, having retained the teachings, does he examine their meaning;
nor, having understood both the meaning and the teaching, does he practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Furthermore, he is not a speaker of what is good, nor one possessed of a good delivery, endowed with speech that is polished, distinct, and free from indistinctness.
He understands the meaning, yet he does not instruct, encourage, inspire, or gladden his fellow celibates.
In this way, monks, a person is practicing neither for their own welfare nor for the welfare of others.
And how, monks, is a person practicing both for their own welfare and for the welfare of others?
In this case, monks, a certain person is quick to comprehend wholesome states;
he is of a nature to retain the teachings he has heard; having retained those teachings, he examines their meaning;
having understood the meaning and understood the teaching, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma.

He is one of lovely speech, with lovely enunciation, endowed with polite language that is distinct, flawless, and expressive of the meaning; he is one who instructs, rouses, inspires, and gladdens his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
It is in this way, monks, that a person practices for their own welfare and for the welfare of others.
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.98 10.
Asura Vagga (The Chapter on Asuras)
Attahitasutta: “Bhikkhus,
these four persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
One who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others;
one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit; [and so forth].
One who practices neither for his own welfare nor for the welfare of others;
and one who practices both for his own welfare and for the welfare of others.
These, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.99 10.
Asura Vagga (The Chapter on Asuras)
Sikkhāpadasutta: “Bhikkhus,
these four types of persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
One who is practicing for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others;
one who is practicing for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit;
One who practices neither for their own welfare nor for the welfare of others;
and one who practices both for their own welfare and for the welfare of others.
And how, monks, is a person practicing for their own welfare, but not for the welfare of others?
In this case, monks, a certain person refrains from taking life himself, but does not encourage others to refrain from taking life;
he refrains from taking what is not given himself, but does not encourage others to refrain from taking what is not given;
he refrains from sexual misconduct himself, but does not encourage others to refrain from sexual misconduct.
He himself abstains from false speech, but does not encourage others in the abstinence from false speech;

he himself abstains from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which cause heedlessness, but does not encourage others in the abstinence from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which cause heedlessness.
In this way, monks, a person is practicing for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of others.
And how, monks, is a person practicing for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit?
Here, monks, a certain person himself does not abstain from taking life, yet he encourages another to abstain from taking life;
he himself does not abstain from taking what is not given, yet he encourages another to abstain from taking what is not given.
He himself does not abstain from sexual misconduct, yet he encourages others to abstain from sexual misconduct;
he himself does not abstain from false speech, yet he encourages others to abstain from false speech;

he himself does not abstain from the use of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, yet he encourages others to abstain from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
"In this way, monks, a person practices for the benefit of others, but not for his own benefit.
And how, monks, does a person practice neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others?
Here, monks, a certain person himself abstains from the destruction of life, but does not cause another to abstain from the destruction of life."

He encourages others to abstain from taking life... [and so on] ...he himself does not refrain from the occasion of negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, nor does he encourage others to abstain from the occasion of negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.
In this way, monks, a person is practicing neither for his own welfare nor for the welfare of others.
And how, monks, is a person practicing for his own benefit and for the benefit of others?
Here, monks, a certain person himself abstains from the destruction of life and encourages others in the abstention from the destruction of life...
[and so on] ...he himself abstains from the use of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which cause negligence.
Furthermore, he encourages others to abstain from fermented and distilled liquors, which are the basis for negligence.
It is in this way, monks, that a person practices both for his own welfare and for the welfare of others.
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.100 10.
Asura Vagga (The Chapter on Asuras)
Then the wanderer Potaliya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As the wanderer Potaliya was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Potaliya, these four types of persons are found existing in the world.
Which four?"

"In this case, Potaliya, a certain person speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.

Furthermore, Potaliya, another person speaks praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time."

"Furthermore, Potaliya, here a certain person neither speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—nor speaks praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.

Furthermore, Potaliya, here a certain person speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—and speaks praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.
These, Potaliya, are the four types of persons found existing in the world."
“Of these four types of persons, Potaliya, which one do you find most excellent and sublime?
“There are, Master Gotama, these four types of persons found existing in the world. Which four? [The text continues with the description of each.]”

"In this case, Master Gotama, a certain person speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time.

Furthermore, Master Gotama, another person speaks praise of one who deserves praise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time—but does not speak dispraise of one who deserves dispraise—truthfully, accurately, and at the proper time."

"Furthermore, Master Gotama, here one person does not speak dispraise of one who deserves dispraise, even when it is true, factual, and timely; nor does he speak praise of one who deserves praise, even when it is true, factual, and timely.

Furthermore, Master Gotama, here another person speaks dispraise of one who deserves dispraise, when it is true, factual, and timely, and he also speaks praise of one who deserves praise, when it is true, factual, and timely.
These, Master Gotama, are the four types of persons found existing in the world."

"Of these four types of persons, Master Gotama, that person who neither speaks dispraise of one deserving of dispraise in a way that is true, real, and timely, nor speaks praise of one deserving of praise in a way that is true, real, and timely—
this person is acceptable to me as the most excellent and the most sublime among these four. And why is that?"
“Indeed, Master Gotama, this equanimity is excellent.
“Potaliya, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world.
Which four? … [as above] … These, Potaliya, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

Potaliya, among these four types of persons, the one who speaks dispraise of one deserving of dispraise in a way that is factual, true, and timely, and who speaks praise of one deserving of praise in a way that is factual, true, and timely—
this person is the most excellent and the most sublime of these four. Why is that?
"For this is excellent, Potaliya, namely, knowing the right time for each respective occasion.
"There are, Master Gotama, these four types of persons found existing in the world.
Which four? ... [omitted] ... These, Master Gotama, are the four types of persons found existing in the world."

Of these four types of persons, Master Gotama, the one who speaks dispraise of one deserving dispraise at the proper time—truthfully and accurately—and who speaks praise of one deserving praise at the proper time—truthfully and accurately:
this person is acceptable to me as the most excellent and the most sublime among these four.
For what reason?
"Excellent indeed, Master Gotama, is this knowledge of the right time for each occasion.
Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost..."
Or one might show the way, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been elucidated by Master Gotama in many ways.
Therefore, I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
Tenth. The Fifth Chapter on Asuras.
Its summary verse:
The asura, the three concentrations,
and the charred brand as the fifth.
"Lust, tranquility, one's own welfare,
and training by Potaliya.
The second fiftieth chapter is finished.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.101 11. Valāhakavagga Paṭhamavalāhakasutta (The First Discourse on Clouds) “Monks, there are these four kinds of clouds. What four? The cloud that rains down upon a single region; the cloud that rains down upon two regions; the cloud that rains down upon four regions; and the cloud that rains down upon the entire world-system. These, monks, are the four kinds of clouds.

In the same way, monks, there are these four kinds of individuals who are like clouds. What four? The individual who rains down upon a single region; the individual who rains down upon two regions; the individual who rains down upon four regions; and the individual who rains down upon the entire world-system. These, monks, are the four kinds of individuals who are like clouds. And how, monks, is one an individual who rains down upon a single region? Here, monks, a certain person gives gifts to one person, not to two; he gives gifts to two, not to many; he gives gifts to many, not to the Saṅgha. This, monks, is called an individual who rains down upon a single region. And how, monks, is one an individual who rains down upon two regions? Here, monks, a certain person gives gifts to one person, not to two; he gives gifts to two, not to many; he gives gifts to many, and also to the Saṅgha. This, monks, is called an individual who rains down upon two regions. And how, monks, is one an individual who rains down upon four regions? Here, monks, a certain person gives gifts to one person, not to two; he gives gifts to two, not to many; he gives gifts to many, and also to the Saṅgha. This, monks, is called an individual who rains down upon four regions. And how, monks, is one an individual who rains down upon the entire world-system? Here, monks, a certain person does not give gifts to one person, nor to two, nor to many, nor to the Saṅgha; rather, he makes a vow: ‘May I become a Cakravartin monarch, a Wheel-turning King, a righteous king of the law, a conqueror of the four quarters, a stabilizer of the land, possessed of the seven treasures. Having made this vow, he practices the ten royal virtues. He abstains from taking life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, from idle chatter, and he is free from covetousness, free from ill will, and holds right view. This, monks, is called an individual who rains down upon the entire world-system. These, monks, are the four kinds of individuals who are like clouds.”
(AN 4.101, PTS AN ii 102) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clouds. Which four?
Thundering but not raining,
raining but not thundering,
neither thundering nor raining.
The one that thunders but does not rain; the one that rains but does not thunder; the one that both thunders and rains; and the one that neither thunders nor rains. These, monks, are the four clouds.
In the same way, monks, there are these four types of persons resembling clouds found existing in the world.
Which four?
One who thunders but does not rain; one who rains but does not thunder; [one who both thunders and rains]; and one who neither thunders nor rains.
Neither one who thunders but does not rain,
nor one who both thunders and rains.
And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
In this case, monks, a certain person is a speaker but not a doer.
In this way, monks, such a person thunders but does not rain.
Just as that cloud, monks, thunders but does not rain;
"Monks, I say that this person is like that.
And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
Here, monks, a certain person is a doer, but not a speaker."
In this way, monks, a person is one who rains but does not thunder.
Just as that cloud, monks, rains but does not thunder,
even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor rains?
Here, monks, a certain person is neither a speaker nor a doer.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is one who neither thunders nor rains.
"Just as that cloud, monks, neither thunders nor rains,
even so, monks, do I describe this person. And how, monks,
is a person one who both thunders and rains?"
"Here, monks, a certain person is both a speaker and a doer.
In this way, monks, a person is both a thunderer and a rainer,
just like that cloud, monks, which is both a thunderer and a rainer."
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
These, monks, are the four cloud-like persons existing and found in the world. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.102 11. Valāhakavagga The Second Discourse on Clouds “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clouds. What four? The cloud that rains down upon a single district; the cloud that rains down upon a whole country; the cloud that rains down upon the great ocean; and the cloud that rains down upon the great earth. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of clouds. “So too, bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons similar to clouds. What four? The person who rains down upon a single district; the person who rains down upon a whole country; the person who rains down upon the great ocean; and the person who rains down upon the great earth. “And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who rains down upon a single district? Here, someone has faith in the Buddha, but not in the Dhamma; he has faith in the Saṅgha, but not in the Dhamma; he has faith in the Dhamma, but not in the Saṅgha; he has faith in the Saṅgha, but not in the Dhamma; he has faith in the Dhamma, but not in the training; he has faith in the training, but not in the Dhamma. He does not have the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who rains down upon a single district. “And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who rains down upon a whole country? Here, someone has faith in the Buddha and in the Dhamma; he has faith in the Saṅgha and in the Dhamma; he has faith in the Dhamma and in the Saṅgha; he has faith in the Saṅgha and in the training; he has faith in the training and in the Dhamma. He has the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who rains down upon a whole country. “And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who rains down upon the great ocean? Here, someone has entered the stream, is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, is firmly established, and is destined for full enlightenment. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who rains down upon the great ocean. “And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who rains down upon the great earth? Here, someone is a non-returner, one who, having completely destroyed the five lower fetters, will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and will attain final nibbāna there without ever returning from that world. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who rains down upon the great earth. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons similar to clouds.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clouds. What are the four? [The Sutta continues with the description of each type.]”
Thundering but not raining;
raining but not thundering;
neither thundering nor raining.
The one that thunders but does not rain; the one that rains but does not thunder; the one that neither thunders nor rains; and the one that both thunders and rains. These, monks, are the four clouds.
In the same way, monks, there are four types of persons resembling clouds found existing in the world.
Which four?
One who thunders but does not rain; one who rains but does not thunder; [one who both thunders and rains]; and one who neither thunders nor rains.
Neither one who thunders but does not rain,
nor one who both thunders and rains.
And how, monks, is a person one who thunders but does not rain?
In this case, monks, a certain person masters the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and questions-and-answers—
but he does not understand, as it really is, "This is suffering," nor does he understand, as it really is, "This is the origin of suffering."
He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is one who thunders but does not rain.
"Just as, monks, that cloud thunders but does not rain,
even so, monks, do I describe this person. And how, monks,
is a person one who rains but does not thunder?"

Here, monks, a certain person does not master the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "Thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical expositions.
Yet he understands as it really is: “This is suffering” … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
In this way, monks, a person is one who rains but does not thunder.
Just as that cloud, monks, is one that rains but does not thunder,
even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person one who neither thunders nor rains?
Here, monks, a certain person does not master the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "Thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers.
Thus, one does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is neither a thunderer nor a rainer.
Just like that cloud, monks, which is neither a thunderer nor a rainer.
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
And how, monks, is a person one who both thunders and rains?
Here, monks, a certain person masters the Dhamma—”
The discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analyses.
He understands as it really is: “This is suffering” … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is both a thunderer and a rainer.
“Just as that cloud, monks, both thunders and rains,
even so, monks, do I describe this person. These, monks,
are the four types of persons resembling clouds who exist and are found in the world.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.103 11.
Valāhakavagga (The Chapter on Clouds)
Kumbhasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these four kinds of jars.”
Which four?
The empty and closed, the full and open, [the full and closed, and the empty and open].
Empty and open,
full and closed—
these, monks, are the four kinds of jars.

In the same way, monks, there are four types of persons comparable to jars found existing in the world. Which four? The empty and covered jar; [the empty and uncovered jar; the full and uncovered jar; and the full and covered jar].
An open vessel that is full,
an open vessel that is empty,
and a closed vessel that is full.
And how, monks, is a person empty yet covered?
Here, monks, a certain person’s advancing and retreating, looking forward and looking aside, drawing in and extending the limbs, and the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes are graceful.
Yet he does not understand as it really is: “This is suffering”; ... [and so on] ... he does not understand as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
"In this way, monks, a person is empty and covered.
Just as that jar, monks, is empty and covered,
even so, monks, do I describe this person."
And how, bhikkhus, is a person full yet open?

Here, bhikkhus, for a certain person, his advancing and retreating, looking forward and looking aside, bending and stretching, and his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe are not graceful.
Yet he understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, monks, a person is full and open.
Just as that jar, monks, is full and open,
even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person empty and exposed?

Here, monks, a certain person’s advancing and retreating, looking forward and looking away, drawing back and stretching forth, and his wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe are not inspiring.
He does not understand as it really is: “This is suffering”; ... [and so on] ... he does not understand as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
In this way, monks, a person is empty and exposed.
Just as that jar, monks, is empty and exposed,
even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person full yet covered?

Here, monks, a certain person is pleasing in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching, and in his manner of wearing the outer robe, the bowl, and the inner robe.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
In this way, monks, a person is full and covered,
just like that jar which is full and covered;
it is with such a simile, monks, that I speak of this person.
“Monks, these four types of persons, comparable to jars, are found existing in the world. Thus [ends] the third [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.104.

11. Valāhakavagga Udakarahadasutta (AN 4.104, AN 4.105, PTS AN ii 105) “Monks, suppose there were a pool of water that was clear, serene, and limpid. A person with good eyesight standing on the bank would see shells, gravel, and pebbles, as well as shoals of fish swimming about and resting. It would occur to him: ‘This pool of water is clear, serene, and limpid. Here there are shells, gravel, and pebbles, and here there are shoals of fish swimming about and resting. In the same way, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I am now possessed of faith, just as that pool of water is clear; I am now possessed of virtuous conduct, just as that pool of water is serene; I am now possessed of learning, just as that pool of water is limpid. Seeing this, he becomes even more intent upon the goal, thinking: ‘May I soon attain the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry!’”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four bodies of water. Which four?
One that is shallow but appears deep;”
The profound appearing superficial,
the superficial appearing superficial,
and the profound appearing profound.
“Monks, these are the four bodies of water.
In the same way, monks, there are four kinds of persons comparable to bodies of water found existing in the world.
Which four?”
Shallow yet appearing deep,
deep yet appearing shallow,
shallow and appearing shallow.
Profound yet appearing profound.
And how, monks, is a person shallow yet appearing profound?

Here, monks, a certain person’s manner of advancing and retreating, looking forward and looking aside, drawing in and extending the limbs, and carrying the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes is inspiring.
Thus, one does not understand as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... nor does one understand as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is shallow but appears deep, just like that pool of water, monks, which is shallow but appears deep.
“Monks, I say that this person is like that.
And how, monks, is a person deep but of superficial appearance?

Here, monks, a certain person’s going forth and returning, his looking ahead and looking aside, his drawing in and extending of the limbs, and his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes are not graceful.”
Thus, “This is suffering,” he understands as it really is …pe… “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,” he understands as it really is.
In this way, monks, a person is deep but appears shallow,
just like that pool of water, monks, which is deep but appears shallow.
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
And how, monks, is a person shallow and shallow in appearance?

Here, monks, a certain person’s advancing and retreating, looking ahead and looking aside, drawing back and stretching forth, and his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe are not inspiring.
Thus, one does not understand as it really is: “This is suffering” ... [and so on] ... one does not understand as it really is:
“This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. In this way, monks, a person is shallow and appears shallow, just like that pool of water, monks, which is shallow and appears shallow.
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
And how, monks, is a person deep and appearing deep?

Here, monks, a certain person’s advancing and retreating, looking ahead and looking aside, bending and stretching, and the manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robes are graceful and inspiring.”
Thus he understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is deep and appears deep, just like that pool of water, monks, which is deep and appears deep.
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
These, monks, are the four types of persons comparable to pools of water who are found existing in the world.
This is the fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.105 11.
Valāhakavagga Ambasutta (The Mango Sutta)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of mangoes. What are the four? [Text continues]”
The unripe appearing as ripe,
the ripe appearing as unripe,
and the unripe appearing as unripe.
"The ripe one with the appearance of being ripe—
these, monks, are the four mangoes.
In the same way, monks, there are these four types of persons resembling mangoes existing in the world."
Which four?
One that is raw but has the appearance of being ripe; one that is ripe but has the appearance of being raw.
The raw is of a raw appearance;
the ripe is of a ripe appearance.
And how, monks, is a person raw but of a ripe appearance?

“Here, monks, a certain person is pleasing in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching, and in his manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe.
Yet he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is unripe but has the appearance of being ripe.”
"Just as, monks, that mango might be unripe but have the color of a ripe one;
even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person ripe but with the color of the unripe?"

“Here, monks, a certain person’s manner of going forward and returning, looking ahead and looking aside, drawing in and extending the limbs, and carrying the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe is not inspiring.
Yet he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ …pe… he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is ripe but has the appearance of being unripe.”
“Just as, monks, that mango is ripe but has the color of the unripe—
so too, monks, do I describe this person. And how, monks,
is a person unripe and having the color of the unripe?

“Here, monks, a certain person’s going forth and returning, looking ahead and looking aside, drawing in and extending the limbs, and the manner of wearing the outer robe, bowl, and inner robe are not inspiring.
Such a one does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is unripe and has the appearance of being unripe.”
"Just as, monks, that mango is unripe and has the color of the unripe,
even so, monks, do I describe this person. And how, monks,
is a person ripe and has the color of the ripe?"

“Here, monks, a certain person’s going forth and returning, looking ahead and looking aside, drawing in and extending the limbs, and carrying the outer robe, bowl, and upper robe, are graceful and inspiring.
He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a person is ripe and has the appearance of being ripe.”
“Just as that mango, monks, is ripe and has the color of ripeness,
so too, monks, do I describe this person. These, monks,
are the four types of persons comparable to mangoes who exist and are found in the world.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.106 11.

so too, monks, do I describe this person. And how, monks,
is a person neither a maker of a burrow nor a dweller?"

In this case, monks, a certain person does not master the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "Thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and questions-and-answers.
He does not understand, as it really is, "This is suffering"... [and so on] ...he does not understand, as it really is, "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."
"In this way, monks, a person is neither a maker of a footing nor a dweller.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.108 11.
Valāhakavagga Balībaddasutta (The Discourse on the Oxen)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four oxen. Which four? [The text continues as follows:]”
One who is fierce toward his own cattle but not toward the cattle of others;
one who is fierce toward the cattle of others but not toward his own cattle;
and one who is fierce toward both his own cattle and the cattle of others.
"Neither fierce toward his own cattle nor fierce toward the cattle of others—
these, monks, are the four oxen.
In the same way, monks, there are these four types of persons resembling oxen who exist and are found in the world."
Which four?
One who is fierce toward his own cattle but not toward the cattle of others;
one who is fierce toward the cattle of others but not toward his own cattle; [and so on].
One who is fierce toward oneself and fierce toward others,
and one who is neither fierce toward oneself nor fierce toward others.
And how, monks, is a person fierce toward oneself but not fierce toward others?
"In this case, monks, a certain person intimidates his own assembly but not the assembly of others.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is fierce toward his own cattle but not fierce toward the cattle of others—
just like that ox, monks, who is fierce toward its own cattle but not fierce toward the cattle of others."
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
And how, monks, is a person fierce toward the cattle of others but not toward his own cattle?
Here, monks, a certain person is one who intimidates the assemblies of others, but not his own assembly.”
In this way, monks, a person is fierce toward the cattle of others, but not toward his own cattle.
Just as that ox, monks, is fierce toward the cattle of others but not toward its own,
even so, monks, I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person fierce toward his own cattle and fierce toward the cattle of others?
Here, monks, a certain person intimidates his own assembly and that of others.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is fierce toward his own cattle and fierce toward the cattle of others.
"Just as that ox, monks, is fierce toward his own cattle and fierce toward other cattle,
even so, monks, do I describe this person. And how, monks,
is a person neither fierce toward his own cattle nor fierce toward other cattle?"
In this case, monks, a certain person neither terrifies his own assembly nor that of others.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is neither fierce toward his own cattle nor fierce toward the cattle of others;
just as, monks, that ox is neither fierce toward its own cattle nor fierce toward the cattle of others.
“Monks, I say that this person is just like that.
These, monks, are the four types of persons comparable to oxen who exist and are found in the world.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.109 11. Valāhakavagga Rukkhasutta (The Discourse on the Tree) “Monks, there are these four kinds of trees. What four? The tree that bears fruit but does not yield its fruit; the tree that yields its fruit but does not bear fruit; the tree that both bears fruit and yields its fruit;

and the tree that neither bears fruit nor yields its fruit. These, monks, are the four kinds of trees. Just so, monks, there are these four kinds of persons similar to trees. What four? The person who bears the fruit of recluseship but does not yield its fruit; the person who yields the fruit of recluseship but does not bear its fruit; the person who both bears the fruit of recluseship and yields its fruit; and the person who neither bears the fruit of recluseship nor yields its fruit. And how, monks, is one a person who bears the fruit of recluseship but does not yield its fruit? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters. With the complete destruction of the three fetters and with the weakening of greed, hatred, and delusion, he is a once-returner who, after returning to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering. This, monks, is called a person who bears the fruit of recluseship but does not yield its fruit. And how, monks, is one a person who yields the fruit of recluseship but does not bear its fruit? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters. With the complete destruction of the three fetters, he is a non-returner who, having attained final knowledge in the interval, will make an end of suffering. This, monks, is called a person who yields the fruit of recluseship but does not bear its fruit. And how, monks, is one a person who both bears the fruit of recluseship and yields its fruit? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters. With the complete destruction of the three fetters, he is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, bound for enlightenment, assured, and destined to attain full awakening. This, monks, is called a person who both bears the fruit of recluseship and yields its fruit. And how, monks, is one a person who neither bears the fruit of recluseship nor yields its fruit? Here, monks, a certain person is possessed of unwholesome qualities and is far from wholesome qualities. This, monks, is called a person who neither bears the fruit of recluseship nor yields its fruit. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons similar to trees.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of trees. Which four? [The text continues as follows:]”
Softwood with a softwood retinue,
softwood with a hardwood retinue,
and hardwood with a softwood retinue.
The heartwood tree with a heartwood retinue—
these, monks, are the four kinds of trees.
In the same way, monks, there are these four types of persons comparable to trees existing in the world.
Which four?
One who is sapwood with a retinue of sapwood;
one who is sapwood with a retinue of heartwood.
There is the core surrounded by sapwood,
and the core surrounded by core.
And how, monks, is a person sapwood with sapwood as his retinue?
In this case, monks, a certain person is immoral and of evil character,
and his retinue is also immoral and of evil character.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is sapwood with a retinue of sapwood.
“Just as that tree, monks, has softwood with softwood surrounding it,
even so, monks, do I describe this person. And how, monks,
is a person softwood with hardwood surrounding him?”
In this case, monks, a certain person is immoral and of evil character,
yet his assembly is virtuous and of good character.
Thus, monks, such a person is like the soft inner bark with a core as its retinue.
“Just as that tree, monks, has softwood at its core but is surrounded by heartwood, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person heartwood with a surrounding of softwood? [The Buddha explains:]”
In this case, monks, a certain person is virtuous and of good character,
yet his retinue is immoral and of evil character.
Thus, monks, such a person is like a tree with a heartwood core surrounded by sapwood.
"Just as, monks, that tree has a heartwood surrounded by sapwood, even so, monks, do I describe this person.
And how, monks, is a person a heartwood-tree with a heartwood retinue? [As follows...]"
In this case, monks, a certain person is virtuous and of good character,
and his retinue is also virtuous and of good character.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is solid and has a solid retinue.
“Just as that tree, monks, has heartwood and is surrounded by heartwood,
even so, monks, do I describe this person.
These, monks, are the four types of persons comparable to trees who exist and are found in the world.”

The Discourse on the Venomous Snake (Āsīvisasutta): “Monks,
there are these four venomous snakes.”
Which four?
One whose venom has spread but is not virulent;
one whose venom is virulent but has not spread.
The one whose venom has spread and whose venom is fierce;
the one whose venom has not spread and whose venom is not fierce—
these, monks, are the four kinds of venomous snakes.
In the same way, monks, there are four types of persons resembling venomous snakes found existing in the world.
What are the four?
One whose venom has been ingested but whose venom is not fierce; [and so on].
One whose venom is fierce but not yet manifested,
one whose venom is both manifested and fierce,
and one whose venom is neither manifested nor fierce.
And how, monks, is a person one whose venom has been neutralized, yet is not of fierce venom?
Here, monks, a certain person frequently becomes angry,
yet that anger of his does not persist for a long time.
"In this way, monks, a person is one whose venom is slow to act but not fierce.
Just as that snake, monks, is one whose venom is slow to act but not fierce,
even so, monks, do I describe this person."
And how, monks, is a person one whose venom is fierce but whose venom does not spread?
Here, monks, a certain person does not indeed become angry frequently;
yet his anger persists for a long time.
"In this way, monks, a person is one whose venom is fierce but whose venom has not yet been released.
Just as that snake, monks, is one whose venom is fierce but whose venom has not yet been released,
even so, monks, do I describe this person."
And how, monks, is a person one whose venom is quick-acting and whose venom is fierce?
Here, monks, a certain person becomes angry frequently,
and that anger of his persists for a long time.
"In this way, monks, a person is one whose venom is both swift-acting and virulent.
Just as that viper, monks, has venom that is both swift-acting and virulent,
even so, monks, do I describe this person."
And how, monks, is a person one whose poison has not been ingested and who is not of fierce venom?
Here, monks, a certain person does not frequently become angry,
and that anger of his does not persist for a long time.
In this way, monks, a person is neither one whose venom has spread nor one with terrible venom.
Just as that snake, monks, is neither one whose venom has spread nor one with terrible venom,
even so, monks, do I describe this person.
“Monks, these four types of persons, comparable to venomous snakes, are found existing in the world.
The tenth [sutta].
The first chapter, the Chapter on Clouds.
Its summary verse:
Two clouds, a water-pot, water,
two lakes, and two mango trees.
The mouse, the ox, and the tree—
these were bitten by a venomous snake.

What five? Here, Kesi, one is virtuous; one dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults; having undertaken the training rules, one trains in them. One has learned much, remembers what has been heard, and accumulates what has been heard; these teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these, one has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well through view. Then Kesi, the trainer of horses, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As Kesi, the trainer of horses, was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Kesi, you are renowned as a trainer of horses.
But how, Kesi, do you train a horse?"
“Venerable sir, I train a horse to be tamed both gently, both harshly, and both gently and harshly.
“If, Kesi, your horse to be tamed does not submit to training through gentleness, nor to training through harshness, nor to training through both gentleness and harshness, what do you do with it?
“Venerable sir, if my horse to be tamed does not submit to training through gentleness, nor to training through harshness, nor to training through both gentleness and harshness;”
"I shall kill him, Bhante.
For what reason?
So that there may be no disrepute for my teacher's lineage."
“But, venerable sir, the Blessed One is the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
How, venerable sir, does the Blessed One train a man to be tamed?
“Kesi, I train a man to be tamed both gently, and I train him harshly, and I train him both gently and harshly.”
In this regard, Kesi, here is what is subtle:

"Such is good conduct of body; such is the result of good conduct of body. Such is good conduct of speech; such is the result of good conduct of speech. Such is good conduct of mind; such is the result of good conduct of mind. Such are the devas; such are human beings.
In this regard, Kesi, here is what is coarse:
"Such is bodily misconduct, such is the result of bodily misconduct; such is verbal misconduct, such is the result of verbal misconduct;
such is mental misconduct, such is the result of mental misconduct; such is hell, such is the animal realm, such is the sphere of hungry ghosts.
In this regard, Kesi, as for what is gentle and harsh:
Thus is bodily good conduct, thus is the result of bodily good conduct; thus is bodily misconduct, thus is the result of bodily misconduct;
thus is verbal good conduct, thus is the result of verbal good conduct; thus is verbal misconduct, thus is the result of verbal misconduct;
thus is mental good conduct, thus is the result of mental good conduct; thus is mental misconduct, thus is the result of mental misconduct.
“...there is ripening of karma; there are gods; there are humans; there is hell; there is the animal realm; there is the sphere of hungry ghosts.
“If, venerable sir, this person to be tamed is not disciplined by gentleness, nor disciplined by harshness, nor disciplined by both gentleness and harshness, what does the Blessed One do with him?
“If, Kesi, this person to be tamed is not disciplined by gentleness, nor disciplined by harshness, nor disciplined by both gentleness and harshness, then I kill him, Kesi.”
“Venerable sir, the taking of life is not permitted for the Blessed One.
And yet the Blessed One says:
‘I shall kill him, Kesī.’”
“It is true, Kesi.
Taking life is not permissible for a Tathāgata.
However, there is the person to be tamed who does not submit to gentle discipline, nor does he submit to harsh discipline, nor does he submit to discipline that is both gentle and harsh.”
He does not come to discipline; the Tathāgata does not consider him one who should be spoken to or instructed, nor do wise fellow-celibates consider him one who should be spoken to or instructed.
For this, Kesi, is a form of execution in the discipline of the Noble One.
"One whom the Tathāgata does not consider worthy of being instructed or exhorted, nor do wise fellow-celibates consider worthy of being instructed or exhorted.
"Indeed, Bhante, he is well-beaten—
one whom the Tathāgata does not consider worthy of being instructed or exhorted, nor do wise fellow-celibates consider worthy of being instructed or exhorted."
