12. Kesivagga Javasutta (AN 4.112, PTS AN ii 113) “Monks, there are these four speeds. What four? The speed of a foot-soldier, the speed of a chariot-warrior, the speed of a bird, and the speed of the wind. These, monks, are the four speeds. Of these four speeds, monks, the speed of the wind is declared to be the foremost. In the same way, monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is slow in both faith and wisdom; the person who is swift in faith but slow in wisdom; the person who is swift in wisdom but slow in faith; and the person who is swift in both faith and wisdom. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Of these four kinds of persons, monks, the one who is swift in both faith and wisdom is declared to be the foremost.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of four factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.
What are the four?
Straightness, speed, patience, and gentleness.”
“Monks, possessed of these four factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu possessed of four qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What are the four? [The text continues with the four qualities.]”
“By straightforwardness, by speediness, by patience, and by gentleness—
endowed with these four qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of gifts … he is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.113 12. Kesivagga Patodasutta (The Goad) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a goad; the person who is like a thorn; the person who is like a boil; and the person who is like a tree. And how, monks, is one a person like a goad? Here, monks, a certain person is well-behaved in body, speech, and mind, yet he does not encourage others to be well-behaved in body, speech, and mind. Just as a goad-stick is used to urge on an ox that is not walking, so too, monks, this is called a person like a goad. And how, monks, is one a person like a thorn? Here, monks, a certain person is himself corrupt in body, speech, and mind, and he encourages others to be corrupt in body, speech, and mind. Just as a thorn causes pain to the one who steps on it, so too, monks, this is called a person like a thorn. And how, monks, is one a person like a boil? Here, monks, a certain person is himself corrupt in body, speech, and mind, yet he does not encourage others to be corrupt in body, speech, and mind. Just as a boil is painful to the one who touches it, so too, monks, this is called a person like a boil. And how, monks, is one a person like a tree? Here, monks, a certain person is himself well-behaved in body, speech, and mind, and he encourages others to be well-behaved in body, speech, and mind. Just as a tree provides shade for those who sit beneath it, so too, monks, this is called a person like a tree. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four noble thoroughbred horses found existing in the world. What are the four? [The text continues as follows:]”
“Here, monks, a certain noble thoroughbred horse, upon seeing the shadow of the goad, is stirred and experiences a sense of urgency, thinking:
‘What task will the trainer have me perform today? How shall I respond?
Such, monks, is one kind of noble thoroughbred horse found here.”
This, monks, is the first noble thoroughbred horse found existing in the world.

Furthermore, monks, here a certain noble thoroughbred horse does not indeed experience a sense of urgency upon seeing the shadow of the goad; rather, he experiences a sense of urgency when pierced by the penetration of the hair:
"What task will the trainer of tame horses have for me today? How shall I respond to it?"
“Monks, such is one kind of noble thoroughbred horse found here.
This, monks, is the second kind of noble thoroughbred horse existing and found in the world.
Furthermore, monks, there is another kind of noble thoroughbred horse who, having seen the shadow of the goad, does not indeed [respond]...”
He does not experience such urgency as to feel a piercing through his hair; nor does he experience such urgency as to feel a piercing through his skin;
rather, he experiences such urgency as to feel a piercing through his hide, thinking:
"What task will the trainer of horses have for me today? How shall I respond to him?"
"Monks, such is one kind of noble thoroughbred horse found here.
This, monks, is the third noble thoroughbred horse existing and to be found in the world.
Furthermore, monks, there is another kind of noble thoroughbred horse who, indeed, does not [react] upon seeing the shadow of the goad..."
He does not experience a sense of urgency when pierced by the hair, nor does he experience a sense of urgency when pierced by the skin;
rather, it is only when pierced by the bone that he experiences a sense of urgency, thinking:
"What task will the trainer of horses have for me today? How shall I perform it?"
"Monks, such is one kind of noble thoroughbred horse found here.
This, monks, is the fourth noble thoroughbred horse existing and to be found in the world.
These, monks, are the four noble thoroughbred horses existing and to be found in the world."

"In the same way, monks, there are these four types of noble thoroughbred persons found existing in the world. What are the four? Here, monks, a certain noble thoroughbred person hears: "Monks, there is this one kind of person who is a speaker but not a doer. Having heard this, he reflects thus: "It would indeed be well for me to be a speaker and a doer, rather than a speaker but not a doer. He then trains himself accordingly, and by so training, he becomes a speaker and a doer. This, monks, is the first type of noble thoroughbred person found existing in the world. "Furthermore, monks, another noble thoroughbred person hears: 'Monks, there is this one kind of person who is a doer but not a speaker. Having heard this, he reflects thus: 'It would indeed be well for me to be a doer and a speaker, rather than a doer but not a speaker. He then trains himself accordingly, and by so training, he becomes a doer and a speaker. This, monks, is the second type of noble thoroughbred person found existing in the world. "Furthermore, monks, another noble thoroughbred person hears: 'Monks, there is this one kind of person who is neither a speaker nor a doer. Having heard this, he reflects thus: 'It would indeed be well for me to be neither a speaker nor a doer, rather than being neither a speaker nor a doer. He then trains himself accordingly, and by so training, he becomes neither a speaker nor a doer. This, monks, is the third type of noble thoroughbred person found existing in the world. "Furthermore, monks, another noble thoroughbred person hears: 'Monks, there is this one kind of person who is both a speaker and a doer. Having heard this, he reflects thus: 'It would indeed be well for me to be both a speaker and a doer, rather than being both a speaker and a doer. He then trains himself accordingly, and by so training, he becomes both a speaker and a doer. This, monks, is the fourth type of noble thoroughbred person found existing in the world."
‘In such and such a village or town, a woman or a man has fallen ill or has died.
Stirred by that, he experiences a sense of spiritual urgency.
Being stirred, he applies himself with wise effort.
Resolute in himself, he realizes the supreme truth with his own body and, having pierced through it with wisdom, sees it.
Just as that noble thoroughbred horse, monks, is stirred and moved upon seeing the shadow of the goad,
even so, monks, do I speak of this noble thoroughbred person.
"Monks, such is one kind of noble thoroughbred person found here in the world.
This, monks, is the first noble thoroughbred person existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, another kind of noble thoroughbred person here does not indeed hear: [that the Tathāgata has arisen in the world...]"
‘In such and such a village or town, a woman or a man has fallen ill or died,’ yet he himself sees a woman or a man who is ill or dead.
He is stirred by this, he experiences a sense of spiritual urgency.
Being stirred, he applies himself with wise effort.
Resolute in himself, he realizes the supreme truth with his very body and, having pierced through it with wisdom, sees it.
Just as that noble thoroughbred horse, monks, when struck by a hair-tuft, is stirred and experiences a sense of urgency,
even so, monks, do I speak of this noble thoroughbred person.
"Monks, such is one kind of noble thoroughbred person found here in the world.
This, monks, is the second noble thoroughbred person existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, there is another kind of noble thoroughbred person who does not indeed hear:"
‘In such and such a village or town, a woman or a man has fallen ill or has died,’ nor does he himself see a woman or a man who is ill or dead; rather,
it is a kinsman or a blood relative of his who is ill or dead.
Thus, by means of that, he becomes stirred; he experiences a sense of spiritual urgency.
Being stirred, he exerts himself with wise attention.
With resolute self, he realizes the supreme truth with the body and, having penetrated it with wisdom, he sees it.
"Just as, monks, that noble thoroughbred horse, pierced by the arrow of the whip, is stirred and experiences a sense of urgency,
even so, monks, do I speak of this noble thoroughbred person.
There is, monks, such a noble thoroughbred person here."
This, monks, is the third kind of excellent thoroughbred person found existing in the world.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain excellent thoroughbred person does not hear:
"In such-and-such a village or town, a woman or a man is suffering or has died."
Nor does he personally see a woman or a man who is suffering or deceased;

nor is his own relative or blood-kinsman suffering or deceased; rather, he himself is personally afflicted by bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
Thus, by means of that, he becomes stirred and experiences a sense of spiritual urgency.
Being stirred, he applies himself with wise reflection.
With resolute self, he realizes the supreme truth with his own body and, having penetrated it through wisdom, sees it.
"Just as, monks, that noble thoroughbred horse, when pierced by the goad, is stirred and experiences a sense of urgency,
even so, monks, do I speak of this noble thoroughbred person.
There is, monks, such a noble thoroughbred person here."
“This, monks, is the fourth kind of excellent thoroughbred person found existing in the world.
These, monks, are the four kinds of excellent thoroughbred persons found existing in the world.
This is the third [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.114 12. Kesivagga Nāgasutta (The Elephant) “Monks, there are these four kinds of elephants. What four? The elephant that is well-bred but not well-trained; the elephant that is well-bred and well-trained; the elephant that is neither well-bred nor well-trained; and the elephant that is neither well-bred nor well-trained, yet when struck by the goad, he bears it with patience. These, monks, are the four kinds of elephants. Just so, monks, there are these four kinds of persons similar to elephants.

What four? The person who is well-bred but not well-trained; the person who is well-bred and well-trained; the person who is neither well-bred nor well-trained; and the person who is neither well-bred nor well-trained, yet when struck by the goad, he bears it with patience. And how, monks, is a person well-bred but not well-trained? Here, monks, a certain person is of noble birth—of high lineage, of pure descent for seven generations back, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth—but he is not one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, having shaved off his hair and beard, putting on the saffron robes, and entered the training in the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata. This, monks, is called a person who is well-bred but not well-trained. And how, monks, is a person well-bred and well-trained? Here, monks, a certain person is of noble birth—of high lineage, of pure descent for seven generations back, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth—and he is one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, having shaved off his hair and beard, putting on the saffron robes, and entered the training in the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata. This, monks, is called a person who is well-bred and well-trained. And how, monks, is a person neither well-bred nor well-trained? Here, monks, a certain person is of lowly birth—of poor lineage, descended from a long line of menial laborers, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth—but he is not one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, having shaved off his hair and beard, putting on the saffron robes, and entered the training in the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata. This, monks, is called a person who is neither well-bred nor well-trained. And how, monks, is a person neither well-bred nor well-trained, yet when struck by the goad, he bears it with patience? Here, monks, a certain person is of lowly birth—of poor lineage, descended from a long line of menial laborers, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth—and he is not one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, having shaved off his hair and beard, putting on the saffron robes, and entered the training in the Dhamma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata. But when reproached by others, he does not respond with reproach; when struck, he does not respond with striking; when scolded, he does not respond with scolding; and when threatened, he does not respond with threatening. This, monks, is called a person who is neither well-bred nor well-trained, yet when struck by the goad, he bears it with patience. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons similar to elephants.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing four factors, a king’s elephant is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What are the four? [The text continues with the description of these four qualities.]”
In this case, monks, a king’s elephant is one who listens, strikes back, endures, and advances.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant one who listens?
Here, monks, whatever task the elephant trainer makes him perform—
Whether it has been done before or not done before,
he attends to that bone, brings it to mind, focuses his entire mind upon it, and listens with an attentive ear.
In this way, monks, the king’s elephant is a listener.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant a slayer?
Here, monks, when a king’s elephant has entered battle, it slays elephants and elephant-riders; it slays horses and horse-riders; it slays chariots and chariot-warriors; it slays foot-soldiers.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is a slayer.
And how, monks, is a king’s elephant patient?

Here, monks, when the king’s elephant has entered the battle, it is patient with blows from spears, blows from swords, blows from javelins, blows from axes, and with the loud clamor of drums, kettledrums, conchs, and cymbals.
It is in this way, monks, that a king’s elephant is patient.
And how, monks, does a king’s elephant go? Here, monks, the king’s elephant goes to whatever direction the elephant trainer sends him—
whether it be a place he has gone before or one he has not gone before.
He goes with great speed.
In this way, monks, a king’s elephant is one who goes.
Endowed with these four factors, monks, a king’s elephant is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with four qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
What are the four?
Here, monks, a monk is a listener, a slayer, a patient, and a goer.
And how, monks, is a monk a listener?

Here, monks, when the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is being taught, a monk listens to the Dhamma with his bones set, his mind set, attending with his whole heart, and with his ear bent forward.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is a listener.
And how, monks, is a monk a slayer?

Here, monks, a monk does not tolerate a thought of sensual desire that has arisen; he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent. [He does not tolerate] a thought of ill will that has arisen... [he does not tolerate] a thought of cruelty that has arisen.
...pe... whatever evil, unwholesome states arise, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, destroys them, brings them to an end, and makes them cease to exist.
In this way, monks, a monk is a destroyer.
And how, monks, is a monk patient?
In this case, monks, a monk is patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
he is one who is accustomed to enduring arisen bodily feelings that are painful,
racking, sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
In this way, monks, a monk is one who endures.
And how, monks, is a monk one who goes?
Here, monks, a monk has not previously gone to that direction which, throughout this long course of time, is the stilling of all formations.
The relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—he is one who goes swiftly to that.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is a goer.
Endowed with these four qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
The Fourth.

Ṭhānasutta (AN 4.115, PTS AN ii 118):
“Bhikkhus, there are these four grounds.”
Which four? There is, monks, a case where one does what is disagreeable;
and that which is being done leads to harm.
"There is, monks, a case of doing what is unpleasant,
yet that which is being done leads to one's welfare.
There is, monks, a case of doing what is pleasant..."
And that which is being done leads to what is harmful.
There is, monks, a case where it is pleasant to do something;
and that which is being done leads to what is beneficial.
In this regard, monks, that which is an unpleasant thing to do,
and which, when done, leads to harm—
this, monks, is considered a situation where one should not act for either reason.
Thinking, "This is an unpleasant thing to do," he considers that it should not be done for this reason as well. Thinking,
"This matter, if carried out, leads to harm," [he considers that it should not be done].
By this [reason] as well, he considers that it should not be done.
Monks, this is a case where he considers that it should not be done for both reasons.
In that regard, monks, as for this matter which is unpleasant to do:
And that which is being done leads to welfare—
in this matter, monks, one should understand the difference between the fool and the wise man by way of human strength, human energy, and human exertion.
For the fool, monks, does not reflect thus:
‘Although this matter is unpleasant to do, nevertheless,
if it were done, it would lead to one’s welfare. Thus, he does not do that thing.
If that course is not undertaken by him, it leads to his harm.
But a wise person, monks, reflects thus:
‘Although this course is unpleasant to do;’
‘Now, if this matter is carried out, it will lead to one’s welfare,’ he carries out that matter.
That matter, being carried out, leads to his welfare.
In this regard, monks, there is a case where a thing that is pleasant to do,
when being done, leads to harm—
in this matter too, monks, the fool and the wise man are to be distinguished by their human strength, human energy, and human exertion.
Monks, a fool does not reflect thus:
"Although this matter may be pleasant to do, nevertheless, when it is done, it leads to harm."
Thus he performs that action.
That action being performed leads to his harm.
But a wise person, monks, reflects thus:
‘Even though this matter might be pleasant to do, nevertheless,
if it were done, it would lead to harm. Thus, he does not do that thing.
That state, when not performed by him, conduces to his welfare. But herein, monks,
that state which is pleasant to perform, when performed, conduces to his welfare—
it is this state, monks, that he considers as something to be done for both reasons.
"Whatever matter is pleasant to do, he thinks it should be done for this reason;
whatever matter, when being done, conduces to one's welfare, he thinks it should be done for this reason.
This, monks, is the matter that he thinks should be done for both reasons."
“Monks, these indeed are the four positions.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.116

12. Kesivagga: Appamādasutta (AN 4.116, PTS AN ii 119) “Monks, diligence is the path to the deathless; negligence is the path to death. Those who are diligent do not die; those who are negligent are as if already dead.”
“Bhikkhus, diligence should be practiced for four reasons.
What are the four?
Abandon bodily misconduct, bhikkhus, and cultivate bodily good conduct;”
And in that regard, do not be negligent.
Abandon verbal misconduct, monks; cultivate verbal good conduct;
and in that regard, do not be negligent.
“Monks, abandon misconduct of the mind; cultivate good conduct of the mind, and do not be negligent therein.
Monks, abandon wrong view; cultivate right view.”
And in this matter, do not be negligent.
For when, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned misconduct of body and cultivated good conduct of body;
has abandoned misconduct of speech and cultivated good conduct of speech; and has abandoned misconduct of mind and cultivated good conduct of mind—
“...when wrong view has been abandoned and right view has been developed, he does not fear death in the future life.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.117

12. Kesivagga Ārakkhasutta (AN 4.117, PTS AN ii 120) “Monks, there are these five dangers in guarding [one’s possessions]. What five? First, monks, one who guards [possessions] experiences fear and anxiety. Second, monks, one who guards [possessions] incurs enmity and hostility. Third, monks, one who guards [possessions] incurs legal disputes. Fourth, monks, one who guards [possessions] incurs feverish distress. Fifth, monks, one who guards [possessions] goes to a state of deprivation after death. These, monks, are the five dangers in guarding [one’s possessions].”
“Bhikkhus, in four instances one should, for one’s own sake, practice heedfulness, maintain mindfulness, and guard the mind.
In which four?
‘May my mind not become lustful toward things that provoke lust’—in this way, for one’s own sake, one should practice heedfulness, maintain mindfulness, and guard the mind.
Thinking, "May my mind not become corrupted by things that cause corruption," one should, for one's own sake, practice diligence, mindfulness, and the guarding of the mind.
Thinking, "May my mind not be deluded by things that cause delusion," one should, for one's own sake, practice diligence, mindfulness, and the guarding of the mind.
Thinking, "May my mind not become intoxicated by things that cause intoxication," one should, for one's own sake, practice diligence, mindfulness, and the guarding of the mind.
But when, monks, a bhikkhu’s mind does not become lustful toward things that provoke lust because he is free from lust;

his mind does not become corrupt toward things that provoke hatred because he is free from hatred; his mind does not become deluded toward things that provoke delusion because he is free from delusion;
and his mind does not become intoxicated by things that provoke intoxication because he is free from intoxication—he does not tremble.
"He does not tremble, he does not shake, he does not fall into fear, nor does he go even for the sake of a recluse’s words.
Thus ends the seventh [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.118.

12. Kesivagga Saṁvejanīyasutta (AN 4.118, PTS AN ii 120) “Monks, there are these five things that cause a sense of spiritual urgency. What five? First, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I am subject to aging; I have not transcended aging. But those beings who have practiced the holy life well, performed what was to be done, laid aside the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and become liberated through final knowledge—they have transcended aging. This, monks, is the first thing that causes a sense of spiritual urgency. Second, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I am subject to illness; I have not transcended illness. But those beings who have practiced the holy life well... they have transcended illness. This, monks, is the second thing that causes a sense of spiritual urgency. Third, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I am subject to death; I have not transcended death. But those beings who have practiced the holy life well... they have transcended death. This, monks, is the third thing that causes a sense of spiritual urgency. Fourth, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I must experience the loss of relatives; I have not transcended the loss of relatives. But those beings who have practiced the holy life well... they have transcended the loss of relatives. This, monks, is the fourth thing that causes a sense of spiritual urgency. Fifth, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I must experience the loss of wealth; I have not transcended the loss of wealth. But those beings who have practiced the holy life well... they have transcended the loss of wealth. This, monks, is the fifth thing that causes a sense of spiritual urgency. These, monks, are the five things that cause a sense of spiritual urgency.”
“Monks, there are these four places that a clansman endowed with faith should visit and find stirring.
What are the four?
‘Here the Tathāgata was born,’ monks, is a place that a clansman endowed with faith should visit and find stirring.”
‘Here the Tathāgata fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,’ monks, is a place worthy of being seen and stirring the heart for a faithful clansman.
‘Here the Tathāgata set in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma,’ monks, is a place worthy of being seen and stirring the heart for a faithful clansman.
‘Here the Tathāgata attained final Nibbāna by the Nibbāna-element without residue,’ monks, is a place worthy of being seen and stirring the heart for a faithful clansman.
“Monks, these are the four places that a clansman endowed with faith should visit and find inspiring.
The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.119

12. Kesivagga The Second Discourse on Fear (Dutiyabhayasutta) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five fears that have not yet arisen which will arise in the future, and for the most part they will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, for the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. What five? (1) ‘In the future, there will be monks who, having abandoned the training and returned to the lower life, will engage in sexual intercourse. This is the first fear that has not yet arisen which will arise in the future, and for the most part it will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, for the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. (2) ‘In the future, there will be monks who, having abandoned the training and returned to the lower life, will take what is not given. This is the second fear... (3) ‘In the future, there will be monks who, having abandoned the training and returned to the lower life, will tell lies. This is the third fear... (4) ‘In the future, there will be monks who, having abandoned the training and returned to the lower life, will indulge in intoxicants, liquor, and fermented spirits, which are the basis for negligence. This is the fourth fear... 13. The Chapter on Fear:
Discourse on Self-Blame (Attānuvādasutta) (AN 4.121, PTS AN ii 121)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four fears. Which four?
The fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of an unhappy destination.”
And what, monks, is the fear of self-reproach?
Here, monks, a certain person reflects thus:
"If I were to engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind, how could my own self not reproach me for my moral conduct?"
Thus, fearing the dread of self-reproach, one abandons bodily misconduct and develops good bodily conduct;
one abandons verbal misconduct and develops good verbal conduct; one abandons mental misconduct and develops good mental conduct; and one maintains oneself in purity.
This, monks, is called the dread of self-reproach.
And what, bhikkhus, is the fear of being censured by others?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person reflects thus:
‘If I were to engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, why would others not censure me for my moral conduct?’”
Thus, being afraid of the fear of reproach by others, one abandons bodily misconduct and develops good bodily conduct;
abandons verbal misconduct and develops good verbal conduct; abandons mental misconduct and develops good mental conduct; and maintains oneself in purity.
This, monks, is called the fear of reproach by others.
And what, monks, is the fear of punishment?
Here, monks, someone sees a thief, a wrongdoer, whom kings have arrested and are subjecting to various forms of torture—
beating him with whips, beating him with canes, beating him with clubs, or cutting off his hand.
Even when they cut off his feet, or cut off his hands and feet, or cut off his ears, or cut off his nose, or cut off both his ears and nose;

even when they make him a *bilaṅgathālika* (one who eats from a skull), or make him a *saṅkhamuṇḍika* (one with a conch-shell-shaven head), or make him a *rāhumukha* (one with a mouth like Rāhu’s), or make him a *jotimālika* (one wearing a garland of fire),
or make him a *hatthapajjotika* (one who carries a torch in his hand), or make him an *erakavattika* (one who wraps himself in *eraka* grass).
They even made them wear garments of bark; they made them wear the skin of an antelope; they made them wear fishhooks as ornaments; they made them wear coins as ornaments;

they made them undergo the punishment of being scraped with salt and wood-shavings; they made them undergo the punishment of rolling over a crossbar; they made them undergo the punishment of sitting on a straw-mat;
they drenched them with boiling oil; they had them devoured by dogs; and they impaled them alive upon stakes.
Even when his head is being cut off with a sword,
it occurs to him:
“It is for the sake of such evil deeds that kings, having seized a thief who has committed a crime, inflict various forms of punishment.”
They cause [others] to be punished; they beat them with whips... even they cut off their heads with swords.
"If I were to commit such an evil deed, kings would also seize me and subject me to various kinds of punishments:
they would beat me with whips, they would beat me with canes, they would beat me with split bamboo rods, and they would cut off my hands and my feet."
They might cut off his hands, they might cut off his feet, they might cut off his ears, they might cut off his nose, they might cut off both his ears and his nose;
they might make him undergo the *bilaṅgathālika* torture, they might make him undergo the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* torture;

they might make him undergo the *rāhumukha* torture, they might make him undergo the *jotimālika* torture, they might make him undergo the *hatthapajjotika* torture, or they might make him undergo the *erakavattika* torture.
They might subject one to the "rag-robe" punishment, they might subject one to the "eneya-deer" punishment,

they might subject one to the "fish-hook" punishment, they might subject one to the "kahāpaṇa" punishment, they might subject one to the "caustic-scratch" punishment, they might subject one to the "rolling-pin" punishment,
they might subject one to the "straw-mat" punishment; they might douse one with boiling oil, or they might have one devoured by dogs.
‘They might impale him alive on a stake or even cut off his head with a sword.
Fearing the threat of punishment, he does not wander about plundering the property of others.
Abandoning bodily misconduct... [and so on] ...he maintains himself in purity.
This, monks, is called the fear of punishment.
And what, monks, is the fear of an evil destination?
Here, monks, a certain person reflects thus:
‘There is indeed an evil result in the future life for misconduct of body, an evil result in the future life for misconduct of speech, and an evil result in the future life for misconduct of mind.
Now, if I were to engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, why should I not—
upon the dissolution of the body after death— fall into a state of deprivation, a bad destination?’
‘May I not fall into ruin and be reborn in hell.
Fearing the danger of an unhappy destination, he abandons bodily misconduct and develops good bodily conduct;
he abandons verbal misconduct and develops good verbal conduct; he abandons mental misconduct and develops good mental conduct, and thus maintains himself in purity.
“This, monks, is called the fear of an unhappy destination.
These, monks, are the four fears. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.122 13. Bhayavagga Ūmibhayasutta – The Discourse on the Fear of Waves “Monks, there are these four fears. What four? The fear of waves, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools, and the fear of sharks. These, monks, are the four fears.

Just as, monks, when a great rain cloud has arisen and a man standing on the bank of a river sees a wave approaching, he thinks: ‘If I do not get out of the way quickly, I shall be struck by this wave and swept away. Thus, monks, does that person experience fear and terror. But when he has gotten out of the way, he no longer experiences fear and terror. In the same way, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘There is the fear of waves within this body; it is not easy to overcome the fear of waves. This, monks, is called the fear of waves. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘There is the fear of crocodiles within this body; it is not easy to overcome the fear of crocodiles. This, monks, is called the fear of crocodiles. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘There is the fear of whirlpools within this body; it is not easy to overcome the fear of whirlpools. This, monks, is called the fear of whirlpools. Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘There is the fear of sharks within this body; it is not easy to overcome the fear of sharks. This, monks, is called the fear of sharks. These, monks, are the four fears. But when, monks, a noble disciple has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust for the form element, the feeling element, the perception element, the volitional formations element, and the consciousness element; when he has abandoned ignorance and given rise to true knowledge, then he has crossed over the flood, gone beyond the mire, and reached the further shore. He is called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.”
“Monks, there are these four fears to be expected for one who descends into water. Which four? [The text continues as follows:]”
The fear of waves, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools,
and the fear of sharks— these, monks, are the four fears to be expected by one who enters the water.
In the same way, monks, these four fears are to be expected here for a certain son of good family who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Which four?
The fear of waves, the fear of crocodiles, the fear of whirlpools, and the fear of sharks.
And what, monks, is the fear of waves?
“Here, monks, a certain clansman goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be discerned.’”
When he has thus gone forth, his fellow celibates advise and instruct him:
“In this way you should step forward; in this way you should step back; in this way you should look ahead; in this way you should look aside; in this way you should bend your limbs;
in this way you should stretch them out; in this way you should wear your outer robe, bowl, and upper robe.”
It occurs to him:
“Formerly, when we were householders, we used to exhort and instruct others.
But now these people—whom I consider as my own sons or grandsons—think that it is they who ought to exhort and instruct me.”
Thus, being angry and displeased, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
This, monks, is called a monk who, terrified by the fear of waves, has renounced the training and reverted to the lower life.
"The fear of waves," monks, is a designation for anger and resentment.

This, monks, is called the danger of waves. And what, monks, is the danger of crocodiles? Here, monks, a certain son of good family, out of faith, goes forth from the home life into homelessness, thinking: [“I am subject to birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and defilement; I am subject to suffering, oppressed by suffering, overwhelmed by suffering; I am not exempt from the nature of suffering. He thus understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Having understood this as it really is, he develops the path leading to the cessation of suffering. While he is developing the path leading to the cessation of suffering, he does not experience revulsion toward suffering; because he does not experience revulsion toward suffering, his mind does not incline toward dispassion; because his mind does not incline toward dispassion, he does not attain final knowledge. This, monks, is called the danger of crocodiles. And what, monks, is the danger of whirlpools? Here, monks, a certain son of good family, out of faith, goes forth from the home life into homelessness... [as above] ...he does not attain final knowledge. “I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.
When he has thus gone forth, his fellow celibates exhort and instruct him:
‘This is for you to eat; this is not for you to eat. This is for you to consume; this is not for you to consume.
This is for you to taste; this is not for you to taste. This is for you to drink; this is not for you to drink.
What is allowable (kappiya) is for you to eat; what is unallowable is not for you to eat. What is allowable is for you to consume; what is unallowable...’
That which is allowable for you must be eaten; that which is not allowable for you must not be tasted.
That which is allowable for you must be drunk; that which is not allowable for you must not be drunk. At the proper time, it must be chewed; at an improper time, it must not be chewed.
At the proper time, it must be eaten; at an improper time, it must not be eaten. At the proper time, it must be tasted; at an improper time, it must not...
‘This must be eaten; this may be drunk by you at the proper time; this must not be drunk by you at the improper time.
Then it occurs to him:
‘Formerly, when we were householders, we ate whatever we desired and did not eat what we did not desire;’
Whatever we desire, that we eat; whatever we do not desire, that we do not eat.
Whatever we desire, that we chew; whatever we do not desire, that we do not chew.
Whatever we desire, that we drink; whatever we do not desire, that we do not drink.
We eat what is allowable and we eat what is unallowable; we consume what is allowable and we consume what is unallowable;
we taste what is allowable and we taste what is unallowable; we drink what is allowable and we drink what is unallowable; we eat at the proper time and we eat at the improper time;
we consume at the proper time and we consume at the improper time; we taste at the proper time and we taste at the improper time; we drink at the proper time and we drink at the improper time.
‘Even when faithful householders give us exquisite staple and non-staple food during the day or at the wrong time, these fellows seem to me to be making a screen for their mouths!
Thus, angry and displeased, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
This, monks, is called a monk who, out of fear of crocodiles, has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
“Monks, ‘the fear of crocodiles’ is a designation for gluttony.
This, monks, is called the fear of crocodiles.
And what, monks, is the fear of whirlpools?”
“Here, monks, a certain son of good family goes forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
‘I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs. I am immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering.
Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.’”
Having thus gone forth, at the time of the morning he dresses himself, takes his bowl and robe,
and enters a village or town for alms with body unguarded, speech unguarded, mind unguarded, with mindfulness unestablished,
and sense faculties unrestrained.
There he sees a householder or a householder’s son endowed with, possessed of, and enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure.
It occurs to him:
“Formerly, when we were householders, we too were endowed with, possessed of, and enjoyed the five cords of sensual pleasure.”
"Indeed, there are riches in my family;
it is possible both to enjoy wealth and to perform meritorious deeds.
What if I were to renounce the training, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds?"
Thus, having renounced the training, he returns to the lower life.
This, monks, is called a monk who, fearing the danger of the whirlpool, has renounced the training and returned to the lower life.
"The danger of the whirlpool," monks, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
This, monks, is called the danger of whirlpools.
And what, monks, is the danger of crocodiles?
Here, monks, a certain son of good family, out of faith, goes forth from the household life into homelessness, thinking: [“I am subject to death; I am not exempt from death”].
“I am immersed in birth, aging, and death; in sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs.
Immersed in suffering, overcome by suffering, perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering might be known.
Having thus gone forth, he dresses in the morning, takes his bowl and robe, and enters a village or town.
Or he enters for alms with body unguarded, speech unguarded, mind unguarded, with mindfulness unestablished,
and sense faculties unrestrained.
There, he sees women dressed immodestly or improperly clad.
Seeing a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust overcomes his mind.
With a mind overcome by lust, he renounces the training and reverts to the lower life.
This, monks, is called a monk who, out of fear of the crocodile, has renounced the training and reverted to the lower life.
“Monks, ‘fear of the shark’ is a designation for womenfolk.
This, monks, is called the fear of the shark.
These, monks, are the four fears that may be expected here by a certain son of good family who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.123 13.
Bhayavagga (The Chapter on Fear)
The First Discourse on Differentiation (Paṭhamanānākaraṇasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these four types of persons found existing in the world.”
Which four?

Here, monks, a certain person, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
He relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
Established therein, intent upon that, dwelling frequently therein, and not falling away from it, one who passes away is reborn in the company of the deities of Brahma’s retinue.
The lifespan of the deities of Brahma’s retinue, monks, is an eon.

Therein, an ordinary person, having remained for as long as their life lasts and having exhausted the entire measure of the lifespan of those deities, may go to hell, may go to the animal realm, or may go to the sphere of hungry ghosts.

But a disciple of the Blessed One, having remained there for as long as his lifespan lasts, and having exhausted the entire measure of the life-span of those devas, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.

This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intent, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, with respect to their destination and rebirth.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, [attains] internal serenity...
With the one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
He relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
Established therein, devoted thereto, dwelling frequently therein, and not falling away from it, when he passes away, he is reborn in the company of the Ābhassara devas.
“Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the Ābhassara devas is two eons.

Therein, an ordinary person (puthujjana), having remained for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, may go to hell, may go to the animal realm, or may go to the sphere of hungry ghosts.
But the Blessed One’s disciple, having remained there for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.”

"This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, with regard to their destination and rebirth.

Furthermore, monks, here a certain person, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He who is equanimous..."
Possessing mindfulness and dwelling in happiness, he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
He relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
Established therein, intent upon it, frequently dwelling therein, and not falling away from it, when he passes away, he is reborn in the company of the Subhakiṇha devas.
“Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the Subhakiṇha devas is four eons.

Therein, an ordinary person (puthujjana), having remained for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, may go to hell, may go to the animal realm, or may go to the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).
But a disciple of the Blessed One, having remained there for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.”
This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling,
namely, with regard to their destination and rebirth. Furthermore, monks, here a certain person, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain,
and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
He enters and dwells in that jhāna.
He relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
Established therein, intent upon it, dwelling frequently therein, and not falling away from it, when he passes away, he is reborn in the company of the Vehapphala devas.
“Bhikkhus, the lifespan of the Vehapphala devas is five hundred eons.

Therein, an ordinary person (puthujjana), having remained for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, goes to hell, goes to the animal realm, or goes to the sphere of hungry ghosts.
But a disciple of the Blessed One, having remained there for the full extent of his life and having exhausted the entire lifespan of those devas, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.”

“This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, with regard to their destination and rebirth.
These, monks, are the four persons found existing in the world. This is the third [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.124 13. Bhayavagga The Second Discourse on Differentiation “Monks, there are these four differentiations. What four? The differentiation of faith, the differentiation of virtue, the differentiation of generosity, and the differentiation of wisdom. These, monks, are the four differentiations. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, is there the differentiation of faith? How is there the differentiation of virtue? How is there the differentiation of generosity? And how is there the differentiation of wisdom? “Here, monk, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This, monk, is called the differentiation of faith. Furthermore, he possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.

This, monk, is called the differentiation of faith. Furthermore, he possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This, monk, is called the differentiation of faith. Furthermore, he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, not adhered to, leading to concentration. This, monk, is called the differentiation of virtue. Furthermore, he is generous, one who dwells as an open-handed giver, one who delights in relinquishing, one who is at home with his hand extended, one who enjoys giving and sharing. This, monk, is called the differentiation of generosity. Furthermore, he possesses wisdom; he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monk, is called the differentiation of wisdom. These, monk, are the four differentiations. When this was said, that monk said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these four differentiations. “Indeed, monk, it is so. It is wonderful, monk, it is amazing, monk, how well this has been stated by the Tathāgata: ‘There are these four differentiations. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four differentiations. What four? The differentiation of faith, the differentiation of virtue, the differentiation of generosity, and the differentiation of wisdom. These, monks, are the four differentiations. “Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;”
Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself,
he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus he relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
Established therein, intent upon that, dwelling frequently therein, and not falling away from it, when he passes away, he is reborn into the company of the deities of Brahma’s retinue.
Monks, the lifespan of the deities of Brahma’s retinue is an eon.

In that regard, an ordinary person (puthujjana), having remained there for the duration of his lifespan and having exhausted the entire measure of the life-span of those devas, may go even to hell, may go to the animal realm, or may go to the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).

But a disciple of the Blessed One, having remained there for the duration of his lifespan and having exhausted the entire measure of the life-span of those devas, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.

“This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intention, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, with respect to their destination and rebirth.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person, with a mind accompanied by compassion … [as before] … with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy … [as before] …”
With a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Thus he relishes it, desires it, and finds satisfaction in it.
Established therein, intent upon it, dwelling frequently in that state, and not falling away from it, when he passes away, he is reborn into the company of the Ābhassara devas.
The lifespan of the Ābhassara devas, monks, is two eons... [and so on] ...he is reborn into the company of the Subhakiṇha devas.
“Bhikkhus, the life span of the Subhakiṇha devas is four eons... [and so on] ...he is reborn in the company of the Vehapphala devas.
Bhikkhus, the life span of the Vehapphala devas is five hundred eons.

Therein, the worldling, having remained for the full length of his life and having exhausted the entire life span of those devas, goes to hell, goes to the animal realm, and goes to the sphere of hungry ghosts.”

But a disciple of the Blessed One, having remained there for as long as his lifespan lasts and having exhausted the entire measure of the life-span of those devas, attains final nibbāna in that very same existence.

This, monks, is the distinction, this is the specific intent, this is the difference between an instructed noble disciple and an uninstructed worldling, namely, with respect to their destination and rebirth.

The First Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata (Paṭhamatathāgataacchariyasutta): “Bhikkhus,
with the manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, four marvelous and wonderful qualities become manifest.”
Which four? When, monks, the Bodhisatta, passing away from the Tusita host, descends into his mother’s womb mindful and clearly comprehending,
then, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—
An immeasurable, sublime radiance appears, surpassing even the divine majesty of the gods.
Even in those intermediate spaces between worlds— void, unsheltered, and shrouded in blinding darkness where even the light of the sun and moon,
despite their such great power and majesty, does not reach— even there, an immeasurable, sublime radiance appears.
It becomes manifest, surpassing even the divine power of the devas.
And those beings who have been reborn there also recognize one another by that light, saying:
"Indeed, friends, there are other beings who have been reborn here as well."
Monks, with the manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, this first wonderful and marvelous quality becomes manifest. Furthermore, monks,
when the Bodhisatta issues from his mother’s womb mindful and clearly comprehending,
then, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—
A measureless, sublime radiance appears, surpassing even the divine power of the devas.
Even in those intermediate spaces between worlds— void, unsheltered, and shrouded in blinding darkness where even the light of the moon and sun,
despite their such great majesty and power, does not reach— even there, a measureless, sublime radiance appears.
It becomes manifest, surpassing even the divine power of the devas.
Those beings who have been reborn there also recognize one another by that light, saying:
"Indeed, friends, there are other beings who have been reborn here as well."
Monks, with the manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, this second wonderful and marvelous quality becomes manifest. Furthermore, monks,
when a Tathāgata awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
then, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—
An immeasurable, sublime radiance appears, surpassing even the divine majesty of the devas.
Even in those intermediate spaces between worlds— void, unsheltered, and shrouded in blinding darkness where even the light of these suns and moons,
so powerful and majestic, does not reach— an immeasurable, sublime radiance appears.
It becomes manifest, surpassing even the divine power of the devas.
Those beings who have been reborn there also recognize one another by that light, saying:
"Indeed, friends, there are other beings who have been reborn here as well."
Monks, with the manifestation of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this third wonderful and marvelous quality becomes manifest. Furthermore, monks,
when the Tathāgata sets in motion the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma,
then in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, an immeasurable and sublime [radiance]...
A radiance appears, surpassing even the divine power of the devas.
Even in those intermediate spaces between worlds— void, open, and shrouded in blinding darkness where even the light of these suns and moons,
so mighty and powerful, does not reach— there too an immeasurable and sublime radiance appears.
It becomes manifest, surpassing even the splendor of the devas.
And those beings who have been reborn there recognize one another by that light, saying:
"Indeed, friends, there are other beings who have also been reborn here."
“Monks, with the manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, this fourth astounding and wonderful quality becomes manifest.

Bhayavagga Dutiyatathāgataacchariyasutta (The Second Discourse on the Marvels of the Tathāgata) “Monks, there are these four marvels in the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, concerning which those who have not heard them from others might well be struck with wonder.

What four? (1) “It may be, monks, that some person here has seen the Tathāgata face-to-face, and yet they do not know him as he really is: ‘This is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) “It may be, monks, that some person here has heard of the Tathāgata from others, and yet they do not know him as he really is: ‘This is the Blessed One... the Buddha, the Blessed One. (3) “It may be, monks, that some person here has neither seen the Tathāgata face-to-face nor heard of him from others, and yet they do not know him as he really is: ‘This is the Blessed One... the Buddha, the Blessed One. (4) “It may be, monks, that some person here has neither seen the Tathāgata face-to-face nor heard of him from others, but nevertheless they know him as he really is: ‘This is the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. These, monks, are the four marvels in the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, concerning which those who have not heard them from others might well be struck with wonder.”
“Bhikkhus, with the manifestation of a Tathāgata,
an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, four wonderful and marvelous qualities become manifest.
What are the four?
“Monks, this generation delights in attachment, revels in attachment, and rejoices in attachment.
When the Dhamma of non-attachment is taught by the Tathāgata, they desire to hear it, they lend an ear, and they apply their minds to understanding.
Monks, with the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this first wonderful and marvelous quality becomes manifest.”
“Monks, this generation delights in conceit, rejoices in conceit, and finds its pleasure in conceit.
When the Dhamma is being taught by the Tathāgata for the removal of conceit, they wish to hear it, they lend an ear, and they apply their minds to understanding.
Monks, with the appearance of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this second wonderful and marvelous quality becomes manifest.”
“Monks, this generation does not delight in peace, does not rejoice in peace, and does not find joy in peace.
Yet, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dhammas conducive to peace, it listens attentively, lends an ear, and applies its mind to understanding.
Monks, with the manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, this third wonderful and marvelous quality becomes manifest.”
“Bhikkhus, this generation is immersed in ignorance, like a bird in an eggshell, completely enveloped.
When the Dhamma for the removal of ignorance is taught by the Tathāgata, it listens intently, lends an ear, and applies its mind to understanding.
With the manifestation of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, this fourth wonderful and marvelous quality becomes manifest.”
“Bhikkhus, with the manifestation of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, these four wonderful and marvelous qualities manifest.
Thus [ends] the eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.129

13. Bhayavagga Ānandaacchariyasutta (AN 4.129, PTS AN ii 132) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated mentally, and penetrated well through view. He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick. He possesses wisdom; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. When a bhikkhu possesses these five qualities, it is wonderful and marvelous that he attains final knowledge for the first time in this very life. “Bhikkhus, there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda.
What are the four?
If, bhikkhus, a company of bhikkhus approaches Ānanda for the purpose of seeing him, they are delighted even by the sight of him.”
If Ānanda speaks the Dhamma there, she is delighted by what he has said.
But while the assembly of bhikkhus remains unsatisfied, Ānanda falls silent.
If, bhikkhus, an assembly of bhikkhunīs approaches to see Ānanda, they are delighted even by the mere sight of him.
If Ānanda speaks the Dhamma there, she is delighted by what he says.
But, monks, while the assembly of bhikkhunīs remains unsatisfied, Ānanda falls silent.
If, monks, an assembly of lay followers approaches Ānanda for the sake of seeing him, they are delighted by the very sight of him.
If Ānanda speaks the Dhamma there, she is delighted by what he has spoken.
But, monks, while the assembly of laymen is still not yet satisfied, Ānanda falls silent.
Monks, if an assembly of laywomen approaches to see Ānanda, they are delighted even by the sight of him.
“If Ānanda speaks on the Dhamma there, the assembly is delighted by what he has said.
But, monks, while the assembly of female lay followers remains unsatisfied, Ānanda falls silent.
These, monks, are the four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.130 13.
Bhayavagga (The Chapter on Fear)
The Discourse on the Wonders of a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavattiacchariyasutta): “Monks,
there are these four wonderful and marvelous qualities in a wheel-turning monarch.”
Which four?
If, monks, an assembly of kshatriyas approaches a wheel-turning monarch to see him, they are delighted even by the sight of him.
And if the wheel-turning monarch speaks there, they are delighted even by his speech.
“Monks, the assembly of khattiyas remains unsatisfied, and then the wheel-turning monarch remains silent.
Monks, if the assembly of brahmins approaches the wheel-turning monarch for an audience, they are pleased even by the sight of him.
And if the wheel-turning monarch speaks to them there, they are pleased even by his speech.”
Monks, the assembly of brahmins remains unsatisfied, and then the wheel-turning monarch becomes silent.
Monks, if the assembly of householders approaches the wheel-turning monarch for an audience, they are delighted even by the sight of him.
And if the wheel-turning monarch speaks to them, they are delighted even by his speech.
“Monks, as long as the assembly of householders is not yet satisfied, the wheel-turning monarch remains silent.
But if, monks, the assembly of recluses approaches to see the wheel-turning monarch, they become delighted even by the mere sight of him.
And if the wheel-turning monarch speaks to them there, they become delighted by his speech as well.”
“Monks, as long as the assembly of recluses is not yet satisfied, the wheel-turning monarch remains silent.
These, monks, are the four wonderful and marvelous qualities found in a wheel-turning monarch.
In the same way, monks, there are four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda.”
Which four?
If, monks, a company of bhikkhus approaches Ānanda to see him, they are delighted even by the sight of him.
If Ānanda speaks the Dhamma there, they are delighted by what he has spoken.
“Monks, as long as the assembly of monks is not yet satisfied, Ānanda remains silent.
Monks, if the assembly of nuns... if the assembly of laymen... if the assembly of laywomen approaches Ānanda for a sight of him, they are delighted by the very sight of him.
If Ānanda speaks the Dhamma there, they are delighted by what he has spoken.”
“Monks, as long as the assembly of female lay followers is not yet satisfied, Ānanda remains silent.
These, monks, are the four wonderful and marvelous qualities in Ānanda.

Puggalavagga Saṃyojana Sutta (The Fetter) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is fettered by all fetters; the person who is freed from some fetters but bound by others; the person who is freed from some fetters and not bound by others; and the person who is neither fettered nor freed from any fetters. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world. Which four? [The text continues with the description of each.]”
In this case, monks, for a certain person the lower fetters are not abandoned;
the fetters leading to rebirth are not abandoned; and the fetters leading to existence are not abandoned.
But in this case, monks, for another person the lower fetters are abandoned.
The fetters pertaining to rebirth have not been abandoned, and the fetters pertaining to existence have not been abandoned.
But here, monks, for a certain person, the lower fetters have been abandoned,
the fetters pertaining to rebirth have been abandoned, and the fetters pertaining to existence have not been abandoned.
"But here, monks, for a certain person the lower fetters have been abandoned,
the fetters leading to rebirth have been abandoned, and the fetters leading to existence have been abandoned.
And for which person, monks, have the lower fetters not been abandoned, the fetters leading to rebirth not been abandoned, and the fetters leading to existence not been abandoned?"
Of the once-returner.
Now, monks, for this person the lower fetters are not abandoned; the fetters that lead to rebirth are not abandoned; the fetters that lead to becoming are not abandoned.
And for which person, monks, are the lower fetters abandoned, while the fetters that lead to rebirth are not abandoned, and the fetters that lead to becoming are not abandoned?
“...of one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

Now, monks, for this person the fetters pertaining to the lower realm have been abandoned, but the fetters pertaining to rebirth have not been abandoned, nor have the fetters pertaining to becoming been abandoned.

And for what kind of person, monks, have the fetters pertaining to the lower realm been abandoned, the fetters pertaining to rebirth been abandoned, but the fetters pertaining to becoming not yet been abandoned?”
Of one who attains parinibbāna in the interval.
Now, monks, for this person the lower fetters are abandoned, the fetters leading to rebirth are abandoned, and the fetters leading to becoming are not yet abandoned.
And for which person, monks, are the lower fetters abandoned, the fetters leading to rebirth abandoned, and the fetters leading to becoming abandoned?
“Of the arahant.

Indeed, monks, for this person the fetters pertaining to the lower realm have been abandoned; the fetters pertaining to rebirth have been abandoned; the fetters pertaining to becoming have been abandoned.
These, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.132 14.
