The Discourse on Inspiration (Paṭibhānasutta): “Bhikkhus,
these four types of persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
One who has ready wit but not ready eloquence; one who has ready eloquence but not ready wit;
[one who has neither]; and one who has both.
One who is prompt in repartee and one who is ready in repartee;
and one who is neither prompt in repartee nor ready in repartee—
these, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.133 14.
Puggalavagga (The Chapter on Persons)
Ugghaṭitaññūsutta: “Bhikkhus,
these four persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
One who gains knowledge through a condensed statement, one who gains knowledge through an elaboration, one who is guidable, and one who is limited to the literal word.
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.”
Third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.134 14.
Puggalavagga (The Chapter on Persons)
Uṭṭhānaphalasutta: “Bhikkhus,
these four persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
One who lives on the fruit of exertion but not on the fruit of action;
one who lives on the fruit of action but not on the fruit of exertion; [and so forth].
"One who lives off the fruits of exertion and the fruits of action;
and one who lives neither off the fruits of exertion nor off the fruits of action—
these, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world."
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.135 14.
Puggalavagga (The Chapter on Persons)
Sāvajjasutta: “Bhikkhus,
these four persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
One who is blameworthy, one who abounds in blame, one who has little blame, and one who is blameless. And how, monks, is a person blameworthy?
“Here, monks, a certain person is possessed of blameworthy bodily action, possessed of blameworthy verbal action, and possessed of blameworthy mental action.
In this way, monks, a person is blameworthy. And how, monks, is a person full of blame?”
In this case, monks, a certain person is possessed of much blameworthy bodily action and little blameless bodily action;
he is possessed of much blameworthy verbal action and little blameless verbal action;
he is possessed of much blameworthy mental action and little blameless mental action.
In this way, monks, a person is full of faults. And how, monks, is a person few in faults?
Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with much faultless bodily action and little faulty bodily action.
He is mostly endowed with blameless verbal action and only rarely with blameworthy verbal action;
he is mostly endowed with blameless mental action and only rarely with blameworthy mental action.
In this way, monks, a person is one who has little fault.
And how, monks, is a person blameless?
Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, and endowed with blameless mental action.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is blameless.
“Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Thus [ends] the fifth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.136.

14. Puggalavagga First Discourse on Virtue (Paṭhamasīlasutta) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is virtuous but not learned; the person who is learned but not virtuous; the person who is neither virtuous nor learned; and the person who is both virtuous and learned. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is not one who fulfills virtuous behavior, is not one who fulfills concentration, and is not one who fulfills wisdom.”
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain person fulfills the precepts but does not fulfill concentration, nor does he fulfill wisdom.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person fulfills the precepts and fulfills concentration, but does not fulfill wisdom.
Furthermore, monks, here a certain person fulfills the precepts, fulfills concentration, and fulfills wisdom."
“Monks, these four persons are found existing in the world.
Thus [ends] the sixth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.137.

14. Puggalavagga The Second Discourse on Virtue (Dutiyasīlasutta) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is virtuous but does not develop concentration; the person who develops concentration but is not virtuous; the person who is neither virtuous nor develops concentration; and the person who is both virtuous and develops concentration. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world.
What are the four?

Here, bhikkhus, a certain person does not value virtuous behavior nor take virtuous behavior as his authority; he does not value concentration nor take concentration as his authority; he does not value wisdom nor take wisdom as his authority.”

"Furthermore, monks, here a certain person values virtue and makes virtue his dominant influence, but does not value concentration nor make concentration his dominant influence, and does not value wisdom nor make wisdom his dominant influence.

Furthermore, monks, here a certain person values virtue and makes virtue his dominant influence, and values concentration and makes concentration his dominant influence, but does not value wisdom nor make wisdom his dominant influence."
"Furthermore, monks, here a certain person values virtue and is dominated by virtue; he values concentration and is dominated by concentration; he values wisdom and is dominated by wisdom.
These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.
This was the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.138 14. Puggalavagga Nikaṭṭhasutta (The One Who Has Abandoned) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who has abandoned what is near; the one who has abandoned what is far; the one who has not abandoned what is near; and the one who has not abandoned what is far. And how, monks, is one a person who has abandoned what is near?

Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned sensual desire, abandoned ill will, abandoned sloth and torpor, abandoned restlessness and remorse, and abandoned doubt. But he has not abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, nor the underlying tendency to aversion, nor the underlying tendency to views, nor the underlying tendency to doubt, nor the underlying tendency to conceit, nor the underlying tendency to craving for existence, nor the underlying tendency to ignorance. This, monks, is called a person who has abandoned what is near. And how, monks, is one a person who has abandoned what is far? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned sensual desire, abandoned ill will, abandoned sloth and torpor, abandoned restlessness and remorse, and abandoned doubt. He has also abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to craving for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. But he has not abandoned the five lower fetters. This, monks, is called a person who has abandoned what is far. And how, monks, is one a person who has not abandoned what is near? Here, monks, a certain person has not abandoned sensual desire, has not abandoned ill will, has not abandoned sloth and torpor, has not abandoned restlessness and remorse, and has not abandoned doubt. This, monks, is called a person who has not abandoned what is near. And how, monks, is one a person who has not abandoned what is far? Here, monks, a certain person has not abandoned sensual desire, has not abandoned ill will, has not abandoned sloth and torpor, has not abandoned restlessness and remorse, and has not abandoned doubt. He has also not abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, nor the underlying tendency to aversion, nor the underlying tendency to views, nor the underlying tendency to doubt, nor the underlying tendency to conceit, nor the underlying tendency to craving for existence, nor the underlying tendency to ignorance. He has also not abandoned the five lower fetters. This, monks, is called a person who has not abandoned what is far. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world. Which four? [The text continues with the description of each.]”
One with body withdrawn but mind not withdrawn;
one with body not withdrawn but mind withdrawn;
and one with both body and mind not withdrawn.
One who has drawn back both in body and in mind.
And how, monks, is a person one who has drawn back in body but not in mind?
Here, monks, a certain person resorts to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.
Thus, in that case, he thinks sensual thoughts, he thinks thoughts of ill will, and he thinks thoughts of cruelty.
In this way, monks, a person is one whose body is drawn away but whose mind is not drawn away.
And how, monks, is a person one whose body is not drawn away but whose mind is drawn away?
In this case, monks, a certain person does not resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.
Yet there, he thinks thoughts of renunciation, he thinks thoughts of non-ill will, and he thinks thoughts of non-cruelty.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is one whose body is distant but whose mind is near.
And how, monks, is a person one whose body is not drawn away and whose mind is not drawn away?
Here, monks, a certain person does not indeed resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.
There, he thinks thoughts of sensual desire, he thinks thoughts of ill will, and he thinks thoughts of cruelty.
"In this way, monks, a person has both body and mind not drawn back.
And how, monks, does a person have both body and mind drawn back?
Here, monks, a certain person resorts to remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves."
Thus, in that case, he thinks thoughts of renunciation, he thinks thoughts of non-ill will, and he thinks thoughts of non-cruelty.
In this way, monks, a person is one whose body is drawn back and whose mind is drawn back.
These, monks, are the four persons existing and found in the world.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.139 14.
Puggalavagga (The Chapter on Persons)
Dhammakathikasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these four kinds of speakers on the Dhamma.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a certain Dhamma-preacher speaks little and what is irrelevant;
and his assembly is not skilled in distinguishing between what is relevant and what is irrelevant.
Monks, such a preacher of the Dhamma is reckoned as a preacher of the Dhamma among such an assembly.
But here, monks, there is another kind of preacher of the Dhamma who speaks little, yet what he says is relevant;
and his assembly is skilled in distinguishing between what is relevant and what is irrelevant.
Monks, such a preacher of the Dhamma is reckoned as a preacher of the Dhamma only in such an assembly.
But here, monks, some preacher of the Dhamma speaks much that is incoherent,
and his assembly is not skilled in distinguishing what is coherent from what is incoherent.
Monks, such a preacher of the Dhamma is reckoned as a preacher of the Dhamma for such an assembly.
But here, monks, a certain preacher of the Dhamma speaks much that is coherent,
and his assembly is skilled in distinguishing what is coherent from what is not.
“Monks, such a Dhamma-preacher is reckoned as a Dhamma-preacher only among such an assembly.
These, monks, are the four kinds of Dhamma-preachers. Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.140 14. Puggalavagga Vādīsutta – The Discourse on the Debater “Monks, there are these four types of debaters. What four? The one who speaks after having investigated; the one who speaks without having investigated;

the one who speaks out of malice; and the one who speaks out of desire for gain. And how, monks, is one a debater who speaks after having investigated? Here, monks, a bhikkhu speaks about the Dhamma after having examined it with the mind, having scrutinized it with wisdom. This, monks, is called a debater who speaks after having investigated. And how, monks, is one a debater who speaks without having investigated? Here, monks, a bhikkhu speaks about the Dhamma without having examined it with the mind, without having scrutinized it with wisdom. This, monks, is called a debater who speaks without having investigated. And how, monks, is one a debater who speaks out of malice? Here, monks, a bhikkhu speaks about the Dhamma with a mind full of ill will, wishing to defeat others. This, monks, is called a debater who speaks out of malice. And how, monks, is one a debater who speaks out of desire for gain? Here, monks, a bhikkhu speaks about the Dhamma for the sake of gain, honor, and fame, thinking: ‘May I obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. This, monks, is called a debater who speaks out of desire for gain. These, monks, are the four types of debaters.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four disputants.
Which four? [The text continues as follows:]”
“Monks, there is a speaker who reaches the exhaustion of the meaning, but not of the phrasing;
there is a speaker, monks, who reaches the exhaustion of the phrasing, but not of the meaning;
there is a speaker, monks, who reaches the exhaustion of both the meaning and the phrasing.”
“There is, bhikkhus, a debater who reaches exhaustion neither in meaning nor in phrasing.
These, bhikkhus, are the four types of debaters.
It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that one endowed with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) should reach exhaustion either in meaning or in phrasing.”

The fourth chapter on persons (Puggalavagga).

the blameworthy, and two kinds of virtue.

15. Ābhāvagga Pabhāsutta (AN 4.142, PTS AN ii 139) “Bhikkhus, there are these three radiances. What three? The radiance of the moon, the radiance of the sun, and the radiance of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the three radiances.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four radiances. Which four?

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.143 15. Ābhāvagga Ālokasutta (The Discourse on Light) “Bhikkhus, there are these four lights. What four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the four lights. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, Bhante, what is the source of the light of wisdom? “Wisdom, bhikkhu, has its source in concentration; concentration has its source in happiness; happiness has its source in tranquility; tranquility has its source in rapture; rapture has its source in faith; faith has its source in hearing the Dhamma; and hearing the Dhamma has its source in association with superior persons. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should associate with superior persons, for by associating with superior persons one hears the Dhamma; by hearing the Dhamma one gains faith; by gaining faith one gains rapture; by gaining rapture one gains happiness; by gaining happiness one gains tranquility; by gaining tranquility one gains concentration; and by gaining concentration one gains wisdom. Wisdom, bhikkhu, is the light. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, that bhikkhu addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, just as if a man were to enter a dark house that had been dark for a hundred years, and by means of a lamp he would see forms, so too, friends, when the Blessed One taught us the Dhamma in brief, we understood it through his teaching.

Friends, the Blessed One taught us the Dhamma in brief: ‘Wisdom, bhikkhu, has its source in concentration; concentration has its source in happiness; happiness has its source in tranquility; tranquility has its source in rapture; rapture has its source in faith; faith has its source in hearing the Dhamma; and hearing the Dhamma has its source in association with superior persons. Then those bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred. “Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu is wise; that bhikkhu has great discernment. For if, bhikkhus, I were to teach the Dhamma to you in detail, it would be exactly like that. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, those bhikkhus addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, let us go to the Blessed One and report to him what the Blessed One said and what he did. “Friends, how could we do so? The Blessed One would rebuke us. “Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One would not rebuke us; the Blessed One would explain to us the meaning of what he said. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, let us go to the Blessed One and report to him what the Blessed One said and what he did. “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with those bhikkhus, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred. “Ānanda, that bhikkhu is wise; that bhikkhu has great discernment. For if, Ānanda, I were to teach the Dhamma to you in detail, it would be exactly like that. Ānanda, there are these four lights. What four? The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom. These, Ānanda, are the four lights. Of these four lights, the light of wisdom is the foremost. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, just as if a man were to enter a dark house that had been dark for a hundred years, and by means of a lamp he would see forms, so too, friends, when the Blessed One taught us the Dhamma in brief, we understood it through his teaching. Friends, the Blessed One taught us the Dhamma in brief: ‘Wisdom, bhikkhu, has its source in concentration; concentration has its source in happiness; happiness has its source in tranquility; tranquility has its source in rapture; rapture has its source in faith; faith has its source in hearing the Dhamma; and hearing the Dhamma has its source in association with superior persons. Then those bhikkhus approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred. “Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu is wise; that bhikkhu has great discernment. For if, bhikkhus, I were to teach the Dhamma to you in detail, it would be exactly like that. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Ābhāvagga Pajjotasutta (AN 4.145, PTS AN ii 140) “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great mass of fire burning for an entire eon; and suppose a man would come along and, having extinguished it, would say: ‘I have extinguished that great mass of fire. Bhikkhus, what do you think? Would he have done much by way of exertion? “Venerable sir, that great mass of fire was vast, extensive, and immeasurable. It is not easy to extinguish such a great mass of fire. Therefore, whatever effort that man would have made to extinguish it, venerable sir, would have been very great. “It is even more so, bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses four things who has extinguished the great mass of fire of craving that has been burning for a long time. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. “When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses these four things, he has extinguished the great mass of fire of craving that has been burning for a long time.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four lights. Which four?
The light of the moon, the light of the sun, the light of fire, and the light of wisdom.”
“Monks, these are the four lights.
Of these four lights, monks, the foremost is this: the light of wisdom. Thus ends the fifth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.146 15.

Ābhāvagga Paṭhamakālasutta (The First Discourse on Time) “Bhikkhus, there are these four times. What four? The time for listening to the Dhamma; the time for discussing the Dhamma; the time for serenity; and the time for insight. These, bhikkhus, are the four times.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four times. What four? [Text continues]”
“Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time, discussing the Dhamma at the proper time, reflecting at the proper time, and insight at the proper time—
these, monks, are the four proper times. The sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.147 15. Ābhāvagga Dutiyakālasutta (The Second Discourse on Time) “Bhikkhus, there are these four times for the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities; and there are these four times for the increase and fulfillment of arisen evil, unwholesome qualities. What are the four? The first time is when one does not attend to the appropriate object of attention and attends instead to an inappropriate object of attention.

This is the first time for the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities; and this is the first time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen evil, unwholesome qualities. The second time is when one does not cultivate wholesome mental states and cultivates unwholesome mental states. This is the second time for the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities; and this is the second time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen evil, unwholesome qualities. The third time is when one does not associate with superior persons, does not listen to the true Dhamma, and does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma. This is the third time for the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities; and this is the third time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen evil, unwholesome qualities. The fourth time is when one has wrong view, distorted vision. This is the fourth time for the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities; and this is the fourth time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen evil, unwholesome qualities. These, bhikkhus, are the four times for the arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome qualities; and these are the four times for the increase and fulfillment of arisen evil, unwholesome qualities. But, bhikkhus, there are these four times for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; and there are these four times for the increase and fulfillment of arisen wholesome qualities. What are the four? The first time is when one attends to the appropriate object of attention and does not attend to an inappropriate object of attention. This is the first time for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; and this is the first time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen wholesome qualities. The second time is when one cultivates wholesome mental states and does not cultivate unwholesome mental states. This is the second time for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; and this is the second time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen wholesome qualities. The third time is when one associates with superior persons, listens to the true Dhamma, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma. This is the third time for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; and this is the third time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen wholesome qualities. The fourth time is when one holds right view, undistorted vision. This is the fourth time for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; and this is the fourth time for the increase and fulfillment of arisen wholesome qualities. These, bhikkhus, are the four times for the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities; and these are the four times for the increase and fulfillment of arisen wholesome qualities.”
“Bhikkhus, these four times, when rightly developed and rightly cultivated, lead gradually to the destruction of the taints. What are the four? [Text continues].”
Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time, discussing the Dhamma at the proper time, reflection at the proper time,
and insight at the proper time— these four times, monks, when rightly developed and rightly pursued, lead gradually to the destruction of the taints. Just as, monks,
when it rains in thick drops from a cloud high above the mountain, that water flows down according to the slope;
As it flows, it fills the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies; the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies being filled, fill the small pools;
the small pools being filled, fill the large pools; the large pools being filled, fill the small streams;
the small streams being filled, fill the great rivers; the great rivers being filled—
They fill the ocean.
In the same way, bhikkhus, when these four times are rightly developed and rightly practiced in succession, they lead, step by step, to the destruction of the taints.
The seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.148 15.

Ābhāvagga Duccaritasutta (The Discourse on Bad Conduct) "Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of bad conduct. What three? Bad conduct of body, bad conduct of speech, and bad conduct of mind. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of bad conduct."
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of verbal misconduct.

Ābhāvagga Sucaritasutta (The Discourse on Good Conduct) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is well-conducted but not one who speaks well; the person who speaks well but is not one who is well-conducted; the person who is neither well-conducted nor one who speaks well; and the person who is both well-conducted and one who speaks well. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of verbal good conduct.
What are the four?
“Truthful speech, speech that is not divisive, gentle speech, and speech that is deliberate—
these, monks, are the four kinds of verbal good conduct. Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.150 15. Ābhāvagga Sārasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a heap of chaff; the person who is like a reed-thicket; the person who is like a lotus stalk; and the person who is like a great sal tree. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a heap of chaff? Here, someone is well-born on both sides, of pure maternal and paternal descent back through seven generations, unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth. Yet he is unlearned, ignorant, and dull-witted; he does not understand the meaning of what has been well spoken and ill spoken. This is called a person like a heap of chaff. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a reed-thicket? Here, someone is well-born on both sides... unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth. He is learned and possesses much that has been heard, but he is dull-witted and does not understand the meaning of what has been well spoken and ill spoken. This is called a person like a reed-thicket. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a lotus stalk? Here, someone is well-born on both sides... unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth. He is learned and possesses much that has been heard, and he is wise and understands the meaning of what has been well spoken and ill spoken. However, he does not live the holy life with a sense of urgency for the complete destruction of suffering. This is called a person like a lotus stalk. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a great sal tree? Here, someone is well-born on both sides... unblemished and irreproachable in respect of birth. He is learned and possesses much that has been heard, and he is wise and understands the meaning of what has been well spoken and ill spoken. And he lives the holy life with a sense of urgency for the complete destruction of suffering. This is called a person like a great sal tree. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four essentials. What four? [The text continues as follows:]”
“Monks, these four are the essentials: the essence of virtue, the essence of concentration, the essence of wisdom, and the essence of liberation.
These, monks, are the four essentials. Tenth.

"for so many years," or "for so many hundreds of years," or "for so many thousands of years," or "for so many hundreds of thousands of years.

“Monks, there are these two kinds of illness. Which two?
Bodily illness and mental illness.”
Bhikkhus, beings are seen who, despite being afflicted by bodily disease,
claim to have been healthy for one year, two years, three years, four years, five years, and even ten years.
claiming [to be healthy], claiming health for twenty years, claiming health for thirty years,
claiming health for forty years, claiming health for fifty years,
or even claiming health for a hundred years and more.
Those beings, monks, are very rare in the world who can claim even for a moment to be free from mental illness, except for those whose taints are destroyed.
Monks, there are these four illnesses of one who has gone forth.
What are the four?
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is full of great desires, troubled, and discontented with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings,

and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive. Being full of great desires, troubled, and discontented with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive,
he forms an evil wish for the sake of gaining honor and for the sake of gaining gain, respect, and fame.
Thus he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort for the sake of obtaining honor and for the sake of obtaining gain, honor, and fame.
He approaches families with calculation, sits down with calculation, speaks the Dhamma with calculation, and holds back his excrement and urine with calculation.
These, monks, are the four diseases of one who has gone forth.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We will not have great desires, we will not be distressed, and we will not be discontented with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick we may receive;
we will not harbor evil desires for the sake of gaining honor, nor for the sake of gaining profit, respect, and fame."
"We shall not rise up, we shall not strive, we shall not exert ourselves for the sake of obtaining respect, nor for the sake of obtaining gain, honor, and renown;
rather, we shall be patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
and with abusive and offensive words, and with arisen bodily feelings that are painful."
‘We shall be of a nature to endure pains that are sharp, harsh, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

The Discourse on the Detailed Exposition (Vitthārasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these four modes of practice.”
Which four?

The painful practice with slow direct knowledge, the painful practice with quick direct knowledge, [the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge].
The pleasant way of practice with slow direct knowledge;
the pleasant way of practice with quick direct knowledge.
And what, monks, is the painful way of practice with slow direct knowledge?
In this case, monks, a certain person is by nature prone to intense lust; he constantly experiences the suffering and dejection born of lust.
By nature he is prone to intense hatred; he constantly experiences the suffering and dejection born of hatred.
By nature he is prone to intense delusion; he constantly experiences the suffering and dejection born of delusion.
In him, these five faculties appear weak:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Because of the weakness of these five faculties, he attains the immediate path to the destruction of the taints with difficulty.
This, monks, is called the painful practice with slow direct knowledge.
And what, monks, is the painful practice with quick direct knowledge?
Here, monks, a certain person is by nature intensely passionate; he constantly experiences the pain and mental distress born of passion.
By nature he is prone to intense hatred and frequently experiences the pain and mental distress born of hatred.
By nature he is prone to intense delusion and frequently experiences the pain and mental distress born of delusion.
In him, these five faculties become especially prominent:
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Because these five faculties are predominant, he quickly attains the state of immediate succession for the destruction of the taints.
This, monks, is called the painful practice with quick direct knowledge.
And what, monks, is the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge?
Here, monks, a certain person is by nature not prone to intense lust, and does not frequently experience the pain and dejection born of lust.
By nature he is not prone to intense hatred, and does not frequently experience the pain and dejection born of hatred.
By nature he is not one of intense delusion, nor does he frequently experience the pain and mental distress born of delusion.
In him these five faculties appear weakly:
the faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom.
Thus, due to the dullness of these five faculties, one attains the state of immediate succession slowly for the destruction of the taints.
This, monks, is called the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge.
And what, monks, is the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge?
In this case, monks, a certain person is by nature not prone to intense passion; he does not frequently experience the pain and mental distress born of passion.
By nature he is not prone to intense hatred; he does not frequently experience the pain and mental distress born of hatred.
By nature he is not prone to intense delusion; he does not frequently experience the pain and mental distress born of delusion.
In him, these five faculties become preeminent:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Because of the preeminence of these five faculties, he quickly attains the state beyond interval for the destruction of the taints.
“This, monks, is called the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge.
These, monks, are the four ways.

And what, bhikkhus, is the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the unattractiveness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world, and contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, the perception of death is well-established within him.
He dwells supported by these five powers of a trainee:
the power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
In him, these five faculties appear weak:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Because of the weakness of these five faculties, he attains the immediate state for the destruction of the taints only slowly.
This, monks, is called the painful practice with slow direct knowledge.
And what, monks, is the painful practice with quick direct knowledge?

Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the foulness of the body, perceiving the repulsiveness of food, perceiving non-delight in the entire world, and contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, the perception of death is well-established within him.
Relying upon these five powers of a trainee, he dwells:
the power of faith … [and so on] … the power of wisdom.
In him, these five faculties appear in an eminent degree—
the faculty of faith …pe… the faculty of wisdom.
Because of the eminence of these five faculties, he quickly attains the state of immediate succession for the destruction of the taints.
This, monks, is called the painful practice with quick direct knowledge.
And what, monks, is the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge?

Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: “He dwells happily, mindful and in equanimity.”

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
He dwells supported by these five powers of a trainee:
the power of faith … [and so on] … the power of wisdom.
In him, these five faculties appear weak:
the faculty of faith ... [and so on] ... the faculty of wisdom.
Because of the weakness of these five faculties, he attains the state of non-returning only sluggishly for the destruction of the taints.
This, monks, is called the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge.
And what, monks, is the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge?
Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought...
He enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is born of seclusion and filled with rapture and pleasure; ...pe... he enters and dwells in the second jhāna;
...pe... he enters and dwells in the third jhāna; ...pe... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He dwells supported by these five powers of a trainee (sekhabala).
The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
In him, these five faculties become preeminent:
the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Thus, through the predominance of these five faculties, one quickly attains the state of immediate succession for the destruction of the taints.
This, monks, is called the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.
These, monks, are the four practices.”

Paṭhamakhamasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are these four ways of practice.”
Which four?
The practice of intolerance, the practice of tolerance, the practice of self-taming, and the practice of tranquility.
And what, monks, is the practice of intolerance?
"Here, monks, a certain person reviles one who reviles him, scolds one who scolds him, and quarrels with one who quarrels with him.
This, monks, is called the practice of non-forgiveness.
And what, monks, is the practice of forgiveness?"
"Here, monks, a certain person does not revile one who reviles him, does not scold one who scolds him, and does not argue with one who argues with him.
This, monks, is called the practice of patience.
And what, monks, is the practice of self-mastery?"
Here, monks, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the eye-faculty; he attains restraint over the eye-faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For if one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.
If mental phenomena were to flow in upon him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the mind-faculty; he achieves restraint over the mind-faculty.
This, monks, is called the practice of taming.
And what, monks, is the practice of calming?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu does not tolerate a thought of sensual desire that has arisen; he abandons it, dispels it, calms it, brings it to an end, and causes it to disappear.
He does not tolerate a thought of ill will that has arisen... a thought of cruelty that has arisen...
nor does he tolerate any evil, unwholesome states that have arisen; he abandons them, dispels them, calms them, brings them to an end, and causes them to disappear.
“This, monks, is called the even way of practice.
These, monks, are the four ways of practice.
The fourth.

Paṭipadāvagga Dutiyakhamasutta (The Second Discourse on Forbearance) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is not patient nor capable of enduring; the person who is patient but not capable of enduring; the person who is not patient but is capable of enduring; and the person who is both patient and capable of enduring. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of practice. Which four?”
The practice of intolerance, the practice of tolerance, the practice of self-mastery, and the practice of equanimity.
And what, monks, is the practice of intolerance?
Here, monks, a certain person is intolerant of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things.
He is one who is by nature unable to endure harsh and offensive paths of speech, nor bodily feelings that have arisen which are painful,
sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening. This, monks,
is called the practice of intolerance.
And what, monks, is the practice of forbearance?
Here, monks, a certain person is forbearing toward cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
toward offensive and unwelcome modes of speech; and toward arisen bodily feelings that are painful.
He is one who is disposed to endure pains that are harsh, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable, and life-threatening.
This, monks, is called the practice of patience.
And what, monks, is the practice of self-mastery?
"Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp at its signs...
having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose..."
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If, when one dwells with this faculty of mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—were to flow in, one practices for its restraint;
one guards the faculty of mind; one attains restraint over the faculty of mind.
This, monks, is called the practice of taming.
And what, bhikkhus, is the balanced way of practice?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, settles it, brings it to an end, and causes it to disappear.
He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will... [and so on] ...an arisen thought of cruelty.
“...whatever evil, unwholesome states have arisen, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, calms them, brings them to an end, and makes them cease to exist.
This, monks, is called the even way of practice.
These, monks, are the four ways of practice.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.169 17. Paṭipadāvagga Sasaṅkhārasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four modes of practice. What four? Practice with exertion, practice with ease, practice with both exertion and ease, and practice that is neither with exertion nor with ease. These, bhikkhus, are the four modes of practice. “Bhikkhus, for one practicing with exertion, there are two possible destinations: either the state of non-percipient beings or the realm of the Subhakiṇha devas. For one practicing with ease, there are two possible destinations: either the state of non-percipient beings or the realm of the Vehapphala devas. For one practicing with both exertion and ease, there are two possible destinations: either the realm of the Aviha devas or the realm of the Atappa devas. For one practicing that is neither with exertion nor with ease, there are two possible destinations: either the realm of the Sudassa devas or the realm of the Sudassi devas. “Bhikkhus, for one practicing with exertion, there are three possible destinations: either the realm of the Aviha devas, the realm of the Atappa devas, or the realm of the Sudassa devas. For one practicing with ease, there are three possible destinations:

either the realm of the Atappa devas, the realm of the Sudassa devas, or the realm of the Sudassi devas. For one practicing with both exertion and ease, there are three possible destinations: either the realm of the Sudassa devas, the realm of the Sudassi devas, or the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas. For one practicing that is neither with exertion nor with ease, there are three possible destinations: either the realm of the Sudassi devas, the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas, or final nibbāna in this very life. “Bhikkhus, for one practicing with exertion, there are four possible destinations: either the realm of the Aviha devas, the realm of the Atappa devas, the realm of the Sudassa devas, or the realm of the Sudassi devas. For one practicing with ease, there are four possible destinations: either the realm of the Atappa devas, the realm of the Sudassa devas, the realm of the Sudassi devas, or the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas. For one practicing with both exertion and ease, there are four possible destinations: either the realm of the Sudassa devas, the realm of the Sudassi devas, the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas, or final nibbāna in this very life. For one practicing that is neither with exertion nor with ease, there are four possible destinations: either the realm of the Sudassi devas, the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas, the realm of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, or final nibbāna in this very life. “Bhikkhus, for one practicing with exertion, there are five possible destinations: either the realm of the Aviha devas, the realm of the Atappa devas, the realm of the Sudassa devas, the realm of the Sudassi devas, or the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas. For one practicing with ease, there are five possible destinations: either the realm of the Atappa devas, the realm of the Sudassa devas, the realm of the Sudassi devas, the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas, or the realm of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. For one practicing with both exertion and ease, there are five possible destinations: either the realm of the Sudassa devas, the realm of the Sudassi devas, the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas, the realm of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, or final nibbāna in this very life. For one practicing that is neither with exertion nor with ease, there are five possible destinations: either the realm of the Sudassi devas, the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas, the realm of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, the realm of the Brahmakāyika devas, or final nibbāna in this very life. “Bhikkhus, for one practicing with exertion, there are six possible destinations: either the realm of the Aviha devas, the realm of the Atappa devas, the realm of the Sudassa devas, the realm of the Sudassi devas, the realm of the Akaniṭṭha devas, or the realm of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.172 18. Sañcetaniyavagga Vibhattisutta (The Discourse on Analysis) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who acts with full awareness regarding the past; the person who acts with full awareness regarding the future; the person who acts with full awareness regarding both the past and the future; and the person who acts with full awareness regarding the present. And how, monks, is one a person who acts with full awareness regarding the past? Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of world-dissolution and evolution: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts with full awareness regarding the past. And how, monks, is one a person who acts with full awareness regarding the future? Here, monks, a noble disciple understands: ‘This is suffering’; he understands: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He understands: ‘These are the defilements’; he understands: ‘This is the origin of the defilements’; he understands: ‘This is the cessation of the defilements’; he understands: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the defilements. And whatever deities there are—whether belonging to the generation of the Four Great Kings, or the generation of the Thirty-Three, or the Yāma generation, or the Tusita generation, or the generation of those who delight in creation, or the generation of those who control the creations of others, or the generation of Brahmā, or the generation of Mahābrahmā, or the generation of the devas who are sovereign lords of all—they all think thus: ‘When the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One—he teaches the Dhamma admirable in its beginning, admirable in its middle, admirable in its end; he proclaims the holy life in its fullness and purity. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts with full awareness regarding the future. And how, monks, is one a person who acts with full awareness regarding both the past and the future? Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects his manifold past lives... [as above] ...in their modes and details. And he understands: ‘This is suffering’... [as above] ...he is the Buddha, the Fortunate One. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts with full awareness regarding both the past and the future. And how, monks, is one a person who acts with full awareness regarding the present? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts with full awareness regarding the present. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:

“Friends,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, having been ordained for half a month, I have realized the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) both in its particulars and in its phrasing.”
I declare, teach, describe, establish, disclose, analyze, and clarify that to him in many ways.
But whoever has doubt or uncertainty, let him ask me;
I am present as the teacher who is most skilled in the Dhammas.

18. Sañcetaniyavagga Upavāṇa Sutta (AN 4.175, PTS AN ii 163) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Upavāṇa, when a bhikkhu is intent on the higher mind, what does he first cultivate, what does he cultivate next, and what is the fruit of that cultivation? “When a bhikkhu is intent on the higher mind, venerable sir, he first cultivates the basis for psychic potency that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving. Having cultivated that, he next cultivates the basis for psychic potency that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving… the basis for psychic potency that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving… the basis for psychic potency that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. When he has cultivated that, the fruit of his cultivation is the attainment of the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. “Good, good, Upavāṇa! When a bhikkhu is intent on the higher mind, Upavāṇa, this is what he first cultivates, this is what he cultivates next, and this is the fruit of that cultivation. Then the Venerable Upavāṇa rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and departed. Not long after the Venerable Upavāṇa had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to say: ‘I will make this great earth float on water without a boat’; he would be speaking about something that is impossible. For what reason? Because the great earth is heavy and solid, and it is water that is light and fluid. So too, when a bhikkhu is intent on the higher mind, he first cultivates the basis for psychic potency that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving… [and so on] …the fruit of his cultivation is the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. But when a bhikkhu is intent on the higher mind, he first cultivates the basis for psychic potency that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving… [and so on] …the fruit of his cultivation is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. This is possible. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the seventeenth sutta of the Sañcetaniyavagga.)
Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upavāṇa said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, how does one become a maker of the end of knowledge?"
“No, friend.
“But then, friend Sāriputta, does one become an end-maker through conduct?
“No, friend.”
“But, friend Sāriputta, does one become an end-maker through knowledge and conduct?
“No indeed, friend.
“But, friend Sāriputta, does one become an end-maker apart from knowledge and conduct?”
“No, friend.
“Then, friend Sāriputta, when asked: ‘Does one who possesses clear knowledge bring about an end [to suffering]?
you replied: ‘No, friend.’”
“Friend Sāriputta, when asked: ‘But does one make an end [of suffering] by means of conduct alone?
you replied: ‘No indeed, friend. When asked:
‘But does one make an end [of suffering] by means of both true knowledge and conduct? you replied:”
“You say, ‘No indeed, friend.
But when asked, ‘Friend Sāriputta, can one make an end [of suffering] apart from knowledge and conduct?
you say, ‘No indeed, friend.’”
“But in what way, friend, does one become an end-maker?
“If, friend, one were an end-maker through true knowledge (*vijjā*), while still possessing clinging (*saupādāna*), one would be an end-maker.
If, friend, one were an end-maker through conduct (*caraṇa*), while still possessing clinging, one would be an end-maker.”
"Friends, if one could bring about an end [to suffering] through knowledge and conduct alone, then even one who still possesses clinging would be able to bring about that end.
Friends, if one could bring about an end apart from knowledge and conduct, then an ordinary person (puthujjana) would be able to bring about that end;
for an ordinary person, friends, exists apart from knowledge and conduct."
"One who has failed in conduct, friend, does not know and does not see things as they really are.
One who is accomplished in conduct knows and sees things as they really are.
Knowing and seeing things as they really are, one makes an end [of suffering]."
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.176 18.
Sañcetaniyavagga (The Chapter on Volitional Intent)
The Discourse on Entreaty (Āyācanasutta):
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with faith, when making a right entreaty, should entreat thus:”
"May I become just like Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Monks, this is the standard, this is the measure for my monk disciples: namely, Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Monks, a nun endowed with faith, making a proper aspiration, should aspire thus:
“May I become just like the bhikkhunīs Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.
Monks, this is the standard, this is the measure for my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs, namely Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.
Monks, a faithful lay follower, making a proper aspiration, should aspire thus:
"May I become just like Citta the householder and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.
Monks, this is the standard, this is the measure for my lay male disciples, namely Citta the householder and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.
Monks, a female disciple endowed with faith who makes a proper request should request thus:
“May I become like the female lay follower Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇḍakī Nandamātā.
Monks, this is the standard, this is the measure for my female lay followers, namely: the female lay follower Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇḍakī Nandamātā.
This is the sixth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.177 18.

Sañcetaniyavagga Rāhulasutta “Rāhula, when a volitional act of body is performed with full awareness, it leads to suffering for a long time. When a volitional act of speech is performed with full awareness, it leads to suffering for a long time. When a volitional act of mind is performed with full awareness, it leads to suffering for a long time. Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: ‘I shall not perform a volitional act of body without full awareness; I shall not perform a volitional act of speech without full awareness; I shall not perform a volitional act of mind without full awareness.’”
(AN 4.177, PTS AN ii 164) Then the Venerable Rāhula approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Rāhula was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Rāhula, whatever is the internal earth element and whatever is the external earth element, all that is simply the earth element.”
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and detaches the mind from the earth element.
And as for the internal water element and the external water element, Rāhula, that is simply the water element.
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus should this be seen with correct wisdom as it actually is.
Having seen this with correct wisdom as it actually is, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and detaches the mind from the water element.
And, Rāhula, whatever internal fire element there is, and whatever external fire element there is—that is simply the fire element.
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Having seen it thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and detaches the mind from the fire element.
And whatever internal air element there is, and whatever external air element there is—that is simply the air element.
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—thus should this be seen with correct wisdom as it actually is.
Having seen this with correct wisdom as it actually is, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and detaches the mind from the air element.
When, Rāhula, a bhikkhu does not regard these four elements as self or as belonging to self, [he is liberated].”
“Rāhula, this bhikkhu is said to have cut off craving, to have removed the fetters, and through the right penetration of conceit,
to have made an end of suffering.
Thus was the seventh [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.178 18. Sañcetaniyavagga Jambālīsutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a mudbank; the person who is like a lotus; the person who is like a blue lotus; and the person who is like a white lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a mudbank?

Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, with a fine complexion, handsome, and attractive. But he does not enjoy sensual pleasures, nor does he abandon them; he does not practice the holy life, nor does he abandon it. He does not gain wealth, nor does he abandon it; he does not go forth from the household life into homelessness, nor does he abandon it. Just as a mudbank is neither a place for enjoying water nor a place for abandoning water, so too, monks, this person is called ‘one like a mudbank. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, with a fine complexion, handsome, and attractive. He enjoys sensual pleasures, but does not abandon them; he practices the holy life, but does not abandon it. He gains wealth, but does not abandon it; he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, but does not abandon it. Just as a lotus is neither a place for enjoying water nor a place for abandoning water, so too, monks, this person is called ‘one like a lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, with a fine complexion, handsome, and attractive. He abandons sensual pleasures, but does not enjoy them; he abandons the holy life, but does not practice it. He abandons wealth, but does not gain it; he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, but does not abandon it. Just as a blue lotus is neither a place for enjoying water nor a place for abandoning water, so too, monks, this person is called ‘one like a blue lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a noble family, with a fine complexion, handsome, and attractive. He abandons sensual pleasures and does not enjoy them; he abandons the holy life and practices it. He abandons wealth and gains it; he goes forth from the household life into homelessness and does not abandon it. Just as a white lotus is neither a place for enjoying water nor a place for abandoning water, so too, monks, this person is called ‘one like a white lotus. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four? [Text continues].”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in a certain peaceful liberation of mind.
He directs his attention to the cessation of identity.

While he is directing his attention to the cessation of identity, his mind does not leap forward toward the cessation of identity; it does not find confidence in it, does not settle in it, and does not resolve upon it.
For such a monk, monks, the cessation of identity is not to be expected.
Just as if a man were to grasp a branch with a hand smeared with resin— his hand would stick,
grip, and become bound— so too, monks, a monk enters and dwells in a certain peaceful liberation of mind.
Thus he attends to the cessation of identity.
As he attends to the cessation of identity, his mind does not leap forward into the cessation of identity, does not find confidence in it, does not settle upon it, and does not resolve upon it.
For such a monk, bhikkhus, the cessation of identity is not to be expected.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu, having attained and dwelling in a certain peaceful liberation of mind,
attends to the cessation of identity.
As he attends to the cessation of identity, his mind leaps forward into the cessation of identity, becomes confident in it, settles upon it, and resolves upon it.
For such a monk, bhikkhus, the cessation of identity is to be expected.
Just as if a man were to grasp a branch with a clean hand— his hand would neither stick,
nor cling, nor be bound— so too, bhikkhus, a monk enters and dwells in a certain peaceful liberation of mind.
Thus he attends to the cessation of identity.
As he attends to the cessation of identity, his mind leaps forward into the cessation of identity, gains confidence in it, becomes settled in it, and resolves upon it.
For a bhikkhu who does so, monks, the cessation of identity is to be expected.
But here, monks, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in a certain peaceful liberation of mind.
He directs his attention to the breaking up of ignorance.
As he directs his attention to the breaking up of ignorance, his mind does not leap forward toward the breaking up of ignorance, nor does it become settled, firm, or resolved upon it.
For such a bhikkhu, monks, the breaking down of ignorance is not to be expected.
It is just as if there were a water-hole that had been dry for many years;
a man would close up its inflow channels and open up its outflow channels, and the sky would not send down rain in proper torrents.
"In this way, monks, the collapse of that embankment is not to be expected.
Even so, monks, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in a certain peaceful liberation of mind.
He then directs his attention to the breaking down of ignorance."
When he attends to the breaking up of ignorance, his mind does not leap forward into the breaking up of ignorance; it does not find confidence, does not settle, and does not resolve upon it.
In such a case, monks, it is not to be expected that this monk will achieve the breaking up of ignorance.
But here, monks, a monk enters and dwells in a certain peaceful liberation of mind.
Thus, he directs his attention to the breaking up of ignorance.
As he directs his attention to the breaking up of ignorance, his mind leaps forward into the breaking up of ignorance, becomes confident in it, settles upon it, and resolves upon it.
For such a monk, bhikkhus, the breaking up of ignorance is to be expected.
“Just as, monks, there might be a water-filled pit that has been so for many years;
and a man were to open its inflow openings and close its outflow openings, and the sky were to send down rain in proper measure—
then, monks, it is to be expected that the embankment of that water-filled pit would break.”
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu, having attained and dwelling in a certain peaceful liberation of mind,
attends to the breaking up of ignorance.
As he attends to the breaking up of ignorance, his mind leaps forward into the breaking up of ignorance, becomes serene, settles, and resolves upon it.
“Monks, for such a monk, the breaking down of ignorance is to be expected.
These, monks, are the four persons found existing in the world.
The eighth.

These, monks, are the four noble truths. (AN 4.179, PTS AN ii 167) Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final nibbāna in this very life?
“Here, friend Ānanda, beings do not understand as it really is: ‘These perceptions lead to decline,’ they do not understand as it really is:
‘These perceptions lead to stability,’ and they do not understand as it really is: ‘These perceptions lead to distinction.’”
“They do not understand as it really is: ‘These perceptions partake of penetration.
This, friend Ānanda, is the cause, this is the condition why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life.
“But what, friend Sāriputta, is the cause, what is the condition why some beings here do attain final Nibbāna in this very life?”
“Here, friend Ānanda, beings understand as they really are: ‘These perceptions lead to decline’; they understand as they really are:
‘These perceptions lead to stability’; they understand as they really are: ‘These perceptions lead to distinction’;
they understand as they really are: ‘These perceptions lead to penetration.’”
“This, friend Ānanda, is the cause, this is the condition, by which some beings here attain final nibbāna in this very life.
(The ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.180

18. Sañcetaniyavagga: Mahāpadesasutta (AN 4.180, PTS AN ii 167) “Monks, there are these four great authorities. What four? ‘This is the Dhamma,’ monks, if it is said, ‘It was spoken by the Blessed One; it was heard by me from his own lips,’ this is the first great authority. ‘This is the Dhamma,’ monks, if it is said, ‘It was spoken by the Blessed One in a certain town or city,’ and it is confirmed by a community of elders who are learned, heirs of the Dhamma, experts in the Dhamma, experts in the Vinaya, and experts in the Matikas, this is the second great authority. ‘This is the Dhamma,’ monks, if it is said, ‘It was spoken by the Blessed One in a certain town or city,’ and it is confirmed by a single elder who is learned, an heir of the Dhamma, an expert in the Dhamma, an expert in the Vinaya, and an expert in the Matikas, this is the third great authority. ‘This is the Dhamma,’ monks, if it is said, ‘It was spoken by the Blessed One in a certain town or city,’ and it is confirmed by a single bhikkhu who is wise, intelligent, and a master of the scriptures, this is the fourth great authority. These, monks, are the four great authorities.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Bhoganagara at the Ānanda Shrine.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the four great authorities.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Monks, what are the four great authorities?
Here, monks, a monk might say:
‘Friends, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from the Blessed One.’”
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.
Monks, the speech of that monk should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without welcoming it and without rejecting it, those words and phrases should be carefully mastered and then compared with the Suttas and verified against the Vinaya.
If, when being compared with the Sutta and examined against the Vinaya, they do not descend into the Sutta nor appear in the Vinaya, one must reach the conclusion:
"Certainly this is not the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
it has been wrongly grasped by this monk."
Therefore, monks, you should discard this.
But here, monks, a monk might say:
"Friends, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from the Blessed One:..."
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.
Monks, the speech of that monk should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without welcoming it and without rejecting it, those words and phrases should be carefully mastered and compared with the Suttas and verified against the Vinaya.
If, when being compared with the Sutta and shown against the Vinaya, they descend into the Sutta and appear in the Vinaya, one should reach the conclusion:
"Truly, this is the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
and it has been well-grasped by this monk."
“Monks, you should remember this as the first great authority (mahāpadesa).
Furthermore, monks, a monk might say:
‘In such-and-such a residence there dwells a Saṅgha with elders and leaders.’”
‘I have heard and received this directly from that Saṅgha:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.
Monks, the speech of that monk should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without approving and without rejecting those words and phrases, having thoroughly mastered them, they should be compared with the Sutta and verified against the Vinaya.
If, when being compared with the Sutta and verified against the Vinaya, they do not enter into the Sutta and are not seen in the Vinaya, one must conclude:
"Certainly this is not the word of that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
‘And that Saṅgha has grasped it wrongly.
Thus, monks, you should discard this.
But here, monks, a monk might say:
‘In such-and-such a residence the Saṅgha dwells, together with its elders and its leaders.
In the presence of that Saṅgha I heard this, I received this:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.”’”
Monks, the speech of that monk should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without welcoming it and without rejecting it, those words and phrases should be carefully mastered and then compared with the Sutta and checked against the Vinaya.

If, when being compared with the Sutta and checked against the Vinaya, they are found to enter into the Sutta and appear in the Vinaya, then one should reach the conclusion: [that this is the word of the Buddha].
‘Surely this is the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
and it has been well grasped by that Saṅgha.
This, monks, you should remember as the second great authority.
"Furthermore, monks, a monk might say this:
'In such-and-such a residence there dwell many elder monks who are learned, masters of the tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Matikas.
From the presence of those elders I have heard it; from their presence I have received it:'"
‘This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.
Monks, the speech of that monk should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without welcoming it and without rejecting it, those words and phrases should be carefully mastered and compared with the Suttas and verified against the Vinaya.
If, when being introduced into the Sutta and compared with the Vinaya, they do not descend into the Sutta nor appear in the Vinaya, one must reach the conclusion:
"Certainly this is not the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
it has been wrongly grasped by those elders."
"Thus, monks, you should discard this.
But suppose, monks, a monk were to say:
'In such-and-such a residence there dwell many elder monks who are learned, masters of the tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā.'"
‘I have heard this directly from those elders, received it directly from them:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.
Monks, the speech of that monk should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without approving and without rejecting those words and phrases, one should thoroughly master them and then compare them with the Sutta and verify them against the Vinaya.
If, when compared with the Sutta and verified against the Vinaya, they are found to enter into the Sutta and appear in the Vinaya, then one should reach the conclusion:
"This is certainly the word of that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
"And those elders have grasped it well.
This, monks, you should remember as the third great authority.
Furthermore, monks, a monk might say this:
‘In such-and-such a residence there dwells a certain elder bhikkhu who is learned, one who has mastered the tradition, a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, and a bearer of the Mātikā.
From the presence of that elder I have heard and received this:
“This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction.”’”
Monks, the speech of that bhikkhu should neither be welcomed nor rejected.
Without welcoming it and without rejecting it, those words and phrases should be carefully mastered and then compared with the Sutta and verified against the Vinaya.

If, when being compared with the Sutta and verified against the Vinaya, they do not enter into the Sutta and are not seen in the Vinaya, then one should reach the conclusion: [that this is not the word of the Buddha].

it has been wrongly grasped by that elder.
