"This is certainly the word of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
and it has been rightly grasped by that Elder."
“Monks, you should remember this as the fourth great authority.
These, monks, are the four great authorities.
The Tenth.
The Third Chapter on Volitional Intention.
Its summary verse:
Volition, Analysis, and the Section on Divisions.
Ānanda, Upavāṇa as the fifth;
the Request, Rāhula, Jambālī,
Nibbāna, and the Great Authorities.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.181 19. Brāhmaṇavagga Yodhājīvasutta (The Warrior) “Monks, there are these four kinds of warriors. What four? The warrior who, when the battle is joined, turns his back and flees; the warrior who, when the battle is joined, stands his ground but does not advance; the warrior who, when the battle is joined, advances but does not retreat; and the warrior who, when the battle is joined, fights on both sides until he emerges victorious. These, monks, are the four kinds of warriors. In the same way, monks, there are these four kinds of persons similar to warriors. What four? The person who, when the battle is joined, turns his back and flees; the person who, when the battle is joined, stands his ground but does not advance; the person who, when the battle is joined, advances but does not retreat; and the person who, when the battle is joined, fights on both sides until he emerges victorious. And how, monks, is one a person who, when the battle is joined, turns his back and flees? Here, monks, a certain person hears: ‘In that place there is abundant wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having heard this, he goes there. When he has gone there, he acquires much wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having acquired them, he becomes intoxicated with that gain, infatuated, and heedless. He indulges in sensual pleasures, neglects his duties, and squanders his wealth. Then, when his wealth is exhausted, he turns his back and flees. This, monks, is called the person who, when the battle is joined, turns his back and flees. And how, monks, is one a person who, when the battle is joined, stands his ground but does not advance? Here, monks, a certain person hears: ‘In that place there is abundant wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having heard this, he goes there. When he has gone there, he acquires much wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having acquired them, he becomes intoxicated with that gain, infatuated, and heedless. He indulges in sensual pleasures, neglects his duties, and squanders his wealth. Then, when his wealth is exhausted, he stands his ground but does not advance. This, monks, is called the person who, when the battle is joined, stands his ground but does not advance. And how, monks, is one a person who, when the battle is joined, advances but does not retreat? Here, monks, a certain person hears: ‘In that place there is abundant wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having heard this, he goes there. When he has gone there, he acquires much wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having acquired them, he does not become intoxicated with that gain, nor infatuated, nor heedless. He does not indulge in sensual pleasures, he does not neglect his duties, and he does not squander his wealth. Then, when his wealth is exhausted, he advances but does not retreat. This, monks, is called the person who, when the battle is joined, advances but does not retreat. And how, monks, is one a person who, when the battle is joined, fights on both sides until he emerges victorious? Here, monks, a certain person hears: ‘In that place there is abundant wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having heard this, he goes there. When he has gone there, he acquires much wealth, grain, gold, silver, property, and possessions. Having acquired them, he does not become intoxicated with that gain, nor infatuated, nor heedless. He does not indulge in sensual pleasures, he does not neglect his duties, and he does not squander his wealth. Then, when his wealth is exhausted, he fights on both sides until he emerges victorious. This, monks, is called the person who, when the battle is joined, fights on both sides until he emerges victorious. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons similar to warriors.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a warrior is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What are the four? [The Sutta continues with the list of qualities.]”
“Here, monks, a warrior is skilled in his stance, a long-distance shooter, one who hits the mark at once, and one who pierces a great body.
Endowed with these four qualities, monks, a warrior is worthy of a king, an attendant of a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu endowed with four qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
What are the four?
Here, monks, a monk is skilled in the target, he is a long-distance shooter, he is a shot-at-no-faults archer, and he is one who can split a great body.
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the target?
"Here, monks, a monk is virtuous... he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training.
In this way, monks, a monk is skilled in the situation.
And how, monks, is a monk one who shoots far?"
“Here, monks, a monk regards whatever form—whether past, future, or present;
internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form as:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Thus he sees it as it really is with correct wisdom.”
Whatever feeling there may be … whatever perception there may be … whatever formations there may be …
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
In this way, monks, a monk is one who shoots from afar.
And how, monks, is a monk one who shoots at the unerring mark?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: “This is suffering” … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
In this way, monks, a monk is one who shoots at the unerring mark.
And how, monks, is a monk a splitter of the great mass?
Here, monks, a monk splits the great mass of ignorance.
"In this way, monks, a monk is one who splits apart a great body.
Endowed with these four qualities, monks, a monk is worthy of offerings... an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.182 19. Brāhmaṇavagga Pāṭibhogasutta (The Discourse on Guarantees) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of guarantees.

What four? The guarantee of a debt, the guarantee of a lawsuit, the guarantee of a wife, and the guarantee of a child. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of guarantees. Just as, bhikkhus, when a person has given a guarantee of a debt, a lawsuit, a wife, or a child, they are not free from anxiety; so too, bhikkhus, when a person has taken up these four things, they are not free from anxiety. What four? Sensual pleasures, existence, views, and self-theories. When a person has taken up these four things, they are not free from anxiety. But, bhikkhus, when a person has abandoned these four things, they are free from anxiety. What four? Sensual pleasures, existence, views, and self-theories. When a person has abandoned these four things, they are free from anxiety.”
“Bhikkhus, for four things there is no guarantor—
whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.”
Of which four?
There is no guarantor—whether ascetic or brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—who can ensure: “May that which is subject to aging not age.”
‘May one subject to illness not fall ill’— there is no guarantor for this,
whether a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world;
‘May one subject to death not die’— there is no guarantor for this.
Whether it be a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, there is no one who can act as a guarantor, saying:
"Let the ripening of those evil deeds previously committed by oneself— which are defiling, conducive to renewed existence,
fraught with danger, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death— not come to pass."
“Whether it be an ascetic, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā,
or anyone else in the world— there is no one, bhikkhus, who can be a guarantor for these four things;
neither an ascetic, nor a brahmin, nor a deva, nor Māra, nor Brahmā, nor anyone else in the world.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.183 19.
Brāhmaṇavagga (The Chapter on Brahmins)
Sutasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, I am of such a doctrine and such a view as this:..."
‘Whoever speaks of what has been seen,
saying, “This is how I have seen it,” there is no fault in that;
whoever speaks of what has been heard— ’
"Thus have I heard"— there is no fault in this;
whoever speaks what they have understood—
"thus have I understood"— there is no fault in this.
"Whoever speaks of what they have cognized,
saying, 'Thus have I cognized,' there is no fault therein.
"Brahmin, I do not say that everything seen should be spoken of."
But I do not say, brahmin, that everything seen should not be spoken;
nor do I say, brahmin, that everything heard should be spoken;
nor do I say, brahmin, that everything heard should not be spoken.
"Brahmin, I do not say that everything that has been sensed should be spoken about;
nor, brahmin, do I say that everything that has been sensed should not be spoken about.
I do not say, brahmin, that everything that has been cognized should be spoken about."
"But, brahmin, I do not say that everything which has been cognized should not be spoken.
For, brahmin, regarding what has been seen, if by speaking of it unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, I say that such a thing seen should not be spoken.
But, brahmin, regarding what has been seen, if by not speaking of it wholesome states decline and unwholesome states increase, I say that such a thing seen should be spoken."
“Brahmin, I say that one should not speak of what has been heard if, by speaking of it, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.
But, Brahmin, I say that one should speak of what has been heard if, by not speaking of it, wholesome states decline and unwholesome states increase.
Likewise, Brahmin, I say that one should not speak of what has been sensed if, by speaking of it, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline.”
“Brahmin, when by speaking of what has been sensed, wholesome states decline and unwholesome states increase, I say that such a thing sensed should be spoken of.
But when by speaking of what has been cognized, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, I say that such a thing cognized should not be spoken of.”
“Furthermore, brahmin, if through not speaking what one has cognized, wholesome states decline and unwholesome states increase, I say that such a thing as has been cognized should be spoken.
Then the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and departed.
This is the third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.184 19.

Brāhmaṇavagga Abhayasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is fearful and apprehensive; the person who is fearful but not apprehensive; the person who is not fearful but apprehensive; and the person who is neither fearful nor apprehensive. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
(AN 4.184, PTS AN ii 173) Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, I am one who speaks thus and holds this view:
‘There is no one subject to death who does not fear it, who does not fall into terror of death.
“Brahmin, there is indeed one subject to death who fears it, who falls into terror of death.”
But there is, brahmin, one who, being subject to death, does not fear death nor fall into terror of death.
And who, brahmin, being subject to death, fears death and falls into terror of death?

Here, brahmin, a certain person is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, and not free from craving for them.
Then a certain severe illness afflicts him.
Being afflicted by that severe illness, it occurs to him:
"Alas, dear sensual pleasures will abandon me, and I shall abandon dear sensual pleasures."
Thus he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he weeps beating his breast and falls into confusion.
This, brahmin, is how one who is subject to death fears and falls into terror at the prospect of death.
Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is not free from lust for the body, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, and not free from craving for it.
Then a certain severe illness afflicts him.
Being afflicted by that severe illness, it occurs to him:
"Alas, this dear body will abandon me, and I shall abandon this dear body."
Thus he sorrows, becomes weary, and laments; he beats his breast and falls into confusion.
This person too, O brahmin, being subject to death, fears death and falls into terror.
Furthermore, O brahmin, here someone has not done what is good, has not done what is wholesome, has not created a refuge from fear; he has done evil, has done cruel deeds, and has committed sins.
Then a certain severe illness afflicts him. Being afflicted by that severe illness, it occurs to him:
"Alas, I have not done what is beautiful; I have not done what is wholesome; I have not made a refuge for myself in times of fear."
‘Evil was done by me, cruel was done by me, sinful was done by me.

To whatever destination those who have not done what is good, who have not done what is wholesome, who have not made a refuge from fear, who have done evil, who have done cruel deeds, who have done sinful deeds go after death—that destination I shall go.
Thus he sorrows, suffers, laments; he beats his breast and falls into confusion.
This person too, brahmin, being subject to death, fears death and falls into terror of it.
Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is full of doubt, wavering, and undecided regarding the true Dhamma.
Then a certain severe illness afflicts him.
When he is afflicted by some severe illness, it occurs to him:
"I am indeed full of doubt, full of uncertainty, and have failed to reach the true Dhamma.
He sorrows, suffers, laments, beats his breast and weeps, and falls into confusion.
This one, too, brahmin, being subject to death, fears death and falls into terror of death.
These four, brahmin, being subject to death, fear death and fall into terror of death.
And who, brahmin, being subject to death, does not fear death and does not fall into terror of death?
"Here, brahmin, a certain person is free from passion for sensual pleasures, devoid of desire, devoid of affection, devoid of thirst, devoid of fever, and devoid of craving.
Yet, he is struck by some severe illness or affliction.
When he is afflicted by that severe illness or affliction, it does not occur to him:"
‘Alas, may dear sensual pleasures leave me, and may I leave dear sensual pleasures.
He does not grieve, he does not languish, he does not lament; he does not beat his breast and weep, nor does he fall into confusion.
This, brahmin, is one who, being subject to death, neither fears nor falls into terror at the prospect of death.
Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is free from lust for the body, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from fever, and free from craving.
Yet he is struck by some severe illness or affliction.
When he is afflicted by that severe illness or affliction, it does not occur to him:
‘Truly, my dear body will leave me, and I shall leave behind my dear body.
Thus he does not grieve, does not suffer, does not lament; he does not weep beating his breast, nor does he fall into confusion.
This too, brahmin, being subject to death, does not fear death, nor does he fall into terror at death.

Furthermore, brahmin, here someone has not committed evil, has not acted with cruelty, has not done what is blameworthy; he has performed what is beautiful, what is wholesome, and what provides a refuge for those in fear.
Then, a certain severe illness and affliction strikes him.
Being afflicted by that severe illness and affliction, it occurs to him:
‘Indeed, no evil has been done by me, no cruelty, no wickedness;
what is beautiful has been done, what is wholesome has been done, and a refuge for those who fear has been made.

To whatever destination belongs those who have not done evil, who have not done cruelty, who have not done wickedness, who have done what is beautiful, who have done what is wholesome, and who have made a refuge for those who fear—to that destination shall I go after passing away.’
Thus he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament; he does not beat his breast and weep, nor does he fall into confusion.
This person too, brahmin, though subject to death, neither fears nor falls into terror at the prospect of death.
Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is free from doubt, without uncertainty, having reached a conclusion regarding the true Dhamma.
Then a certain severe illness afflicts him.
When he is afflicted by that severe illness, it occurs to him:
"I am indeed free from doubt, without uncertainty, and have reached the conclusion regarding the true Dhamma."
Thus he does not grieve, does not weary, does not lament; he does not beat his breast and weep, nor does he fall into confusion.
This person too, brahmin, though subject to death, neither fears nor falls into terror at the prospect of death.
These, brahmin, are the four who, though subject to death, do not fear and do not fall into terror at death.”
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! … [as before] … Let Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.185

19. Brāhmaṇavagga Brāhmaṇasaccasutta (AN 4.185, PTS AN ii 176) “Brahmins, there are these four truths. What four? The truth of the noble ones that is to be fully understood; the truth of the noble ones that is to be abandoned; the truth of the noble ones that is to be developed; and the truth of the noble ones that is to be realized. And what, brahmins, is the truth of the noble ones that is to be fully understood? It is this: ‘This is suffering. This is the truth of the noble ones that is to be fully understood. And what, brahmins, is the truth of the noble ones that is to be abandoned? It is this: ‘This is the origin of suffering. This is the truth of the noble ones that is to be abandoned. And what, brahmins, is the truth of the noble ones that is to be developed? It is this: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. This is the truth of the noble ones that is to be developed. And what, brahmins, is the truth of the noble ones that is to be realized? It is this: ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering. This is the truth of the noble ones that is to be realized. These, brahmins, are the four truths of the noble ones.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, several well-known and renowned wanderers were residing in the Wanderers’ Park on the bank of the Sippinikā River, namely:
Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyin, and other well-known wanderers.
These were well-known wanderers.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the wanderers’ park on the bank of the Sippinikā River.
Now at that time, this discussion arose among those wanderers of other sects as they were sitting together in assembly:
“‘Such indeed are the truths of the brahmins, such indeed are the truths of the brahmins.
Then the Blessed One approached those wanderers; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to those wanderers:
‘Wanderers, with what discussion are you currently seated together, and what was the conversation of yours that remained unfinished?’”
“Here, Master Gotama, while we were sitting together in assembly, this discussion arose among us:
‘Such-and-such are the truths of the brahmins; such-and-such are the truths of the brahmins.
“Wanderers, there are these four truths of the brahmins that have been declared by me after having realized them for myself through direct knowledge.”
Which four?
Here, wanderers, a brahmin says this:
‘All living beings are not to be killed.’
Speaking thus, the brahmin speaks the truth, not a falsehood.

Because of that, he does not conceive "I am an ascetic," nor does he conceive "I am a brahmin"; he does not conceive "I am superior," nor does he conceive "I am equal," nor does he conceive "I am inferior.
Rather, having directly known that which is true therein, he practices out of compassion and sympathy for living beings alone.
Furthermore, wanderers, a brahmin says this:
“All sensual pleasures are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
Speaking thus, the brahmin speaks truth, not falsehood.

Therefore, he does not conceive, "I am an ascetic," nor does he conceive, "I am a brahmin"; he does not conceive, "I am superior," nor does he conceive, "I am equal," nor does he conceive, "I am inferior.
Rather, having directly known whatever truth there is in that regard, he practices for the very sake of disenchantment with sensual pleasures, for their fading away, and for their cessation.
Furthermore, wanderers, a brahmin speaks thus:

‘All states of existence are impermanent’ … [as before] … through direct knowledge of this, he is practicing for disenchantment with states of existence, for dispassion toward them, and for their cessation.
Furthermore, wanderers, a brahmin says thus:
‘I am not anything belonging to anyone anywhere, nor is there anything belonging to me anywhere at all.’”
Speaking thus, the brahmin speaks the truth, not a falsehood.

Because of that, he does not conceive himself as a recluse, nor does he conceive himself as a brahmin; he does not conceive "I am superior," nor does he conceive "I am equal," nor does he conceive "I am inferior.
Rather, having directly known whatever truth there is in that regard, he has entered upon the very practice of nothingness.
“Monks, these four brahmin truths have been proclaimed by me after having realized them for myself through direct higher knowledge.
The fifth.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.186

19. Brāhmaṇavagga Ummaggasutta (The Discourse on the Wrong Path) “Brahmins, there are these four wrong paths. What four? ‘The world is eternal’—this is the first wrong path. ‘The world is not eternal’—this is the second wrong path. ‘The world is finite’—this is the third wrong path. ‘The world is infinite’—this is the fourth wrong path. These, brahmins, are the four wrong paths.”
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“By what, Bhante, is the world led? By what is the world dragged along? And under whose power does it fall once [something] has arisen?
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
“Excellent indeed is your approach, bhikkhu; excellent is your ingenuity; beautiful is your inquiry.
For it is thus that you ask:
‘By what, venerable sir, is the world led? By what is the world dragged along? And under the sway of what, once arisen, does the world fall?’”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“By mind, bhikkhu, the world is led; by mind it is dragged around; it falls under the sway of the mind that has arisen.
“It is well, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu said, and having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, he asked the Blessed One a further question:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma; one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma.
To what extent, venerable sir, is one learned and a bearer of the Dhamma?
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
“Excellent indeed is your approach, bhikkhu; excellent is your ingenuity; beautiful is your inquiry.
For it is thus you ask:
‘Venerable sir, it is said: “one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma.”’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one considered ‘learned’ and ‘a bearer of the Dhamma’?
“So it is, venerable sir.
“Bhikkhu, many teachings have been taught by me—”
“Discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, ‘Thus-it-was-said’ passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analyses.
Even if one understands the meaning and the Dhamma of a single four-line verse, and practices in accordance with the Dhamma, one may be called ‘learned’ and ‘a bearer of the Dhamma.
“Excellent, Bhante! that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, asked the Blessed One a further question:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘one of learned wisdom, one of penetrative wisdom; one of learned wisdom, one of penetrative wisdom.
To what extent, venerable sir, is one a person of learned wisdom and penetrative wisdom?
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhu!
“Excellent indeed is your approach, bhikkhu; excellent is your ingenuity; beautiful is your inquiry. For thus you ask:
‘Venerable sir, it is said: “one of learned and penetrative wisdom, one of learned and penetrative wisdom.”’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one a learned person of penetrative wisdom?
“In this way, bhikkhu.
“In this case, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu has heard: ‘This is suffering,’ and he sees its meaning, having penetrated it with wisdom.”
‘This is the origin of suffering’—this has been heard, and one sees its meaning by penetrating it with wisdom;
‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this has been heard, and one sees its meaning by penetrating it with wisdom;
‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’—this has been heard, and one sees its meaning by penetrating it with wisdom.
“In this way, bhikkhu, one who has heard [the Dhamma] becomes one of penetrative wisdom.
“Excellent, Bhante,” that bhikkhu said, rejoicing and expressing his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words. Then he asked the Blessed One a further question:
“Bhante, it is said: ‘a wise man of great wisdom, a wise man of great wisdom.’”
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one wise and of great wisdom?
“Excellent, excellent, monk!
Your approach is auspicious, your ingenuity is auspicious, and your inquiry is admirable.”
For thus you ask, monk:
“‘Wise, of great wisdom,’ it is said, venerable sir.
In what way, venerable sir, is one wise and of great wisdom?”’”
“Yes, venerable sir.

“Here, bhikkhu, a wise person of great wisdom does not intend for his own affliction, nor does he intend for the affliction of others, nor does he intend for the affliction of both; rather, intending only what is beneficial for himself, beneficial for others, and beneficial for both, he thinks thoughts that are for the welfare of the whole world.
It is in this way, bhikkhu, that one is a wise person of great wisdom.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.187 19.
Brāhmaṇavagga (The Chapter on Brahmins)
The Discourse to Vassakāra (Vassakārasutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
"Could an untrue man, Master Gotama, recognize an untrue man?"
“Is this person an untrue man?
“It is impossible, brahmin, it cannot happen that an untrue man would know of another untrue man:
‘This person is an untrue man.’”
“But could an untrue man, Master Gotama, know an true man, thinking:
‘This venerable one is a true man’?
“That too, brahmin, is impossible, it cannot happen, that an untrue man should know a true man: ‘This venerable one is a true man.’”
“‘This person is a true man.
“But, Master Gotama, would a true man recognize another true man as:
‘This person is a true man’?”
“It is possible, brahmin, that a true person might recognize another true person, thinking:
‘This worthy man is a true person.
But could a true person, Master Gotama, recognize a person who is not a true person?”
“‘This person, sir, is not a true man,’ is that so?
“Indeed, brahmin, it is possible that a true man would know an untrue man:
‘This person, sir, is not a true man.’”
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
How well this has been stated by Master Gotama:
‘It is impossible, brahmin, it cannot happen that an untrue man should know an untrue man—’”
"This person is an untrue man.
This too, brahmin, is impossible, it cannot happen, that an untrue man would know a true man:
"This person is a true man."
"It is indeed possible, brahmin, that a true person might recognize another true person, thinking:
'This one is a true person.
It is also possible, brahmin, that a true person might recognize a person who is not a true person."
“This person is not a true man.
Once, Master Gotama, in the assembly of the brahmin Todeyya, they were speaking in criticism of others:

“This King Eḷeyya is a fool, for he has full confidence in the ascetic Rāmaputta; and he performs such supreme acts of homage toward the ascetic Rāmaputta as bowing down, rising up, joining his palms, and performing proper services.”
These attendants of King Eḷeyya were also fools:
Yamaka, Moggalla, Ugga, Nāvindakī, Gandhabba, and Aggivessa;
they were deeply devoted to the ascetic Rāmaputta and performed such supreme acts of service for him as this, namely, paying him homage.
‘Rising to greet, joining the palms in salutation, and performing acts of respect.
In this manner, the brahmin Todeyya leads them.
“What do you think, sirs?”
“Is King Eḷeyya wise, such that in matters requiring action and in matters requiring speech, he is wiser than those who are already wise?
“Yes, sir, King Eḷeyya is wise; in matters requiring action and in matters requiring speech, he is wiser than those who are already wise.
However, sir, the ascetic Rāmaputta is even wiser than the wise King Eḷeyya in matters requiring action and in matters requiring speech.”

"Among those who are worthy of being spoken to and those who are even more worthy of being spoken to, one who perceives the goal is superior to one who does not; therefore, King Eḷeyya has full confidence in the ascetic Rāmaputta, and he performs such supreme acts of homage toward the ascetic Rāmaputta as these:
salutation, rising from one's seat, joining of palms, and respectful service."
"What do you think, sirs,
wise men as they are— the attendants of King Eḷeyya,

namely Yamaka, Moggalla, Ugga, Nāvindakī, Gandhabba, and Aggivessa— are they more capable of accomplishing what needs to be done and responding to what needs to be said than those who are already highly capable?"

‘It is so, sir; the wise attendants of King Eḷeyya—Yamaka, Moggalla, Ugga, Nāvindakī, Gandhabba, and Aggivessa—are more capable in what must be done and what must be undertaken, more eloquent in speech and response, and more discerning of the goal than others who are themselves discerning of the goal.
Yet, sir, the ascetic Rāmaputta is even wiser than these wise attendants of King Eḷeyya.’
"In matters requiring action and in matters requiring speech, those who are more discerning of the goal are superior to those less discerning.
Therefore, the attendants of King Eḷeyya have placed their full confidence in the ascetics, the followers of Rāma;

and they perform such supreme acts of service toward the ascetics, the followers of Rāma, as bowing down, rising from their seats, joining their palms in salutation, and performing respectful duties."
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
How well this has been expressed by Master Gotama:
‘It is impossible, brahmin, it cannot happen that an untrue man should know an untrue man—’”
"This person is an untrue man.
This too, brahmin, is impossible, it cannot happen, that an untrue man would know a true man:
"This person is a true man."
"It is indeed possible, brahmin, that a true person might recognize another true person, thinking:
'This one is a true person.
It is also possible, brahmin, that a true person might recognize a person who is not a true person."
“This person is not a true man.
Well now, Master Gotama, we must go;
we have many duties and much to do.
“Now, brahmin, you may go at your own convenience.
Then Vassakāra, the brahmin and chief minister of Magadha, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat and departed.
This was the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.188 19. Brāhmaṇavagga Upaka Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. At that time, the wanderer Upaka approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Upaka said this to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I have heard this: ‘The ascetic Gotama knows the path to the state of a Brahmā. Does Master Gotama know the path to the state of a Brahmā? “I know the path to the state of a Brahmā, Upaka; I know it thoroughly. “What is that path to the state of a Brahmā, Master Gotama? “It is, Upaka, when a bhikkhu dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, possessed of the restraint of the sense faculties, and is moderate in eating. He is devoted to wakefulness, possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension, and dwells having abandoned the hindrances. This, Upaka, is the path to the state of a Brahmā. “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. Then the wanderer Upaka, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the wanderer Upaka had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, do you see how the wanderer Upaka’s face is bright and his complexion is serene? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, the wanderer Upaka has seen the Dhamma. “Venerable sir, how is it that the wanderer Upaka has seen the Dhamma? “Bhikkhus, when a person sees the Dhamma, they see the Tathāgata; and when they see the Tathāgata, they see the Dhamma. For the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma, and the Dhamma is the Tathāgata. It is because of this that the wanderer Upaka has seen the Dhamma. When this was said, the wanderer Upaka stopped at a certain place, turned back, and said to the bhikkhus: “Friends, I have seen the Dhamma. “How is it, friend, that you have seen the Dhamma? “Friends, when a person sees the Dhamma, they see the Tathāgata; and when they see the Tathāgata, they see the Dhamma. For the Tathāgata, friends, is the Dhamma, and the Dhamma is the Tathāgata. It is because of this that I have seen the Dhamma. Then the bhikkhus went to the Blessed One and reported this matter to him. The Blessed One then said: “Bhikkhus, the wanderer Upaka has indeed seen the Dhamma. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, the brahmin student Ambaṭṭha was studying under the brahmin Pokkharasāti in the northern country. He had mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual manuals, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as the fifth; he was skilled in philology and grammar, and was fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a Great Man. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala had sent a messenger to the brahmin Pokkharasāti with the message: “Let the brahmin Pokkharasāti come to the king; the king wishes to see him. Then the brahmin student Ambaṭṭha thought: “This is the time to go to the brahmin Pokkharasāti. So he set out for the northern country. Meanwhile, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. The brahmin student Ambaṭṭha saw the Blessed One from afar as he was walking for alms with a steady gaze, with eyes cast down, with limbs withdrawn, with senses calmed, and with a mind composed. Seeing him, he thought: “It would be good if I were to approach this ascetic Gotama and ask him about his lineage. Then the brahmin student Ambaṭṭha approached the Blessed One and said: “Ascetic, what is your clan? “I am of the Sakyans, student. “But the Sakyans are servants, ascetic; the Sakyans are servants, ascetic. “Student, the Sakyans are khattiyas, great khattiyas; the Sakyans are khattiyas, great khattiyas. Then the brahmin student Ambaṭṭha, being angry and displeased, spoke these words of contempt: “Ascetic, you are a slave, a slave’s son, born from the loins of a slave woman, one who was purchased for a price and brought away. How can you claim to be of the Sakyans? The Sakyans are khattiyas, great khattiyas; the Sakyans are khattiyas, great khattiyas. “Student, do you speak thus because you have been told so by others, or because you know it yourself? “I speak thus because I have been told so by others, ascetic, and because I know it myself. “Student, do you know the lineage of the Sakyans? “Yes, ascetic, I know the lineage of the Sakyans. “Then tell us, student, how the Sakyans originated. “Ascetic, the Sakyans originated from the root of a branch of the Sakka tree. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a tree named ‘Sakka’? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a tree. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom, and who was the father of the Sakyans? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom, and who was the grandfather of the Sakyans? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom, and who was the great-grandfather of the Sakyans? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom, and who was the ancestor of the Sakyans? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom, and who was the progenitor of the Sakyans? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom, and who was the founder of the Sakyans? “No, ascetic, I have neither seen nor heard of such a man. “Student, have you ever seen or heard of a man named ‘Sakka’ who was a khattiya, a great khattiya, ruling over a kingdom, and who was the
(AN 4.188, PTS AN ii 181) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture’s Peak Mountain.

Then Upaka Maṇḍikāputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Upaka Maṇḍikāputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I am one who speaks thus and holds this view:
‘Whoever engages in criticism of others, when engaging in such criticism, fails to establish his point.
One who fails to establish his point is censurable and blameworthy.’”

“Upaka, if one engages in attacking others, and while engaging in attacking others one does not provide a justification for it, then by failing to provide a justification, one becomes censurable and blameworthy.
You, Upaka, engage in attacking others, yet while engaging in attacking others you do not provide a justification; by failing to provide a justification, you become censurable and blameworthy.
“It is as if, Bhante, one were to bind with a great snare a person at the very moment they are emerging [from the water].”
“In this very way, Bhante, even as I was just emerging, I have been caught by the Blessed One with the great hook of his teaching.
“Upaka, I have declared: ‘This is unwholesome.
In this regard, there are immeasurable phrases, immeasurable syllables, and immeasurable teachings on the Dhamma from the Tathāgata.”
"Thus this is unwholesome.
Furthermore, Upaka, it has been declared by me that this unwholesome must be abandoned.
In this regard, there are immeasurable words, immeasurable phrases, and immeasurable teachings on the Dhamma by the Tathāgata.
"Thus, this is unwholesome and should be abandoned.
Now, Upaka, "this is wholesome" is how it has been designated by me.
In this regard, there are immeasurable words, immeasurable phrases, and immeasurable teachings on the Dhamma by the Tathāgata.
"Thus this is wholesome.
Furthermore, Upaka, I have declared that this wholesome state is to be developed.
In this regard, there are immeasurable words, immeasurable phrases, and immeasurable teachings on the Dhamma from the Tathāgata.
“Thus, this wholesome state should be developed.
Then Upaka Maṇḍikāputta, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words,
rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, went to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha.
He approached him; having approached, he reported in full to King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha everything that had been the conversation and discussion between him and the Blessed One.
When this was said, King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha, angry and displeased, said this to Upaka Maṇḍikāputta:
“How corrupt indeed is this salt-maker’s son! How talkative! How impudent! For how could he think to offend that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
Begone, Upaka! Perish! May you not see him! This was the eighth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.189 19. Brāhmaṇavagga Sacchikaraṇīyasutta (The Discourse on What Should Be Realized) “Bhikkhus, there are these four things that should be realized. What four? ‘This is suffering’—this, bhikkhus, is the first thing that should be realized. ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this, bhikkhus, is the second thing that should be realized. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this, bhikkhus, is the third thing that should be realized. ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—this, bhikkhus, is the fourth thing that should be realized. These, bhikkhus, are the four things that should be realized.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things to be realized. Which four? [The text continues as follows:]”
"There are, monks, states to be realized by means of the body;
there are, monks, states to be realized by means of mindfulness;
there are, monks, states to be realized by means of the eye."
"There are, monks, states to be realized through wisdom.
And what, monks, are the states to be realized by the body?
The eight liberations, monks, are to be realized by the body."
"And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be realized through mindfulness?
Former lives, bhikkhus, are to be realized through mindfulness.
And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be realized through the eye?"
The passing away and rebirth of beings, monks, is to be realized by means of the eye.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be realized by means of wisdom?
The destruction of the taints, monks, is to be realized by means of wisdom.
“Monks, these are the four things to be realized.
Thus was the ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.190.

19. Brāhmaṇa Vagga: Uposatha Sutta (AN 4.190, PTS AN ii 183) “Brahmins, there are these four kinds of uposatha. What four? The uposatha of the worldlings, the uposatha of the ordinary disciples, the uposatha of the noble ones, and the supreme uposatha. And what, brahmins, is the uposatha of the worldlings? Here, brahmins, some person observes the uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, thinking: ‘May my body be pure, may my speech be pure, may my mind be pure; may I be free from ill-will and hatred. This, brahmins, is called the uposatha of the worldlings. And what, brahmins, is the uposatha of the ordinary disciples? Here, brahmins, some person who is a stream-enterer or one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry observes the uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, thinking: ‘May my body be pure, may my speech be pure, may my mind be pure; may I be free from ill-will and hatred. This, brahmins, is called the uposatha of the ordinary disciples. And what, brahmins, is the uposatha of the noble ones? Here, brahmins, some person who is a once-returner or one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning observes the uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, thinking: ‘May my body be pure, may my speech be pure, may my mind be pure; may I be free from ill-will and hatred. This, brahmins, is called the uposatha of the noble ones. And what, brahmins, is the supreme uposatha? Here, brahmins, some person who is a non-returner or one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning observes the uposatha on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight, thinking: ‘May my body be pure, may my speech be pure, may my mind be pure; may I be free from ill-will and hatred. This, brahmins, is called the supreme uposatha. These, brahmins, are the four kinds of uposatha.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day, the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent Saṅgha of bhikkhus again and again, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, this assembly is free from chaff, monks, this assembly is free from rubbish; it is pure and established in the essence.
Such, monks, is this Saṅgha of bhikkhus; such, monks, is this assembly.
An assembly such as this is difficult to behold even in the world; such, monks, is this Saṅgha of bhikkhus; such, monks, is this assembly.”

“Monks, such is this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, such is this assembly, as an assembly that is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Monks, such is this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, such is this assembly, as an assembly where what is given becomes much, and what is given in abundance becomes even more abundant.”
“Monks, such is this Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and such is this assembly, that it is sufficient to go even for many leagues to see it, even with a shoulder-bag.
Monks, there are bhikkhus in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus who dwell having attained the state of a deva;
monks, there are bhikkhus in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus who dwell having attained the state of a Brahmā.”
"There are, monks, monks in this Saṅgha of monks who dwell having attained the imperturbable;
there are, monks, monks in this Saṅgha of monks who dwell having attained the noble state.
And how, monks, does a monk become one who has attained the divine state?"
“Here, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna;
with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought … [as above] … he enters and dwells in the second jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu has attained the state of a deva.”
And how, monks, does a monk attain to the state of Brahmā?
Here, monks, a monk dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself.
He dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity,
and free from ill will. [He dwells likewise] with compassion...
...with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy ... he dwells pervading one quarter; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.
Thus above, below, across, everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
In this way, monks, a monk has attained the state of Brahmā.
And how, monks, does a monk attain the imperturbable?

“Here, monks, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] ‘space is infinite,’ a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
By completely transcending the base of infinite space, [thinking] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [thinking] ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.”
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In this way, monks, a monk has attained imperturbability.
And how, monks, does a monk attain the noble state?
“Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [as before] … he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a monk has attained the noble state.
The tenth.
The fourth chapter, the Chapter on Brahmins.
Its summary verse:
The Warriors, the Pāṭibhoga, the Discourse, ...
The fearless through truth, O brahmin, is the fifth;
the Ummagga, Vassakāra, Upaka, realization, and the Uposatha.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.191 20. Mahāvagga Sotānugatasutta The Discourse on What Flows Along with the Stream “Monks, there are these four things that flow along with the stream. What four? Flowing along with the stream, one does not cross over; flowing along with the stream, one does not reach the further shore; flowing along with the stream, one does not attain nibbāna; flowing along with the stream, one does not realize the unsurpassed security from bondage. And what, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not cross over? It is sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). This, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not cross over. And what, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not reach the further shore? It is ill will (*vyāpāda*). This, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not reach the further shore. And what, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not attain nibbāna? It is dullness and drowsiness (*thinamiddha*). This, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not attain nibbāna. And what, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not realize the unsurpassed security from bondage? It is restlessness and remorse (*uddhaccakukkucca*). This, monks, is the thing that flows along with the stream by which one does not realize the unsurpassed security from bondage. These, monks, are the four things that flow along with the stream.”
“Bhikkhus, for teachings that have been followed by ear,
mastered by word of mouth, examined by the mind, and well penetrated by view, four benefits are to be expected. What four?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and analytical expositions.
Those teachings have entered his ear, been mastered by his speech, examined by his mind, and well-penetrated by his view.
Thus, one who dies with a muddled mindfulness is reborn in a certain order of devas.
While there, being happy, the words of the Dhamma float before them.
But, bhikkhus, the arising of their mindfulness is slow.
Then that being quickly becomes one who attains distinction.
Monks, when teachings have been entered into by the ear, mastered by speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view, this is the first benefit to be expected.
Furthermore, monks, a monk masters the Dhamma—
The discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and analytical expositions—
these teachings have entered his ear, been mastered by speech, examined by the mind,
and well-penetrated by view. Dying with muddled mindfulness, he is reborn in a certain order of devas.
In that situation, not only do verses of Dhamma float up for him;
rather, a bhikkhu who possesses psychic power and has attained mastery over his mind teaches the Dhamma in an assembly of devas,
and it occurs to him:
‘This indeed is that Dhamma and Vinaya wherein I formerly practiced the holy life.
Slow, monks, is the arising of mindfulness;
yet that being very quickly becomes one who attains distinction.
"Just as if, monks, there were a man skilled in the sound of a drum, who,
while traveling along a highway, were to hear the sound of a drum;
he would have no doubt or perplexity regarding it."
‘Is this the sound of a drum, or is it not the sound of a drum? Then he would come to the conclusion that it is indeed the sound of a drum.
In the same way, monks, a monk masters the Dhamma.
The discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "thus-it-was-said" passages, birth stories, accounts of marvelous phenomena, and analytical expositions.
These teachings have entered his ear, been mastered by him through speech, examined by him with the mind, and well-penetrated by him through right view.
Dying with muddled mindfulness, he is reborn in a certain order of devas.
In that situation, not only do joyful verses of Dhamma float to him;
rather, a bhikkhu who possesses supernormal power and has attained mastery over his mind teaches the Dhamma in an assembly of devas.
It occurs to him thus:
‘This indeed is that Dhamma and Discipline in which I formerly practiced the holy life.
Slow, monks, is the arising of mindfulness;
yet that being very quickly becomes one who attains distinction.
“Monks, for those teachings that have been entered into by hearing, mastered by recitation, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view, this second benefit is to be expected.
Furthermore, monks, a monk masters the Dhamma:

discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), legends (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical expositions (vedalla).”
Those teachings have entered his ear, been mastered by him through speech, examined by him with the mind, and well-penetrated by him through right view.
When he passes away with muddled mindfulness, he is reborn in a certain assembly of devas.

There, however, the words of the Dhamma do not float before him as they do for one who is happy, nor does a bhikkhu possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over his mind teach the Dhamma in that assembly of devas.
Moreover, a son of the gods teaches the Dhamma in an assembly of gods.
It occurs to him:
"This indeed is that Dhamma and Discipline in which I formerly practiced the holy life."
“Slow, bhikkhus, is the arising of mindfulness;
yet that being quickly becomes one who goes to distinction.
It is just as if, bhikkhus, there were a man skilled in the sound of a conch.”
Suppose a person traveling along a highway were to hear the sound of a conch shell.
He would have no doubt or perplexity as to whether it was indeed the sound of a conch shell or not.
Then one would simply conclude that it was the sound of a conch.
In the same way, monks, a monk masters the Dhamma:

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical teachings (vedalla).
Those teachings have entered his ear, been mastered by him through speech, examined by him with the mind, and well-penetrated by him through right view.
When he passes away with muddled mindfulness, he is reborn in a certain company of devas.

There, however, the words of the Dhamma do not float before him as they did when he was happy, nor does a bhikkhu possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind teach the Dhamma in that assembly of devas.
Moreover, a son of the gods teaches the Dhamma in an assembly of gods.
It occurs to him:
"This is that Dhamma and Discipline in which I formerly practiced the holy life."
“Slow, monks, is the arising of mindfulness;
yet that being very quickly becomes one who attains distinction.
This, monks, is the third benefit to be expected for those teachings that have been followed by ear, mastered by word of mouth, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view.”
Furthermore, monks, a monk masters the Dhamma—
the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, "Thus it was said" sayings, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers.
Those teachings have entered his ear, are mastered by his speech, examined by his mind, and well-penetrated by his view.
Thus, one who dies with a muddled mindfulness is reborn in a certain class of devas.

There, the words of the Dhamma do not float before him as they do for those who are happy; nor does a bhikkhu possessing psychic power and mastery over his own mind teach the Dhamma to the assembly of devas, nor does a son of the devas teach the Dhamma to the assembly of devas;
rather, it is simply that one being born by spontaneous generation reminds another being born by spontaneous generation.
‘Do you remember, dear sir? Do you remember, dear sir, where we formerly practiced the holy life?
He replied:
‘I remember, dear sir; I remember, dear sirs.’
“Bhikkhus, the arising of mindfulness is slow,
yet that being very quickly becomes one who attains distinction.
It is just as if, bhikkhus, there were two friends who played together in the dust.”
At some time or another, they might meet one another.
Then one companion might say to the other:
“Do you remember this, friend? Do you remember that, friend?”
He would say:
‘I remember, friend, I remember, friend.
In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma.

The discourses (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), inspired utterances (*udāna*), "thus-it-was-said" (*itivuttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), marvelous qualities (*abbhutadhamma*), and analytical expositions (*vedalla*).
Those teachings have entered his ear, been mastered by speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view.
Dying with mindfulness lost, he is reborn in a certain order of devas.

There, not only do verses on the Dhamma not float to him as he experiences happiness, nor does a bhikkhu possessing psychic power who has attained mastery over his mind teach the Dhamma to the assembly of devas, nor does a son of the devas teach the Dhamma to the assembly of devas;
rather, one being of spontaneous birth reminds another being of spontaneous birth:
"Do you remember, dear sir? Do you remember, dear sir? Where we formerly practiced the holy life."
So he spoke thus:
“I remember, dear sir; I remember, dear sir.
Slow, monks, is the arising of mindfulness.
Then that being very quickly becomes one who attains distinction.
Monks, for teachings that have been heard, mastered through speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view, this fourth benefit is to be expected.
Monks, for teachings that have been heard, mastered through speech, examined by the mind, and well-penetrated by view, these four benefits are to be expected.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.192 20. Mahāvagga
The Discourse on the Bases (Ṭhānasutta). “Bhikkhus,
these four bases are to be understood by means of four bases.”
Which four?

Monks, virtue is to be known through cohabitation, and that only over a long period, not a short one; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is wise, not by one who is unwise.
Purity is to be known through dealings, and that only over a long period, not a short one; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is wise, not by one who is unwise.

"In times of adversity, monks, fortitude is to be known; and that only over a long period, not briefly; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted.

In conversation, monks, wisdom is to be known; and that only over a long period, not briefly; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted."
“‘By living together, monks, virtue is to be known; and that, moreover, over a long period of time, not briefly; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive;
by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted’—this is what was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, a person living together with another person knows thus:”
‘For a long time, indeed, this venerable one has been a doer of brokenness, a doer of flaws, a doer of blemishes, and a doer of stains; he is not a doer of continuity, nor is his conduct continuous.
This venerable one is immoral regarding the precepts; this venerable one is not virtuous.
But here, monks, when one person lives together with another, he knows thus:
‘For a long time this venerable one has acted without flaw, without breach, without defect, without impurity; he acts continuously and lives a continuous life;
this venerable one is virtuous in his conduct, this venerable one is not immoral.
‘Monks, virtue is to be known through association, and that too over a long period, not a short one; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive.’

‘It is by means of commerce, monks, that purity is to be known, and that only over a long period of time, not briefly; by one who attends to it, not one who does not attend to it; by one who possesses wisdom, not by one who lacks wisdom. This is what was said. And with reference to what was this said?

‘It is by means of commerce, monks, that purity is to be known, and that only over a long period of time, not briefly; by one who attends to it, not one who does not attend to it; by one who possesses wisdom, not by one who lacks wisdom.
This, indeed, was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this case, monks, when a person is conducting business with another person, he knows:
"This venerable one conducts himself in one way when alone, in another way when with two, in another way when with three, and in another way when with many;
this venerable one deviates from his earlier conduct to a later conduct."
‘This venerable one’s dealings are impure; this venerable one is not pure in his dealings.
But here, monks, when a person is conducting business with another person, he knows:
‘Just as this venerable one deals with one person alone, so does he deal with two, so with three, and so with many.’
‘This venerable one does not deviate from his former mode of speech to a later mode of speech;
this venerable one’s mode of speech is pure, this venerable one is not of impure speech.
‘Monks, purity should be understood through one’s dealings, and that over a long period of time, not a short one;’
‘It is by one who attends, not by one who does not attend; by one who is wise, not by one who is unwise. This is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.

‘In times of misfortune, monks, fortitude is to be recognized, and that indeed over a long period of time, not briefly; by one who attends, not by one who does not attend; by one who is wise, not by one who is unwise.
So it was said. With reference to what was this said?
“Here, monks, when someone is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by illness, they do not reflect thus:
‘Such indeed is this dwelling in the world, such is this acquisition of an individual existence;
in such a dwelling in the world, in such an acquisition of an individual existence, the eight worldly conditions revolve around the world.’”
The world revolves around eight worldly conditions:
gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.

When he is touched by the ruin of relatives, or touched by the ruin of wealth, or touched by the ruin of health, he sorrows, languishes, and laments; he weeps beating his breast and falls into confusion.

"Furthermore, monks, here someone, when touched by misfortune concerning relatives, or touched by misfortune concerning wealth, or touched by misfortune concerning illness, reflects thus: ‘Such indeed is this worldly existence,
such is this acquisition of a selfhood, that in such a worldly existence and such an acquisition of a selfhood,
the eight worldly conditions revolve around the world.’"
And the world revolves around these eight worldly conditions:
gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.

When he is touched by the ruin of relatives, or touched by the ruin of wealth, or touched by the ruin of health, he does not grieve, he does not languish, he does not lament; he does not beat his breast and weep, nor does he fall into confusion.
“‘In times of adversity, bhikkhus, fortitude is to be known—this indeed over a long period of time, not briefly; by one who attends to it, not by one who does not attend to it;
by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted. Thus, what was said was said with reference to this.

‘In discussion, bhikkhus, wisdom is to be known—this indeed over a long period of time, not briefly; by one who attends to it, not by one who does not attend to it; by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted.’”
Thus indeed it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, when one person is engaged in discussion with another, he knows thus:

"From the way this venerable one’s approach is, from the way his aim is directed, and from the way he puts forward his questions, this venerable one is of little wisdom; this venerable one is not wise."

For what reason? Because this venerable one does not utter words of deep meaning— peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise— and he is not capable of explaining,
teaching, making known, establishing, revealing, analyzing, or clarifying the meaning of the Dhamma that this venerable one speaks, whether in brief or in detail.
‘This venerable one is lacking in wisdom; this venerable one is not possessed of wisdom.
Just as if, monks, a man with good eyesight, standing on the bank of a body of water, were to see a small fish surfacing, it would occur to him:
"Just as one would know of this fish: 'From the way it surfaces, from the way it is struck by the waves, and from its manner of darting about, this fish is small;
this fish is not large,' even so, bhikkhus, when one person is conversing with another, he knows:
'From the way this venerable one's approach is, from the way his application is, and from the way his posing of questions is, this venerable one is of dull wisdom; this venerable one is not wise.'"
For what reason? Because this venerable one does not utter profound words of meaning— words that are peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle,

and to be experienced by the wise— and he is not capable of explaining, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, or clarifying the meaning of the Dharma that this venerable one speaks, whether in brief or in detail.
‘This venerable one is lacking in wisdom; this venerable one is not possessed of wisdom.
But here, monks, when one person is engaged in discussion with another, he knows thus:

‘From the way this venerable one’s approach is, from the way his direction is, and from the way his posing of questions is, this venerable one is possessed of wisdom; this venerable one is not lacking in wisdom.’”
For what reason?
Because this venerable one utters a profound word concerning the goal—peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.

And as for the Dhamma that this venerable one speaks, he is capable of explaining its meaning, both in brief and in detail; he is capable of teaching it, making it known, establishing it, revealing it, analyzing it, and making it clear.
‘This venerable one is wise; this venerable one is not dull-witted.
Just as, monks, a man with good eyesight standing on the bank of a body of water might see a large fish rising up, and it would occur to him:
‘Just as this fish’s leap, its surge against the waves, and its vigorous movement indicate that this fish is large and not small,’ so too, monks, when one person is conversing with another, he knows:
‘From the way this venerable one’s approach, his direction, and his formulation of questions, this venerable one is wise; this venerable one is not dull-witted.’
For what reason?
Because this venerable one utters words of meaning that are profound, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise;
and he is capable of explaining, teaching, laying down, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and clarifying the meaning of whatever Dhamma he speaks, whether in brief or in detail.
‘This venerable one is wise, this venerable one is not dull-witted.
‘Wise, bhikkhus, is wisdom to be known through discussion, and that over a long period, not a short one; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive;
by one who is wise, not by one who is dull-witted. It was with reference to this that it was said.
“Monks, these four states are to be understood by means of these four grounds.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.193

20. Mahāvagga Bhaddiyasutta (AN 4.193, PTS AN ii 190) At Sāvatthī. “Bhaddiya, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, Bhaddiya, are the five aggregates subject to clinging.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.

Then Bhaddiya the Licchavi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Bhaddiya the Licchavi said this to the Blessed One:
"I have heard this, venerable sir: [that...]"
“The ascetic Gotama is a magician; he knows the converting magic by which he converts the disciples of other sectarians.
Venerable sir, as for those who say:
“The ascetic Gotama is a magician; he knows the converting magic by which he converts the disciples of other sectarians,” [they speak thus].
"Venerable sir, do they speak in accordance with what has been said by the Blessed One? Do they not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false?
Do they explain the Dhamma in conformity with the Dhamma? Is there no point of censure that can be legitimately raised against them by anyone who follows the Dhamma?
For we, venerable sir, do not wish to misrepresent the Blessed One."
“Come now, Bhaddiya, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the scriptures,
do not go by reasoned conjecture, do not go by inferential reasoning, do not go by reflection on appearances, do not go by approval after pondering a view,
do not go by the thought ‘He is our respected teacher.’”
“Bhaddiya, when you yourself should know:

‘These states are unwholesome; these states are blameworthy; these states are censured by the wise; these states, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering,’ then, Bhaddiya, you should abandon them.
What do you think, Bhaddiya?”
“Does greed, when arising within a person, arise for his benefit or for his harm?
“For his harm, Bhante.
“But, Bhaddiya, when a greedy person is overcome by greed and his mind is consumed by it, he might even [take] the life of a living being...”
“He kills, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood, and encourages others to do likewise—
this leads to his harm and suffering for a long time.
“It is so, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Bhaddiya:
when hatred arises within a person... or delusion arises within a person... or aggression arises within a person, does it arise for one’s welfare or for one’s harm?
“For one’s harm, Bhante.”
“Moreover, Bhaddiya, an agitated person— one overcome by resentment and with a mind consumed by it—
kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits adultery, speaks falsehood,
and even incites others to do the same, which leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.”
“Yes, Bhante.
“What do you think, Bhaddiya, are these things wholesome or unwholesome?
“Unwholesome, Bhante.”
“Is it blameworthy or blameless?
“It is blameworthy, venerable sir.
“Is it censured by the wise or praised by the wise?”
“Censured by the wise, venerable sir.
“When fully undertaken and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not?
Or how does it stand in this matter?”
“Venerable sir, when they have been undertaken and observed, they lead to harm and suffering.
This is how it appears to us in this matter.
“In that case, Bhaddiya, as for what we said to you:”
"Come, Bhaddiya, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the scriptures,
do not go by reasoned conjecture, do not go by the result of inference, do not go by reflection on appearances, do not go by approval after pondering a view,
do not go by the thought 'He is our respected teacher.'"
“Bhaddiya, when you yourself should know:

‘These states are unwholesome; these states are blameworthy; these states are censured by the wise; these states, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering’—then, Bhaddiya, you should abandon them.
It was with reference to this that it was said.
"Come, Bhaddiya, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of scriptures,
do not go by reasoned conjecture, do not go by inferential reasoning, do not go by reflection on appearances, do not go by approval after pondering a view,
do not go by the thought 'the recluse is our teacher.'"
“Bhaddiya, when you yourself know:

‘These states are wholesome; these states are blameless; these states are praised by the wise; these states, when fully undertaken and observed, lead to welfare and happiness,’ then, Bhaddiya, you should enter upon and abide in them.
What do you think, Bhaddiya?”
“Does non-greed, when arising within a person, arise for his welfare or for his harm?
“For his welfare, Bhante.
“But, Bhaddiya, a person who is not greedy, who is not overcome by greed, and whose mind is not consumed by it, does not [act]... [for his harm].”
“He does not kill living beings, he does not take what is not given, he does not go to another’s wife, he does not speak falsehood,
and he does not encourage others to do likewise— this leads to his welfare and happiness for a long time.
“So it is, Bhante.”

“What do you think, Bhaddiya, when non-hatred arises within a person... [and so on] ...when non-delusion arises within a person... [and so on] ...when non-aggression arises within a person, does it arise for their welfare or for their harm?
“For their welfare, Bhante.
“But when this person, Bhaddiya, is not agitated and is not overcome by aggression, with a mind that is not overwhelmed...”
“He does not kill living beings, he does not take what is not given, he does not commit adultery, he does not speak falsehood,
and he does not incite others to do likewise— this leads to his welfare and happiness for a long time.
“It is so, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Bhaddiya, are these states wholesome or unwholesome?
“Wholesome, venerable sir.
“Are they blameworthy or blameless?”
“Blameless, venerable sir.
“Is it censured by the wise or praised by the wise?
“It is praised by the wise, venerable sir.”
“Do those things undertaken and practiced lead to welfare and happiness, or not?
Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, those things undertaken and practiced do lead to welfare and happiness.”
“This is how it appears to us in this matter.
“Thus indeed, Bhaddiya, as to what we said to you:
‘Come, Bhaddiya, do not go by oral tradition, do not go by lineage, do not go by hearsay, do not go by the authority of the scriptures...’”
Do not [judge] by reason of logic, do not by reason of inference, do not by reflection on the manner [of his speech],
do not by approval of your views after deliberation, do not because of his venerable appearance, and do not because of the thought, “The ascetic is our teacher.
But when you, Bhaddiya, know for yourselves:
‘These things are wholesome; these things are blameless; these things are praised by the wise; these things, when fully undertaken and observed, lead to welfare and happiness.
It was with reference to this that it was said:

“Bhaddiya, when those who are good and true persons in the world thus encourage a disciple, you should enter upon and abide in them. Bhaddiya, those who are good and true persons in the world encourage their disciple in this way.
"Come, good man, dwell having overcome greed.
