Dwelling having overcome greed, you will not perform any action born of greed by way of body, speech, or mind.
Dwell having overcome hatred."
Dwelling having removed hatred, you will not perform action born of hatred through body, speech, or mind.
Dwelling having removed delusion, so should you dwell.
Dwelling having removed delusion, you will not perform action born of delusion through body, speech, or mind.
“Abandoning aggression, dwell [thus].
Dwelling having abandoned aggression, you will not perform action born of aggression by way of body, speech, or mind.
When this was said, Bhaddiya the Licchavi spoke thus to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! … [as before] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
“But, Bhaddiya, did I ever speak to you thus:
‘Come, Bhaddiya, be my disciple’?”
‘I shall be the Teacher’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”— “Bhaddiya,
when I speak thus and declare this, certain ascetics and brahmins falsely, vainly, and deceitfully misrepresent me with what is untrue and unreal:”
“The ascetic Gotama is a magician; he knows the converting magic by which he converts the disciples of other sectarians.
“Bhante, that converting magic is auspicious.
Bhante, that converting magic is beautiful.”

“Venerable sir, if my beloved kinsmen and blood relatives were to be turned back by this turning-back, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of those beloved kinsmen and blood relatives for a long time.
Venerable sir, if all the khattiyas were to be turned back by this turning-back, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of all those khattiyas for a long time.
Venerable sir, if all the brahmins… all the vessas… all the suddas were to be turned back by this turning-back, it would lead to the welfare and happiness of all those suddas for a long time.”
“So it is, Bhaddiya; so it is, Bhaddiya.

If all the khattiyas were to turn themselves around by means of this turning-around for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, that would lead to the welfare and happiness of those khattiyas for a long time.

If all the brahmins… all the vessas… and all the suddas were to turn themselves around by means of this turning-around for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, that would lead to the welfare and happiness of those suddas for a long time.”
Bhaddiya, even if the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans,
were to be converted by this conversion for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states,
it would lead to the welfare and happiness of that world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and of this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, for a long time.

“Bhaddiya, if even these great sal trees were to be turned by this turning [of the mind] toward the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states, it would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.
What need then to speak of one who has become human? This is the third [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.194 20. Mahāvagga Sāmugiyasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a stone boat; the person who is like a leaking boat; the person who is like a boat with a hole; and the person who is like a well-constructed boat. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a stone boat? Here, bhikkhus, a person is not accomplished in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This is called a person like a stone boat. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a leaking boat? Here, bhikkhus, a person is accomplished in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, yet they do not dwell with diligence in order to abandon the arisen lustful thoughts, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt that have arisen. This is called a person like a leaking boat. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a boat with a hole? Here, bhikkhus, a person is accomplished in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, and they dwell with diligence in order to abandon the arisen lustful thoughts, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt that have arisen, yet they do not gain the rapture and pleasure that are apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, which are born of seclusion and constitute the first jhāna. This is called a person like a boat with a hole. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a well-constructed boat? Here, bhikkhus, a person is accomplished in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom; they dwell with diligence in order to abandon the arisen lustful thoughts, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt that have arisen; and they gain the rapture and pleasure that are apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states, which are born of seclusion and constitute the first jhāna. This is called a person like a well-constructed boat. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
(AN 4.194, PTS AN ii 194) On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling among the Koliyans at a town of the Koliyans named Sāmagama.
Then a number of Koliyan youths from Sāmagama approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to those Sāmugiyas, the sons of the Koliyans:
“Veyyagghapajjas, there are these four factors of striving for purity, which have been taught by the Blessed One, who knows and sees.”
These four things have been rightly expounded by the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation,
for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna. What are the four?
The factor of striving for purity of virtue, the factor of striving for purity of mind, the factor of striving for purity of view, and the factor of striving for purity of liberation.
And what, Byagghapajja, is the factor of striving for purity of virtue?
Here, Byagghapajja, a bhikkhu is virtuous... [as before] ...he trains himself in the training precepts he has undertaken.
This, Byagghapajja, is called purity of virtue.

Thus, thinking: "I shall fulfill such purity of virtue as is not yet fulfilled, or I shall maintain with wisdom here and there that which is already fulfilled," whatever desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, and indefatigability there is therein—this is called the basis for spiritual power.
And mindfulness and clear comprehension while abiding—this, Byagghapajjas, is called the factor of striving for the purification of virtue.
And what, Byagghapajjas, is the factor of striving for the purification of mind?
Here, Byagghapajjas, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, Byagghapajja, is called purity of mind. Thus, thinking,
"I will fulfill this kind of purity of mind that is not yet fulfilled,

or I will support with wisdom here and there that which is already fulfilled," whatever desire, effort, exertion, ardor, and perseverance one has therein— without turning back— [this is called right effort].
And mindfulness and clear comprehension—this, Byagghapajjas, is called the factor of striving for purity of mind.
And what, Byagghapajjas, is the factor of striving for purity of view?
Here, Byagghapajjas, a bhikkhu understands as it really is: “This is suffering” … [as above] … he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
This, Byagghapajja, is called purity of view.
Thus, regarding such purity of view that is either incomplete...
[or] "I shall support it here and there with wisdom"—whatever desire, effort, exertion, ardor, non-remissness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension there is therein.
This, Byagghapajja, is called the factor of striving for purity of view.
And what, Byagghapajja, is the factor of striving for purity of liberation?
That noble disciple, Byagghapajja, being endowed with this factor of striving for purity of virtue...
Endowed with this factor of striving for purity of mind and endowed with this factor of striving for purity of view,
he causes the mind to fade away from things that cause passion and liberates the mind from things that lead to liberation.
Having caused the mind to fade away from things that cause passion and having liberated the mind from things that lead to liberation, he touches right liberation.
This, Byagghapajja, is called purity of liberation. Thus,
"I shall fulfill this kind of purity of liberation that is not yet fulfilled, or I shall support with wisdom wherever it is already fulfilled"—
the desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, and indefatigability therein is what is meant.
And mindfulness and clear comprehension— this, Byagghapajja, is called the factor of striving for the purification of liberation. These, Byagghapajja,
are the four factors of striving for purification rightly proclaimed by the Blessed One— the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One,
the Perfectly Enlightened One— for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation.
"For the cessation of suffering and sorrow, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.
Thus ends the fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.195.

20. Mahāvagga Vappasutta (AN 4.195, PTS AN ii 196) At Sāvatthī. Then the householder Vappa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him: “Householder, if one were to say: ‘I do not see even a single thing that, when abandoned, leads to the cessation of suffering,’ it would be in reference to this very thing. Householder, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. [The same is repeated for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. “Therefore, householder, whatever form—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling... Whatever perception... Whatever volitional formations... Whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus with right wisdom exactly as it is, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, [the mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. When this was said, the householder Vappa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts. Then the householder Vappa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed keeping him on his right. Not long after the householder Vappa had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this householder Vappa is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the householder Vappa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him: “Householder, if one were to say: ‘I do not see even a single thing that, when fully understood, leads to the cessation of suffering,’ it would be in reference to this very thing. Householder, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. [The same is repeated for feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. “Therefore, householder, whatever form—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling... Whatever perception... Whatever volitional formations... Whatever consciousness—whether past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen with right wisdom exactly as it is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. When one sees it thus with right wisdom exactly as it is, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, [the mind] is liberated. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being. When this was said, the householder Vappa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts. Then the householder Vappa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed keeping him on his right. Not long after the householder Vappa had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, this householder Vappa is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then Vappa the Sakyan, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and sat down to one side. As Vappa was sitting to one side...
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to Sakka, the disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas:
"Suppose, Vappa, there were one who was restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind; through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge.
Do you see, Vappa, any ground on account of which the taints productive of painful feeling would flow into such a person in the future life?"
“I see that possibility, venerable sir.
Suppose, venerable sir, a person has previously committed an evil deed whose result has not yet ripened.
On that account, taints productive of suffering might flow into that person in the future.”
Now, this conversation between the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and Vappa the Sakyan, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, had been left unfinished.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall;
having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Once seated, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“Moggallāna, for what discussion are you sitting together here now? And what was the conversation of yours that was left unfinished?
“Just now, Bhante, I said this to Vappa the Sakyan, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas:
‘In this case, Vappa, one is restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind; through the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge...’”
“Do you see, Vappa, any ground on account of which taints productive of suffering might flow into a person in future lives?
When this was said, venerable sir, Vappa the Sakyan, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, said this to me:
“I do see such a ground, venerable sir.”
“Venerable sir, there is the case where evil kamma has been performed by this person in the past, the result of which has not yet ripened.
On that account, taints productive of painful feeling might flow in upon him in future lives.
This, venerable sir, was our conversation with Vappa the Sakyan, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, which was left unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.
Then the Blessed One said this to Vappa, the disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas:

“Vappa, if you would grant what is worthy of being granted to me, and refute what is worthy of being refuted; and if you do not understand the meaning of what I have said, you should ask me further about it:
‘Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this? Then there might be a discussion and an exchange of views between us on this matter.”
“Venerable sir, I shall accept what the Blessed One says when it is to be accepted, and I shall reject what is to be rejected;
and whenever I do not understand the meaning of something spoken by the Blessed One, I shall inquire further of the Blessed One himself:
‘Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’”
“Let there be a discussion here between us.
“What do you think, Vappa?
Those taints, distresses, and fevers that arise conditioned by bodily undertakings—do those taints, distresses, and fevers not cease for one who abstains from bodily undertakings?”

Thus, one does not perform new karma and, by experiencing it as it arises, one brings old karma to an end. This wearing away is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
Do you see, Vappa, any ground on account of which the taints productive of suffering might flow into a person in the future life?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Vappa?
Those taints, distressing and feverish, that arise conditioned by verbal undertakings—do those taints, distressing and feverish, not exist for one who abstains from verbal undertakings?
Such a person does not create new karma, and he brings to an end old karma as it arises.”
“Wearing away [of defilements] is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.
Do you see, Vappa, any ground on account of which effluents leading to painful feeling might flow into a person in future lives?
“No, Bhante.”
“What do you think, Vappa?
Those taints, distressing and feverish, that arise conditioned by mental activity—do they not cease for one who abstains from such mental activity?
Such a person does not create new karma, and he wears away old karma as it comes into contact with him.”
“Wearing away [of defilements] is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
Do you see, Vappa, any ground on account of which the taints productive of painful feeling might flow into a person in the future life?
“No, venerable sir.”
“What do you think, Vappa?

Those taints, distressing and feverish, that arise with ignorance as condition—when there is the fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge, those taints, distressing and feverish, no longer exist.
Such a person does not create new karma, and he makes an end of old karma by experiencing it as it arises.”
“Wearing away [of defilements] is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.
Do you see, Vappa, any ground on account of which effluents leading to painful feeling might flow in upon a person in future lives?
“No, Bhante.”
“Vappa, for a bhikkhu whose mind is thus rightly liberated, six constant abidings have been attained.
Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad; he abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear … [and so on] …”
Having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe… having touched a tangible object with the body …pe…
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.

Experiencing a feeling limited to the body, he understands: ‘I experience a feeling limited to the body. Experiencing a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I experience a feeling limited to life. He understands:
‘With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’
"Just as, Vappa, a shadow is perceived in dependence upon a pillar,
and then a man might come along carrying a spade and a basket,
and he might cut that pillar at its base;
Having cut it at the root, he would dig it up;
having dug it up, he would pull out the roots, even down to the size of a grass-blade.
He would then cut that pillar into pieces.
Having cut it into pieces, one would split them apart.
Having split them apart, one would reduce them to fragments.
Having reduced them to fragments, one would dry them in the wind and sun.
Having dried it in the wind and heat, one would burn it with fire.
Having burned it with fire, one would reduce it to ash.
Having reduced it to ash, one would scatter it in a great wind or carry it away by a swift-flowing river.
"For in this way, Vappa, whatever shadow depended on that pillar has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
In the same way, Vappa, for a bhikkhu whose mind is thus rightly liberated, six constant abidings have been attained.
Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending."
Having heard a sound with the ear …pe… having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe…
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.

Experiencing a feeling that ends with the body, he understands: "I experience a feeling that ends with the body. Experiencing a feeling that ends with life, he understands: "I experience a feeling that ends with life."
‘With the breakup of the body, after the exhaustion of life, all that is felt here, not being delighted in, will become cool right here,’ he understands.
When this was said, Vappa the Sakyan, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, said to the Blessed One:
“Just as if, venerable sir, a man seeking profit were to raise a horse for sale.”
"In that case, one would neither attain prosperity nor avoid further exhaustion and distress.
Even so, venerable sir, seeking prosperity, I attended upon the foolish Nigaṇṭhas.
But I attained neither prosperity nor did I avoid further exhaustion and distress."
“Venerable sir, from this day forth, I shall blow away with a great wind whatever confidence I had in those foolish Nigaṇṭhas, or wash it away in the swift current of a river.
Excellent, venerable sir! … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The fifth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.196 20. Mahāvagga Sāḷhasutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward himself, but he does not dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward others—whether they are a certain class of beings or all beings. This, monks, is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward others—whether they are a certain class of beings or all beings—but he does not dwell having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward himself. This, monks, is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, monks, is one a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having generated a mind of loving-kindness neither toward himself nor toward others—whether they are a certain class of beings or all beings. This, monks, is called a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward himself and also dwells having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward others—whether they are a certain class of beings or all beings. This, monks, is called a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
(AN 4.196, PTS AN ii 200) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
Then Sāḷha the Licchavi and Abhaya the Licchavi approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, Sāḷha the Licchavi said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, there are some ascetics and brahmins who prescribe a twofold way for crossing over the flood.”
“For the sake of purification of virtue and for the sake of austerity and self-disgust.
What does the Blessed One say about this, venerable sir?
“Sāḷha, I say that purification of virtue is one factor of asceticism.”

“Sāḷha, those ascetics and brahmins who advocate self-mortification and loathing, who take self-mortification and loathing as their essence, and who dwell clinging to self-mortification and loathing—they are incapable of crossing the flood.

And those ascetics and brahmins, Sāḷha, whose conduct of body is impure, whose conduct of speech is impure, whose conduct of mind is impure, and whose livelihood is impure—they are incapable of knowledge and vision, and of unsurpassed enlightenment.
It is just as if, Sāḷha, a man wishing to cross a river were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest.”
Suppose he were to see there a great sal-tree trunk, straight, fresh, and not yet worm-eaten.
He would cut it at the root;
having cut it at the root, he would cut it at the top.
Having cut off the top, one should thoroughly clear away the branches and foliage;
having thoroughly cleared away the branches and foliage, one should hew it with axes;
having hewed it with axes, one should hew it with adzes.
Having carved it with an adze, one should write upon it with a stylus;
having written with a stylus, one should polish it with a stone pellet;
having polished it with a stone pellet, one should cast it into a river.
“What do you think, Sāḷha,
would that man be able to cross the river?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“And why is that? “Because, Bhante, that sāl-tree trunk was well-worked on the outside but impure within.
It is to be expected that the sāl-tree trunk will sink down and the man will meet with disaster and ruin.”

“In the same way, Sāḷha, those ascetics and brahmins who advocate self-mortification and loathing, who take self-mortification and loathing as their essence, and who dwell clinging to self-mortification and loathing—they are incapable of crossing over the flood.

And those ascetics and brahmins, Sāḷha, whose bodily conduct is impure, whose verbal conduct is impure, whose mental conduct is impure, and whose livelihood is impure—they are incapable of knowledge and vision, and of unsurpassed enlightenment.”

But those ascetics and brahmins, Sāḷha, who do not advocate self-mortification and loathing, who do not take self-mortification and loathing as their core, and who do not dwell clinging to self-mortification and loathing—they are capable of crossing over the flood.

And those ascetics and brahmins, Sāḷha, whose bodily conduct is pure, whose verbal conduct is pure, whose mental conduct is pure, and whose livelihood is pure—they are capable of attaining knowledge and vision and unsurpassed enlightenment.
It is just as if, Sāḷha, a man wishing to cross a river were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest.
Suppose he were to see there a great sal-tree trunk, straight, fresh, and not yet worm-eaten.
Having cut it at the root, he would then cut it at the top.
Having cut off the top, one should thoroughly clear away the branches and foliage;
having thoroughly cleared away the branches and foliage, one should hew it with axes;
having hewed it with axes, one should hew it with adzes.
Having cut it with axes, one should take a chisel and polish the interior thoroughly;
having polished the interior thoroughly, one should engrave it with a stylus;
having engraved it with a stylus, one should wash it with a stone-powder.
Having washed it with a stone ball, one would fashion a boat;
having fashioned the boat, one would lash on a rudder;
and having lashed on the rudder, one would cross over the river.
“What do you think, Sāḷha,
would that man be able to cross the river?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“And for what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, that sal-tree trunk was well-worked on the outside, thoroughly cleaned out within, hollowed out, and bound with lashings.
It is to be expected of it:”
‘The boat will not sink; the man will reach the far shore in safety.

‘In the same way, Sāḷha, those ascetics and brahmins who do not speak in praise of austerity and self-reproach, who do not have austerity and self-reproach as their core, and who do not dwell clinging to austerity and self-reproach, are capable of crossing the flood.

And those ascetics and brahmins, Sāḷha, who are pure in bodily conduct, pure in verbal conduct, pure in mental conduct, and pure in livelihood, are capable of attaining supreme knowledge and vision, that is, unsurpassed enlightenment.’”
"Just as, Sāḷha, even if a warrior knows many kinds of variegated arrows,
he still becomes worthy of a king, an enjoyer of a king’s wealth, and is reckoned as a limb of the king for three reasons.
What are these three?"
He is one who shoots from afar, one who pierces the mark, and one who splits a great body. Just as, Sāḷha,
a warrior is one who shoots from afar, even so, Sāḷha,
is the noble disciple one who possesses right concentration.
Sāḷha, a noble disciple with right concentration regards whatever form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form as it actually is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
Whatever feeling there may be … whatever perception there may be … whatever formations there may be …
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
"Just as, Sāḷha, a warrior is one who shoots at a small target, even so, Sāḷha, a noble disciple possesses right view.

Possessing right view, Sāḷha, a noble disciple understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ ... [and so on] ... he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’"
"Just as, Sāḷha, a warrior is one who pierces through a great host,
even so, Sāḷha, a noble disciple possesses right liberation.
Possessing right liberation, Sāḷha, the noble disciple pierces through the great mass of ignorance."
The Sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.197 20. Mahāvagga
The Discourse to Queen Mallikā (AN 4.197).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then Queen Mallikā approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side. As she was sitting there, Queen Mallikā said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some woman is ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to look upon;
and is poor, ownerless, without possessions, and of little influence?”
"But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some woman is ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to look at, yet she is wealthy,
possessing great riches and great wealth,
and of high status? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some woman is beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion?"
“Why is it, Bhante, that some woman here is poor, with little property, few possessions, and of low status;
while what is the cause, what is the reason, by which another woman here is beautiful, handsome, pleasing,
endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, wealthy, possessing great riches and great possessions, and of high status?”
“Here, Mallikā, a certain woman is prone to anger and full of resentment.
Even when spoken to only slightly, she becomes agitated, becomes angry, becomes malevolent, and becomes stubborn; she manifests anger, hatred, and ill-will.
She does not give food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps to ascetics or brahmins.”
Furthermore, she is envious:
she envies, resents, and harbors envy toward the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship received by others.
When she passes away from there and comes back to this human state, wherever she is reborn, she is ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to behold.
She is poor, possessing little, having few enjoyments, and lacking influence.
Furthermore, Mallikā, here a certain woman is prone to anger and full of resentment;
even when spoken to only slightly, she becomes agitated, becomes angry, becomes malevolent, and becomes stubborn, manifesting anger, hatred, and ill-will.
She is a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or brahmins.
Furthermore, she is not envious;
she does not envy, does not become ill-willed toward, and does not harbor envy regarding the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship received by others.
If, having passed away from there, she returns to this human state, wherever she is reborn, she is ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to behold;
yet she is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, and is of high status.
Furthermore, Mallikā, some woman here is not prone to anger and does not experience much distress.
Even when spoken to much, she does not become resentful, does not become angry, does not become malicious, and does not become obstinate; she does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
Yet she is not a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, bedding, dwellings, or lamps to ascetics or brahmins.
Moreover, she is envious and stingy.
She envies, becomes ill-disposed toward, and harbors jealousy regarding the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship received by others.
If, after passing away from there, she returns to this human state, wherever she is reborn, she is beautiful, handsome, pleasing, and endowed with supreme beauty of complexion;
yet she is poor, possessing little, having few enjoyments, and lacking in influence.
Furthermore, Mallikā, here a certain woman is not prone to anger and does not frequently experience distress.
Even when spoken to much, she does not become resentful, does not become agitated, does not harbor ill will, and does not remain obstinate; she does not manifest anger, hatred, or resentment.
She is a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or brahmins.
Furthermore, she is free from envy:
regarding the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship of others, she does not envy, does not become malicious, and does not harbor envy.
If, passing away from there, she comes to this state of existence, wherever she is reborn, she is beautiful, handsome, pleasing, and endowed with supreme beauty of complexion.
She becomes wealthy, possessing great riches, great enjoyments, and great influence.
This, Mallikā, is the cause, this is the condition, by which some woman here is ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to behold;
she is poor, possessing little, having few enjoyments, and having little influence.
But this, Mallikā, is the cause, this is the condition, why some woman here is ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to behold, yet she is wealthy,
possessing great riches and great enjoyments,
and of high status. This, Mallikā, is the cause, this is the condition, why some woman here is beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.
"She is poor, possessing little, with few enjoyments, and of little influence.
But this, Mallikā, is the cause, this is the condition, by which a certain woman here is beautiful, handsome, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion;
she is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, and of great influence."
When this was said, Queen Mallikā said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, perhaps in another birth I was prone to anger and full of distress;
even when addressed with only a little, I became resentful, I grew angry, I harbored ill will, I stood firm in resentment, and I manifested anger, hatred, and dissatisfaction."
"Venerable sir, I am now ugly, misshapen, and unpleasant to behold.

It must be, venerable sir, that in another birth I gave to a recluse or a brahmin food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps; for it is because of that, venerable sir, that I am now..."
"I am wealthy, of great riches, and of great possessions.

Yet, Bhante, whatever lack of envy I had toward another birth—wherein I was not envious, did not feel ill will, and did not harbor jealousy regarding the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship [received by others]—by that, Bhante, I have now become one of great influence.
Furthermore, Bhante, in this royal family there are daughters of kshatriyas, daughters of brahmins, and daughters of householders; over them, I exercise lordship and sovereignty."
“Venerable sir, from this day forward, I shall be free from anger and free from much distress.

Even when spoken to harshly, I will not be resentful, I will not become agitated, I will not harbor ill will, and I will not stand my ground in opposition; I will manifest neither anger, nor hatred, nor resentment.
I will give food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or brahmins.”
“I shall not be envious; I will not be jealous, I will not be malicious, and I will not bind myself with envy toward the gains, honors, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship of others.
Excellent, Bhante! … [as before] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
This was the seventh [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.198 20. Mahāvagga Attantapasutta (The Discourse on Self-Torment) “Monks, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who torments himself; the person who torments others; the person who torments both himself and others; and the person who torments neither himself nor others, but dwells having attained the bliss of concentration here and now. And how, monks, is one a person who torments himself? Here, someone goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not stopping when asked; he does not accept food brought or food specially prepared; he does not accept an invitation; he does not accept food from a pregnant woman, from a woman nursing a child, or from a woman having intercourse with a man; he accepts no fish or meat; he drinks no liquor, wine, or fermented brew. He visits houses only for alms once a day; he eats only from a single bowl; he eats only what he receives; he eats only standing up; he eats only after taking a mirror; he eats only one mouthful;

he lives on vegetables, on millet, on wild rice, on water hyacinth seeds, on the seeds of the snake-gourd, on oil-seeds, on rice-husk powder, on rice-straw, or on forest roots and fruits. He clothes himself in hemp, in hemp-mixed cloth, in shrouds, in refuse rags, in tree bark, in antelope hide, in strips of antelope hide, in kusa-grass fabric, in wood-shavings fabric, in woven human hair, in woven horse-tail hair, or in owls’ wings. He is a ‘plucker-out,’ plucking out his hair and beard; he is a ‘stander-on-his-heels,’ constantly standing on his heels; he is a ‘croucher-in-dust,’ crouching in dust; he is a ‘swallower-of-hot-food,’ constantly eating hot food; he is a ‘fire-worshipper,’ constantly tending the fire; he is a ‘sun-worshipper,’ standing facing the sun; he is a ‘water-dweller,’ constantly living in water; he is a ‘cow-pen-dweller,’ constantly living in a cow-pen; he is a ‘goat-pen-dweller,’ constantly living in a goat-pen; he is a ‘dog-pen-dweller,’ constantly living in a dog-pen; he is a ‘charnel-ground-dweller,’ constantly living in a charnel ground; he is a ‘tree-root-dweller,’ constantly living at the root of a tree; he is a ‘open-air-dweller,’ constantly living in the open air; he is a ‘any-bed-user,’ constantly using any bed that is offered; he is a ‘sitter,’ refusing to lie down; he is a ‘one-leg-stander,’ constantly standing on one leg. In this way, he dwells pursuing the practice of tormenting and mortifying the body in various ways. This is called a person who torments himself. And how, monks, is one a person who torments others? Here, someone is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a trapper of wild beasts, a hunter, a fisherman, a thief, an executioner, a prison warden, or one who follows any other such bloody occupation. This is called a person who torments others. And how, monks, is one a person who torments both himself and others? Here, someone is a head-anointed noble king or a well-to-do brahmin. Having had a new sacrificial hall built to the east of the city, and having shaved off his hair and beard, dressed himself in rough animal hides, and afflicted himself with the austerity of the five fires, he makes a fire offering while uttering the words: ‘May Indra together with the Maruts, Brahmā together with the Brahmakāyikas, and the Four Great Kings protect me in this place! And he has many hundreds of animals—such as goats, rams, oxen, calves, and various kinds of birds and deer—brought before him, and he causes them to be slaughtered by his servants. And he thinks: ‘I shall sacrifice to the gods with these freshly slaughtered, warm, blood-dripping, freshly killed animals. This is called a person who torments both himself and others. And how, monks, is one a person who torments neither himself nor others, but dwells having attained the bliss of concentration here and now? Here, monks, a Tathāgata appears in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened... [as in the standard formula] ...he teaches the Dhamma that is lovely in its beginning, lovely in its middle, and lovely in its ending, in the spirit and in the letter, and displays the fully-perfected holy life. A householder hears that Dhamma, or a householder’s son hears it, or one born into some other clan hears it. Having heard it, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata. Endowed with that faith, he considers: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, put on the saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. Later on, having abandoned a small or a large fortune, having abandoned a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; he is perfect in conduct and resort; he sees danger in the slightest faults; he trains himself by undertaking the training precepts. In this way, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; he is perfect in conduct and resort; he sees danger in the slightest faults; he trains himself by undertaking the training precepts. With the abandoning of ill will and hatred, with the absence of enmity and affliction, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells suffusing one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells suffusing the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without affliction. With the abandoning of ill will and hatred, with the absence of enmity and affliction, with a mind imbued with compassion, he dwells suffusing one quarter... [as above] ...the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without affliction. With the abandoning of ill will and hatred, with the absence of enmity and affliction, with a mind imbued with altruistic joy, he dwells suffusing one quarter... [as above] ...the entire world with a mind imbued with altruistic joy, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without affliction. With the abandoning of ill will and hatred, with the absence of enmity and affliction, with a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells suffusing one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells suffusing the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without affliction. This, monks, is called a person who torments neither himself nor others, but dwells having attained the bliss of concentration here and now. These, monks, are the four types of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world. Which four? [The text continues with the description of each.]”
In this case, monks, a certain person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment.
In this case, monks, another person torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
In this case, monks, yet another person both torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
"But here, monks, a certain person is neither a tormentor of self nor devoted to the practice of tormenting self, nor is he a tormentor of others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Being neither a tormentor of self nor a tormentor of others, in this very life he is free from craving, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, and dwells with a self that has become sublime.
And how, monks, is a person a tormentor of self, devoted to the practice of tormenting self?"

"Here, monks, a certain person goes naked, disregarding conventions, licking his hands; he does not accept [food] when invited to come, nor when one stands waiting; he does not accept food brought to him, nor food specially prepared for him, nor an invitation.
He does not accept it from the mouth of a pot, nor from the mouth of a basket; he does not accept it across a woolen blanket, nor across a staff, nor across a pestle;
he does not accept it from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing."
He does not go to another man’s wife, nor to crowded places, nor where she is present, nor where flies are swarming;
he drinks no fish, no meat, no liquor, no wine, and no fermented grain-water.
He becomes a "one-house" man or a "one-bite" eater, or a "two-house" man or a "two-bite" eater... [and so on] ...or he becomes a "seven-house" man or a "seven-bite" eater.
He subsists on one alms-meal, or he subsists on two alms-meals... up to seven alms-meals;
he takes food once a day, or he takes food every second day... up to taking food every seventh day. Thus, he dwells engaged in such practice of consuming food at intervals, even for half a month.
He becomes one who eats greens, one who eats millet, one who eats wild rice, and one who eats coarse grain.
He subsists on fallen leaves, he subsists on husks, he subsists on rice-scum, he subsists on oil-cake, he subsists on grass, and he subsists on cow dung;
he maintains himself by feeding on forest roots and fruits, eating only what has fallen of its own accord.
He wears hempen garments, he wears bark garments, he wears shrouds from cemeteries, and he wears rag-robes.
He wears garments of tirīṭa cloth, he wears deerskins, he wears a cloak made of many deerskins, he wears a dress of kusa grass, he wears a dress of bark,
he wears a dress of wood-shavings, he wears a blanket of human hair, he wears a blanket of animal wool, or he wears a cloak of owl feathers;
he is one who plucks out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard.
He is one who stands continuously, refusing to sit;
he is one who squats, devoted to the practice of squatting;
he is one who uses a bed of thorns, spreading his sleep upon a bed of thorns.
He dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water for a third time at night.
Thus, in such a manner, he dwells devoted to various kinds of practices involving the tormenting and mortification of the body.
In this way, monks, a person is one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment.
And how, monks, is a person one who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others?

Here, monks, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a hunter, a trapper, a fisherman, a thief, an executioner, a butcher of cattle, a jailer, or anyone else engaged in cruel occupations.
It is in this way, monks, that a person is one who torments others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And how, monks, is a person one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of torturing himself, and also one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of torturing others?
Here, monks, a certain person is either a consecrated Khattiya king or a wealthy Brahmin.
Having had a new assembly hall built to the east of the city, and having shaved off his hair and beard and put on a rough antelope skin...

Having dressed himself and anointed his body with ghee and oil, he enters the new assembly hall together with his chief queen and the brahmin family priest, scratching his back with a deer horn. There,
he makes his bed upon the bare ground smeared with green cow dung.
Of a single cow with calves of similar appearance, the milk from one udder sustains the king;
the milk from the second udder sustains the chief queen; the milk from the third udder sustains the brahmin family priest;
and the milk from the fourth udder is used to offer oblations to the sacrificial fire.
He sustained himself on the remainder of the calf.
He spoke thus:
“Let so many bulls be slaughtered for the sake of the sacrifice; let so many young oxen be slaughtered for the sake of the sacrifice; let so many...”
“Let so many heifers be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many goats be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many rams be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice;
let so many horses be slaughtered for the sake of sacrifice; let so many trees be cut down for the sake of sacrificial posts;
let so much grass be mown for the sake of the sacrificial strew.”
And those who are their slaves, messengers, or laborers—they too perform their tasks while driven by punishment and driven by fear, weeping with tearful faces.
In this way, monks, a person is one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and also one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And how, monks, is a person neither one who torments himself nor devoted to the practice of self-torment, nor one who torments others nor devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
Thus, not tormented by himself and not tormented by others, in this very life—free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, and experiencing happiness—he dwells with a self that has become sublime.

Here, monks, a Tathāgata arises in the world: an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

Thus, having realized for himself through direct higher knowledge this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Possessed of that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is the open air."
"It is not easy for one living in a household to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) that is entirely complete, entirely pure, and polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or a large mass of wealth, he went forth.

Having abandoned a small circle of relatives, or having abandoned a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, endowed with the training and livelihood of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life; from the taking of life...
He abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the sword, and dwells conscientious and compassionate, sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft, pure and clean.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he dwells remote, abstaining from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to the truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech;

he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here for the purpose of dividing these people, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere for the purpose of dividing those people; thus, he does not bring about division among those who are divided...
He is a reconciler or one who provides for those who have been reconciled; he delights in harmony, rejoices in harmony, finds joy in harmony, and speaks words that bring about harmony.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-warming, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, and speaks what is meaningful.
He is one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma and speaks in accordance with the Vinaya; he speaks words that are worth treasuring, timely, grounded in reason, measured, and beneficial.
He abstains from injuring seeds and plants.
He eats only once a day, refraining from food at night and abstaining from eating outside the proper time.
He abstains from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and witnessing performances.
He abstains from wearing garlands, using scents and unguents, and from the practice of beautifying and adorning himself.
He abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats.
He abstains from accepting gold and silver.
He abstains from accepting raw grain.
He abstains from accepting raw meat.
He abstains from accepting women and girls;
he abstains from accepting male and female slaves;
he abstains from accepting goats and sheep.
He abstains from accepting chickens and pigs;
he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares;
he abstains from accepting fields and land.
He abstains from engaging in the business of running errands and acting as a messenger.
He abstains from buying and selling.
He abstains from cheating with false weights, false metals, and false measures.
He abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud.
He abstains from mutilation, execution, imprisonment, plunder, and violence.
He is content with robes to protect his body and almsfood to sustain his belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him.

Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden, even so a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes having taken these up.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness that is blameless.
Thus, having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye; he attains mastery over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If one dwells with this faculty of the mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—[might arise].
If unwholesome states of mind were to flow in upon him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the mind and achieves mastery over the faculty of the mind.
Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the unsullied happiness.
He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside.
He acts with clear comprehension when bending and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating;
and he acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment,
endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension,
he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Then, having returned from his alms round after the meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly calmed; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from indecision regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
Thus, having abandoned these five hindrances— defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— he,
quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the recollection of past lives … [as above] …
He directs his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings... [and] toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands, as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands, as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering."
He understands as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
He understands as it really is: “These are the taints”; he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of the taints.”
‘This is the cessation of the taints,’ he understands as it really is; ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints,’ he understands as it really is.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
In this way, monks, a person neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Thus, neither tormenting oneself nor tormenting others, one dwells in this very life free from craving, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, having become Brahma through oneself.
These, monks, are the four persons found existing in the world.
This is the eighth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.199 20.

Mahāvagga Taṇhāsutta (The Discourse on Craving) “Monks, there are these four kinds of craving. What four? Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence, and craving for formlessness. These, monks, are the four kinds of craving.”
The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus,
I will teach you craving— the ensnarer, the flowing, the spreading, the clinging— by which this world [is bound].”

“Tossed about, enveloped, like a tangled skein, like a knotted ball of thread, like matted rushes and reeds, they do not pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realms, the cycle of existence.
Listen to that; attend closely, and I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is that craving—spider-web-like, streaming, spreading, and clinging—by which this world is tossed about?”
Enveloped, entangled like a ball of thread, matted like a tuft of wool, and become like reeds and rushes, one does not transcend states of deprivation, the bad destination,
the lower realms, and saṃsāra. Furthermore, monks,
there are these eighteen modes of craving’s wandering based on the internal, and eighteen modes of craving’s wandering based on the external.
What are the eighteen modes of craving’s wandering based on the internal?
Monks, when there is the thought "I am," there occurs:
"I am thus," "I am so," "I am otherwise," "I am not," "I am existing," "I am thus existing," "I am so existing," "I am otherwise existing."
"There is," "there is thus," "there is in this way," "there is so," "there is otherwise";
"there will be," "there will be thus," "there will be in this way," "there will be so," "there will be otherwise."
These eighteen modes of craving’s wandering are based on the internal.
What are the eighteen modes of craving’s wandering based on the external?

Monks, when there is the thought “I am this,” there occurs the thought “I am such-and-such by means of this,” there occurs the thought “I am thus by means of this,” and there occurs the thought “I am otherwise by means of this.”
By this, one thinks "I am"; by this, one thinks "I am such-and-such"; by this, one thinks "I am existing"; by this, one thinks "I am existing thus";
by this, one thinks "I am existing in this way"; by this, one thinks "I am existing otherwise"; by this, one thinks "I am existing here";
by this, one thinks "I am existing here thus"; by this, one thinks "I am existing here in this way"; by this, one thinks "I am existing here otherwise."
"There will be by this," "there will be through this," "there will be thus by this," "there will be in such a way by this," "there will be otherwise by this.
These eighteen modes of craving's roaming are based on the external.
Thus there are eighteen modes of craving's wandering based on the internal, and eighteen modes of craving's wandering based on the external.
These, monks, are called the thirty-six modes of craving's wandering.
Thus there are these kinds of thirty-six modes of craving's wandering in the past, thirty-six modes of craving's wandering in the future, and thirty-six modes of craving's wandering in the present.
Thus there are one hundred and eight modes of craving’s wandering.
This, monks, is that craving which is ensnaring, flowing, spreading, and clinging;
by which this world is tossed about, enveloped, become like a tangled skein, like a knotted ball of thread, like matted rushes and reeds, and goes to ruin, to a state of misery, to perdition.
“He does not transcend saṃsāra.
Thus [ends] the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.200

20. Mahāvagga Pemasutta (AN 4.200, PTS AN ii 213) “Monks, there are these five kinds of love. What five? Love that is like a mother’s for her child; love that is like a father’s for his child; love that is like a brother’s for his brother; love that is like a sister’s for her brother; and love that is like a friend’s or companion’s for a friend or companion. These, monks, are the five kinds of love.”
“Monks, these four kinds of affection arise. Which four?
Affection arises from affection;”
From affection, aversion arises;
from aversion, affection arises;
from aversion, further aversion arises.
And how, monks, does affection arise from affection?
Here, monks, a person is dear, beloved, and pleasing to another person.
Others treat that person with what is dear, beloved, and pleasing.
It occurs to him:
"This person who is dear, beloved, and pleasing to me is treated with what is dear, beloved, and pleasing by others.
He conceives affection for them.
In this way, monks, affection arises from affection.
And how, monks, does aversion arise from affection?
Here, monks, a person is dear, beloved, and pleasing to another person.
Others treat that person with what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable. He thinks:
“This person who is desirable, lovely, and agreeable to me is being treated by others with what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable.”
Thus he conceives hatred toward them.
In this way, monks, hatred arises from affection.
And how, monks, does affection arise from hatred?
In this case, monks, a person is disliked, unloved, and unpleasant to another person.
Others treat that person with what is disliked, unloved, and unpleasant.
It occurs to him:
‘This person who is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable to me is being treated with what is undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable by others.
Thus he conceives affection for them.
In this way, monks, affection arises from aversion.
And how, monks, does hatred arise from hatred?
Here, monks, a person is disliked, unloved, and unpleasant to another person.
Others then treat that person with what is liked, loved, and pleasant.
It occurs to him:
“This person who is undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasant to me is being treated by others with what is desirable, lovely, and pleasant.
He conceives hatred toward them.

In this way, monks, hatred is born from hatred. These, monks, are the four kinds of love that arise. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the first jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of thought and examination … [as above] … enters and dwells in the second jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the second jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, with the fading away as well of rapture … [as above] … enters and dwells in the third jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the third jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the fourth jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. These, monks, are the four kinds of love that arise. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the first jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of thought and examination … [as above] … enters and dwells in the second jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the second jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, with the fading away as well of rapture … [as above] … enters and dwells in the third jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the third jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. At whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain … [as above] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, at that time, monks, there is love for the fourth jhāna. It is in this way that love is born from non-hatred. These, monks, are the four kinds of love that arise. Whatever affection arises from affection does not exist for him at that time;

“Monks, this is called a monk who neither flares up nor smolders, nor blazes, nor burns, nor is consumed by fire.
And how, monks, does a monk flare up?
Here, monks, a monk regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.”
One regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as being in self, or self as being in feeling;
one regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as being in self, or self as being in perception;
one regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as being in self, or self as being in volitional formations.
One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
In this way, monks, a monk exalts himself.
And how, monks, does a monk not exalt himself?
In this case, monks, a monk does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form;
he does not regard feeling as self, nor self as possessing feeling, nor feeling as in self, nor self as in feeling;
he does not regard perception as self, nor self as possessing perception, nor perception as in self, nor self as in perception.
He does not regard volitional formations as self, nor self as possessing volitional formations, nor volitional formations as in self, nor self as in volitional formations;
he does not regard consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as in self, nor self as in consciousness.
In this way, monks, a monk does not exalt himself.
And how, monks, does a monk retaliate?
Here, monks, a monk reviles one who reviles him, scolds one who scolds him, and quarrels with one who quarrels with him.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk retaliates.
And how, monks, does a monk not retaliate?
Here, monks, a monk does not revile one who reviles him, does not scold one who scolds him, and does not argue with one who argues with him.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk does not retaliate.
And how, monks, does a monk smoke? When there is the thought "I am," monks,

there occurs the thought "I am this way," there occurs the thought "I am like this," there occurs the thought "I am otherwise," there occurs the thought "I am not," there occurs the thought "I am so-and-so," there occurs the thought "I exist," there occurs the thought "I exist this way," there occurs the thought "I exist like this," there occurs the thought "I exist otherwise."
There is "I am," there is "I am this," there is "I am such," there is "I am so," there is "I am otherwise";
there is "I shall be," there is "I shall be this," there is "I shall be such," there is "I shall be so," there is "I shall be otherwise."
In this way, monks, a monk smokes. And how, monks, does a monk not smoke?
When there is no "I am," monks, there is no "I am this," there is no "I am thus," and there is no "I am otherwise."
"I am" does not occur; "I am this" does not occur; "I exist" does not occur; "I exist thus" does not occur;
"I exist in such a way" does not occur; "I exist otherwise" does not occur; "I exist here" does not occur;
"I exist here thus" does not occur; "I exist here in such a way" does not occur; "I exist here otherwise" does not occur; "I shall be" does not occur; "I shall be thus"...
"It will not be thus," "it will not be so," "it will not be otherwise"—
in this way, monks, a monk does not smolder.
And how, monks, does a monk blaze up?

"By means of this, monks, when there is the thought 'I am,' there arises the thought 'I am thus'; by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am such'; by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am otherwise';
by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am not'; by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am existing';

by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am existing thus'; by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am existing such'; by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am existing otherwise'; by means of this, there arises the thought 'I am here.'"

"By this there is existence in this way," "by this there is existence thus," "by this there is existence otherwise," "by this there will be existence," "by this there will be existence in this way," "by this there will be existence thus," "by this there will be existence otherwise."
In this way, monks, a monk burns. And how, monks, does a monk not burn?
When there is "I am by means of this," monks, then "I am such-and-such" does not occur; "I am thus-and-so" does not occur.
By this, "I am otherwise" does not occur; by this, "I am permanent" does not occur; by this, "I am eternal" does not occur;
by this, "I am" does not occur; by this, "I am thus" does not occur; by this, "I am in such a way" does not occur;
by this, "I am otherwise" does not occur; by this, "I am here" does not occur; by this, "I am here thus" does not occur; by this...
"By this means there is no such existence; by this means there is not otherwise an existence;
by this means there will be no such existence; by this means there will not be thus an existence;
by this means there will not be otherwise an existence."
In this way, monks, a monk does not blaze up.
And how, monks, does a monk burn away?
Here, monks, a monk’s conceit “I am” has not been abandoned; it is not cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and subject to non-arising in the future.
In this way, monks, a monk broods. And how, monks, does a monk not brood?
Here, monks, a monk’s conceit “I am” has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
“It is in this way, monks, that a monk does not brood.

Sappurisavagga Sikkhāpadasutta (The Discourse on the Training Rules) “Monks, there are these four training rules for a noble person. What four? ‘I will not take life,’ this is the first training rule for a noble person. ‘I will not take what is not given,’ this is the second training rule for a noble person. ‘I will not engage in sexual misconduct,’ this is the third training rule for a noble person. ‘I will not speak falsely,’ this is the fourth training rule for a noble person. These, monks, are the four training rules for a noble person.”
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the person who is not a true man, and one even more base than the person who is not a true man; and I will teach you the true man,
and one even more excellent than the true man.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
