The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is not a true man?
Here, bhikkhus, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence.
This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is not a true man.”
And who, monks, is the person more ignoble than the ignoble?
Here, monks, a certain person himself takes life and encourages others to take life;
he himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given.
One engages in sexual misconduct oneself and encourages others to engage in sexual misconduct;
one speaks falsehood oneself and encourages others to speak falsehood;

one consumes intoxicants such as fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence oneself and encourages others to consume intoxicants such as fermented and distilled liquors that cause negligence.
This, monks, is called one who is more of an untrue person than an untrue person.
And who, monks, is a true person?
Here, monks, a certain person abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
He abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from false speech, and he abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
This, monks, is called a true person.
And who, monks, is even more of a true person than a true person?
In this case, monks, a certain person refrains from taking life themselves and encourages others to refrain from taking life;
they refrain from taking what is not given themselves and encourage others to refrain from taking what is not given;
they refrain from sexual misconduct themselves and encourage others to refrain from sexual misconduct.
“He himself abstains from false speech and encourages others in the refraining from false speech;

he himself abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, and encourages others in the refraining from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
This, monks, is called one who is more of a true person than a true person.”
First.

Here, monks, a certain person is himself devoid of faith, and he encourages another in lack of faith.
One is oneself shameless and encourages others in shamelessness;
one is oneself lacking moral dread and encourages others in the lack of moral dread;
one is oneself of little learning and encourages others in having little learning.
One is lazy oneself and encourages others in laziness;
one is muddle-minded oneself and encourages others in muddle-mindedness;
one is unwise oneself and encourages others in lack of wisdom.
This, monks, is called one who is more of an untrue person than an untrue person.

One is oneself possessed of a sense of shame, and encourages others in the possession of a sense of shame;

21. Sappurisavagga Sattakammasutta (The Discourse on the Seven Kinds of Action) “Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of action. What seven? There is action that is dark with dark result; there is action that is bright with bright result; there is action that is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result; there is action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action. And what, bhikkhus, is action that is dark with dark result? Here, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, or indulges in idle chatter; they are full of longing, have a mind of ill will, and hold wrong view. This is called action that is dark with dark result. And what, bhikkhus, is action that is bright with bright result? Here, someone abstains from destroying life, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from divisive speech, from harsh speech, and from idle chatter; they are without longing, have a mind of good will, and hold right view. This is called action that is bright with bright result. And what, bhikkhus, is action that is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result? Here, someone both destroys life and abstains from destroying life; takes what is not given and refrains from taking what is not given; engages in sexual misconduct and refrains from sexual misconduct; speaks falsely and speaks truthfully; speaks divisively and speaks harmoniously; speaks harshly and speaks gently; indulges in idle chatter and indulges in purposeful speech; is full of longing and also free from longing; has a mind of ill will and also a mind of good will; holds wrong view and also holds right view. This is called action that is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result. And what, bhikkhus, is action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action? It is volition for the abandoning of the aforementioned three kinds of action. This is called action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of action.”
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the person who is not a true man, and one even more base than the person who is not a true man;
I will also teach you the true man, and one even more excellent than the true man. Listen to that… [as above]… And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is not a true man?”
“Here, monks, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, and indulges in idle chatter.
This, monks, is called an untrue person.
And who, monks, is more of an untrue person than that?”
In this case, monks, a certain person himself destroys life and encourages others to destroy life;
he himself takes what is not given and encourages others to take what is not given;
he himself engages in sexual misconduct and encourages others to engage in sexual misconduct.
One is oneself a speaker of falsehood and incites others to speak falsehood;
one is oneself a speaker of divisive speech and incites others to divisive speech;
one is oneself a speaker of harsh speech and incites others to harsh speech.
One who speaks idle chatter oneself and encourages another to speak idle chatter—
this, monks, is called one who is more of an untrue person than an untrue person.
And who, monks, is a true person?
In this case, monks, a certain person abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct,
abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech,
abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter.
This, monks, is called a true person.
And who, monks, is a person even more of a true person than a true person?
Here, monks, a certain person refrains from taking life himself and encourages others in the abstention from taking life.
He himself abstains from taking what is not given and encourages others to refrain from taking what is not given;
he himself abstains from sexual misconduct and encourages others to refrain from sexual misconduct;
he himself abstains from false speech and encourages others to refrain from false speech.
He himself abstains from divisive speech and encourages others to refrain from divisive speech;
he himself abstains from harsh speech and encourages others to refrain from harsh speech;
he himself abstains from idle chatter and encourages others to refrain from idle chatter.
“This, monks, is called a person who is even more of a true person than a true person.
The third [sutta].

21. Sappurisavagga Dasakammasutta (AN 4.204, PTS AN ii 219) “Monks, there are these ten wholesome actions. What ten? (1) Here, monks, a noble disciple abstains from taking life; he lays down the rod and the sword, and dwells modest, compassionate, and kind toward all living beings. (2) He abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a mind free from theft. (3) He abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, father, parents, brother, sister, or relatives, nor with those protected by their Dhamma, or with those who have a husband, or even with those who are garlanded [as betrothed]. (4) He abstains from false speech; when summoned to a court or to a gathering, or as a witness for others, he does not speak falsely regarding what he has seen or heard. (5) He abstains from divisive speech; he does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide people from those there, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide these from those. Thus, he is one who reconciles those who are divided and encourages those who are united, delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, and being a speaker of words that create concord. (6) He abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-warming, courteous, and agreeable to many people. (7) He abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks truthfully, speaks meaningfully, speaks on the Dhamma and the Vinaya; at the proper time, he speaks such words as are worth treasuring, reasonable, moderate, and beneficial. (8) He is devoid of covetousness; he does not covet the wealth and property of others, thinking, ‘Oh, may what belongs to another be mine! (9) He is devoid of ill will and malevolence; his mind is free from hate, and he dwells with thoughts of loving-kindness toward all living beings. (10) He holds right view; he possesses a perspective that is straight, not crooked, leading to the state of the Noble Ones, and resulting in the cessation of suffering. These, monks, are the ten wholesome actions.”
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the person who is not a true man, and one even more base than the person who is not a true man;
the true man, and one even more excellent than the true man. Listen to that… [as above]… And what, bhikkhus, is the person who is not a true man?”
In this case, monks, a certain person destroys living beings, takes what is not given,
engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter,
is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong views.
This, monks, is called an untrue person.
And who, monks, is an even more untrue person than an untrue person?
Here, monks, a certain person himself destroys life and encourages others to destroy life... he himself is covetous and encourages others in covetousness.

One who is himself malevolent and encourages others toward ill will; one who is himself possessed of wrong view and encourages others toward wrong view—this, monks, is called a person worse than an inferior person.
And who, monks, is the superior person?
“Here, monks, a certain person abstains from taking life … [as before] … he is without covetousness, he has a mind free from ill will, and he holds right view.
This, monks, is called a true person.
And who, monks, is a person even more excellent than a true person?”

In this case, monks, a certain person refrains from taking life themselves and encourages others to abstain from taking life... [and so on] ... they themselves are free from covetousness and encourage others in non-covetousness;
they themselves have a mind free from ill will and encourage others in non-ill will;
they themselves possess right view and encourage others in right view.
“This, monks, is called a person who is even more of a true person than a true person.
The fourth.

21. Sappurisavagga The Discourse on the Ten Paths (Dasamaggasutta) (AN 4.206, PTS AN ii 221) “Monks, there are these ten paths of wholesome action. What ten? Taking life is a path of unwholesome action; abstaining from taking life is a path of wholesome action. Taking what is not given is a path of unwholesome action; abstaining from taking what is not given is a path of wholesome action. Sexual misconduct is a path of unwholesome action; abstaining from sexual misconduct is a path of wholesome action. False speech is a path of unwholesome action; abstaining from false speech is a path of wholesome action. Divisive speech is a path of unwholesome action; abstaining from divisive speech is a path of wholesome action. 22. The Chapter on Purification: The Discourse on the Immoral (Dussīlasutta) “Monks, there are these five dangers for one who is immoral. What five? First, monks, the immoral person dwells in fear, trembling, and with a mind full of dread. This is the first danger for one who is immoral. Second, monks, whatever assembly the immoral person approaches—whether an assembly of noble warriors, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics—he does so with a lack of confidence and with a shamed heart. This is the second danger for one who is immoral. Third, monks, the immoral person dies confused and with a troubled mind. This is the third danger for one who is immoral. This is the fourth danger for one who is immoral. Fifth, monks, when the immoral person is examined by the wise, they are found to be blameworthy. This is the fifth danger for one who is immoral. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.221 23. Duccaritavagga Duccaritasutta: On Bad Conduct “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is bad in conduct; the person who is bad in speech; the person who is bad in both conduct and speech; and the person who is good in conduct, good in speech, and good in both conduct and speech. And how, monks, is one a person who is bad in conduct? Here, monks, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, and engages in sexual misconduct. This, monks, is called a person who is bad in conduct. And how, monks, is one a person who is bad in speech? Here, monks, someone speaks falsehood, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, and indulges in idle chatter. This, monks, is called a person who is bad in speech. And how, monks, is one a person who is bad in both conduct and speech? Here, monks, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, and indulges in idle chatter. This, monks, is called a person who is bad in both conduct and speech. And how, monks, is one a person who is good in conduct, good in speech, and good in both conduct and speech? Here, monks, someone abstains from destroying life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct; they abstain from speaking falsehood, abstain from speaking maliciously, abstain from speaking harshly, and abstain from idle chatter. This, monks, is called a person who is good in conduct, good in speech, and good in both conduct and speech. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

23. Duccaritavagga The Second Discourse on the Path (Dutiyamaggasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these three unwholesome courses of action. What three? The unwholesome course of bodily action, the unwholesome course of verbal action, and the unwholesome course of mental action. These, bhikkhus, are the three unwholesome courses of action. There are, bhikkhus, these three wholesome courses of action. What three? The wholesome course of bodily action, the wholesome course of verbal action, and the wholesome course of mental action. These, bhikkhus, are the three wholesome courses of action. Just as, bhikkhus, from a cow comes milk; from milk, curd; from curd, butter; from butter, ghee; and from ghee, cream-of-ghee—which is reckoned the foremost of all these—so too, bhikkhus, when one has abandoned the three unwholesome courses of action and cultivated the three wholesome courses of action, this is reckoned the foremost of all these. What, bhikkhus, is the noble path with eight factors? It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the noble path with eight factors.”

Here, bhikkhus, someone has heard with his own ears that a deed was badly done. Having heard it, he composes verses about it. This is called a poet who composes verses based on what he has heard. And how, bhikkhus, is one a poet who composes verses based on what he has sensed? Here, bhikkhus, someone has sensed with his own mind a state that was badly done. Having sensed it, he composes verses about it. This is called a poet who composes verses based on what he has sensed. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of poets.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four poets. Which four?
The poet of thought, the poet of what has been heard, the poet of meaning, and the poet of inspired speech.”
“Monks, these are the four poets.
The eleventh [sutta].
The third chapter on Misconduct is finished.
Its summary verse:
Misconduct, wrong view, and ingratitude;
killing living beings, and the two paths.
Two courses of speech have been declared:
shamelessness and lack of wisdom, O wise one.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.232)

24. Kamma Chapter: The Short Discourse (Saṅkhittasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five results of giving. What five? One acquires wealth; one gains a good reputation; one is dear to human beings; one is dear to non-human beings; after the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a heavenly world. These, bhikkhus, are the five results of giving.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kamma that have been realized by me through direct higher knowledge and have been declared.
What are the four?
There is, bhikkhus, kamma that is dark with dark result;”
“Monks, there is action that is bright with a bright result;
there is action that is black with a black result;
there is action that is neither black nor bright with neither black nor bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.”
“Monks, these four kinds of kamma have been declared by me after having realized them for myself through direct knowledge.
Thus was the first [discourse]. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.233.

24. Kamma Chapter: The Detailed Discourse (Vitthārasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of kamma. What three? There is dark kamma with dark result; there is bright kamma with bright result; and there is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma. And what, bhikkhus, is dark kamma with dark result? Here, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called dark kamma with dark result. And what, bhikkhus, is bright kamma with bright result? Here, someone abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for heedlessness. This is called bright kamma with bright result. And what, bhikkhus, is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma? It is this noble eightfold path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is called kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of kamma. What three? There is dark kamma with dark result; there is bright kamma with bright result; and there is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma. [The Buddha then spoke in detail as above. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the twenty-third and twenty-second discourses of the Kamma Chapter.)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kamma that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge and have proclaimed.
What are the four?
There is, bhikkhus, kamma that is dark with dark result;”
“Monks, there is action that is bright with a bright result;
there is action that is dark with a dark result;
there is action that is neither dark nor bright with neither dark nor bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.”
And what, monks, is dark action with dark result?
Here, monks, someone performs a harmful bodily formation, performs a harmful verbal formation, and performs a harmful mental formation.
Having performed a harmful bodily formation, having performed a harmful verbal formation, and having performed a harmful mental formation, he is reborn in a harmful world.
When he has been reborn in a world that is afflicted, afflicted contacts touch him.
Being touched by afflicted contacts, he experiences afflicted feelings, exclusively painful, just like beings in hell.
This, monks, is called black karma with black result.
"And what, monks, is white action with white result?
Here, monks, a certain person performs a non-afflictive bodily formation, performs a non-afflictive verbal formation, and performs a non-afflictive mental formation.

Having performed a non-afflictive bodily formation, having performed a non-afflictive verbal formation, and having performed a non-afflictive mental formation, he reappears in a non-afflictive world."
When he has been reborn in a non-afflictive world, non-afflictive contacts touch him.
Being touched by non-afflictive contacts, he experiences non-afflictive feeling, which is exclusively pleasant, just like the Subhakiṇha devas.
This, monks, is called white action with white result.
And what, monks, is action that is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result?
Here, monks, someone performs a bodily formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive;
he performs a verbal formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive; [he performs a mental formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive...]
He forms a mental formation.
Having formed a bodily formation that is both harmful and harmless,
having formed a verbal formation that is both harmful and harmless, and having formed a mental formation that is both harmful and harmless, he...
One is reborn into a world that is both afflicted and unafflicted.
Having been reborn into a world that is both afflicted and unafflicted, one is touched by contacts that are both afflicted and unafflicted.

Being touched by both afflicted and unafflicted contacts, one experiences feelings that are both afflicted and unafflicted—a mixture of pleasure and pain—just like humans, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This, monks, is called action that is black-and-white with black-and-white result.
And what, monks, is action that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the destruction of action?

In this regard, monks, the volition for the abandoning of that action which is black with black result—this, monks, [is action that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the destruction of action].
The volition for the abandoning of white kamma with white result, and the volition for the abandoning of kamma that is both black and white with black-and-white result— this, monks,
is called kamma that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the destruction of kamma.
“Monks, these four kinds of kamma have been declared by me after having realized them for myself through direct higher knowledge.
This is the second [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.234

24. Kamma Chapter: The Discourse on the Soṇakāyana (AN 4.234, AN 4.233, PTS AN ii 232) At Sāvatthī. “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who acts for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others; the person who acts for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit; and the person who acts both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. “And how, monks, is one a person who acts for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others? Here, monks, someone has undertaken training rules that are wholesome and conducive to the goal, yet he does not encourage others to undertake them. He himself is established in virtuous behavior, yet he does not encourage others to be established in virtuous behavior. He himself has attained concentration, yet he does not encourage others to attain concentration. He himself has attained wisdom, yet he does not encourage others to attain wisdom. He himself has attained liberation, yet he does not encourage others to attain liberation. He himself has attained the knowledge and vision of liberation, yet he does not encourage others to attain the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others. “And how, monks, is one a person who acts for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit? Here, monks, someone has not undertaken training rules that are wholesome and conducive to the goal, yet he encourages others to undertake them. He himself is not established in virtuous behavior, yet he encourages others to be established in virtuous behavior. He himself has not attained concentration, yet he encourages others to attain concentration. He himself has not attained wisdom, yet he encourages others to attain wisdom. He himself has not attained liberation, yet he encourages others to attain liberation. He himself has not attained the knowledge and vision of liberation, yet he encourages others to attain the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit. “And how, monks, is one a person who acts both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others? Here, monks, someone has undertaken training rules that are wholesome and conducive to the goal, and he encourages others to undertake them. He himself is established in virtuous behavior, and he encourages others to be established in virtuous behavior. He himself has attained concentration, and he encourages others to attain concentration. He himself has attained wisdom, and he encourages others to attain wisdom. He himself has attained liberation, and he encourages others to attain liberation. He himself has attained the knowledge and vision of liberation, and he encourages others to attain the knowledge and vision of liberation. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who acts both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others. “Of these three persons, monks, the one who acts for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others is inferior and lowly, while the one who acts for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit is superior. But the one who acts both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others is the most excellent of all.”
Then the brahmin Sikhāmoggallāna approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Sikhāmoggallāna said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, some days ago, even earlier than that, the young brahmin Soṇakāyana approached me and said this to me:"
“The ascetic Gotama teaches the non-performance of all kamma; by teaching the non-performance of all kamma, he asserts the annihilation of the world.
“Sir, this world is established on the truth of kamma and subsists through the undertaking of kamma.
“Brahmin, I do not even recall having met with the young brahmin Soṇakāyana.”
But from where does such a conversation arise?
Brahmin, there are these four kinds of action that I have realized for myself through direct higher knowledge and have proclaimed.
What are the four?
"There is, brahmin, black kamma with black result;
there is, brahmin, white kamma with white result;
there is, brahmin, black-and-white kamma with black-and-white result."
"There is, brahmin, action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.
And what, brahmin, is action that is dark with dark result?
Here, brahmin, someone performs a harmful bodily formation, performs a harmful verbal formation, and performs a harmful mental formation."

Thus, having performed a bodily formation that is afflictive, having performed a verbal formation that is afflictive, and having performed a mental formation that is afflictive, one is reborn in an afflictive world.
Having been reborn in an afflictive world, afflictive contacts touch him.
Being touched by afflictive contacts, he experiences afflictive feeling, which is exclusively painful, just like the beings in hell.
This, brahmin, is called dark action with dark result.
And what, brahmin, is bright action with bright result?
Here, brahmin, someone performs a wholesome bodily formation, performs a wholesome verbal formation, and performs a wholesome mental formation.
Having performed an unafflictive bodily formation, having performed an unafflictive verbal formation, and having performed an unafflictive mental formation, one is reborn in an unafflictive world.
Being reborn in that unafflictive world, unafflictive contacts touch him.
Touched by those unafflictive contacts, he experiences unafflictive feeling, which is exclusively pleasant, just like the Subhakiṇha devas.
This, brahmin, is called white action with white result.
And what, brahmin, is black-and-white action with black-and-white result?
Here, brahmin, someone performs a bodily formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive.
He performs verbal formations that are both harmful and harmless; he performs mental formations that are both harmful and harmless.
Having performed bodily formations that are both harmful and harmless, as well as verbal and mental formations that are both harmful and harmless...
Having formed a verbal formation, and having formed a mental formation that is either afflictive or non-afflictive,
one is reborn into a world that is either afflictive or non-afflictive.
Being reborn into such an afflictive or non-afflictive world, one is touched by contacts that are either afflictive or non-afflictive.

Thus, being touched by both afflictive and non-afflictive contacts, one experiences both afflictive and non-afflictive feelings, mixed with pleasure and pain—just like humans, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This, brahmin, is called black-and-white karma with black-and-white result.
And what, brahmin, is the karma that is neither black nor white, with neither black nor white result, which leads to the destruction of karma?
In this regard, brahmin, there is the volition for the abandoning of that action which is dark with dark result;
the volition for the abandoning of that action which is bright with bright result; and the volition for the abandoning of that action which is both dark and bright with dark-and-bright result.
“This, brahmin, is called the action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.
These, brahmin, are the four kinds of action that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge and have declared.
The third [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.235 24. Kamma-vagga Paṭhama-sikkhāpada-sutta (The First Training Rule) “Monks, there are these four training rules. What four? ‘I will not take life’—this is a training rule to be observed with full understanding. ‘I will not take what is not given’—this is a training rule to be observed with full understanding. ‘I will not engage in sexual misconduct’—this is a training rule to be observed with full understanding. ‘I will not speak falsehood’—this is a training rule to be observed with full understanding. These, monks, are the four training rules.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kamma that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge and have declared.
What are the four?
There is, monks, black karma with black result;
there is, monks, white karma with white result;
there is, monks, black-and-white karma with black-and-white result.
"There is, monks, action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.
And what, monks, is action that is dark with dark result?

Here, monks, someone is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehood, and one who indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence."
This, monks, is called black action with black result.
And what, monks, is white action with white result?
Here, monks, a certain person abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
He abstains from taking what is not given, he abstains from false speech, and he abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.
This, monks, is called action that is bright with a bright result.
And what, monks, is action that is black-and-white with a black-and-white result?
“Here, monks, a certain person performs a bodily formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive... This, monks, is called action that is black-and-white with black-and-white result.
“And what, monks, is action that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the destruction of action?

In this regard, monks, whatever action is black with black result... [as before] ...this, monks, is called action that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the destruction of action.”
“Monks, these four kinds of kamma have been declared by me after having realized them for myself through direct knowledge.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.236
24. Kamma Chapter:
The Second Training Rule Discourse (AN 4.236, AN 4.234, PTS AN ii 234)
“Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of kamma that have been realized by me through direct higher knowledge and declared.
What are the four?
There is, bhikkhus, dark kamma with dark result;”
“Monks, there is action that is bright with a bright result;
there is action that is black with a black result;
there is action that is neither black nor bright with neither black nor bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.”
And what, monks, is the black action with black result?
Here, monks, someone has deprived his mother of life, deprived his father of life, deprived an arahant of life;
with a mind of hatred he has shed the blood of a Tathāgata; or he has caused a schism in the Saṅgha.
This, monks, is called dark action with dark result.
And what, monks, is bright action with bright result?
Here, monks, a certain person abstains from the destruction of life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct.
He abstains from taking what is not given; he abstains from false speech; he abstains from malicious speech;
he abstains from harsh speech; he abstains from idle chatter; he is free from covetousness;
he is of a mind without ill will; he holds right view.
This, monks, is called white action with white result.
And what, monks, is black-and-white action with black-and-white result?
Here, monks, someone performs a bodily formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive... [as before] ... This, monks, is called black-and-white action with black-and-white result.
"And what, bhikkhus, is the action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action?

Here, bhikkhus, whatever action is dark with dark result... [as before] ...this, bhikkhus, is called the action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.
These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of action proclaimed by me after having realized them for myself through direct knowledge."
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.237 24.
Kamma-vagga (The Chapter on Kamma)
The Noble Path Discourse (Ariyamaggasutta): “Monks,
there are these four kinds of kamma that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge and have proclaimed.”
Which four?
There is, monks, black karma with black result;
there is, monks, white karma with white result.
“Monks, there is action that is dark with dark result; there is action that is bright with bright result;
and there is action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the exhaustion of action.
And what, monks, is action that is dark with dark result?”
"Here, monks, a certain person performs a bodily formation that is afflictive... [as before] ...this, monks, is called black karma with black result.
And what, monks, is white karma with white result?
Here, monks, a certain person performs a bodily formation that is non-afflictive... [as before] ...this, monks, is called white karma with white result."
"And what, monks, is action that is black-and-white with black-and-white result?
Here, monks, someone performs a bodily formation that is both afflictive and non-afflictive... This, monks, is called action that is black-and-white with black-and-white result.
And what, monks, is action that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the destruction of action?"
“Right view ... right concentration.
This, monks, is called action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action.
These, monks, are the four kinds of action that have been realized by me through direct knowledge and have been declared.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.238 24.
Kamma-vagga (The Chapter on Kamma)
The Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgasutta) (AN 4.238, AN 4.236, PTS AN ii 236):
“Monks, there are these four kinds of kamma … [as before] … dark with dark result … [as before] …”
"Here, monks, a certain person performs a bodily formation that is afflictive... [as before] ...this, monks, is called black karma with black result.
And what, monks, is white karma with white result?
Here, monks, a certain person performs a bodily formation that is non-afflictive... [as before] ...this, monks, is called white karma with white result."
"And what, monks, is the action that is black-and-white with black-and-white result?
Here, monks, someone performs a bodily formation that is both harmful and harmless... This, monks, is called the action that is black-and-white with black-and-white result.
And what, monks, is the action that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result, which leads to the destruction of action?"

The mindfulness enlightenment factor, the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor, the energy enlightenment factor, the rapture enlightenment factor, the tranquility enlightenment factor, the concentration enlightenment factor, and the equanimity enlightenment factor— this, monks,
is called the action that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of action. These, monks,
are the four kinds of action that have been realized by me through direct knowledge and declared.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.239 24.
Chapter on Kamma (Kammavagga)
Sāvajjasutta:
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. What four? [The text continues with the specific qualities.]”
Which four?
Blameworthy bodily action, blameworthy verbal action, blameworthy mental action, and blameworthy view.
Endowed with these four things, monks, one is placed in hell as if carried there.
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses four qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the four?
Faultless bodily action, faultless verbal action, faultless mental action, and faultless view.”
“Monks, one who possesses these four qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
The eighth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 4.240.

24. Kamma Chapter: The Discourse on Harmlessness (Abyābajjha-sutta) “Monks, there are these three kinds of kamma that have been taught by me after being directly known and realized through higher knowledge. What three? There is dark kamma with dark result; there is bright kamma with bright result; and there is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma. And what, monks, is dark kamma with dark result? Here, someone performs an action that is harmful to others and brings them suffering, and they experience the result of that action as something harmful and painful. This is called dark kamma with dark result. And what, monks, is bright kamma with bright result? Here, someone performs an action that is beneficial to others and brings them happiness, and they experience the result of that action as something beneficial and pleasant. This is called bright kamma with bright result. And what, monks, is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma? Here, one dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. One dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This is called kamma that is neither dark nor bright with neither-dark-nor-bright result, which leads to the destruction of kamma.”
“Monks, one who possesses four qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. Which four?
Harmful bodily action, harmful verbal action, harmful mental action, and a harmful view.”
"Monks, one who possesses these four qualities is placed in hell as if carried there.
Monks, one who possesses four qualities is placed in heaven as if carried there.
Which four?"
“By means of non-afflictive bodily action, non-afflictive verbal action, non-afflictive mental action, and a non-afflictive view—
it is by being endowed with these four qualities, monks, that one is placed in heaven as if carried there. Thus ends the ninth discourse.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.241 24. Chapter on Action (Kammavagga) Samaṇa Sutta: The Ascetic “Monks, there are these four kinds of ascetics who are found existing in the world. What four? The one who is an ascetic by way of livelihood; the one who is an ascetic by way of outward appearance; the one who is an ascetic by way of mere talk; and the one who is an ascetic by way of the destruction of the taints. And how, monks, is one an ascetic by way of livelihood? Here, monks, a certain person goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, considering: ‘I am one who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of the holy life. Yet he lives the holy life for the sake of gain, honor, and renown, and for the sake of the next world. He does not train himself in accordance with the Dhamma, nor does he practice the Dhamma in its entirety. This, monks, is called an ascetic by way of livelihood. And how, monks, is one an ascetic by way of outward appearance? Here, monks, a certain person goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness… [as before] …He trains himself in accordance with the Dhamma and practices the Dhamma in its entirety, yet he wears robes made of rags from the dustheap, carries an alms bowl, and maintains the outward marks of a recluse. This, monks, is called an ascetic by way of outward appearance. And how, monks, is one an ascetic by way of mere talk? Here, monks, a certain person goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness… [as before] …He trains himself in accordance with the Dhamma and practices the Dhamma in its entirety, yet he merely utters various forms of talk, such as: ‘The Tathāgata is omniscient, all-seeing; he knows all things, sees all things; he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the welfare and happiness of gods and humans. This, monks, is called an ascetic by way of mere talk. And how, monks, is one an ascetic by way of the destruction of the taints? Here, monks, a certain person goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness… [as before] …He trains himself in accordance with the Dhamma and practices the Dhamma in its entirety. By realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, which is devoid of clinging. This, monks, is called an ascetic by way of the destruction of the taints. These, monks, are the four kinds of ascetics who are found existing in the world.”
“Right here, monks, is the first ascetic;
right here is the second ascetic; right here is the third ascetic; right here is the fourth ascetic.
Empty are the teachings of others of other ascetics.”
"It is so, monks; roar this true lion’s roar.
And who, monks, is the first kind of ascetic?

Here, monks, a monk, through the total destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination."
This, monks, is the first ascetic.
And what, monks, is the second ascetic?

Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the complete destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, becomes a once-returner; returning to this world only once more, he makes an end of suffering.
This, monks, is the second ascetic.
And who, monks, is the third ascetic?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
This, monks, is the third kind of ascetic.
And what, monks, is the fourth kind of ascetic?

Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
“This, monks, is the fourth ascetic.
‘Right here, monks, is the first ascetic; right here is the second ascetic; right here is the third ascetic; right here is the fourth ascetic;
empty are the teachings of others of other ascetics.’”
“It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should rightly roar your lion’s roar.
The tenth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.242

24. Section on Kamma: Discourse on the Benefits of a True Person (Sappurisānisaṁsasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits for a true person. What five? First, bhikkhus, a true person does not do anything that would lead to his own affliction, nor does he do anything that would lead to the affliction of others, nor does he do anything that would lead to the affliction of both. He practices for his own welfare, for the welfare of others, and for the welfare of both. And he dwells with a mind free from enmity, free from ill will, compassionate, and sympathetic toward all living beings. This, bhikkhus, is the first benefit for a true person. Second, bhikkhus, a true person does not do anything that would lead to his own harm, nor does he do anything that would lead to the harm of others, nor does he do anything that would lead to the harm of both. He practices for his own welfare, for the welfare of others, and for the welfare of both. And he dwells with a mind free from enmity, free from ill will, compassionate, and sympathetic toward all living beings. This, bhikkhus, is the second benefit for a true person. Third, bhikkhus, a true person does not do anything that would lead to his own suffering, nor does he do anything that would lead to the suffering of others, nor does he do anything that would lead to the suffering of both. He practices for his own welfare, for the welfare of others, and for the welfare of both. And he dwells with a mind free from enmity, free from ill will, compassionate, and sympathetic toward all living beings. This, bhikkhus, is the third benefit for a true person. Fourth, bhikkhus, a true person does not do anything that would lead to his own disadvantage, nor does he do anything that would lead to the disadvantage of others, nor does he do anything that would lead to the disadvantage of both. He practices for his own welfare, for the welfare of others, and for the welfare of both. And he dwells with a mind free from enmity, free from ill will, compassionate, and sympathetic toward all living beings. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth benefit for a true person. Fifth, bhikkhus, a true person does not do anything that would lead to his own defilement, nor does he do anything that would lead to the defilement of others, nor does he do anything that would lead to the defilement of both. He practices for his own welfare, for the welfare of others, and for the welfare of both. And he dwells with a mind free from enmity, free from ill will, compassionate, and sympathetic toward all living beings. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth benefit for a true person. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits for a true person.”
“Monks, by relying on a true person, four benefits are to be expected. What four?
One grows in noble virtue; one grows in noble concentration; one grows in noble wisdom; one grows in noble liberation.”
“Bhikkhus, by relying on a true person, these four benefits are to be expected.
The eleventh [sutta].
The fourth chapter on Action is finished.
Its summary verse:
The brief and the detailed, Soṇa and Kāyana,
the training rule, the noble path, and the factors of enlightenment.
That which is blameworthy yet harmless,
and the benefit of being a true person for a recluse.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.243)

25. The Chapter on Fear of Offenses: Discourse on the Schism of the Saṅgha (Āpattibhayavagga Saṅghabhedakasutta) “Monks, there are these five fears of offenses. What five? The fear of being accused of a grave offense; the fear of being accused of a minor offense; the fear of being censured by the Saṅgha; the fear of being suspended from the Saṅgha; and the fear of being reborn in hell after death. These, monks, are the five fears of offenses. “Monks, there are these five benefits of not causing a schism in the Saṅgha. What five? One does not incur the fear of being accused of a grave offense; one does not incur the fear of being accused of a minor offense; one does not incur the fear of being censured by the Saṅgha; one does not incur the fear of being suspended from the Saṅgha; and one does not incur the fear of being reborn in hell after death. These, monks, are the five benefits of not causing a schism in the Saṅgha. “Monks, there are these five things that lead to the schism of the Saṅgha. What five? Here, monks, a monk is himself full of lust and incites others who are full of lust; he is himself full of hatred and incites others who are full of hatred; he is himself full of delusion and incites others who are full of delusion; he is himself full of agitation and incites others who are full of agitation; and he speaks in praise of those who are full of lust, hatred, delusion, and agitation. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the schism of the Saṅgha. “Monks, there are these five things that lead to the non-schism of the Saṅgha. What five? Here, monks, a monk is himself free from lust and does not incite others who are full of lust; he is himself free from hatred and does not incite others who are full of hatred; he is himself free from delusion and does not incite others who are full of delusion; he is himself free from agitation and does not incite others who are full of agitation; and he speaks in dispraise of those who are full of lust, hatred, delusion, and agitation. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the non-schism of the Saṅgha. “Monks, there are these five causes for the schism of the Saṅgha. What five? Here, monks, a monk teaches a Dhamma that is contrary to the Dhamma as being the Dhamma, and he teaches a Dhamma that is not the Dhamma as being contrary to the Dhamma;

he teaches a discipline that is contrary to the discipline as being the discipline, and he teaches a discipline that is not the discipline as being contrary to the discipline. These, monks, are the five causes for the schism of the Saṅgha. “Monks, there are these five causes for the non-schism of the Saṅgha. What five? These, monks, are the five causes for the non-schism of the Saṅgha. “Monks, there are these five causes for the schism of the Saṅgha. What five? These, monks, are the five causes for the schism of the Saṅgha. “Monks, there are these five causes for the non-schism of the Saṅgha. What five? Here, monks, a monk teaches a Dhamma that is contrary to the Dhamma
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Ānanda, has that legal dispute been settled?”
“Venerable sir, from where will that legal dispute be settled?
Venerable sir, a co-resident of the venerable Anuruddha named Bāhiya has stood firm for the schism of the Saṅgha throughout its entirety.
In this matter, the venerable Anuruddha does not consider even a single word to be said.”
“But when, Ānanda, does Anuruddha apply himself to legal matters in the midst of the Saṅgha?
Is it not the case, Ānanda, that whatever legal matters arise, you and Sāriputta and Moggallāna should all together settle them?
Seeing four reasons for his welfare, Ānanda, a wicked bhikkhu delights in a schism in the Saṅgha.”
Which four?

Here, Ānanda, a wicked bhikkhu is immoral, of evil nature, impure, of suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions; he is not a recluse though claiming to be a recluse, not one who lives the holy life though claiming to live the holy life; he is inwardly rotten, leaking, and full of filth.
It occurs to him thus:
‘If the monks should know me as one who is immoral,

of evil character, impure, of suspicious conduct, secretive in his actions, not a recluse though claiming to be a recluse, not living the holy life though claiming to live the holy life, inwardly rotten, leaking, and putrid, they will,
being united, expel me; but if they are divided, they will not expel me.’
"Ānanda, seeing this first advantage, a wicked bhikkhu rejoices in a schism in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a wicked bhikkhu holds wrong view and is possessed of extremist views.
It occurs to him thus:"
‘If the monks should know me as one of wrong view,
possessed of extremist views, then when they are united they will exclude me,
but when they are divided they will not exclude me.’
Seeing this second reason for its benefit, Ānanda, a wicked bhikkhu delights in causing a schism in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a wicked bhikkhu lives by a wrong livelihood; he maintains his life through wrong livelihood.
It occurs to him thus:
‘If the monks should know me as one who lives by wrong livelihood,
maintaining his life by wrong livelihood, they will expel me when they are in concord;
but when they are divided, they will not expel me.’
"Ānanda, seeing this third advantage, a wicked bhikkhu delights in causing a schism in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a wicked bhikkhu is desirous of gain, desirous of honor, and desirous of not being despised.
It occurs to him thus:"
‘If the monks should know me as one who desires gain,

who desires honor, and who desires not to be treated with contempt, then while they are in concord, they will not honor me, they will not revere me, they will not esteem me, and they will not worship me;
but when they are divided, they will honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me.’
“Ānanda, seeing this fourth reason, a wicked bhikkhu delights in a schism in the Saṅgha.
It is these four reasons, Ānanda, that a wicked bhikkhu sees when he delights in a schism in the Saṅgha.
The first.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.244 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Āpattibhayasutta (The Discourse on Fear of Offenses) "Bhikkhus, there are these four fears regarding offenses. What four? The fear of committing an offense; the fear of being reproved for an offense; the fear of being censured by wise companions in the holy life; and the fear of falling into the states of misery, the bad destinations, the lower realms, and hell because of an offense. These, bhikkhus, are the four fears regarding offenses."
“Bhikkhus, there are these four fears regarding offenses.
What are the four?
“Monks, it is just as if they were to seize a thief, a wrongdoer, and present him to the king, saying:
‘Sire, this is a thief, a wrongdoer.
May Your Majesty decree a punishment for him.’”
Then the king would say to him:
“Go, sirs, bind this man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope,
shave his head, and lead him from street to street and from square to square with a harsh-sounding drum.”
‘Having led him out through the southern gate, cut off his head to the south of the city. Then the king’s men,
having bound him with firm ropes behind the arms in tight shackles, shaved his head,
and led him along from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads with the shrill sound of drums, parading him about.
Having led him out through the southern gate, they would cut off his head to the south of the city.
Then, a certain man standing on dry land there might think:
"Alas, sir, this man has committed a wicked, blameworthy deed deserving of decapitation."
For indeed, there are men of the king who, having bound a man with his arms tied tightly behind his back with a strong rope,
having shaved his head, and having led him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the accompaniment of a harsh-sounding drum,
shall lead him out through the southern gate and cut off his head to the south of the city.
“‘Oh, may I never commit such an evil, censurable deed that would result in the cutting off of my head!
In the same way, monks, for whichever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī such a keen perception of danger has been established regarding the offenses entailing defeat, it can be expected of them:
either they will not commit an offense entailing defeat if they have not already done so, or if they have committed one, they will make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma.”
“Monks, suppose a man were to put on black garments, let his hair hang down, place a pestle upon his shoulder, and approach a great crowd of people, saying:
‘Venerable sirs, I have committed a blameworthy evil deed that deserves a pestle; I shall do whatever makes you venerable ones pleased.
Then, a certain man standing on dry ground would think thus:”
“Alas, sirs, this man has committed a wicked, censurable deed deserving of the wooden pestle!
For he has indeed put on black garments, disheveled his hair, placed a wooden pestle upon his shoulder, approached a great crowd of people, and said:
‘Venerable sirs, I have committed a wicked, censurable deed deserving of the wooden pestle; I shall do whatever makes you venerable ones pleased.’”
"Alas, may I not commit such an evil, censurable deed that leads to remorse!
In the same way, monks, for whichever monk or nun such a keen perception of danger is established regarding the offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa),
it can be expected of them that they will not commit a saṅghādisesa offense, or— if already committed— will confess it.
He will not commit an offense, or if he has committed an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*), he will make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma.
Just as if, monks, a man were to put on black garments, dishevel his hair, place a basket of ashes upon his shoulder, approach a great crowd of people, and say:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed a wicked deed, a censurable act; here is my basket of ashes."
‘I shall do whatever will please these venerable ones.
Then, a certain man standing on dry land might think:
‘Alas, this man has committed a wicked deed; he has made a censurable ash-bag!’”
For indeed, having put on a black garment, having disheveled his hair, and having placed a basket of ashes upon his shoulder, he would approach a great crowd of people and say:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed a blameworthy evil deed;
I shall do whatever makes you venerable ones pleased."
"Alas, may I not commit such a blameworthy evil deed as this, which is like being wrapped in ashes!
In the same way, monks, for whichever monk or nun such a keen perception of danger is established regarding the *pācittiya* rules,
it can be expected of them that they will either not have committed a *pācittiya* offense, or...
He will not commit an offense, or if he has committed one, he will make amends for that offense requiring expiation in accordance with the Dhamma.
Just as if, monks, a man were to put on black clothes, dishevel his hair, and approach a great crowd of people, saying:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed an evil deed, one that is censurable and blameworthy."
‘I shall do whatever will make these venerable ones pleased.
Then, a certain man standing on dry land might think:
‘Alas, this man has committed an evil deed, one that is censurable and blameworthy!’”
For it is indeed remarkable that one who has put on black garments and disheveled his hair should approach a great multitude of people and say:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed an evil deed, blameworthy and censurable;
I shall do whatever makes you venerable ones pleased."
"Alas, may I not commit such an evil deed, which is censurable and blameworthy!
In the same way, monks, for any monk or nun who has established such a keen perception of danger regarding the *pāṭidesanīya* offenses,
it is to be expected that they will either not commit a *pāṭidesanīya* offense...
“He will not commit an offense, or if he has committed one, he will make amends for the offense entailing confession in accordance with the Dhamma.
These, monks, are the four fears regarding offenses. This is the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.245 25. Āpattibhayavagga Sikkhānisaṁsasutta:

The Benefits of Training “Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits of training. What five? One trains for the sake of restraint; one trains for the sake of non-transgression; one trains for the sake of full understanding; one trains for the sake of abandoning; one trains for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five benefits of training.”
“Monks, this holy life is lived for the sake of the benefit of training; it has wisdom as its summit, liberation as its essence, and mindfulness as its governing principle.
And how, monks, is there the benefit of training?

“Here, monks, I have prescribed for my disciples the training in higher conduct for the purpose of inspiring confidence in those without confidence and for increasing the confidence of those who already have it.

In whatever way, monks, I have prescribed the training in higher conduct for my disciples for the purpose of inspiring confidence in those without confidence and for increasing the confidence of those who already have it, in that very way, he becomes one who practices that training without breaking it.”
He acts without flaw, acts without blemish, and acts without impurity; he trains himself, undertaking the rules of training.
Furthermore, monks, the training fundamental to the holy life has been prescribed by me for my disciples for the complete and utter destruction of suffering.
In whatever way, monks, the training fundamental to the holy life has been prescribed by me for my disciples for the complete and utter...
In such a way that it leads to the complete destruction of suffering, he practices that training unbrokenly, without gaps, without flaws, and without blemish;
having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.
In this way, monks, there is the fruit of training.
And how, bhikkhus, is there wisdom as the superior?
Here, bhikkhus, the Dhammas have been taught by me to my disciples for the complete and perfect destruction of suffering.
In whatever way those Dhammas have been taught by me to my disciples for the complete and perfect destruction of suffering, in that very way they have been thoroughly examined with wisdom.
"In this way, monks, wisdom is supreme.
And how, monks, is liberation the essence?
Here, monks, the Dhamma has been taught by me to my disciples for the complete and total destruction of suffering."
“Bhikkhus, in whatever way the Dhamma has been taught by me to my disciples for the complete and total destruction of suffering, in that very way those teachings have touched liberation.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is a core of liberation.
And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness predominant?”

‘Thus, I will fulfill the training in higher conduct that is not yet fulfilled, or I will support with wisdom here and there the training in higher conduct that is already fulfilled’—in this way, mindfulness is well-established within oneself.

‘Thus, I will fulfill the training fundamental to the holy life that is not yet fulfilled, or I will support with wisdom here and there the training fundamental to the holy life that is already fulfilled’—in this way, mindfulness is well-established within oneself.

‘Thus, I shall examine with wisdom a state not yet examined, or I shall further assist with wisdom here and there a state already examined’—in this way, mindfulness is well-established within oneself.

‘Thus, I shall touch with liberation a state not yet touched, or I shall further assist with wisdom here and there a state already touched’—in this way, mindfulness is well-established within oneself.
It is in this manner, monks, that mindfulness is predominant.
“‘This holy life, bhikkhus, is lived with training as its benefit, with wisdom as its supreme goal, with liberation as its essence, and with mindfulness as its overlord’—
it was with reference to this that this was said. Thus was the third [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.246 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Seyyāsutta (The Discourse on the Bed) “Monks, there are these four kinds of beds. What four? The bed of one who has committed an offense; the bed of one who is angry and resentful; the bed of one who is intoxicated and negligent; and the bed of one who is heedless. These, monks, are the four kinds of beds.”
“Monks, there are these four kinds of sleepers. Which four? [Text continues as in AN 4.246 and AN 4.244].”
The posture of the hungry ghosts, the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures, the lion’s posture, and the Tathāgata’s posture.
And what, monks, is the posture of the hungry ghosts?
For the most part, monks, hungry ghosts lie on their backs.
This, monks, is called the posture of the hungry ghosts.
And what, monks, is the posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures?
For the most part, monks, those who enjoy sensual pleasures lie on their left side.
This, monks, is called the reclining posture of those who enjoy sensual pleasures.
And what, monks, is the lion’s reclining posture?
The lion, monks, the king of beasts, lies down on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, and tucking his tail between his thighs.
Having thus awakened, he raises his forequarters and surveys his hindquarters.
If, monks, the lion, the king of beasts, sees anything of his body that is scattered or disheveled, then, monks, the lion, the king of beasts, is displeased.
But if, monks, the lion, the king of beasts, sees nothing of his body that is scattered or disheveled, then, monks, the lion, the king of beasts, is pleased.
This, monks, is called the lion’s posture.
And what, monks, is the Tathāgata’s posture?
Here, monks, the Tathāgata, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
“Monks, this is called the Tathāgata’s reclining.
These, monks, are the four kinds of reclining.
The fourth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.247 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Thūpārahasutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons worthy of a stupa. What four? The person who is a Perfectly Awakened One, an Arahant Buddha; the person who is a Paccekabuddha; the person who is a disciple of the Tathāgata, a stream-enterer; and the person who is a disciple of the Tathāgata, one who has attained the fruit of non-returning. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons worthy of a stupa.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four who are worthy of a stupa. Which four? [Text continues]”

“The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is worthy of a stupa; a Paccekabuddha is worthy of a stupa; a disciple of the Tathāgata is worthy of a stupa; a wheel-turning monarch is worthy of a stupa.
These, monks, are the four who are worthy of a stupa.
Thus was the fifth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.248 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Paññāvuddhisutta: The Discourse on the Growth of Wisdom “Monks, there are these four things that lead to the growth of wisdom. What four? Association with superior persons, listening to the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma. These, monks, are the four things that lead to the growth of wisdom.”
“Bhikkhus, these four things lead to the increase of wisdom. What four? [The text continues with the list of four.]”
“Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma—
these, monks, are the four things that lead to the increase of wisdom.
This is the sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.249 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Bahukārasutta “Monks, there are these four persons who are of great service. What four? The person who provides one with robes; the person who provides one with almsfood; the person who provides one with a dwelling; and the person who provides one with medicinal requisites for the sick. These, monks, are the four persons who are of great service.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things that are of great benefit to one who has become human.
What are the four?
“Association with superior persons, hearing the true Dhamma, careful attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma—
these, monks, are the four things that are of great benefit to one who has become human.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.250 25. The Chapter on Fear of Offenses First Discourse on Conventional Expression "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of conventional expression. What four? 'One who has not been ordained is called "one who has not been ordained. This is the first kind of conventional expression. 'One who has been ordained is called "one who has been ordained. This is the second kind of conventional expression. 'One who is not a bhikkhu is called "not a bhikkhu. This is the third kind of conventional expression. 'One who is a bhikkhu is called "a bhikkhu. This is the fourth kind of conventional expression. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of conventional expression."* *The remainder of this discourse follows the pattern of the preceding suttas in this section, detailing various categories of persons and their respective designations.*
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ignoble modes of speech. What are the four? [The text continues with the list of these four.]”
“Claiming to have seen what was not seen; claiming to have heard what was not heard; claiming to have sensed what was not sensed;
claiming to have cognized what was not cognized—these, monks, are the four ignoble modes of speech.
The eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.251 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Dutiyavohārasutta (The Second Discourse on Conventional Expression) “Monks, there are these four kinds of conventional expression. What four? ‘This is form,’ monks, is a conventional expression; ‘this is feeling’ is a conventional expression; ‘this is perception’ is a conventional expression; ‘these are volitional formations’ are conventional expressions. These, monks, are the four kinds of conventional expression.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four noble modes of speech.
What are the four? [The text continues with the list of the four noble modes of speech.]”

“Bhikkhus, there are these four noble modes of speech: speaking of what has not been seen as ‘not seen,’ speaking of what has not been heard as ‘not heard,’ speaking of what has not been sensed as ‘not sensed,’ and speaking of what has not been cognized as ‘not cognized.
These, bhikkhus, are the four noble modes of speech.
The ninth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.252 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Tatiyavohārasutta (The Third Discourse on Modes of Speech) "Bhikkhus, there are these four modes of speech. What four? There is a mode of speech that is true and factual; there is a mode of speech that is untrue but factual; there is a mode of speech that is untrue and unfactual; and there is a mode of speech that is neither true nor factual. These, bhikkhus, are the four modes of speech."
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ignoble modes of speech. What are the four? [The text continues with the list.]”
“Claiming not to have seen what was seen; claiming not to have heard what was heard; claiming not to have sensed what was sensed;
claiming not to have cognized what was cognized—these, monks, are the four ignoble modes of speech. Tenth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.253 25.

Āpattibhayavagga Catutthavohārasutta (The Fourth Discourse on Designation) "Bhikkhus, there are these four designations. What four? Designation by way of name, designation by way of clan, designation by way of occupation, and designation by way of personal characteristics. These, bhikkhus, are the four designations."
“Bhikkhus, there are these four noble modes of speech.
What are the four?

these, bhikkhus, are the four noble modes of speech. (The eleventh.)

Schism, offense, and training;
A bed [is for one] worthy of a stupa;
the increase of wisdom is of great benefit;
the four modes of conduct are established.
The Fifth Fifty is completed. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.254, Chapter 26:

26. Chapter on Direct Knowledge:

Then the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said this to the Blessed One:

“In this matter, Māluṅkyaputta, what shall we say to the young bhikkhus now?”
“Indeed, since you, being aged, elderly, and advanced in years, request a brief exhortation from the Tathāgata.
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief; let the Sugata teach me the Dhamma in brief.
It is possible that I might understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said; it is possible that I might become an heir to what the Blessed One has spoken.”
“Māluṅkyaputta, there are these four origins of craving where craving arises in a bhikkhu as it arises.
What are the four?
Craving arises in a bhikkhu on account of robes, Māluṅkyaputta.”
“Māluṅkyaputta, craving arises in a bhikkhu because of almsfood;
Māluṅkyaputta, craving arises in a bhikkhu because of lodging;
or, Māluṅkyaputta, craving arises in a bhikkhu because of the pursuit of ‘it may be thus’ or ‘it may be otherwise.’”
“Māluṅkyaputta, these are the four origins of craving where craving arises in a bhikkhu when it arises.
But when, Māluṅkyaputta, a bhikkhu’s craving has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with,
and is no longer subject to future arising— this, Māluṅkyaputta, is called a bhikkhu who has cut off craving and turned away [from the round].”
“...the fetter; through the perfect realization of conceit, he has made an end of suffering.

These sons of noble family went forth from the home life into homelessness in the right way;
and having realized for themselves with direct knowledge, he dwelt having attained that supreme goal of the holy life, even in this very life.
