26. Abhiññāvagga Kulasutta (AN 4.258, AN 4.255, PTS AN ii 249) “Monks, there are these four kinds of families. What four? The family that is well-behaved but not wealthy; the family that is wealthy but not well-behaved; the family that is neither well-behaved nor wealthy; and the family that is both well-behaved and wealthy. These, monks, are the four kinds of families.”
“Bhikkhus, whatever families have attained great wealth but do not endure for long, all of them do so for one or another of four reasons.
What are the four?

They do not search for what has been lost; they do not repair what is worn out; they consume food and drink in immoderate amounts; and they place a woman or a man of immoral conduct in a position of authority.
“Bhikkhus, whatever families have attained great wealth but do not remain long-term, all of them do so for one or another of these four reasons.
Bhikkhus, whatever families have attained great wealth and do remain long-term, all of them do so for one or another of these four reasons.
What are the four?”
They search for what is lost; they repair what is worn out; they are moderate in food and drink; and they appoint a virtuous woman or man to the position of authority.
Monks, whatever families have attained great wealth and endure for a long time, all of them do so through these four factors or one of them.
Thus ends the fifth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.259 26. Chapter on Direct Knowledge (Abhiññāvagga) First Discourse on the Noble Steed (Paṭhama-ājānīya-sutta) “Monks, there are these four types of noble steeds. What four? The one who, when struck by a whip-stroke, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort; the one who, when struck by a mere touch, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort; the one who, when merely seeing the shadow of the whip, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort; and the one who, through mere hearing of the words ‘I shall strike you,’ exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. These, monks, are the four types of noble steeds. In the same way, monks, there are these four types of noble individuals. What four? The one who, when struck by a whip-stroke, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort; the one who, when struck by a mere touch, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort; the one who, when merely seeing the shadow of the whip, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort; and the one who, through mere hearing of the words ‘I shall strike you,’ exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. And how, monks, is the noble individual one who, when struck by a whip-stroke, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort? Here, monks, a certain noble individual is reproved by the Teacher or by one similar to the Teacher, or by a companion in the holy life, or by a fellow disciple, saying: ‘It is not fitting for you, friend, thus to act; it is not proper for you, friend, thus to conduct yourself. Being reproved in this way, he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. But even while exerting himself, striving, and making an effort, he does not attain that state of further distinction, higher than the human, which is peaceful and sublime, and which he had not attained before. This, monks, is called the noble individual who, when struck by a whip-stroke, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. And how, monks, is the noble individual one who, when struck by a mere touch, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort? Here, monks, a certain noble individual is reproved by the Teacher or by one similar to the Teacher... [as above] ...But even while exerting himself, striving, and making an effort, he does not attain that state of further distinction, higher than the human, which is peaceful and sublime, and which he had not attained before. This, monks, is called the noble individual who, when struck by a mere touch, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. And how, monks, is the noble individual one who, when merely seeing the shadow of the whip, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort? Here, monks, a certain noble individual is reproved by the Teacher or by one similar to the Teacher... [as above] ...But even while exerting himself, striving, and making an effort, he does not attain that state of further distinction, higher than the human, which is peaceful and sublime, and which he had not attained before. This, monks, is called the noble individual who, when merely seeing the shadow of the whip, exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. And how, monks, is the noble individual one who, through mere hearing of the words ‘I shall strike you,’ exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort? Here, monks, a certain noble individual hears: ‘The Teacher or one similar to the Teacher will reprove such-and-such a person. Having heard this, he exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. And having exerted himself, strived, and made an effort, he attains that state of further distinction, higher than the human, which is peaceful and sublime, and which he had not attained before. This, monks, is called the noble individual who, through mere hearing of the words ‘I shall strike you,’ exerts himself, strives, and makes an effort. These, monks, are the four types of noble individuals.”
“Bhikkhus, possessing four factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.
What are the four? [Text follows].”
“Here, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse possesses four qualities: it is endowed with beauty, strength, speed, and the right proportions of height and girth.
Endowed with these four factors, monks, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king.

In the same way, monks, a bhikkhu endowed with four qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
Which four?
Here, monks, a monk is endowed with beauty, endowed with strength, endowed with speed, and endowed with height and proportion.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with beauty?
“Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous… he trains himself by undertaking the training precepts.
In this way, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with beauty.
And how, monks, is a bhikkhu endowed with strength?”

"Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.
In this way, monks, a monk is endowed with strength.
And how, monks, is a monk endowed with speed?"
“Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
In this way, monks, a monk is possessed of speed.
And how, monks, is a monk possessed of stature and girth?
“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is endowed with physical stature and proportion.
Possessing these four qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.260 26.

“Bhikkhus, endowed with four factors, a king’s noble thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, an asset to a king, and is reckoned as a very limb of the king. What four? [The text continues with the description of these four qualities.]”

“In the same way, monks, a monk endowed with four qualities is worthy of offerings … an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

Here, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is endowed with strength.

26. Abhiññāvagga Araññasutta (AN 4.262, AN 4.259, PTS AN ii 252) “Monks, there are these five kinds of forest-dwelling. What five? Yet he does not gain internal serenity of mind, and his body remains uncalmed. This is the first kind of forest-dweller. Again, monks, a bhikkhu dwells in a forest… or on a heap of straw. He gains internal serenity of mind, but his body remains uncalmed. This is the second kind of forest-dweller. Again, monks, a bhikkhu dwells in a forest… or on a heap of straw. He gains internal serenity of mind, and his body becomes calmed. However, he does not dwell having attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, having realized for himself with direct knowledge. This is the third kind of forest-dweller. Again, monks, a bhikkhu dwells in a forest… or on a heap of straw. He gains internal serenity of mind, and his body becomes calmed. And he dwells having attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, having realized for himself with direct knowledge. This is the fourth kind of forest-dweller. Again, monks, a bhikkhu dwells in a forest… or on a heap of straw. He gains internal serenity of mind, and his body becomes calmed. And he dwells having attained the destruction of the taints in this very life, having realized for himself with direct knowledge. Furthermore, when he has attained final Nibbāna, the devas proclaim: ‘He was a forest-dweller, one who frequented remote lodgings; it is fitting that he should attain final Nibbāna in the forest. This is the fifth kind of forest-dweller. These, monks, are the five kinds of forest-dwellers.”
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with four qualities is not fit to resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets.
With which four?
He is obsessed by thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty; and he is dull-witted, stupid, and mute-like.
“Monks, a monk who possesses these four qualities is not fit to resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats.
Monks, a monk who possesses four qualities is fit to resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats.
Which four?”
“By means of thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-cruelty, he is wise, unconfused, and not dull-witted or mute.
Possessing these four qualities, monks, a bhikkhu is fit to resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle groves.
Thus was the ninth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.263 26. Abhiññāvagga Kammasutta “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who performs a dark deed and experiences a dark result; the person who performs a bright deed and experiences a bright result; the person who performs a dark-and-bright deed and experiences a dark-and-bright result;

and the person who performs a deed that is neither dark nor bright and experiences a result that is neither dark nor bright. And how, monks, is one a person who performs a dark deed and experiences a dark result? Here, monks, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This, monks, is called a person who performs a dark deed and experiences a dark result. And how, monks, is one a person who performs a bright deed and experiences a bright result? Here, monks, someone abstains from destroying life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This, monks, is called a person who performs a bright deed and experiences a bright result. And how, monks, is one a person who performs a dark-and-bright deed and experiences a dark-and-bright result? Here, monks, someone both destroys life and abstains from destroying life... [and so on through the other courses of action] ...indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence, and abstains from them. This, monks, is called a person who performs a dark-and-bright deed and experiences a dark-and-bright result. And how, monks, is one a person who performs a deed that is neither dark nor bright and experiences a result that is neither dark nor bright? Here, monks, someone is a noble disciple who has abandoned the five lower fetters and is one bound upstream, heading toward the Akaniṭṭha realm. This, monks, is called a person who performs a deed that is neither dark nor bright and experiences a result that is neither dark nor bright. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

“Bhikkhus, possessed of four qualities, a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man, maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit. What are the four? [The text continues with the list of these four qualities.]”

"By means of blameworthy bodily action, blameworthy verbal action, blameworthy mental action, and blameworthy view—with these four qualities, monks, a fool, an incompetent person, an untrue man maintains himself wounded and injured; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit."
“Bhikkhus, possessing four qualities, a wise, competent, true person preserves himself unscarred and uninjured; he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit.
What are the four?
Blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, blameless mental action, and blameless view.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of these four qualities, a wise, competent, true person preserves himself unscarred and uninjured;
he is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise, and he generates much merit. This is the tenth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.266 27. Kammapathavagga Micchācārīsutta (The Discourse on the One Who Engages in Sexual Misconduct) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who engages in sexual misconduct; the person who does not engage in sexual misconduct; the person who both engages in sexual misconduct and does not engage in sexual misconduct; and the person who neither engages in sexual misconduct nor does not engage in sexual misconduct. And how, monks, is one a person who engages in sexual misconduct? Here, monks, someone has sexual relations with women who have a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, or relatives; with those protected by Dhamma; with those who have taken refuge [in the Triple Gem]; with those who have been promised to another; or with those who are under royal protection. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who engages in sexual misconduct. And how, monks, is one a person who does not engage in sexual misconduct? Here, monks, someone has no sexual relations with women who have a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, or relatives; with those protected by Dhamma; with those who have taken refuge; with those who have been promised to another; or with those who are under royal protection. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who does not engage in sexual misconduct. And how, monks, is one a person who both engages in sexual misconduct and does not engage in sexual misconduct? Here, monks, someone has sexual relations with some women who have a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, or relatives; with those protected by Dhamma; with those who have taken refuge; with those who have been promised to another; or with those who are under royal protection, but he does not have sexual relations with other women who do not have a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, or relatives; who are not protected by Dhamma; who have not taken refuge; who have not been promised to another; or who are not under royal protection. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who both engages in sexual misconduct and does not engage in sexual misconduct. And how, monks, is one a person who neither engages in sexual misconduct nor does not engage in sexual misconduct? Here, monks, someone has no sexual relations with women who have a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, or relatives; with those protected by Dhamma; with those who have taken refuge; with those who have been promised to another; or with those who are under royal protection, and he also has no sexual relations with women who do not have a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, or relatives; who are not protected by Dhamma; who have not taken refuge; who have not been promised to another; or who are not under royal protection. It is in this way, monks, that one is a person who neither engages in sexual misconduct nor does not engage in sexual misconduct. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
…pe… One is oneself an adulterer,

Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.270 27. Kammapathavagga Samphappalāpasutta (Idle Chatter) “Monks, there are these four kinds of idle chatter. What four? There is the case where a certain person, when asked about something that has occurred, says: ‘I didn’t say that; you’re misquoting me; it wasn’t said by me in that way. Thus he argues with them, quarrels with them, disputes with them, and engages in a battle of words with them: ‘Say what was said by me as having been said by me; don’t say what wasn’t said by me as having been said by me. Explain what was said by me as having been said by me; don’t explain what wasn’t said by me as having been said by me. Let the matter stand as it was said by me. This is the first kind of idle chatter. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, when asked about something that has not occurred, says: ‘It happened like this; it happened like that. Thus he argues with them, quarrels with them, disputes with them, and engages in a battle of words with them: ‘Say what happened as having happened; don’t say what didn’t happen as having happened. Explain what happened as having happened; don’t explain what didn’t happen as having happened. This is the second kind of idle chatter. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, when asked about something that has occurred, says: ‘I didn’t say that; you’re misquoting me; it wasn’t said by me in that way. Thus he argues with them, quarrels with them, disputes with them, and engages in a battle of words with them: ‘Say what was said by me as having been said by me; don’t say what wasn’t said by me as having been said by me. Explain what was said by me as having been said by me; don’t explain what wasn’t said by me as having been said by me. Let the matter stand as it was said by me. This is the third kind of idle chatter. Furthermore, there is the case where a certain person, when asked about something that has not occurred, says: ‘It didn’t happen like this; it didn’t happen like that. Thus he argues with them, quarrels with them, disputes with them, and engages in a battle of words with them: ‘Say what didn’t happen as not having happened; don’t say what did happen as not having happened. Explain what didn’t happen as not having happened; don’t explain what did happen as not having happened. This is the fourth kind of idle chatter. These, monks, are the four kinds of idle chatter.”
…pe… One speaks idle chatter oneself,
encourages others to speak idle chatter, approves of idle chatter, and speaks in praise of idle chatter— by these [factors] …pe….
One abstains from idle chatter oneself, and encourages others to refrain from idle chatter.
He approves of abstaining from idle chatter and speaks in praise of abstaining from idle chatter— by these,
monks, … [as before] … This is the seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.271 27.

and speaks in praise of covetousness …pe…. One is not covetous oneself, encourages others in non-covetousness, approves of non-covetousness, and speaks in praise of non-covetousness— it is by these …pe….

27. The Chapter on Courses of Action: The Discourse on Wrong View (Micchādiṭṭhisutta) “Monks, there are these three courses of action that are unwholesome. What three? The course of action of bodily misconduct, the course of action of verbal misconduct, and the course of action of mental misconduct. These, monks, are the three courses of action that are unwholesome. There are, monks, these three courses of action that are wholesome. What three? The course of action of bodily good conduct, the course of action of verbal good conduct, and the course of action of mental good conduct. These, monks, are the three courses of action that are wholesome. There are, monks, these three kinds of wrong view. What three? ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously born; there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. These, monks, are the three kinds of wrong view. There are, monks, these three kinds of right view. What three? ‘There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings spontaneously born; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. These, monks, are the three kinds of right view. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has spoken in brief regarding the three courses of action that are unwholesome, the three courses of action that are wholesome, the three kinds of wrong view, and the three kinds of right view. It would be good if the venerable ones were to expand upon the meaning of this in detail. “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Ānanda. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, there are these three courses of action that are unwholesome. What three? The course of action of bodily misconduct, the course of action of verbal misconduct, and the course of action of mental misconduct. These, friends, are the three courses of action that are unwholesome. There are, friends, these three courses of action that are wholesome. What three? The course of action of bodily good conduct, the course of action of verbal good conduct, and the course of action of mental good conduct. These, friends, are the three courses of action that are wholesome. There are, friends, these three kinds of wrong view. What three? ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously born; there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. These, friends, are the three kinds of wrong view. There are, friends, these three kinds of right view. What three? ‘There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings spontaneously born; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. These, friends, are the three kinds of right view. When the venerable Ānanda had thus spoken, the venerable Sāriputta said to him: “Friend Ānanda, it is as if one were to set upright what was overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. Even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the venerable Ānanda in many ways. And I, friend Ānanda, go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
...pe... One is oneself possessed of wrong view, one encourages others in wrong view, one approves of wrong view, and one speaks in praise of wrong view—by these ...pe...

One is oneself possessed of right view, one encourages others in right view, one approves of right view, and one speaks in praise of right view—it is by possessing these four qualities, monks, that one goes to heaven as if carried there.

28. The Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness from the Series on Passion (Rāgapeyyāla Satipaṭṭhānasutta) (AN 4.274, AN 4.271, PTS AN ii 256)
“Monks, for the direct knowledge of lust, four things are to be developed. What four?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”
“He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
For the direct knowledge of lust, monks, these four things are to be developed. Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.275 28.
Rāgapeyyāla Sammappadhānasutta (The Discourse on the Right Exertions)
“Bhikkhus, for the direct knowledge of lust, four things are to be developed. What four?”
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states;
for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states; ... [and so on] ... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states;
... [and so on] ... for the stability, non-confusion, increase, and abundance of arisen wholesome states.
He generates desire for the fulfillment of development; he exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives.
For the direct knowledge of lust, monks, these four things are to be developed. Thus ends the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.276 28.
Rāgapeyyāla Iddhipādasutta (The Discourse on the Bases for Spiritual Power)
“Monks, for the direct knowledge of lust, four things are to be developed. What four?

Here, monks, a monk develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration through energy … [and so on] … he develops the basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration through mind … [and so on] …
“He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with the concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
For the direct knowledge of lust, bhikkhus, these four things are to be developed. Thus was the third [discourse].
